en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Brahman, who is attainable through yoga.
Salutations to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Salutations to the Gurus, to the Goddesses, to the Yogis, and salutations to Hari!

[I bow to that which is] eternally most subtle, consisting of the single essence of consciousness, liberated, pure, auspicious, with all conceptual constructions shaken off, accessible through the Upanishads, and beyond the reach of ordinary means of knowledge.

We worship incessantly that great light, the manifestation of one's own Self, which is intense bliss, and which the yogis—having mastered their vital breaths and minds—behold as the fullness of the Abode. || 1 ||
May he— the one whose splendor is like ten million suns, who is a fierce sun at the end of the eon known as saṃsāra, who is a full moon scorched by the rays of that sun,
and who is a violent wind at the end of the eon for the ocean of suffering; may he, the very ground of compassion and beauty, be mine.
The venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who brings about the awakening to all objects of knowledge. || 2 ||

I bow to the pot-bellied one of fierce valor, who resembles a fire to the cotton of the multitude of obstacles; who is a wish-fulfilling gem for contemplated objects and possesses a beautiful form; and whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
Having bowed down to Śrī Vyāsa, the ascetic Śaṅkara, the spiritual preceptor Bhava, the teacher Śrī Rāmacandra whose lotus feet are dense bliss, and all the lords of yogis,
[I shall extract] the *Śrī Yogacintāmaṇi*— which contains the complete meaning and has fallen into the midst of the ocean of various scriptures.
Śivānanda composes this clearly, with equal distribution of the metrical feet. || 4 ||
Yoga, however, is precisely non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpaka-samādhi*); thus Patañjali said: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaś-citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*).

That state of the mind which, preceded by the cessation of mental fluctuations directed toward the meaning of a sentence, abides in the form of Brahman, is called non-conceptual meditative absorption, known as cessation (*nirodha*), and is termed Yoga.
In grammar, it is stated that [the suffix] *yuc* is used for the sake of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
this is also found in the *Vāsiṣṭha*.
O Raghava, there are two methods for the destruction of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is the restraint of its fluctuations; knowledge is correct discernment.
Thus ends the speech of the Lord in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Yoga consists in focusing the mind one-pointedly upon Me through the cessation of other mental activities,
wherein one's own true nature is contemplated as entirely empty and free from appearances.
The yoga of non-existence has been fully described, by which one perceives the Self,
wherein one beholds the Self as eternal bliss and stainless.
"But the supreme yoga is taught as being directed toward me alone," thus it is stated in the Āditya Purāṇa as well.
"From yoga knowledge is born; yoga is one-pointedness of mind upon Me," as stated in the *Yogabīja*.
The Goddess said:
O God, what is called yoga? What is the practice of yoga like?
And what might be attained through yoga? Tell me all that, O Śaṅkara.
The Lord said:
The union of the lower and upper apertures, as well as that of the vital breaths; likewise, the union of the voice, the seed, and the semen;
the union of the sun and the moon; and the union of the individual self and the supreme self.
Thus, the conjunction of the net of pairs is called yoga;
however, it should be understood that others are merely its constituent parts, as will be explained in detail.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having rendered the mind free from activity and having unified the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self, one is liberated; he is said to be "yoked in yoga."
Having indeed turned all the external openings inward,
one should withdraw the collection of senses into the mind, and then apply the mind to the Self.
One should dissolve the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is liberated from all existents, into Brahman;
this is both meditation and yoga, while everything else is merely an expansion of books.
The wise say that the conjunction of the self and the mind is called *yoga*;
others, however, maintain that the union of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is *yoga*.
"The conjunction of the sense objects and the senses is yoga," so say the wise;

however, because breath control (prāṇāyāma) is well known in all Yoga scriptures as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*) and not as yoga itself, the presentation of this alternative view by some is intended solely to bring out its lack of natural appropriateness.

By the phrase "through the conjunction of the sense objects and the senses," the intended meaning is the contemplation of the internal sound (*nāda*) and the observation of the space between the eyebrows, the nose,
and so forth; for the possibility of *samādhi* through these means as well has been stated by Patañjali and other yogis.
And it will be explained in detail in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
O Khāṇḍikya, hear from me as I speak the true nature of yoga,
established in which the sage, having attained absorption into Brahman, does not fall away.
The specific movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort,
and its union with Brahman is designated as yoga.
Thus, he whose yoga consists of the discernment of dharmas endowed with such absolute distinction is indeed called a yogi seeking liberation.

This is the meaning: the movement (*gati*)— that is, knowledge (*jñāna*)— produced by the mind acting as an instrument, which is distinct from the state of being a living soul (*jīva-rūpa*), and which depends upon the effort of the self consisting in turning inward the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that is naturally disposed toward external objects by withdrawing it from them and making it face within.

The meaning of the two [previous] verses is that the conjunction of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman as its object, arising from the contemplation of its non-difference from Brahman, is said to be the *samādhi* characterized as *saṃprajñāta*. However, the meaning of the third [verse] is that for one possessing such practice, there occurs the complete dissolution of the mind into the Supreme Brahman known as Viṣṇu.

The yoga of that yogin whose yoga is characterized by the dharma of distinguished union is called a "seeker of liberation" (mumukṣu) in the scriptures because he possesses the practice of yoga which is the direct means to liberation. By this, the samādhi characterized as "non-cognitive" (asaṃprajñāta) has been described.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
This root *yuj* in the sense of "union" has reached its ultimate state;
because that [state] is united by him, he is therefore called a *yogin*.
The supreme state, known as the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, has been reached and attained by the Creator;

however, that state is not merely their conjunction (*yoga*). That state is called *yoga* because it is fit for one who practices non-duality, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "it is called *yoga* because that state is fit" (*yujyate*). By this, the *asaṃprajñāta* [samādhi] is indicated.

Concentration (samādhi) has been described. Likewise, in that very same [text], cessation is considered by yogis to be the union of the mind; by this, the non-conceptual state is expressed. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
Know that knowledge consists of yoga, and yoga is endowed with eight limbs;
the union of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is called yoga.
By this, the dissolution of the mind and the characteristics of dissolution have been stated in brief as *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta*, as recorded in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"O King, that which is the oneness of the self with the Supreme Brahman..."
That alone is celebrated as Yoga; what other characteristic of Yoga could there be?
O protector of the earth, listen now to the characteristics of that yoga which brings about the complete exhaustion even of the karma that constitutes one's own body.
That which is declared to be the supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, pure and immutable—
the dissolution of the mind therein is designated as Yoga.
When that mind has dissolved through the awakening born of yoga,
the Puruṣa, due to the absence of a cause, no longer perceives differentiation at all.
O Lord of Men, the distinction between the self and the other is constructed by cognition;
when that [cognition] ceases, the distinction between self and other is indeed nothing but a mental state.
O scorcher of foes, that very distinction between the Supreme Self and the individual self which you asked about is indeed the supreme yoga; it has been explained to you in brief.
Here, by the words "by the Supreme Brahman" and so forth, the samādhi characterized as *saṃprajñāta* (cognitive) has been described.
By the words "of that which initiates the body" and so forth, the samādhi in the form of *asaṃprajñāta* (non-cognitive) has been described. Now, [one might ask]:
what of restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*)?

If it is argued that since "the concentrations are the eight limbs of yoga," and so forth, concentration (*samādhi*) is enumerated as an ancillary limb (*aṅga*) of yoga in all yoga treatises, it is therefore understood that yoga is something entirely different [from concentration], this is true. For concentration is of two kinds, distinguished as *saṃprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asaṃprajñāta* (non-cognitive). Among these, the *asaṃprajñāta*...

Samādhi has *saṃprajñāta* as its constituent (*aṅga*). In this regard, the relationship between the constituent and the possessor of the constituent (*aṅgāṅgin*) is established in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtra]. It is stated that the triad beginning with *dhāraṇā* (concentration) constitutes the "inner limb" (*antaraṅga*) because they provide direct assistance [to *samādhi*].

However, the five beginning with *yama* are "external limbs" (*bahir-aṅga*) because they assist *samādhi* by means of uprooting discursive thoughts such as violence, which are its opposites. Once *āsana* has been mastered, there is steadiness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth. Likewise, *dhāraṇā* and *dhyāna* [assist] *saṃprajñāta-samādhi*.

Although these three are "inner" (antaraṅga) in comparison to the other limbs because they directly bring about [samādhi], they are nonetheless "outer" (bahiraṅga) with respect to the seedless samādhi known as *asaṃprajñāta*, because they assist it only through a mediated succession. This is established by the two sūtras: "The three are inner compared to the previous ones," and "Even those are outer with respect to the seedless [samādhi]."
Vasiṣṭha and Yājñavalkya, however, state that while the four beginning with restraint (yama) are external limbs, the four beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra) are internal limbs.
Yājñavalkya.
At the beginning, four are external; those other than these are indeed internal. These four limbs of yoga have been described, O fair-faced one.
Vasiṣṭha.

"Listen to the four internal [aids], beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra). Here, this should be understood: from the restraints (yama) up to meditation (dhyāna), these are "external" to seedless (nirbīja) samādhi because they bring about cognitive (saṃprajñāta) samādhi by way of being successive auxiliaries.

"Concentration alone is the limb. That by which the nature of the object of meditation is correctly and pre-eminently known—that is, through the absence of erroneous determination—is *samprajñāta* concentration, a specific form of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And that which is a specific form of cultivation is called *samprajñāta* concentration; and it is as follows:

It is fourfold according to the distinctions of *vitarka* and so forth: with *vitarka*, with *vicāra*, with *ānanda*, and with *asmitā*. Thus says the venerable Patañjali: "Cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) [samādhi] arises from the accompaniment of the forms of *vitarka*, *vicāra*, *ānanda*, and *asmitā*. Furthermore, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated fixing of the object of meditation by means of the exclusion of other objects.
The object of contemplation (*bhāvya*) is twofold: the Lord (*īśa*) and the principles (*tattva*).

The principles are also twofold: insentient (*jaḍa*) and sentient (*ajaḍa*). The insentient consist of twenty-four [categories], divided into *prakṛti*, the Great One (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). In brief, however, they are simply *prakṛti*.

That which is designated as the power of Īśvara and as *māyā* is described in such Vedic passages as: "One should know *prakṛti* as *māyā*, and the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) as the wielder of *māyā*," and "The power of the divine Self is concealed by its own qualities. Furthermore, the non-inert *puruṣa* and those other [entities] are also of two kinds; [the latter being] the gross.

And [the objects] are subtle. In that regard, when meditation is performed by taking the gross elements and the sense organs as its objects, accompanied by the intermingling of the verbal expression and the synthesis of what precedes and what follows, then that samādhi is designated as "with vitarka" (vitarka-savicāra). [The phrase] "synthesis of what precedes and what follows" [is explained as follows:]

If it is devoid of the mention of words (*śabdollekha*), then it is designated as *nirvitarka* (non-discursive). Likewise, if it takes as its object subtle internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and objects, characterized by distinctions of space, time, and qualities (*dharma*), then it is designated as *savitaraka* (discursive). If, however, it has as its object only the substratum (*dharmī*) unqualified by those [distinctions], then...

This samādhi, known as *nirvicāra*, is designated as the "cognitive attainment" (*grāhya-samāpatti*). When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), in the form of *sattva*, is cultivated while still permeated by subtle traces of *rajas* and *tamas*, then, due to the predominance of *sattva*— which consists of bliss and illumination arising from the subsidence of the [other] *guṇas*— the samādhi called "blissful" (*sānanda*) occurs.
Those whose steadiness consists of this alone are called the "bodiless" (videha). This is called the "grasping" (grahaṇa) meditative attainment.

Beyond this, when cultivation proceeds by taking as its object pure *sattva*—unoverpowered by even a trace of *rajas* and *tamas*—therein, due to the subordination of the grasped *sattva* and the surging forth of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*), [the yogin attains the attainment of the "greatness of the knower"].

Samādhi, in which only pure existence remains, is called *sāsmita*. Nor should one suspect there is no difference between the ego-function (*ahaṃkāra*) and the "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*). Therein, when the internal organ perceives objects by delineating them as "I," that is *ahaṃkāra*; but where, through an inward-turning and inverse transformation, the mind has dissolved into its primal nature (*prakṛti*), there is only pure existence.

Only the *mātra* (the pure ego) shines forth; this is called *sāsmita*. Those who delight in this *mātra* alone are designated by the term "dissolution into *prakṛti*. However, for those who, having known the Supreme Puruṣa, proceed toward meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), this discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is called "absorption as the grasper" (*grahītṛ-samāpatti*). This [samādhi] consists of four stages.

Cognitive absorption (*samprajñāta-samādhi*)—which is characterized by conceptualization—is designated in the Yoga treatises by such terms as "having seeds," "the state of seed," and "contemplation" (*nididhyāsana*). Regarding the definition of non-cognitive absorption (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*), the venerable Patañjali says: "The other [absorption] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and is characterized by residual mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: *virāma* (cessation) is that by which one ceases; it is the abandonment of thoughts such as *vitarka* (discursive reasoning). This cessation is itself the *pratyaya* (cognitive state), hence it is called the "cessation-cognition" (*virāma-pratyaya*). Its "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated application of it to the mind. In this regard, whatever mental fluctuation (*vṛtti*) arises, one attends to it continuously with the thought, "not this, not this. This is its constant cultivation.

The meaning is that the *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* (non-cognitive absorption) is a specific *saṃskāra* (latent impression) preceded by that [cognitive absorption], yet distinct from it; for in that state, nothing whatsoever is cognized, hence it is called *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*. This is also termed *nirbīja* (seedless), *nirvikalpa* (non-conceptual), *nirālamba* (unsupported), and *rājayoga* (royal yoga).
In Rajayoga.
Vāmadeva said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, beautiful with supreme bliss! By your grace, I have obtained the ancient yoga in its full detail.
Furthermore, that which was uttered by you is indeed the name of Mahādeva, who is difficult to describe.
The former is endowed with external mudrās and consists of external yoga;
the other, however, is endowed with internal mudrās and is indeed internal yoga itself.
And that very [configuration] has been described by the best of sages as Rājayoga;
it shines among all yogas and is thus known as Rājayoga.
That which leads the embodied soul to the King who is radiant, the imperishable Supreme Brahman, is called Rājayoga.
The names common to the two types of samādhi are given in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
Rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, manonmanī, amaraugha, ogha, cāndrā, nirālamba, and nirañjana.
It has been shown and illustrated that "amanaska," "laya," "śūnyāśūnya," "parāpara," "jīvanmukti," "sahaja," and "turya" are synonymous terms;
furthermore, the two-fold nature of samādhi has already been explained in the Purāṇas and other scriptures.
Is it not the case that there are mantra-yoga, laya-yoga, rāja-yoga, and likewise haṭha-yoga?
Yoga is declared to be fourfold by the seers of reality; for this fourfold nature of yoga is heard in various places,

and because the term "yoga" is observed to be employed in the Gītā and other texts in reference to Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth, as well as in the contexts of *karmayoga*, *bhaktiyoga*, *vairāgyayoga*, and *sāṃkhyayoga*.
If it is asked, "Since the word *yoga* is perceived to have multiple meanings, how is it determined that this specific [practice] alone is *yoga*?"—the answer is true.

Just as the word "livelihood" (*jīvana*) is applied to a plow because it is a means of livelihood, the application of the word *yoga* to mantra-yoga and other such practices is justified because they are means for achieving yoga, whether directly or indirectly. To illustrate:
Yoga and the attainment of yogic perfection arise solely through the grace of the Lord when He has been propitiated by means of mantra-recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth;
it is not otherwise. In the Āditya Purāṇa, there is this statement of Śiva:
"He is omniscient, perfectly complete, and free from old age and death."
"O destroyer of Krauñca, by my grace one becomes a yogi, and not otherwise," as stated in the *Mānasollāsa*.
"Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains yoga characterized by its eight limbs;
and through the grace of Śiva, one obtains eternal perfection in yoga."
In the Śaiva [tradition].
"Mantra-yoga is accomplished by those skilled in the recitation of mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, just as it was by Vatsarāja and others," as stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
"Whether seeking knowledge, seeking yoga, or especially seeking liberation,
one should indeed take refuge in Virūpākṣa, who bestows the fruits of all desires."

Moreover, it is clearly seen in all the Yoga scriptures that the recitation of the mantra of Īśvara, worship, and so forth, constitute limbs of yoga; and as will be stated: "Rājayoga is indeed seedless samādhi; laya is cognitive absorption (samprajñāta); and Haṭha is simply breath control (prāṇāyāma)."
And likewise, in the Yogabīja:
Mantra, Haṭha, Laya, and Rājayoga—these are the stages in succession;
this single Great Yoga is said to be fourfold.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, please explain to me, in due order and exactly as it is, this fourfold reality of yoga according to the divisions of the stages.
Īśvara said:
With the letter *sa*, the vital breath (*marut*) goes outward; with the letter *ha*, it enters.
The living soul (*jīva*) constantly recites this mantra: "Haṃsa, Haṃsa."
Through the word of the Guru, the recitation (japa) becomes reversed within the Suṣumṇā;
when "so'ham, so'ham" is attained, that is then called Mantra-yoga.
And through the application of mere cognition on the final path, it arises;
by the letter *ha* the sun is indicated, and by the letter *sa-uṭha* the moon is said to be expressed.
The unification of the sun and the moon is designated as *haṭha*;
by means of *haṭha*, the brilliance and so forth arising from all defects are swallowed up.
When the knower of the field and the supreme self become one,
O Goddess, once that unity is accomplished, the mind attains dissolution.
When the yoga of absorption (layayoga) arises, the vital breath attains stability;
through absorption, one attains perfection, which is the supreme state of self-bliss.
Having attained the state of *aṇimā* and the other powers, one shines through *rājayoga*;
the fourfold yoga is to be understood as occurring in the union of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.

Previously, mantra-yoga was described as external; this, however, is internal—this is the distinction. Haṭha-yoga is said to be prāṇāyāma, characterized by the unification of the prāṇa and apāna known as the sun and the moon. [As stated] in the Vasiṣṭha:
The apāna, as the moon, nourishes the body from the outside;
the prāṇa, as the sun or the fire, digests this internal frame.

In another tradition, however, the designations are reversed, as stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*: "Prāṇa should be known as consisting of the moon, and apāna likewise as consisting of the sun; both are the leaders of the body and perform the coming and going [of the breath].
The union of these two must always be practiced with effort by those seeking liberation."
Through this gateway, all accomplishments arise for the wise.

Based on the statement in the *Gītā*, "Having restrained the movements of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one is devoted to *prāṇāyāma*," and according to the statement of Yājñavalkya, "The union of *prāṇa* and *apāna* is *prāṇāyāma*," it is *prāṇāyāma* itself that is expressed by the term *haṭha*. For the yogi who is merged in the Supreme Self within that meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the following occurs].

The manifestation of the bliss of Brahman, accompanied by a specific state of contemplation (*sabhāvanā-viśe��ṣa*), is called *samprajñāta-samādhi* and *laya-yoga*. Even in *laya-yoga*, it is said that *laya-yoga* consists of the dissolution of both the vital breath (*marut*) and the mind (*manas*) within the nine *cakras*.
That by which the yogi, endowed with the supreme sovereignty beginning with *aṇimā*, shines throughout the three worlds, being of the nature of seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi, is called *rājayoga*.
Thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Under the sway of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the individual soul runs up and down;
flickering along the left and right channels, it finds no stability.
Just as a bird bound by a string is drawn back even though it has flown away,
so too the individual soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), is drawn along by the out-breath and in-breath (prāṇa-apāna).
The *apāna* draws up the *prāṇa*, and the *prāṇa* draws up the *apāna*; the knower of yoga joins these two as they are situated above and below.
By the letter *ha* it goes out, and by the letter *sa* it enters again.
The individual soul constantly recites this mantra: "Haṃsa, haṃsa."
Twenty-one thousand six hundred (21,600) times— this is the number of mantras that the individual soul (jīva) recites constantly day and night.
This Gāyatrī, known as Ajapā, bestows liberation upon yogis.
By the mere resolve for this [practice], one is liberated from all sins.
There is no knowledge equal to this, no recitation equal to this;
there has been no wisdom equal to this, nor will there ever be.
All three are indeed limbs of Rājayoga, according to the Haṭhapradīpikā.
The various *pīṭhas*, *kuṃbhakas*, and divine *karaṇas*—
all these lead to the perfection of *rājayoga* through the practice of *haṭhayoga*.
A person who has ascended to the Royal Yoga (rājayoga) is a deceiver of time.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the six types of ritual actions (ṣaṭkarman) are included.
The term "seat" (pīṭha) is an elliptical expression for restraint (yama) and observance (niyama).
Because both of these are stated in all the Yoga-shastras to be constituent parts (aṅgas) of yoga.

In this verse, although it appears that all the practices beginning with *yama* and *niyama* directly assist *rājayoga*, nevertheless, upon a thorough examination of the preceding and following texts,
such is not the established conclusion. [Rather,] the eight limbs beginning with *yama* [assist] either directly or indirectly.
The utility of supreme meditative concentration (*parayāsamādhi*) has already been explained previously.
In that regard, the six actions (*karma*) of the seals (*mudrā*) constitute the very limbs of *haṭha*.

The mudrās for the six actions will be explained below. In that regard, the six actions assist Haṭha-yoga by means of removing the humors (doṣas) such as phlegm; however, in the absence of such humors, they are of no use at all. Others, however, do not desire the performance of the six actions because, even when humors are present, [Haṭha] is crowded with many other means.
They say that since all tasks are accomplished through *prāṇāyāma* alone, even *haṭha* is not necessarily a required limb [of yoga].
Thus says Ātmārāma:
"When grossness, phlegm, fat, diseases, and so forth have been removed by the six practices (*ṣatkarma*),"...
One should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); it is accomplished without effort.
One should perform the six purificatory actions (ṣaṭkarma) for the purpose of eliminating fat and phlegm;
otherwise, one should not perform them, since their purpose is the restoration of the equilibrium of the humors (doṣas).

"By all forms of *prāṇāyāma* alone, the impurities are dried up from their very source. Thus it is said. However, for certain teachers, another sequence is not accepted. As for the *mudrās*, they are:
*mūlabandha*, *jālandhara*, *uḍḍīyāna*, *mahāmudrā*, *mahāvedha*, *mahābandha*, and *śakti*.

The distinction is this: while the *cālanī* acts as an aid to Haṭha yoga directly, the *viparītakaraṇī* and *khecarī* act through the medium of bodily perfection (*śarīrasiddhi*). However, in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, it is stated that even *khecarī* is useful for Haṭha yoga directly; for instance: "Having forcibly drawn [the tongue] back from the root of the palate..."
"When the breath has reached the upper aperture at the uvula, the vibration of the breath is restrained. Thus it is said. In the *Mānasollāsa*:
"The contraction of the apāna, the restraint of the prāṇa, and the placing of the tongue upon the uvula—this is the practice of yoga."
In the *Nandikeśvaratārāvalī*:
"When the consort of the Great Lord (Umā) is awakened by the *uḍḍīna*, *jālandhara*,
and *mūlabandha* postures, the wind— releasing its outward flow and entering the *suṣumṇā*— abandons both going and coming."

In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*: "When the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*) has been awakened by means of various postures (*āsana*), breath-retentions (*kumbhaka*), and diverse yogic exercises (*karaṇa*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) dissolves into the void (*śūnya*)."
When the power of awakening has arisen and all karma has been completely abandoned, the state of *sahaja* (the innate) arises spontaneously for the yogi.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through the *suṣumnā* and the wind enters the void (*śūnya*), the knower of yoga likewise eradicates all karmas from their very root. As stated in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
Through the contraction of the anus and other locations by means of the sequential practices of *sthānaka* and so forth,
through the purification of posture and food, and through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous;
Through one's own right conduct, through association with virtuous people, through total renunciation, through a comfortable posture,
and by the intense practice of breath control at a certain time, [one attains success].
O observer of noble vows, through the abandonment of anger and greed, and by relinquishing their respective portions,
they become thoroughly submissive when the processes of giving up and taking up are restrained.

"All the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are like servants to the man who knows that [Self], because of its sovereignty. Now, one might object: "Since many fruits are heard of in the case of *mudrās*, *haṭhayoga*, and so forth, why should they not be considered primary? We say no; for those [passages] are merely *arthavāda* (laudatory statements). And thus it is stated in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*: "In the case of auxiliary parts..."

The mention of a fruit is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), according to the principle that "that which is without fruit [is subordinate] when it occurs in proximity to that which possesses fruit. However, the practice of *karma-yoga* is indeed the propitiation of the Lord. And this is enumerated among the observances (*niyamas*) that constitute the limbs of yoga in all yoga scriptures. To this effect are two *pātañjala* sūtras: "Austerity, self-study, and the worship of the Lord... (YS 2.32).

The application of practice consists of the aspirational vows (*praṇidhāna*). Purity, contentment, austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*) are the observances (*niyama*). Austerity includes the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances; self-study is the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava* and other sacred texts.
The dedication of all actions to the Supreme Lord without regard for their fruits is *praṇidhāna*.
These are called the *kriyā-yogas*. Through the practice of these, *samādhi* arises. Regarding how *kriyā-yoga* serves as an aid to *samādhi*, Patañjali states the means by which this occurs:
It is for the purpose of cultivating samādhi and for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (kleśas).
The afflictions are ignorance (avidyā), egoism (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and clinging to existence (abhiniveśa).

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the delusion consisting of the cognition of something as what it is not; it is the ground for the production of the four afflictions (*kleśa*), namely egoism (*asmitā*) and the rest, which take the form of permanence, purity, pleasure, and selfhood with respect to that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. Egoism (*asmitā*) is a particular mental modification (*mano-vṛtti*) whose object is the identity of the intellect (*sattva*) and the person (*puruṣa*); it is the sense of "I. Attachment (*rāga*)...
The desire "May this happiness remain thus" is *rāga* (attachment); *dveṣa* (aversion) is the censure of the causes of suffering; and *abhiniveśa* (clinging) is stubborn adherence.
These five, being denoted by the term "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they generate suffering, are conducive to the great misfortune called *saṃsāra* and are obstacles to *samādhi*.

The purpose of *kriyā-yoga* is to serve as a cause for *samādhi* by means of the removal and weakening of the root sins (*mūla-bhūta-pāpa*). Furthermore, those afflictions (*kleśa*) which are gross and have already begun to produce effects are removed by *dhyāna*, characterized by one-pointedness of mind; however, those remaining in the form of subtle latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are [removed] by the reverse process.
They cease through transformation. And thus there are two Sūtras:
"Their fluctuations are to be abandoned by means of meditation (dhyāna)," and "The subtle ones are to be abandoned by their re-absorption.
Furthermore, these afflictions have ignorance as their root, and their fruit is characterized by the auspicious and the inauspicious.

The fruit of action—defined as that which has been described—is the experience of pleasure and pain, as well as the acquisition of birth, lifespan, objects, and sense-faculties corresponding to that karma. In this context, the gateway [to the fruit] exists when the root [karma] is present; its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and enjoyment. Here, the mention of both birth and lifespan as fruits of karma is made specifically with respect to enjoyment (*bhoga*).

Although pleasure may serve as a gateway for that which is to be produced [liberation], it must be understood as nothing but suffering for the discerning person, because one observes its transformation into bitterness and so forth. These afflictions (kleśas), rooted in ignorance, have as their fruit of maturation (vipāka) the latent impressions of karma known as virtuous and non-virtuous actions, as well as birth, lifespan, and experience; they are to be abandoned by the discerning person.

Thus, renunciation is rooted in knowledge; it is to be accomplished through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), and right knowledge is to be accomplished through the scripture (*śāstra*). This scripture consists of four divisions known as the *caturvyūha*, comprising four stages (*parva*) designated as that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), its cause (*tatkāraṇa*), its abandonment (*hāna*), and the means of that abandonment (*tatkāraṇa*). They are as follows:

Saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering, is that which is to be abandoned; the conjunction of the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*) is the cause of what is to be abandoned; the cause of that [conjunction] is ignorance (*avidyā*). The absolute cessation of the conjunction of the primary matter and the spirit is the abandonment, and that itself is isolation (*kaivalya*).
The cause for that is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). And thus the aphorisms state: "That which is to be abandoned is future suffering for the seer..."

The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of suffering; its cause is ignorance (*avidyā*). From the absence of that [ignorance] comes the absence of conjunction, which is liberation (*hāna*).
Isolation (*kaivalya*) for that seer consists in the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the means of liberation (*hānopāya*). These and other such points concern the seer.

The subsequent aphorisms concern the seer, the seen, and their conjunction: "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, it perceives the mental modifications. The seen consists of the elements and the senses, having the nature of illumination, activity, and inertia, and exists for the purpose of experience and liberation. Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the respective natures of the owner and the owned."

The meaning of this is as follows: the Puruṣa, whose nature is consciousness, is the Seer; by the mere proximity of the unconditioned [Puruṣa], the mental modification (vṛtti) becomes colored by the object. [The objective world] consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas—characterized by illumination, activity, and restraint—and takes the form of the graspable (grāhya). It comprises gross and subtle transformations such as the elements beginning with earth and the subtle elements (tanmātras), as well as the sense organs (buddhīndriya).

The object of perception (*dṛśya*)— consisting of the organs of action, the organs of cognition, and the internal organ, which undergoes transformation and serves as the means for experience and liberation— is [to be understood] during the stage of non-perception (*asaṃvedya-parvaṇi*) with respect to the two eternal and all-pervading entities called the "power of the object" (*sva-śakti*) and the "power of the master" (*svāmi-śakti*), which are the natures of the perceived and the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*).

The conjunction that is the cause for perceiving the essential nature of two things that exist [simultaneously] is beginningless, and its inherent nature is that of the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed;

this very thing is what is called the "conjunction of the seer and the seen. Here, the following should be considered: in the phrase "the seer is pure consciousness alone" (*draṣṭā dṛśi-mātra*), the word "alone" (*mātra*) is intended to exclude the relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*) as maintained by the Naiyāyikas.

Having bowed to that which wards off the state of being mere bliss (ānanda-svarūpatā), the Sarvajñātmamunis have stated in this context that the ultimate goal is one's own essential nature, which consists of pure consciousness (caitanya-mātra).
This very state is indicated by the mark of unconditional love, according to the Vedic scripture: "This is dearer than a son... and so forth.
Because the nature of the Self as bliss is established by the experience, "I slept happily," for this very reason the Śruti passage, "Verily,

that which is bodiless is not touched by pleasure or pain," is intended to negate objective pleasure and pain; otherwise, [it would contradict the fact that] all other beings [subsist] upon this very bliss.

"There is bliss only in abundance; for who indeed could breathe or live if this space were not bliss? For it is this that brings bliss. There would thus be a contradiction with endless scriptural passages such as "The knower of the bliss of Brahman," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss."

Nor should it be said that these [scriptural passages] are intended solely to reveal the bliss of Brahman and not that of the individual soul (jīva). For the identity of the jīva and Brahman is revealed by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), "That which is Brahman, immediate and direct," and "The Self that is within all. Therefore, the word "only" (*mātra*) does not exclude the nature of bliss.
However, it is more logical that it is the relationship between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) that is the delimiter.

The meaning of the sūtra, "The discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means for the cessation of the flow [of suffering]," is as follows: the discernment consisting of the realization that "the qualities (*guṇas*) are one thing and the Puruṣa is another"—such discernment, which is wisdom (*prajñā*), is the means for cessation.

The means for the abandonment of the visible [world] is as follows: For a person in whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has been produced by both scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*), this [discernment] is not the means [for final liberation], because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*) still persist.
This is what is meant by the term "unshaken" (*aviplava*); it means being free from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). This is what is intended: [the authority of] the Śruti...
Having grasped discernment through wisdom consisting of hearing, and having established it through wisdom consisting of reasoning, discriminative discernment—

which has attained direct perception as the culmination of excellence through long-term, uninterrupted practice and cultivation— becomes the unimpeded means for the removal of false knowledge along with its latent impressions once that false knowledge has been overturned.
Vācaspati Miśra [states]: As for the commentary of Bhojadeva: "That [samādhi] in which no *viplava*—that is, no interruption or emergence in the form of distraction—exists;

[a state] in which, through the power of cultivating the counter-thesis that 'the qualities (*guṇas*) are one thing and the *puruṣa* is another,' ignorance (*avidyā*) has dissolved, and thus the false conceits of being a knower and an agent have ceased, and which is not overwhelmed by the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*."

The power of consciousness belonging to the inward-turned intellect is called discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). When that [discernment] proceeds as a complete reality, there occurs liberation (*kaivalya*) due to the cessation of the duty of the object of perception.
This must be considered here: the mere cognition of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is not itself the means of liberation.

However, the true nature of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is that it is the first stage. Thereafter, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— the pure *sattva*— is freed from even the slightest trace of *rajas* and *tamas*, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that arises, characterized by identity with the object, is what is described in the Sūtra as "the seer abiding in his own nature."

The realization that Brahman is the singular essence of perfect consciousness—characterized by the form "I am Brahman"—is itself the supreme means for attaining liberation (*kaivalya*), which is defined as the attainment of the true nature of Brahman as the Self of all and is designated by the term "cessation" (*hāna*). Other qualities are one thing, and the Puruṣa is another; such is the knowledge [that leads to this].

The exposition of the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, serves exclusively for the purpose of distinguishing between the insentient and the sentient, by virtue of being the uncommon cause of the mental modification consisting of the false identification with the inert body and so forth— the root of all beginningless misfortune; for this very reason, liberation even in this dissolution is expressed by such terms as "cessation" (*hāna*) and "absolute isolation" (*kaivalya*).

That which manifests as one's own essential nature (nijātmasvarūpa) during the state of liberation, and that essential nature delimited by the uncommon object of the means to liberation— these have been directly explained by the venerable Patañjali primarily and specifically as "the Self" (ātmā), characterized by the relinquishment [of all else] through the very function [of the mind].

And likewise in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all. Thus, in the Sūtra on Knowledge, with reference to liberation in the form of the state of being the Self of all, [the text] states "I am Brahman" as the means to that end.

Knowledge was introduced as the means [to liberation] and has now been concluded; furthermore, it has been shown in that very same *Avidyāsūtra* how "I am Brahman" and "he becomes this All"—just as everything else—constitute knowledge, while its opposite constitutes ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, as for any other...

"One worships a deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another'—he is not a god," and so forth; enough of this digression. This is what is meant: for one whose internal organ (svānta) has become utterly pure through all actions performed for the sake of the Lord—excluding those motivated by desire and those that are prohibited—the perception of the defects of sense-objects [arises].

For one who has developed dispassion and seeks self-knowledge— the knowledge of the Self that eradicates all suffering along with its root, as understood from the Vedic statement, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"— there arises purification of the intellect through the practice of *nididhyāsana* (contemplation), which is augmented by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) under a true guru, leading to the attainment of seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*).

By the very gateway of the nature of samādhi, actions whose purpose has been fulfilled cease of their own accord. And so it is stated in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "Once the intellect has attained proficiency directed toward the inner Self through the purification of the intellect, actions cease, just as clouds do at the end of the rainy season. Thus it is said in the *Rājayoga*.
A yogi should not abandon actions, for he is liberated by means of actions;
this occurs through the destruction of *saṃkalpa* (volitional intention) alone, which is the very root of action.
To the extent that the dissolution of conceptual construction occurs through constant practice,
to that same extent the renunciation of action becomes more excellent for the yogi.
One who is himself ever-delighted in the practice of lofty innate bliss,
having completely abandoned all volitional thoughts and possessing true knowledge, should renounce ritual action.

One should abandon like an outcaste that person who is engaged in worldly activities, who claims "I am a knower of Brahman," and who has fallen away from both ritual action and the realization of Brahman.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Dharma must be practiced with effort, especially by yogins;
"there is no yoga without dharma"—thus do those who know yoga understand. In the *Yājñavalkya-gītā*, Gārgī said:
O Lord, how can a man engaged in yoga perform his daily rites during the two twilights or at night?
And what is the expiation for one who performs them [at such times]?
Yājñavalkya said:
O beautiful lady, whatever ought to be performed by a person engaged in yoga during the two twilights or at night is indeed accomplished through yoga.
When the fire of one's own Ātma-agnihotra has been intensified by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
for one who performs pure action with the oblation of a purified mind—
His deceit was indeed fulfilled when the separation between the individual self and the supreme self was attained.
The actions prescribed by the injunctions must be performed constantly by those who know Brahman;
and at the time of separation, the yogi should not abandon them, thinking, "This is suffering."
For him, karma is proclaimed to be the source of rebirth in hell;
for it is not possible for a yogin to abandon actions entirely.
Therefore, until death, a yogi should always practice this twofold discipline;
as stated in the Bhagavad Gītā.
"For a sage desiring to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means," as stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Therefore, remaining with every effort established in the ordinances of the castes and stages of life,
the wise man who has taken refuge in the ultimate state shall cross over the power of Māyā.
One who is constantly devoted to his own duty and whose mind is offered to the Lord attains the supreme state described by the exponents of the Vedas.
O best of beings, for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
their respective duties as ordained by their own castes should be performed free from attachment and aversion.
"The state of being the cause of knowledge arises solely for one who has attained [the goal]," as stated in the *Yogabīja*.
O Goddess, without action, the perfection of yoga does not arise;
nor can knowledge, heaven, or enjoyments be obtained by those devoid of merit.
Therefore, that very task must be performed quickly if there is indeed a means;
for success is not attained otherwise. Thus has Śiva spoken.
Moreover, the propitiation of Īśvara alone is the primary means for yoga;
and so it is stated in the Pātañjala [Yoga Sūtra]:

In the exposition of the means to yoga, it is said: "Or by devotion to Īśvara. Here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*). It means that through the grace of Īśvara alone—when propitiated by a particular form of devotion consisting of bodily, vocal, and mental service—yoga and the fruit of yoga are attained.

This is the meaning of the Sūtra: in the Vedānta, there is the Vyāsa-sūtra which states, "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical. By this, it should be understood that even *bhakti-yoga* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to *rāja-yoga*. Furthermore, since Patañjali has stated that even *vairāgya-yoga* is an auxiliary to *rāja-yoga*, it does not possess the status of the primary yoga. For instance, [Patañjali says]: "Cessation [of mental fluctuations] results from practice and detachment (*abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṃ tan-nirodhaḥ*)."

Thus [it is said]. This is its meaning: the suppression (*nirodha*) of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), which consist of illumination, activity, and restriction, by means of the practice and dispassion to be described hereafter—that is *nirodha*. When these fluctuations—characterized by attachment to objects of speech—cease, they exist in a state of potentiality (*śaktirūpatayā*) within their own cause, the mind (*citta*), by virtue of being turned inward.
Stability:

herein, through detachment born from perceiving the defects of sense objects, aversion toward them is produced; and through practice, by means of demonstrating a peaceful flow that generates happiness, firm steadfastness is produced.

Therefore, from those two [abhyāsa and vairāgya], there arises samādhi, which is called the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. He states the general and specific definitions of *abhyāsa* in two sūtras: "In that regard, effort toward stability is *abhyāsa*; it becomes firmly grounded when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. The meaning of this is: for one who is free from mental fluctuations...

The transformation of the mind that abides in its own true nature is "stability" (sthiti). The effort toward that, the enthusiasm, the repeated settling of the mind in that state—this is called "practice" (abhyāsa). The meaning is that this very practice, when cultivated over a long period of time with continuity and with an excess of reverence, becomes firmly grounded and stable.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Liberation comes through self-knowledge, and that indeed cannot be attained without yoga;
and that yoga is perfected only through long-term practice.
Yoga is not attained by resorting to the forest, nor by reflecting on various scriptures,
nor by gifts, nor by vows, nor even by austerities or sacrifices.
Neither through the lotus posture and such yogic practices, nor by gazing at the tip of the nose;
neither through ritual purity, nor through silence, nor even through the propitiation of mantras.
Through application, constant practice, and firm conviction in that very [path], and by not becoming despondent again and again, yoga will be accomplished; and not otherwise.
For one who constantly sports with the Self, who is always united with the Self,
and who is perfectly satisfied in the Self alone, the perfection of yoga is not far off.
He who does not perceive a second thing here apart from the Self—
that lord of yogis, delighting in the Self, becomes Brahman even in this world.
For that Brahman is to be realized by oneself, just as a young girl experiences sexual pleasure;
one who is not a yogi does not know it at all, like a person born blind does not perceive color.
Through constant practice of ethical conduct, that state indeed becomes self-evident;
because of its subtlety, it is the supreme, eternal Brahman, which is inexpressible.
In the Āgama, the Pārameśvara Tantra.
Therefore, those who desire liberation must practice constantly;
from practice comes perfection, and through practice one attains liberation.
Through practice one attains realization; yoga proceeds from practice.
The accomplishment of mantras comes from practice, and the mastery of the vital winds comes from practice.
And through such practice, mastery over time and likewise victory over death shall occur;
through practice, the perfection of speech and the power to act at will will certainly come to pass.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Whether young, childish, old, diseased, or even weak,
one who is untiring attains perfection in all yogas through practice.
In the *Amṛtasiddhi*.
After the description of mudrās and prāṇāyāma, it was stated:
"Thus, practice should always be performed by the wise who desire liberation."
Through practice yoga is born; through yoga, everything is accomplished.
By means of hearing and the yoga of practice, the vital wind (vāyu) becomes mastered.
Through the practice of breath control, the digestive fire increases greatly day by day;
and as the fire grows stronger, food is indeed digested with ease.
Through the digestion of food, the increase of the nutrient essence (rasa) is produced;
when the essence has increased, the bodily constituents (dhātus) then constantly grow.
From the nourishment of the constituent element (dhātu) alone, the primary essence (rasa) increases;
when the primary essence is perfected, one possesses a firm body and great strength.
The great bandha and the great practice arise by force alone;
from the great bandha and the great practice, the digestion of the rasa occurs.
All impurities, such as filth, urine, and perspiration, are purified;
and all sins committed throughout ten million lifetimes are consumed by fire.
Right here, through the yoga of practice, just as grasses are consumed by fire,
so too are all divine austerities— whether ten thousand or even millions— consumed.
Through the yoga of practice, these [powers] become millions upon millions;
likewise, the qualities and defects of nature manifest as various diseases in the body.
"Just as clouds are destroyed by the wind through the practice of yoga," so too are the two supreme aphorisms concerning the characteristics of general and specific detachment.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the perception of mastery in one who is free from thirst for the objects of the seen and the heard;
that which follows is the absence of thirst for the *guṇas* due to the discernment of the *puruṣa*.
The meaning of this is as follows: the "seen" object is that which is perceived right here, such as sound and so forth;

the "heard" object is that which is heard from the mouth of a teacher regarding the world of the gods and other realms—the term *ānuśravika* means that which comes from the *anuśrava*, which is the Veda—and thus it pertains to both of these types of objects.

When one is free from longing through the perception of the insipidity of transformation, that state of mastery—the discernment that "these are under my control" or "I am under their control"—is called detachment (*vairāgya*). The first [type of] detachment has the objects of the senses as its domain; the second—

[This refers to] the object that is the *guṇas*. Among these, dispassion (*vairāgya*) whose object is the *guṇas* is called "supreme" (*param*). This dispassion arises only for one who has produced the discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*, because it is extremely conducive to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*). By this, it is stated that even Sāṃkhya-yoga, which consists of the expression of discriminative discernment, is useful for yoga. And thus...

In the second stage, there is the restriction of *śravaṇa*— which consists of ascertaining the intended meaning of the Vedānta texts— and *manana*— which consists of reflecting upon the meaning of the scriptures through reasoning; and in the third stage, there is the restriction of *nididhyāsana*, which consists of establishing a continuous flow of similar mental impressions by setting aside heterogeneous impressions, within the context of *dhyāna*.
Its inclusion within *samprajñāta-samādhi* should be understood; likewise, Yājñavalkya states in his exposition of the restraints (*niyama*):

"The hearing of the established doctrine is declared by the wise to be the hearing of the Vedānta; while performing the hearing of the Vedānta, one should practice yoga therein. Therefore, it is not [among] the eight limbs.

It should be noted that there exists something external to yoga which is denoted by the word "yoga. Now, in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, regarding the crossing over of saṃsāra, it is said: "The power [to cross] is called by the word 'yoga,' as well as the method of self-knowledge and the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)."
Although both types have indeed been declared by the word "yoga,"...
Nevertheless, since it has been stated that "this [yoga] is firmly established when joined with breath," one might ask:

how can the restraint of the mind alone be called yoga? This is true; however, it was stated with the intention that the restraint of the mind consists in the restraint of the breath. For this very reason, through the sequence of practice, it is indeed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) [that becomes yoga].
It is expressed by the terms *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*. And so says Dattātreya:
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally defined as the restraint of the vital breaths;
it is that by which the senses, which have been directed toward sound and other objects, are withdrawn by those of self-controlled mind.
They are withdrawn by means of yoga; therefore, it is known as withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
That which is held steady by the wise is called concentration (dhāraṇā).
Prāṇāyāma and recitation are proclaimed as Dhāraṇā;
Yoga is remembered by the seers of reality as being twofold through these means.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is said to consist of twelve rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
concentration (dhāraṇā) is proclaimed to consist of twelve rounds of withdrawal.
For the sake of union with Īśvara, there is meditation (dhyāna) and twelvefold retention (dhāraṇā);
when meditation has reached its twelfth stage, it is designated as samādhi.
Beyond samādhi is the infinite light, self-luminous;
when that is seen, the coming and going of the realm of ritual action ceases.
Likewise, the duration for dhāraṇā and so forth has been stated: dhāraṇā lasts five nāḍīs, and dhyāna should last sixty nāḍīs.
"Through the restraint of the vital breath for twelve days, samādhi shall arise. Regarding the measure of a *ghaṭikā*, Vasiṣṭha says:
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* constitute one *ghaṭikā*.
Five *ghaṭikās* constitute one *rāśi*, and twelve *rāśis* constitute one day.
Thus, five *ghaṭikās* are one-twelfth [of a day], which is two and a half *prāṇas*.
The breath held for that duration is called *pratyāhāra*.
Likewise, two and a half *prāṇas* constitute a twelfth part; twelve and a half breaths held for that duration becomes the first *prāṇāyāma*. It ends with twenty-four breaths.
The middling [prāṇāyāma] ends with thirty-six breaths, while the superior ends with forty-eight; thus it is stated in the Rāddha.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "A single breath constitutes one mātrā, and this is defined as prāṇāyāma."

Thus, for one who has fallen under the sway of sleep, the duration of time it takes for a single breath to go out and return is the measure of one *prāṇāyāma*. Furthermore, in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, it is stated that the vibration (*spanda*) of both the mind and the vital breath is indeed one and the same.
The vibration of the vital breath is indeed the very vibration of the mind;
therefore, a wise person should exert great effort in conquering the vibration of the vital breath.

For this very reason, it is well known in all the Yoga Śāstras that samādhi consists precisely of fear and dissolution; as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "When the vital breath is completely exhausted and the mind is dissolved, that which is the state of equal flavor (samarasatva) is here called samādhi. Therefore, knowledge arises only when fear has been destroyed.
And regarding the statement that "liberation occurs," there is this word of Śiva: "O Goddess, as long as the mind lives, how can knowledge [arise]?
As long as the mind does not die, the vital breath also lives.
He who brings both of these—the breath and the mind—to dissolution, that man attains liberation; how could it be otherwise?"
Consciousness is something else;
[this is stated] in the Vāsiṣṭha.
Intense practice of a single principle, the dissolution of the vital breaths,
and the restraint of the mind— this is the summary of the meaning of the word "liberation."
Is it not true that for this disease of saṃsāra, which causes all manner of afflictions, there is but one single remedy: the restraint of one's own mind?
"The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra, endowed with desire, anger, and so forth"— this and more is complete in the Vāsiṣṭha.
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
attached to sense-objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense-objects, it is considered the path to liberation," and so forth.
Furthermore, since other scriptures also declare that saṃsāra is rooted in the mind,

and since they likewise declare that both the knowledge of reality and liberation are dependent upon the conquest of the mind, it follows that the goal consisting of liberation— which is preceded by the uprooting of ignorance along with its manifestations, the cause of all misfortune— is possible only through the restraint of the mind.
If it be argued, "What is the use of this difficult-to-accomplish restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which causes the suffering of disease and illness?"—it is not so;
for without mastery over the *prāṇas*, mastery of the mind (*citta*) cannot be achieved. And thus it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
When the breath moves, the mind moves; when it is still, the mind is likewise still.
The yogi attains the state of an immovable pillar; therefore, he should restrain the vital air.
Just as water, even for a single moment, does not attain stability when struck by the wind, so too is the mind; therefore, one should not place trust in it.
Then, for the sake of stabilizing the *citta*, one should restrain the *nīla* [wind];
for the purpose of restraining the vital breaths (*marut*), one should practice the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).
"As long as the breath is bound within, for that long the mind is free from affliction;
as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, for that long, whence can there be fear of death?
Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Thus has this been told to you, O King; now understand this yoga as well, by attaining which a Brahmin yogi shall never again fall into a state of otherness from the eternal.
When that which is difficult to conquer already exists, the yogi should first make an effort to conquer his own self; hear from me the means for that conquest.
Just as the impurities of mountain ores are burned away when they are smelted,
so too are the defects produced by the senses burned away through the restraint of the vital breath.
One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
When the channel-wheel has been purified by various breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
the vital air (māruta) pierces the opening of the Suṣumṇā and enters through its mouth.
When the vital breath moves through the middle channel, stability of mind arises;
that state in which the mind becomes steady is itself the state of *manonmanī*.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā]:
For the sake of pacifying the mind, the yogi should practice the restraint of the vital breath through breath-control exercises,
meditations, and applications devised by reason.
The wise know that the restraint of the vital breath bestows the fruit of pacifying all disturbances, is the supreme cause of peace, brings good fortune, and results in the health of consciousness.
For one who observes vows, there are two seeds for the tree of the mind's activity:
the first is the movement of the vital breath, and the second is firm latent impression (*vāsanā*).
The masters of the Āgamas say that the mind is the vibration of the vital breath;
when that [breath] is restrained, the mind will surely become tranquil.
Through the cessation of the vibration of the mind, saṃsāra dissolves,
just as the movement of the world ceases when the radiance of the sun subsides.
"When the movement of the vital breaths has come to an end through practice, the mind attains tranquility; only nirvāṇa remains. Thus it is said in another scripture.
The dull-witted person who attempts to accomplish yoga without breath-control (prāṇāyāma) does not attain the state of perfection,
just as a cripple cannot achieve the gait of a horse.
In the Yogabīja.
The mind is bound by the vital breath, and that [breath] resides within living beings;
just as a bull is tied with a rope, so too is this mind bound.
The mind cannot be mastered through various kinds of analytical reflections;
therefore, the means for its conquest is indeed the conquest of the vital breath (prāṇa).
O Beloved, through logic, disputation, the web of scriptures, reasoning, mantras, and medicines,
the vital breath is not restored to life anew without the perfected means (siddhopāya).
Without understanding that means, one proceeds upon the path of yoga;
by that very fragmented knowledge, a person becomes a partaker of affliction.
That yogi who, out of delusion, desires to practice yoga after having conquered the vital breath (prāṇa) is like one who,
having climbed onto a heated pot, desires to cross the ocean.
If one's vital breaths have dissolved while the practitioner is still alive and the physical body has not yet fallen,
his mind is liberated from defects.
When the mind is stilled, the knowledge of one's own true self shines forth.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, knowledge arises from yoga within a single lifetime;
for that reason, the practitioner should constantly practice that very yoga at the outset.
"Those desiring liberation must practice the conquest of the vital breaths for the sake of liberation"—
thus says the venerable Patañjali.

"By means of vomiting and splitting, [there is the conquest] of the vital breath"— the meaning is that there would be the cessation of the mind. Thus, it is only when the mind is conquered that the vital breath is conquered,
because the two are mutually dependent in their respective functions.
And likewise in the Vāsiṣṭha:
Inseparable from one another and ever-present in the breath and mind of living beings,
they exist like fragrance in a flower or oil in sesame seeds.
These two are like the support and the supported; in the absence of one, both perish.
Through their own destruction, they accomplish the supreme goal known as liberation.
In the Rājayoga.

Like milk and water, these two always remain mixed within the same vessel; when the breath flows through both nostrils, its specific restraint is *prāṇāyāma*. Through these two, one should achieve steadiness of mind. As long as the mind and the vital air are engaged in activity, the vital air remains there with the mind.

As long as there is activity of the vital air (*marut*), there is activity of the mind (*manas*). From the destruction of one, there is the destruction of the other; from the activity of one, there is the activity of the other. When both are undestroyed, there is the increase of their respective groups of sense organs; when both are destroyed, there is the attainment of the state of liberation (*mokṣa-pada*). Even in that case, the destruction of the vital air is to be accomplished by the practice of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-yoga*) and so forth.

But the destruction of the mind is indeed easily accomplished in a mere moment through the grace of the Guru. Just as the steadiness of the mind arises from constant practice, so too does the steadiness of the [inner] wind, the body, and the vision arise.
Therefore, one should strive for the destruction of the mind, for by its destruction even the fierce wind is destroyed.
Thus, through the dissolution of one's own body, senses, and intellect, the innate perception of duality simply ceases to exist.
Sureśvarācārya.
When the mind has attained immobility, the vital breath becomes immobile;
therefore, one should practice the eightfold yoga for the sake of the mind's immobility.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.

When the mind is steady, the vital air becomes steady; from that, the seminal drop (bindu) becomes steady. From the steadiness of the drop, the steadiness of the physical body (piṇḍa) is then produced.
Thus, in the Amṛtasiddhi.
Death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*; life comes from holding the *bindu*.
When the *bindu* has been mastered as the great elixir (*mahārasa*), all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise.
The Bindu is Brahmā, the Bindu is Viṣṇu, the Bindu is the Lord Sadāśiva;
the Bindu is the all-pervading God, the Bindu is the mirror of the three worlds.
The God who transcends all principles, whose form is existence and who is stainless,
dwells within all living beings in the form of the Bindu.
That *bindu* should be known as twofold: that which arises from the male and that which arises from the female.
The seed is declared to be the male, and the menstrual flow (*rajas*) is that which originates from the female.
Through external yoga, the creation of men arises;
when yoga is internal, then one is celebrated as a yogin.
The *bindu* is said to consist of the moon, and likewise, the *rajas* consists of the sun;
from the union of these two alone, the supreme state is attained.
The Bindu bestows heaven, bestows liberation, bestows merit, and likewise bestows dharma;
within it, all deities abide in a subtle form.
This is the reality, this is the seed; it is called the essence of all.
Without the wind, the drop does not fall, nor is there any other means for the realization of the drop.
The vital wind (vāyu) reaches whatever state the drop (bindu) attains;
for just as the wind is mastered, so too is the mastery of the drop accomplished.
When swooning, it removes disease; when bound, it leads to the power of moving through the air;
when absorbed, it grants all accomplishments; and when motionless, it bestows liberation.
In whatever state the *bindu* may be, such is the state of the mind.
When this wind moves, then the *bindu* is said to move.
The *bindu* moves within his body, and his mind is likewise unsteady;
as long as the *bindu* is moving, the mind is moving, and the vital breath (*vāyu*) is always moving.
The world is born and dies; this word is the truth, the absolute truth. That which is the sound "nāda" is indeed the drop "bindu," and that is proclaimed to be the mind (citta).
Nāda, bindu, and citta— the practice for the unification of these three is that,
although they exist externally as distinct entities within the body, they are established as one.
Nevertheless, once the vital air (vāyu) is mastered, everything is certainly accomplished;
when this middle air is brought to rest through the practice of the middle yoga, one dies.
Then the drop (bindu) and the mind (citta) die together with the vital wind (vāyu);
all the principles of the drop (bindu-tattva) likewise reside within the body.
"The movement of the vital breaths proceeds; they die because of the destruction of the vital breaths," so it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha.
Rāma said:
How can the movement of the vital winds— such as prāṇa and the rest— which move incessantly within the body-house and course through its depths, be obstructed?
Vasiṣṭha:
Through association with the scriptures and virtuous people, through the practice of dispassion, and through yoga,
one establishes a lack of reliance upon former worldly activities and instead establishes reliance [upon the means of liberation].
From meditating for a long time with one-pointedness upon whatever is desired,
and from the intense practice of a single reality, the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
Through the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*) and other breath-control techniques, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained;
this occurs through firm practice of the restraint of the breath via inhalation and the rest, performed without causing fatigue.
Through the application of one-pointed meditation,
the vibration of the vital breath is arrested by contemplating the reality of the sound at the conclusion of the utterance of the syllable *Oṃ*.
Through meditation on the mind free from latent impressions, the vibration of the vital breath is ceased at the tip of the nose,
within the twelve-finger space of the stainless sky.
When consciousness and the object of perception are stilled,
the vibration of the vital breath ceases through the firm practice of breath control and by means of the method imparted by the Guru.
Through the practice of postures and breath control, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained;
and through repeated practice, these methods of yoga become free from obstacles.
They become the means for the fortunate one to break through cyclic existence;
having reached firmness through practice, they are characterized by dispassion.
The life-force of Māyā is considered fruitful according to one's latent impressions (vāsanā),
because from it arise the afflictions accompanied by the conceptualization of mental constructs.

"By means of the notion of conceptualization, that state remains for the living being. There are other methods for the conquest of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as well, but they are not written here for fear of prolixity.
Therefore, these two—*haṭhayoga* and *rājayoga*—having been considered, should be practiced.
In the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"Without Haṭha, Rājayoga is not accomplished; without Rājayoga, Haṭha is not accomplished. Therefore, these two should be practiced together as a pair by the wise."
Those who practice Rajayoga without Hatha, or Hatha without Rajayoga,
I consider them to be devoid of the fruits of their efforts.
Also in the Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti]:
As long as the mind has not dissolved, so long there is no destruction of latent impressions;
and as long as the latent impressions have not been destroyed, so long the mind does not become tranquil.
As long as there is no realization of reality, so long is there no destruction of the mind;
as long as there is no pacification of the mind, so long is there no knowledge of reality.
As long as there is no destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), how can there be realization of reality?
As long as there is no attainment of reality, there is no exhaustion of latent impressions.
Knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—
since these mutually serve as causes for one another, they remain difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, O King, with effort and human exertion through discernment, one should cast attachment to enjoyments far away and take refuge in these three.
As long as these three are not practiced equally again and again,
the attainment of reality will not occur even in hundreds of aeons.
O Mahāmati, for the Sage, the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the destruction of consciousness (*vijñāna*),
and the dissolution of the mind (*manas*) become fruit-bearing when practiced simultaneously.
If each of these is practiced individually for a long time and sufficiently,
they bestow accomplishment there, just like the mantras that have been proclaimed.
The firm knots of the heart, long-practiced through the three [types of] craving,
are severed without a doubt, like fibers from a lotus stalk.
The persistence of worldly existence, cultivated through hundreds of previous births,
is never extinguished without the yoga of immediate practice.
The knowers of reality understand that the complete abandonment of latent impressions is equal to the restraint of the vital breaths; therefore, one should practice both of these together.
Through the complete relinquishing of latent tendencies, the mind attains the state of pure consciousness;
through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, do as you wish.
Because one acts without attachment, because one has abandoned the cultivation of existence,
and because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent tendencies do not arise.
When the manifestation of latent impressions is destroyed, the mind no longer functions.
O Rāma, there are two seeds for the mind: the vibration of the vital breath and latent impressions.
"When one thought has perished, both [the preceding and succeeding thoughts] quickly perish. Now follows the determination of the means to yoga (*yogopāya*).
Among those, some taught by Patañjali have already been mentioned previously in passing. This is the sequence of means here:
first, one who has attained delight in the mind toward the reality of the object through scripture, inference, and the instruction of a teacher...

From that, faith in yoga which serves as the means of accomplishment is produced; immediately after that, enthusiasm arises. For one possessed of enthusiasm, mindfulness occurs regarding the subsequent stages. Through that recollection, the mind becomes undisturbed and established in the restraints (yamas), observances (niyamas), and so forth, whereby it becomes endowed with the limb of yoga known as concentration (samādhi). Thereafter, for one who has perfected all the limbs of yoga:

From the excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*), there arises *samprajñāta* (cognitive) *samādhi*. Through the practice of that [wisdom] and from supreme dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward its objects, there arises *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive) *samādhi*. And that is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*). For the cessation [of mental activity] preceded by the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa* has fulfilled the mind’s purpose through the performance of all its functions.

Based on the context, he causes [the mind] to settle. In that regard, first, the yogi must purify the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables], because a mind possessed by envy and the like cannot be directed.
And so it is said in the *Gītā*:
Yoga is difficult to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my conviction.
But by one whose self is controlled and who strives with the proper means, it can be attained.
Thus, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
As long as the activity of the mind, which is difficult to restrain, does not cease, how can even the slightest state of yoga be attained? How much less so the great?
Thus ends the section on Rājayoga.
As long as there is even a trace of the ancient [world], as long as there is conceptualization and imagination,
and as long as the mind is agitated, there is no true celibacy for those who possess it.
It is intermingled with old age and death and is the basis for all afflictions;
likewise,
as long as the wind follows the wrong path and does not remain motionless within the center.
"Since even the attainment of reality is unestablished, what talk can there be [of its realization]?"—
thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
As long as the vital breath (māruta) does not enter the central path for a long time,

as long as the life-force (prāṇavāta) has not become firmly awakened as the bindu, and as long as the reality that resembles the innate state (sahaja) is not known within the fire of the lower abdomen (dhoma)—
all this that one speaks is merely hypocrisy and false prattle.
Thus, in the Amṛtasiddhi.
