A man is considered bound by the worldly cycle and unperfected for as long as this mercury,
which has the nature of the Brahman within the body, remains in a liquid state.
One should know that to be unaccomplished; one should know it to be accompanied by the qualities of the action of wind, as long as the mind vibrates toward external and internal objects.
One should know that mind to be unestablished when it follows the power of karma;
likewise, the Sūtra of Patañjali states: [Yoga Sūtra 1.5].

The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which have as their objects happiness and suffering, and merit and demerit. Here, the words "happiness" and so forth refer to those possessing such qualities. For a person whose disposition is defiled by passion and aversion, there is envy when seeing one who is happy, and hatred toward one who possesses merit.

Toward those who suffer, equanimity arises; toward those who are evil, rejoicing arises. By cultivating loving-kindness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, sympathetic joy toward the meritorious, and equanimity toward the evil, the yogi uproots passion and hatred—the very roots of all weariness—along with their foundations.

Thereupon the mind becomes serene; for one whose mind is serene, yoga is easily attained. Thus it has been stated by the aphorism, "Or from meditation on whatever is desired," that the mind becomes steady even through meditation on an object of one's own choice. As it is said in the *Vasiṣṭha*:
The mind is the cause of all objects; when it exists, the three worlds exist. When it is extinguished, the world is extinguished; therefore, it should be treated with diligent effort.
Having crushed hand with hand and ground teeth against teeth,
and having pressed limb against limb, one should first conquer one's own mind.
O son, abandon all sense-objects entirely;
for this supreme lack of reliance upon them is the very method for conquering the mind.
This alone is the supreme application;
by this very means, the great elephant of one's own intoxicated mind is instantly subdued.
One should fill two parts of the mind with enjoyments, one part with the scriptures, and one part with service to the guru; this is the proper sequence for one who is unlearned.
One should fill one part of that which is endowed with some proficiency with enjoyments;
two parts with service to the teacher; and one part with reflection on the meaning of the scriptures.
Day by day, one should fill the mind according to its capacity:
two parts with scriptural learning and dispassion, and two parts with meditation and the worship of the Guru.
O noble son, by the power of wisdom and investigation, the mind cannot be conquered at all times without blameless reasoning.
Just as a wicked elephant, when intoxicated, cannot be controlled without a goad,
so too [the mind] cannot be restrained without the acquisition of inner science (adhyātmavidyā) and association with the virtuous.
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the simultaneous restraint of the vital breaths—
these indeed are the most excellent methods for the conquest of the mind.
Those who, despite these rational methods existing, forcibly restrain their minds,
are like those who discard a lamp and attempt to destroy darkness with collyrium.
Those deluded ones who strive to conquer the mind by force are like those who attempt to bind a furious elephant-king with lotus fibers; they only bring about their own destruction.
Now, the means of yoga, beginning with the taking up and joining of the breaths, are described in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"The mind is the master of the senses, and the vital air (māruta) is the master of the mind; the master of the vital air is its dissolution, and the master of that [dissolution] is its dissolution."
It is based on *nāda*.
Let this alone be what is called liberation, or even according to other doctrines;
the dissolution of mind and breath is *nāda*, and there is no distinction whatsoever between them.
This sound, acting as a sharp goad, is capable of restraining the lordly elephant of the mind as it wanders through the garden of the sense-objects.
Just as a bee drinking nectar does not look toward other fragrances,
so the mind attached to the Sound (nāda) does not desire sense objects.
Fire kindled in wood is extinguished along with the wood;
the mind kindled by the *nāda* dissolves along with the *nāda*.
Having forgotten all that is external, like milk and water mixed together, the person suddenly becomes one with the sound and then dissolves into the space of consciousness.
The glorious Ādinātha has proclaimed seventy million methods of dissolution (*laya*); may they be victorious!
We consider that the practice of contemplation upon *nāda* alone is the task among all these dissolutions.
Having become supremely indifferent through constant practice, the self-controlled one [attains liberation].
One should immediately focus one's attention on the *nāda* alone in order to achieve the state of *unmanī*.
What kind of indifference is it?

At the time of conduct, boiled milk or cow’s milk is wholesome; for food, alms or a cluster of wild tubers; for eating, a wooden bowl or the vessel of another’s meal. For the swift attainment of the state beyond the mind (*unmanī*), these two paths are my preference.
Whether it be reality, supreme bliss, or indeed the practice of Nāda.
For those whose minds are engaged in bliss, even for the hidden ones,
the dissolution of the *nāda* and *jyotis* arises, instantly bestowing joy.
Seated in the liberated posture (muktāsana), the yogi, maintaining the Śāmbhavī mudrā,
should constantly hear the internal sound within the right ear.
Having abandoned all thought with an attentive mind,
one established in the sovereignty of yoga focuses exclusively upon the internal sound (nāda).
Covering his ears with his hands, the sage should steady his mind for as long as it takes to hear a sound, until it reaches a state of stability.
This internal sound, when practiced, causes the external river of breath to turn back;
thereafter, having conquered all distraction, the yogi becomes happy.
It is heard that during the initial practice, various kinds of great sounds arise;
as the practice continues, however, they are heard to become increasingly subtle.
At the beginning, there is the ocean, the clouds, the kettledrum, and the sound arising from the eyebrows;
in the middle, there are the mṛdaṅga drum, the conch, as well as the bell and the kāhala trumpet.
But at the front, the sounds of clusters of small bells, lutes, and bees are heard;
thus, various kinds of sounds are perceived arising from within the body.
Even when great sounds such as those of clouds or kettledrums are being heard,
one should thus contemplate the sound itself, subtler than the subtle.
Having abandoned the gross for the subtle, or having proceeded from the subtle to the gross,
one should cast the mind into that very [subtle state] and not move it elsewhere.
Wherever in any sound the mind first becomes well-established, there one should make it steady; by that means, it dissolves together with it.
The sound is the seed, Haṭha is the field, and equanimity is known as the water;
thus the wish-fulfilling creeper of the Transmental state will immediately sprout.
In the Rājayoga.
Where vision dissolves, there lies the eternal power of the elements and the senses;
the vision of all beings is united with its objective focus.

With the gaze directed upward, the piercing is downward; with the gaze directed downward, the piercing is upward. By means of this method of the "journey of blindness," one shall become liberated while living.
With his vision expanded everywhere and then gradually withdrawn,
he beholds the supreme reality, which is beyond all reflection, as the Self by means of the self.
First, the vision that has emerged becomes attached to whatever it encounters;
having become fixed right there, it perishes very gradually.
Constantly vigilant in crushing the successive series of volitions by force,
the vision— gradually diminishing due to the loss of its objective support— attains peace.
The floods of the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas are like common courtesans.
The Śāmbhavī Mudrā alone is like a secret, unmanifest bride.
The inner focus with the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening—
the Śāmbhavī Mudrā is this, hidden in all scriptures.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā:

When the yogi exists with the mind and breath dissolved within the internal object of focus, and by means of this stainless vision, he sees outwardly yet does not see [anything external], this indeed is the Śāmbhavī Mudrā. By your grace, O Guru, may that reality— the Śāmbhava state— which shines forth as being devoid of both the void and the non-void, manifest.
Only the Guru-Natha knows that single reality— the one bliss, ineffable by words, hidden within the hearts of the lords of yogis who partake in the samādhi of the pursuit of the inner sound (nāda)—
with his mind steady and his eyes half-opened.
When the gaze is fixed on the tip of the nose, even the moon and sun are brought to dissolution within the state of motionlessness;
then, one attains that supreme reality, the highest state, which is of the nature of light, entirely devoid of externality, and intensely radiant— what more need be said here of this supreme object?
The states of Śrīśāmbhavī and Khecarī differ according to their movement;
having joined [the breath] with the light in the Tārā, one should slightly raise the eyebrows.
This is the path of the ancient yoga, by which one attains the state of Unmanī in an instant;
some rely on the web of scriptures, while others are burdened by restrictive observances.
Some are deluded by reasoning and do not know the Savior at all;
the distinction of the fourfold yogic states is heard [only] through the internal sound (nāda).
And the states will be explained.
The Knot of Brahmā becomes pierced; bliss arises from the Void.
Within the diverse body, at every moment, the resonance of sound is heard.
When the Viṣṇugranthi is pierced, indicating supreme bliss,
and there is the penetration of the Great Void (atiśūnya), then the sound of a kettledrum arises.
Then, on the third [day], having burst through that, the sound of the drum,
free from conceptualization, likewise enters the Great Void, which is the refuge of all accomplishments.
Then, having conquered the bliss of the mind, he who is the source of sudden joy pierces the Rudra-knot; thereafter, the Blue One (Nīla) reaches all the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The sound of a flute is indeed a *nirghāta*, while the resonance of a vibrating lute is a *kvaṇa*;
likewise, when the mind becomes unified, it is designated as *rājayoga*.
Sureśvarācārya.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the suṣumnā, the internal sound (nāda) is heard in eight ways,
like the sounds of a bell, a drum, the ocean, a lute, a flute, and so forth.
When the vital breath has entered the Brahma-nāḍī, Tanūnapāt, Trita, and Tāratāra— resembling the sun— reveal the form of the Cosmic Man (Bimbarūpa).
The Procedure for the Arising of Nāda in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
Now, with the heel of the left foot pressed against the base of the right heel, the root of the navel, and the anus; with the body and neck held straight;
with the self restrained and the senses withdrawn from their objects.
O enemy of Mura, having repeatedly filled the cavity of the abdomen with winds drawn in like a female crow,

one of steady and pure intellect should block the two ear-openings with both thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, and the nostrils with the two middle fingers, while blocking the mouth with the remaining fingers.

One should firmly fix one's own mind within the abode born of the lotus (the heart). For one who practices thus every day according to their capacity, this vital breath (pavana) gradually flows into the *suṣumṇā*.
Then the innate sound (*nāda*) arises, which generates innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), progressively like the sweet resonance of a lute being struck.
It is like the sky. At first, it possesses the resonance of a swarm of intoxicated bees and carries the sound of all-pervading *bhūṃkāra*;

then it is equal to the sound of a flute-player’s shining flute filled with air; thereafter, it imitates the ringing of bells and the roar of thundering clouds from the ocean; yet another [sound] exists here within this cave.
The Brahman-Channel: He whose innate resonance has arisen through the conquered breath is victorious;

for him of immeasurable merit and the abode of great qualities, the powers such as *aṇimā* come to pass. Having blocked the aperture of the vital breath with two fingers of his own hand, he [hears] within a sound like the deep roar of the ocean, as if the body of the King of the Gods were being crushed by force.

A mortal suddenly hears this sound spreading forth; even while contemplating this roar produced by the enemies of the Son of the Lord of the Thirty-three, there is the constant attainment of virtues for the person who is slain [by it] and freed from impurity. Who, having properly blocked the horns with his fingers... [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The final line is incomplete, but based on the context of the preceding verses regarding the *śrīkhaṇḍābhidha* (sandalwood) mountain and the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, the missing portion likely describes the ritual procedure.]

Between the two staffs, the wise man immediately beholds for himself that supreme light of Triputra— the best of bulls whose vital breath is restrained, who is the sixth sense, Yama himself, the song of whom is sung with gradual shyness, and whose radiance is marked by hundreds of thousands of moons, yet remains unmarked.
Yājñavalkya.
Thus, O fair-faced one, is the method for conquering the vital breath (prāṇa) through the mastery of the winds;
this can be accomplished by assuming a steady posture with a concentrated mind.
Having brought the organs under control by force from their objects, the wise man,
being composed, draws the *apāna* upward with the *praṇava*.
One should properly bind the sense organs, such as the ears and so forth, with both hands:
the two ears with the two thumbs, and the two eyes with the two index fingers.
Having likewise covered the two nostrils with the other [two fingers],
one should indeed hold [the breath] upon the head for as long as the experience of bliss lasts.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is not directed [outward] at all; therefore, it does not cause the destruction of life.
It resides within the Brahma-randhra in the Suṣumṇā, like a thread within the interior of a lotus stalk.
The arising of the *nāda* within the *anāhata* is indeed like a pure crystal;
the *nāda* revolves upward from the head, having arisen like the sound of a lute being played.
At first it resembles the sound of a conch shell, then in the middle it is like the roar of clouds;
when the sound has reached the path of the sky, it is like a mountain torrent.
When the vital air has entered the aperture of space and the mind is established in the Self, the yogi shall be in a state of perpetual bliss; by that, the vital air becomes conquered.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
When the wind has reached the sky, a great sound arises from sounding objects such as bells; therefore, accomplishment is not far off.
Thus, in the Haṭhapradīpikā.

One should block the ears, eyes, and nostrils; then, clearly and stainlessly, the sound (nāda) is heard within the path of the auspicious, pure Suṣumṇā. While engaged in conversation with pieces of wood, listen to the sound that resides within.
O Purāmatsyendra, for the sake of awakening, the word spoken by Ādinātha— namely,
the practice called *Nirālamba*— brings about the ripening of the mind.
Therefore, the yogi must constantly apply himself to the worship of *nāda*;
for by hearing the *nāda*, the mind—the inner steed—is brought under control.
All is utterly empty; the mind does not run toward anything at all.
Like a deer within its inner enclosure, it is bound fast by the sound.
It also dissolves into the binding of the inner horse,
which is intent upon the resonance of the bell and devoted to the production of sound.
Of that unstruck sound, there is the resonance;
within the resonance is the light, and within the light is the mind.
That state where the mind dissolves is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
the conceptualization of space persists only as long as sound continues to function.
That which is soundless is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman, the Paramātman;
whatever is heard by way of name and form is indeed that very power (śakti).
He who hears that is formless; he alone is the Supreme Lord.
There are thousands of millions of *nādas* and hundreds of millions of *bindus*.
"All dissolve there where the stainless God resides"—
thus it is said in the Rājayoga.
When the mind moves, saṃsāra arises; when it is unmoving, dissolution occurs.
Therefore, one who is devoted to equanimity should make the mind steady.
One should always remain indifferent; then reality shines forth. When reality has been self-revealed, one's own bliss arises in that very instant.
One should always remain devoted to practice, satisfied with bliss;
for one who has become firm through constant practice, the ritual procedure is no longer required.
The yogi should not think of anything at all, for he should become supreme in equanimity;
by the very absence of thinking anything, reality itself is revealed spontaneously.
When reality is revealed by itself, one becomes identical with it at that very moment;
for this entire visible world, whatever exists moving or unmoving, is nothing but the mind.
They declare that non-duality arises from the state of the mind being beyond the mind (unmanī);
it occurs for one who remains indifferent while the mind is being born [into its own nature].
Both softness and submissiveness arise even in the body when it has been uprooted from its very foundation by the mindless spade.
When the internal organ is set in motion, the sage becomes happy;
it is accompanied by the thread of breath and crowded with the abode of the senses.
Having cast the net of the mind, one becomes happy like a fish;
this group of senses is thoroughly pacified and endowed with the power of intelligence.
Having conquered the enemy that is the mind, which is joined with the abode of the vital breath (vāyu), one shall become happy;
[one must sever] the very firm rope composed of the three qualities (guṇas) that binds the self to the Self.
Having severed [the bonds] with the razor of the mindless state, one may attain liberation;
just as everything dissolves and sets when the sun has gone down.
Likewise, the entire web of karma dissolves in the state of no-mind (amanaska),
which is free from the grasp of the senses, windless, and pure nectar.
One who has bathed in the state of mindlessness (amanaska) partakes of the supreme nectar;
with inhalation and exhalation destroyed and the grasping of sense objects shattered.
Free from activity and devoid of all exertion, the practitioner of yoga brings joy; with all mental constructs severed and all residual movements gone,
a certain dissolution arises that is self-realized and beyond the reach of words.
Likewise, the single staff, the triple staff, and so forth, as well as matted hair, ashes, and the like.
Neither the shaving of hair nor nakedness, nor the wearing of dyed garments,
belongs to one who has attained self-awakening and remains forever indifferent.
For one who is always delighted in practice, that [attainment] is not required anywhere;
at that time, there are various special visions and diverse postures (āsanas).
The states of the internal organ do not apply to the yogi;
he always remains as if asleep even while in the waking state.
Devoid of inhalation and exhalation, he is certainly liberated;
that state which arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking is indeed the Tūpa.
The yogi who meditates upon that state is certainly liberated;
he is like someone who, having awakened from sleep, encounters sense objects.
Therefore, the yogi remains truly awake due to the exhaustion of the sleep of yoga (yoganidrā),
as he is nourished by the ever-increasing flood of the nectar of equanimity.
Once the root of the mind has been uprooted, the tree of the world will fall; for wherever, however, and from whatever cause the mind remains steady, there the world-tree falls.
Therefore, one should never move from that state there in that manner;
wherever the mind goes, it should not be restrained from that place.
Therefore, the mind that is left unrestrained dissolves by itself;
however, when it is being restrained with effort, it cannot be made to cease its activity.
It arises in an instant by the power of the wind;
the mind is indeed difficult to restrain as long as one has not found the reality.
But when the supreme reality is known, the mind becomes as steady as a crow perched on a pillar;
just as a skilled weigher makes a swaying scale steady.

When happiness has arisen through constant practice, the mental state likewise [becomes established] in the Self. Having abandoned distraction, singleness, and multiplicity, just as turbid water becomes pure when situated in a windless place— clear, tranquil, and of supreme nature— so too, having suddenly abandoned all this, it shines forth brilliantly.
When the mind has arisen, that partless reality, which is innate and stainless by nature, becomes certain.
Therefore, having abandoned all objects of the senses, through the yoga of the partless self, there follows the destruction of the vital breath (*vāyu*), and thereafter the destruction of the mind;
that destruction is liberation. [One attains] the God who is Being-Consciousness.
O wise ones, strive from the very beginning to attain that which is stainless, partless, and changeless— the state beyond the mind. A sage must understand the fourfold states of the mind.
And it is separated from the grasping of conceptual objects, which involve coming and going.
If it becomes well-integrated, of excellent character, and removes the objects of conceptual construction through the application of practice,
then it may become supportless.
Then, having become equanimous, that very mind becomes supreme bliss; being joyful and immovable, it is therefore called "well-united."
For one who practices, the mind— having first become exceedingly steady and blissful like a flute— is liberated once it has been detached from its objects.
Then, there is some movement, both mobile and immobile, along with joyful coming and going;
such are the actions of one who has become thus—both meritorious deeds and doubts.
"They pass by and do not smear [the wise man], for they are performed as being done by the virtuous.

Thus, while describing the nature of one who has ascended to yoga, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva speaks of the manifestation of the bliss of Brahman during the stage of practice in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). For it is thus:
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, one is said to be ever-yoked in yoga.
"Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker— this is the simile taught for the yogin of restrained mind who practices yoga of the self."
Wherein the mind is restrained through the practice of yoga according to the supreme view,
and wherein, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds contentment within the self.
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; [that is Brahman].
Having obtained another gain, he does not consider it to be superior to that [previous one];
established in that state, he is not shaken even by heavy suffering.
One should know that the separation from union with suffering is designated as yoga;
that yoga must be practiced with determination and an undistracted mind.
Having abandoned all desires born of volitional thought without remainder,
he should then restrain the entire collection of senses with the mind alone, making them even.
One should gradually come to rest by means of the intellect held with firmness;
having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone.
Supreme bliss comes to this yogi whose mind is perfectly tranquil,
whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from all taint.
Yoking himself thus at all times, the yogi, freed from defilement,
easily attains the infinite bliss that is the touch of Brahman.
One whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he perceives the same everywhere with an equal vision.
And such is the Vedic revelation.

"When the mind has its impurities shaken off by meditative concentration (samādhi) and is established within the Self, there arises a bliss that cannot be described by speech; it is grasped only by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) itself.
— Śrīpāda Vidyāraṇya.
To the extent that the ego-sense is blended through the yoga of practice,
to that same extent is one's own bliss inferred by the subtle vision.
Although this samādhi is difficult for humans to attain even over a long period of time,
nevertheless, even for a moment, it causes one to realize the bliss of Brahman.
Thus it is also stated in the Pātañjala [Yogaśāstra].

The four states of the mind have been described according to the differentiation of its qualities: the state of emergence (vyutthāna), the commencement of meditative absorption (samādhi-prārambha), one-pointedness (ekāgratā), and cessation (nirodha). This is the process therein. Since the mind is an effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), the mind itself is also composed of the three qualities. That primordial nature was already explained previously during the investigation of the principles (tattva-nirūpaṇa).

The qualities (*guṇas*), however, are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among them, *sattva* has the nature of luminosity, clarity, and virtue; *rajas* has the nature of activity, distress, grief, and so forth; while *tamas* has the nature of obstruction to activity, known as stability, and possesses the qualities of heaviness, concealment, delusion, and so on. And such are these [qualities] of the mind.

Because the three *guṇas* possess the quality of being mutually suppressive and supportive, there arise five states—designated by the term "stages" (*bhūmi*)—due to their diverse transformations: the distracted (*kṣipta*), the deluded (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*nirodha*). Among these, the "distracted" state occurs when [the mind], through the influence of *rajas*, is directed toward external objects such as pleasure and the like.

The *prerita* (agitated) mind is extremely unstable; it is deluded by *tamas*, characterized by sleep, possessed of fainting and the like, filled with anger and other passions, devoid of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done, and intent on harming others. The *vikṣipta* (distracted) mind is distinguished from the *kṣipta* (deranged); its distinction lies in the fact that while the *kṣipta* is predominantly unstable, the *vikṣipta* possesses occasional stability.
Although there is no increase of *sattva* here, nevertheless,

because it is touched by a slight degree of *rajas* and *tamas*, one finds pleasure in sovereignty and in objects such as sound; and due to the predominance of *sattva*, even though reality (*tattva*) exists, it is obscured by *tamas*.

Thinking that the powers such as *aṇimā* constitute true sovereignty, one desires to direct the mind [toward them] and directs it for a moment. Then, being cast away by a portion of *rajas*, it fails to find stability there and becomes merely fond of them. This is the state of being established in love for sound and other objects due to their constant flow; in the state of being "cast" (*kṣipta*), this occurs only occasionally.

Because it does not eliminate distraction from concentration, [the state of] one-pointedness is useless for yoga. Even though there is a cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*) here, because it lacks the quality of being a means to liberation even indirectly, it is to be abandoned; thus, all three of these stages are indeed to be abandoned. However, the two stages of one-pointedness and suppression (*niruddha*), due to the excellence of *sattva*, lead respectively to external activity...

Cessation (*nirodha*) is one-pointedness and continuous flow toward that which is to be adopted— namely, meditative absorption (*samādhi*)— by means of the dissolution of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). For here, the mind, having manifested as consisting of pure goodness (*sattva*) and being free from the veil of darkness (*tamas*), yet still touched by a mere trace of passion (*rajas*), attains virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

It becomes like the mental essence (*cittasattva*) of a middling yogi who possesses the light of wisdom (*prajñājyotis*) belonging to the two stages of honeyed concentration (*madhubhūmika*), which is fully conscious; however, when all fluctuations have been restrained and only the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain, it is understood as the mental essence of the yogi who has transcended that which is to be cultivated.

The intellect, which is like refined gold, having its impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* shaken off by the continuous process of smelting through practice and dispassion, becomes established in its own true nature. For that intellect, which has withdrawn from objects and senses and whose functional mandate is now concluded, there remains only the task of abiding in oneness with its own essential form.

For one who acts thus, only the supreme task remains: the discernment of the distinction (*vivekakhyāti*). In this context, the word "supreme" (*param*) should be understood as that reality which is distinct from the self (*ātman*). And so, there is the cessation of outward mental fluctuations through one-pointedness; and when all fluctuations, together with their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), have been ceased, they dissolve away.

Thus, there is the possibility of a conjunction between these two stages of the mind that are devoid of purpose. Among them, the stages of the *kṣipta* (distracted) and *mūḍha* (infatuated) minds constitute the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). The stage of *kṣipta* begins with the onset of concentration due to the predominance of *sattva*. One-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are the final stages. And for each transformation, there are latent impressions (*saṃskāras*). Among these, [the first] is emergence.

The formations produced by the initial application of concentration are destroyed by the formations born of that [concentration]; those born of one-pointedness are destroyed by the formations born of cessation; and even those cessations are destroyed by those very same formations. Just as lead mixed with gold, when being smelted, destroys its own impurities and becomes gold.

In this way, one-pointedness consumes the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) produced [by the mind], and that which is born of cessation consumes itself as well. Then, for the yogi whose mind has become steady through the aforementioned means, the various types of conceptualized meditative absorption (*savikalpa-samādhi*) gradually manifest. Thereafter, the seedless meditative absorption known as *samprajñāta* manifests; such is the process.

The *sūtras* of Patañjali, which are intended for demonstration, are presented here along with their commentary: "Samādhi is the state of the mind—whose fluctuations have been stilled—being established in and colored by the object of perception, the act of perceiving, and the perceiver, like a gem of pure birth. This refers to the mind that has attained stability through the aforementioned means, which, like a crystal gem, is naturally [transparent].

For one who is established in stability and is unassailed by *rajas* and *tamas*, there occurs the attainment of the ungraspable (*agrāhya-samāpatti*), which is preceded by one-pointedness regarding the gross and subtle forms of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and consists of the state of being absorbed in that [object] such that it is no longer graspable. Following that, there is the non-perception of the form consisting of absorption in that [object], preceded by one-pointedness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is permeated by minute traces of *rajas* and *tamas*.

There is meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Following that, there occurs the so-called "smile" (*smitā*), which is a state of identification (*tanmayatā*) preceded by one-pointedness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), and it takes the form of a non-grasping subject. In the Sūtra, it is said: "Abiding in that, one-pointedness toward that, being born from that, and identification with that [occur] when the mind has become subservient to the object being contemplated."

The term *cotkarṣaḥ* means that such an attainment (*samāpatti*) is a transformation into that very form. Furthermore, that attainment is fourfold, distinguished as with-discursive-thought (*savitarka*), without-discursive-thought (*nirvitarka*), with-deliberation (*savicāra*), and without-deliberation (*nirvicāra*). Among these, *savitarkā* is that attainment which is intermingled with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and knowledge; in this attainment, the word and the object—

The meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) accompanied by deliberation (*savitarkā*) is that in which there is a coarse appearance, permeated by the conceptualization of knowledge. When memory is purified and [the mind] is as if empty of its own nature, there is the appearance of the object alone; this is the attainment without deliberation (*nirvitarkā*), which follows upon the necessary consequence of that practice when the mind is inclined toward the object alone and absorbed in the object alone.

The memory of conventional signs is abandoned, and when that [memory] is joined with [the object], the non-conceptualizations following from hearing are also abandoned as being rooted in that [memory].

Then, in the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) which is empty of those [signs], the object remains by its very own nature alone. It exists by its very own nature alone, and not even by way of a conceptualized form; thus, it is non-existent as a coarse object.

The attainment without deliberation (*nirvitarkāsamāpatti*). By this very [attainment], the one with reflection (*savicārā*) and the one without reflection (*nirvicārā*) are also explained as having subtle objects.

That attainment in which a subtle object—consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth—appears, accompanied by verbal conceptualization (*śabdārthavikalpa*) and unconditioned by space, time, or specific qualities (*dharmādi*), is the attainment with reflection (*savicārasamāpatti*). That [is it].
These alone are directly perceived by yogins, because there is not even a trace of the superimposition of non-existence.

Among these meditative attainments (*samāpattis*), the state without discursive thought (*nirvitarka*) is superior in comparison to that with discursive thought (*savitarka*), which has gross objects;
superior to that is the state with subtle objects (*savicāra*); and superior even to that is the state consisting of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

When that non-discursive [samādhi], which has extremely subtle objects as its limit, also becomes stainless through the power of habitual practice, the mind—freed from the latent impressions of the afflictions—becomes fit for a continuous flow of stability. Therein arises the wisdom that "bears truth" (*ṛtaṃbhara*). And at that time, it is not even tainted by the scent of error.

When [the mind] is thus touched, the wisdom that bears truth (*ṛtambharā prajñā*) arises. Being of a different object than the wisdom derived from scripture (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*), because it concerns particulars (*viśeṣārthatvāt*), this wisdom that bears truth— which is distinct from the knowledge of words and inference— illuminates subtle and concealed objects in a perfectly clear form.
And thus two verses have been cited by the authors of the Bhāṣya:
"Having ascended the clarity of wisdom, the wise man, who is beyond grief, looks down upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain peak looking at those on the ground, the wise man observes everyone."
"By means of scripture, inference, and the power of the practice of meditation,
one who cultivates wisdom in these three ways attains supreme yoga."

The impression (*saṃskāra*) born from that [state] is an obstacle to other impressions. And by means of the impressions produced by this [state], the impressions born of distraction become incapable of producing their effects.
This very state is "samādhi with seed" (*sabīja-samādhi*); these are the four attainments (*samāpatti*) together with their seeds and objective supports (*ālambana*).

By the etymological derivation "it proceeds" (*vartate*), that is called "seeded concentration" (*sabīja-samādhi*). That which was previously described as "cognitive concentration with mental constructs" (*savikalpaka-samprajñāta-samādhi*)—upon the cessation of even that, because of the cessation of everything, there is "seedless concentration" (*nirbīja-samādhi*).
When even that seeded [concentration] dissolves, due to the dissolution of all mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti*) back into their own cause, that [state arises].

When a mental modification arises from mere latent impressions (*saṃskāramātra*), that [modification] is removed solely by means of negation—“not this, not this” (*neti neti*)—and there occurs the non-discursive, seedless (*nirbīja*) cognitive absorption (*samprajñāta-samādhi*).
When this exists, the Person (*puruṣa*) becomes established in the light of his own essential nature alone and is purified. This indeed is the seedless [absorption].
The yoga known as samādhi is the cause of the supreme goal of human life; apart from this, there is not even the possibility of liberation.
And in this regard, he cites as authority the statements of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti]:
The cholera-like onset of the poison of cyclic existence, which is difficult to endure,
is pacified by the purifying mantra of Yoga-Garuḍa.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Thus, O Mātaṅgī, supreme nirvāṇa will not be attained otherwise;
it is obtained through yoga, and by no other means whatsoever.
For those tormented by the heat of worldly existence, yoga is indeed the supreme medicine;
it is that from which arises detachment, whose intellect is fixed upon both the higher and the lower.
And he, whose entire accumulation of afflictions has been consumed by the fire of yoga, attains supreme and complete nirvāṇa; of this there is no doubt.
But you, who have attained the perfection of yoga and are fulfilled through the vision of the Self, see no task whatsoever remaining; indeed, everything has been accomplished by you.
Delighting in the Self, ever full, and having attained ultimate bliss,
he is therefore free from world-weariness, being eternally composed of bliss.
"Yogins whose selves are purified by austerity and whose senses are restrained—
those great-souled ones cross over the ocean of existence by means of yoga alone."
In the Smṛti of Yājñavalkya.
Among the acts of sacrifice, restraint, non-violence, charity, and self-study, this indeed is the supreme dharma: the realization of the Self through yoga.
The great seer Mātaṅga.
Having abandoned sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, the best of the twice-born,
devoted to the practice of yoga and tranquil, attains the Supreme Brahman.
For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike, yoga is the purifier;
for the pacification of actions and for liberation, there is nothing else besides yoga.
The words of Śiva in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the yoga that is most difficult to attain,
by which they behold the Self as the Lord, resplendent like the sun.
The fire of yoga quickly burns away the entire cage of sin;
clear knowledge arises, which directly bestows the attainment of nirvāṇa.
For renunciants, householders, forest-dwellers,
and students who are constantly devoted to these [practices], the principle of Māyā has arisen.
I shall dispel all darkness without delay by means of the lamp of knowledge,
just as:
Having attained the unsurpassed yoga and shaken off the turbidity of delusion, even a householder is released from bondage; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Likewise, in the section concerning the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).

"One should be devoted to the practice of yoga and should constantly recite the Rudrādhyāya," says Saṃvarta. "Having established the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born man should become a wandering mendicant."
"Constantly devoted to the practice of yoga and dedicated to the knowledge of the Self"—
thus Manu [states] in the section on the duties of an ascetic.
Through yoga, one should contemplate the existence of beings as belonging to the Supreme Self,
as well as their manifestation within bodies and within the highest duties.
Thus it is stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
The sin of a man who delights in the practice of yoga in this world perishes;
he is a man endowed with knowledge and austerity who is devoted to yoga.
Having abandoned the two bodies, he is swiftly liberated from bondage;
thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Just as even a very small lamp can destroy a vast darkness,
so too even a slight practice of yoga destroys great sin.
In the Viṣṇudharma.
Tell us that supreme good which is beneficial for all castes and even for women,
and which is a benefit even for insects and winged creatures.
Thus was Kapila previously addressed by the gods and likewise by the celestial rishis;
he had formerly declared to them that yoga alone is the supreme good.
In the Mahābhārata, regarding the path of yoga, Vyāsa has declared:
"Even one who is of the lowest caste, or even a woman, if they desire righteousness..."
By this very path, both may attain the supreme goal—
whether they be a man who knows all dharmas or one who is devoid of merit.
Whether he be a most excellent righteous man, or the worst of evildoers;
whether he be a tiger among men, or one who merely wears hair.
One certainly crosses over the great ocean of suffering—of old age and death—even one who merely desires to know it; even one who has realized the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) is liberated.
Thus, in the Bhagavadgītā.
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has conquered the self and subdued the senses,
whose inner self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, such a person is not tainted.
For one who is not disciplined, there is no discernment; for one who is not disciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; and for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness?
The yogi who constantly disciplines himself with a restrained mind attains the supreme peace, which is Nirvana and abides in Me.
In this, there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a little of this dharma protects one from great fear.

Whatever merit and fruit is declared to come from the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—all that transcends when one has realized this; and the yogi attains the supreme, primordial state. Therefore, apply yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
Thus, in the Yogaśāstra.
This is the ladder to liberation; this is the deception of time:
that the mind, having turned away from enjoyment, is attached to the Supreme Self.
Dattātreya [states] in the Yogatattvaprakāśa:
Whether a brahmin or a śramaṇa, a Buddhist or even one who has fallen from his status, a kāpālika or a cārvāka— provided he is wise and endowed with faith.
One who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga shall attain all perfections;
[as stated] in the *Yogabīja*.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to you, the Primordial Lord; salutations to you, the Lord of the Universe.
Salutations to you, whose form is the universe; salutations to you, who transcends the universe.
Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, who cause creation, sustenance, and dissolution, and who remove the afflictions; salutations to you, the Supreme Self.
Salutations to you, the perfectly complete one, the cause of joy for the world;
O Sadāśiva, Lord of the Universe, ocean of the nectar of compassion.
All living beings are enveloped by the net of illusion through pleasures and pains;
O Lord Śaṅkara, tell me out of compassion how their liberation may be attained.
This path brings about all accomplishments and cuts through the net of illusion;
it is that which destroys birth, death, old age, and disease, and bestows happiness.
O Lord Maheśvara, various paths have been described by you;
now, O preeminent among the knowers of Yoga, speak of the path that bestows liberation.
The Lord said:
O Goddess, those who are bound are liberated by this path;
beyond this, O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall describe it to you out of affection for you.
The supreme state of absolute liberation is difficult to attain through various paths;
it is obtained only by the path of the perfected ones, and not otherwise—so has Śiva declared.
By means of hundreds of various systems such as logic and grammar,
they have fallen into the snares of the scriptures and are utterly deluded by their own intellectual acumen.
That state which is ineffable cannot be described even by the gods;
since it is of the nature of the self-luminous consciousness, how could it be illuminated by a scripture?
That which is partless, stainless, peaceful, transcending all, and free from affliction— this very same [reality],
enveloped by the fruits of merit and demerit, exists in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, tell me how that eternal state of the Supreme Self, which transcends all principles, came to be attained by living beings. How can this be explained?
Īśvara said:
Transcending the state of all existent things, the stainless form of knowledge flashes forth within itself like water; therein, the ego-sense arises.
The body-mass consists of the five elements, is bound by the constituents, and is composed of qualities;
it is always joined with pleasure and pain, and is agitated by the notion of being a living soul.
Therefore, the designation "living being" (jīva) is said to apply to the pure Supreme Self;
yet desire, anger, fear, anxiety, greed, delusion, pride, and disease [belong to the individual].
Old age and death, wretchedness, grief, lassitude, hunger, thirst, hatred, shame, pleasure, pain, despondency, and even joy.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as doubt and pride— one who is completely free from these defects is indeed the individual soul (jīva) that is Śiva himself.
Therefore, I shall tell you the means for the destruction of faults;
some say that here knowledge alone leads to the realization of reality.
O Īśvarī, how can knowledge devoid of yoga bestow liberation?
And yoga devoid of knowledge is likewise incapable of the task of liberation.
The Goddess said:
Samsara arises from ignorance alone, and one is liberated through knowledge alone;
what need then have I for yoga? Tell me with your gracious speech.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall tell you that which has been spoken to me as the truth:
first, the nature of knowledge itself is to be known, and through knowledge is the means [attained].
Having investigated what ignorance is like,
the discerning person [should realize] that knowledge is one's own true nature, which is absolute liberation and supreme auspiciousness.
If the soul were initially free from defects such as desire, anger, fear, and the like, how could it—
being enveloped by all these defects— be liberated through knowledge?
The Goddess said:
When knowledge of one's own true nature is complete, it is then all-pervasive;
at that time, there is no distinction between the defects such as desire and anger and one's essential nature.
Afterwards, what injunction could there be for him, or how could there even be a prohibition? The man of discernment is forever liberated, free from the delusion of saṃsāra.
Īśvara said:
O fair-faced one, if that is the nature of the Full, then this is the truth;
for it is indeed both with parts and without parts, precisely because of its fullness.
From the state of being with parts, it has come to undergo the delusion of saṃsāra in the form of manifestation;
yet its true nature is partless, stainless, directly evident, and comparable to the sky.
Devoid of the knowledge of arising, abiding, and dissolution,
how could he of such a nature fall into the ocean of delusion through *māyā*?
O lady of excellent limbs, one who has abandoned knowledge sinks again and again into delusions such as pleasure and pain, just like the condition of worldly beings.
Just as the knower remains when he is permeated by latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
there is no difference between the two here, for their contemplation of saṃsāra is the same.
If knowledge has arisen as something visible, what then is ignorance?
One who is established in knowledge, though detached, knows the Dharma and has conquered the senses.
"O beloved, even a god does not attain liberation without yoga.
The Goddess said:
O Śaṅkara, for those who possess knowledge and whose souls are established in dispassion, there is nothing further to be fully known;
how then could liberation not be theirs?
The Lord said:
Embodied beings are known to be of two kinds: the unripe and the fully ripe.
Those devoid of yoga are unripe, while those endowed with yoga are the ripe ones.
The embodied soul matured by the fire of yoga is non-inert and free from sorrow;
however, that which is inert should be known as earthen, for being unripe, it becomes a source of suffering.
Even while established in meditative absorption, he may thus remain powerless over his senses;
even though he restrains them firmly, he is nonetheless afflicted by others.
By cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and the like; by diseases as well as by humans;
by various other kinds of living beings; and by weapons, fire, water, and wind.
By those [impurities], the body is afflicted and the mind is consequently agitated;
likewise, upon the failure of the vital breaths, it falls into agitation due to the winds.
Then, at the time of the body's end, whatever one contemplates in the mind will cause that mind to become agitated and pervaded by hundreds of sufferings for human beings.
"That very thing becomes the living soul (jīva)"; such is the cause of birth. Men do not know what kind of birth there might be at the end of the body.
Therefore, knowledge, detachment, and even mere recitation are but labor;
for when an ant has attached itself to the body, one is liberated through knowledge alone.
"Is he bitten by scorpions, or how can there be happiness at the end of the body?
Therefore, fools do not understand, being occupied with false reasoning."
When one's sense of ego has perished from the body, that person indeed does not perish; how much less, then, can diseases affect him?
By whom will death by water, fire, weapons, or blows come to pass?
In whatever manner one's external form becomes utterly wasted away, [so shall it be].
By that measure, all his ailments and the like perish;
for an effect can never exist without a cause.
"Without egoism, how could there likewise be bodily suffering? The Goddess said:
When yogins are being described, what do they employ in their worldly discourse?
And how, O Śaṅkara, does that discourse come to an end? Tell me.
Or what is the nature of their end of the body?
O Purifier, O Lord, you ought to sever this doubt of mine.
The Lord said:
All things are conquered by the body, yet the body itself has been conquered by yogis;
how then can it produce for them results such as pleasure and pain?
He by whom the senses and so forth, as well as the mind, intellect, desire, anger, and the like, have been conquered—by him alone is everything conquered; he is not oppressed by anything whatsoever.
The great elements and the principles are withdrawn in due order;
the body, composed of the seven constituents, is consumed by the fires of yoga that destroy [all things].
Even by the gods, his body of yoga could not be perceived;
he was of great strength, liberated from cutting and binding, and possessed of various supreme powers.
As is space, so is the body; yet the body is even purer than space.
The body is subtler than the subtle, grosser than the gross, and more inert than the inert.
The body of the yogi, which takes on forms at will, is independent, ageless, and immortal;
it sports as it pleases in the three worlds, wherever it may be.
The yogi, possessing inconceivable power and having conquered his senses, may assume various forms and then withdraw them again at his own will.
O Goddess, why do you ask about his death, he who is equal to the moon?
He does not meet with death, for by the power of yoga he returns again.
He was already immortal long ago; how could there be death for one who is dead?
O friend, he lives where death exists for all.
Wherever fools live, there he always dies;
he has no duty to perform, nor is he tainted by what has been done.
The one liberated while living is ever pure and free from all defects;
others who possess knowledge and are dispassionate are likewise always victorious over the body.
"How can those wretched embodied beings, who are mere lumps of flesh, be equal to yogins?
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, ocean of the nectar of compassion, tell me: what kind of destination awaits those wise ones when they have indeed passed away?
The Lord said:
At the end of the body, for the knower, no fruit is obtained from merit or from sin;
whatever [state] may arise there, having experienced it, the knower shall be born again.
Afterwards, through merit, one obtains a meeting with a Siddha;
then, by the grace of that Siddha, one becomes a yogi, and not otherwise.
"Then cyclic existence is destroyed; it is not otherwise, as Śiva has spoken. The Goddess said:
For the wise always declare that liberation comes from knowledge alone;
how then could yoga not be accomplished thereby, and would it not be the giver of liberation?
The Lord said:
For liberation occurs through knowledge alone; their statement is not otherwise.
Everyone says that victory comes by means of a sword; what then?
How could one attain victory without valor in battle? Likewise, how could knowledge devoid of yoga be a path to liberation?
Even without knowledge, liberation is never accomplished;
therefore, O lady of excellent limbs, there is no separation between these two here.
Union with knowledge is attained through many successive births;
however, knowledge itself arises from yoga in a single birth.
"Therefore, there is no path superior to this yoga that bestows liberation.
The Goddess said:
How is yoga attained through knowledge over many lifetimes?
And how is knowledge attained through yoga in a single lifetime?
The Lord said:
Having deliberated for a long time through knowledge, he thinks, "I am liberated.
Does his liberation occur at that very moment simply from such reflection?
A person is liberated from yoga after hundreds of other births;
yet, through yoga, there will no longer be birth and death again and again.
Through the union of prāṇa and apāna, the oneness of the moon and sun occurs;
the wise one should digest the body composed of the seven constituents by means of the fire.
His diseases, as well as injuries such as cuts and blows, perish;
thus he remains as an embodied being in the form of the supreme aspect.
But what is the use of saying more? Indeed, there is no death for him; even though he possesses a body, he is seen in the world like burnt camphor itself.
There is no merit greater than yoga; there is no state higher than yoga;
there is nothing more subtle than yoga; indeed, there is nothing superior to the path of yoga.
In the Mahābhārata.
Just as fire, when driven by the wind, may burn even the entire earth,
so too the yogi, having gained power, becomes possessed of blazing splendor and great strength.
Like a blazing fire at the time of the end of an eon, it would dry up the entire world;
and those endowed with the power of yoga and ayoga enter it helplessly, O Pārtha.
Neither the Lords of Procreation, nor the Sages, nor the Gods, nor the Great Elements have power over them; neither Yama, nor Antaka, nor even Death of terrifying prowess, when enraged, can prevail.
O King, lord of men, all are capable of attaining yoga of immeasurable splendor,
as are many thousands of individual selves, O bull among the Bharatas.
Having attained power, the yogi should traverse the earth with all these [attainments];
he may experience some sense-object, and then again practice fierce austerity.
"And again, O dear one, the sun withdraws its rays like a multitude [of attendants]," as stated in the *Mānasollāsa*.
When the realization of one's own self occurs through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, by the power of the practice of yoga, and also through the favor of the Lord;
Just as food eaten and residing in the stomach does not perceive itself as being other than its own nature,
so too the Lord of Yogis perceives the entire universe swallowed by the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃtā) as being nothing but Himself.
The words of Śiva addressed to Vāmadeva regarding the Rājayoga.
Who indeed knows the true greatness of Rājayoga?
Wherever a knower of that resides, that place becomes a vessel of merit.

By seeing and worshipping him, those joined with twenty-one generations of their lineage attain the state of liberation from ignorance; how much more so those who are devoted to him as their supreme goal?
He who understands inner yoga and outer yoga in their particular distinctions—he is to be venerated by you and by me as well; how much more so by the rest?
In the Brahmavaivarta and Kūrma Purāṇas.
Those who practice the great yoga once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or constantly at all times, should be known as Maheśvaras.
Thus it is said in the Gītā.
"The yogi is superior to the ascetics, he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge, and the yogi is superior to those who perform ritual actions; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Yoga alone is superior to a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand celibate students.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
By him his parents have achieved their purpose; blessed is that country and that family.
He who possesses such a practitioner of yoga becomes truly fortunate, and whatever is given by him attains imperishability.
One who has seen, conversed with, or touched [this person], and who possesses discrimination between the male essence and its nature,
purifies the sins of men accumulated over nine hundred million births.
"But this is the supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga," thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha.
Those whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it reaches the limit of direct experience—
everyone within the range of their vision is liberated from all sins.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Through the practice of posture (āsana), one destroys physical disease; through breath control (prāṇāyāma), one destroys sin;
and through sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the yogi releases mental affliction.
Through the *dhāraṇās* one attains steadiness of mind; through meditation (*dhyāna*), the vision of the Lord;
and through *samādhi*, one attains liberation, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Now, an objection may be raised: since yoga, defined as the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, falls outside the category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can ignorance be removed by the knowledge produced thereby? Indeed, there is not even the possibility of liberation without the removal of ignorance; and thus says the Śruti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path."
If it is argued that [liberation] is for the sake of liberation, we say no; for it is true that it must be attained by the mind alone.

However, on the strength of such scriptural passages as, "But it is seen by those of subtle vision through a subtle intellect," the mind is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and others, however—

When the position is maintained that [knowledge] produces only indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), then the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self would arise through a mind whose defects have been entirely dispelled by the practice of yoga. However, when [the position is taken that it is direct], then by the force of such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back, along with the mind, not having attained it; this is the eternal, consisting of bliss," [it is established as] a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, if one accepts the position that the mind is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it acts as a cooperative factor— just like the mental impressions (saṃskāra)— and that immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge arises from sentences such as "That thou art" alone, even then, for a person whose defects have been entirely eliminated through meditative absorption (samādhi), the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) is possible from the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) alone.
And likewise, Vidyāraṇya [says]:
"Having abandoned both the meditator and the meditation, when the mind gradually becomes focused solely on the object of meditation, like a lamp in a windless place, that is called samādhi."
When this entire web of latent impressions has been utterly destroyed,
and when the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit has been uprooted from its very foundation;
Being unobstructed externally,
it produces a non-mediated cognition— like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand— within that which is manifested as mediated.

Furthermore, since the practice of Sāṃkhya-yoga—which removes the threefold doubt residing in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—has been enjoined by the Śruti itself for the purpose of direct realization, [it is as follows]: "The Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. And the Śruti says: "It is to be heard..."

It has been stated that the rule of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) consists in the fact that [the Truth] is to be reflected upon through the words of the scriptures and through logical arguments, and having reflected, it is to be constantly meditated upon; these are the causes for realization. Furthermore, profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*)—which takes the form of meditation (*dhyāna*) as the worship of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), or in the form of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*)—must be fully matured.
That becomes seedless samādhi;
and thus [it was said by] the venerable Vidyāraṇya Svāmī:
The worship of the attributeless [Brahman] becomes matured as samādhi;
thereafter, that samādhi known as nirodha (cessation) is attained without effort.
Upon the attainment of samādhi, only the internal connection with the object remains for the person;
when this has been cultivated again and again, the wisdom of reality arises from that statement.
The practice of yoga is for this very purpose, as heard in the *Mṛtabindu* and other scriptures;
those most skilled in yoga call this samādhi "dharmamegha" (the cloud of dharma).
Since he rains down thousands of streams of the nectar of Dharma,
the millions of karmas accumulated here in this beginningless saṃsāra [are destroyed].
"By this [practice], dissolution occurs and pure Dharma increases. Although,
in the scriptural passages from the Purāṇas and other sources cited here, the eligibility for Yoga is found to belong to all living beings whatsoever,
nevertheless, with respect to Yoga— which bears the fruit of liberation— it is appropriate that only those who possess dispassion (virakta) are eligible.
And likewise, in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
He whose mind is detached from objects, both those perceived in this world and those heard of in sacred tradition, is qualified for this yoga; no one else is.
Sureśvarācārya.

For those who are dispassionate toward this world and the next, who desire to abandon transmigratory existence, and who seek to know the oneness of the Self— it is precisely such persons who are qualified for the Upanishads (the end of the three Vedas).
In this matter, the established rule is as follows: among the four castes, it applies only to the Brāhmaṇa; even there, only to one who has renounced the world (saṃnyāsin);

and even there, only to one in whom has arisen that direct realization which—through yoga practiced with dispassion throughout this life and previous lives—acts as a sublater of the notion of the body being the self, just as the knowledge of the Self sublates the notion of the body being the self. For such a person, liberation consists in that very realization.
It occurs in the Gītā.
"Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection;
and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth."

But for others— namely Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and Śūdras— even if they are established in the ultimate reality through the practice of yoga, liberation occurs only after they have gradually attained birth as Brāhmaṇas.
And likewise in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
For those men who have no practice of yoga from previous births,
the sequence for attaining yoga begins with the status of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and so forth.
Due to being female, he attains the status of a Śūdra; from there, he may attain the status of a Vaiśya;
and thereafter, he becomes a Kṣatriya, and then a Brahmin devoid of ritual action.

"From that he becomes a learned reciter (anūcāna), from that a performer of sacrifices (yajvā), and beyond that, one who has renounced action (karmayāsin); thereafter he attains the state of a knower (jñānitva) and gradually obtains the liberation of a yogin."

For those women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas who lack the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) cultivated in previous births, there is now the attainment of yoga and the acquisition of liberation either through the practice of that very yoga or through the performance of the duties prescribed for their own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*).

Alternatively, for those who have attained birth as Brahmins through other intense and subtle dharmas, who have performed renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and practiced yoga for a long time, liberation occurs; this is the sequence.
However, for those in whom the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) practiced in previous births persist, [liberation occurs] by those very [impressions] from before.

The meaning is that for those who repeatedly attain yoga through spiritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), liberation occurs gradually by means of attaining birth as a Brahmin. In the *Dānadharma*, however, this matter was explained in detail to Mataṅga by Śakra while he was performing austerities for the sake of attaining Brahminhood.
"O river, when will our liberation occur, or will it not?
Thus questioned, the brahmin replied: "When [the time] shall come."
Requested by Mucukunda for the sake of liberation, Keśava, having become his elder brother, said: "You shall be released from the bondage of worldly existence."
The protector of the earth named Bharata, as well as Dharmavyādha and others,
were foremost among those devoted to the practice of yoga and were also intent upon the knowledge of Brahman.
It is heard that having attained birth as Brahmins, they were liberated;
their words are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

This being the case, it is determined that Janaka and others were Kṣatriyas, Tulādhāra and others were Vaiśyas, Gārgī, Sulabhā, and others were women, and Vidura, Paiṅgala, and others were Śūdras, yet they attained such [realization] only after reaching birth as Brāhmaṇas.
Now, one might object: "But for those in whom all stains of doubt have been cast off and who have realized the true nature of Brahman as the Self..."
If it is argued that even for those who have attained direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), there is rebirth—which thus appears to be incoherent—it is not so;
for we hear of many births even for Vasiṣṭha and others, who were the crest-jewels among all knowers of Brahman.
And thus, in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, Bhuśuṇḍa speaks to Vasiṣṭha:
O Sage, this is indeed your eighth birth as the son of Brahmā;
I remember that in that eighth creation, you were united with me.
Sometimes it is born from the sky, sometimes it is born from water;
sometimes it is born from a mountain, and sometimes it is born from a reed.
For the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now descend to earth;
his eleventh birth shall take place under the name of Rāma.
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of relieving the burden of the earth, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
"Triṇuka attained birth for the sixth time as this Hari;
and a hundred Kali Yugas and a hundred Buddha-states of Hari— thus I remember," [this is] the connection with what follows in the Gītā.
Many births have passed for both you and me, O Arjuna;
I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of foes.
If it is argued that their birth is for the purpose of protecting the world and maintaining the cosmic order (*niyati*), then in this case as well,

only a Brāhmaṇa is entitled to liberation because the supreme Lord’s cosmic order remains in force. If it is further argued that knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is useless because the cycle of saṃsāra— characterized by birth and death— does not cease [for them], we say no.

For liberation is inevitable once the obstructing *prārabdha* karma—which can only be exhausted through experience—is removed; moreover, even during that period of experiencing [the fruits], there is the state of *jīvanmukti*. Thus says the Śruti: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body; then he shall attain [Brahman]," and so forth.

Furthermore, this matter is well-known from the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth. And how liberation belongs only to the yogin has already been demonstrated here by the author citing the "Yogabīja" passages. Now, it may be objected: since it is heard that liberation occurs for every living being through death in Kāśī, how can it be said that only a Brāhmaṇa possesses the qualification for such liberation?

If you say this, it is true; even in that case, [the teaching] is for one who has indeed abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, who has attained a divine body, and who is qualified for the instruction of Viśvanātha. This is because such a divine body is mentioned in scripture, and because a divine body possesses qualities equal to those of a Brāhmaṇa body;
and this meaning is clearly evident.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa].

Others, however, maintain that those who possess faith in yoga are eligible for all [levels] of practice upon hearing the teachings; thus, through the knowledge of reality arising from yoga, everyone is liberated, while for those such as Kṣatriyas who are deficient in yoga, there is liberation by stages.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa, the sages said:
O Blessed One, O God, O Destroyer of the obstacle Hiraṇyākṣa!
Four stages of life have indeed been proclaimed, but for yogis, one alone is spoken of.
The tortoise said:
Having renounced all actions and having resorted to unwavering meditative absorption,
the yogin who remains thus is a true renunciant, not one of the other five types.
Therefore, this fourfold system of stages of life for those of different classes does not find support as a fifth [category] in any of the Vedic scriptures.
He who has attained seedless samādhi is to be known as a true renunciant (saṃnyāsī),
because he has abandoned all actions without exception.

And because [the householder] possesses the direct qualification for liberation; for this very reason, in the absence of yoga, renunciation is difficult to accomplish and obstacles arise at every step.
As stated in the Bhagavad Gītā:
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogi without having renounced all volitional intentions.
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman without delay.

Now, one might object: for a person who has begun a yoga practice that is to be accomplished over a long period of time, it would not be appropriate for a wise person to engage in this [yoga] if—due to fate, they die midway; or out of fear that their exertion is in vain; or because they have abandoned the yoga due to fierce obstacles or the defect of contact with poison; or out of apprehension regarding the transgression of a downfall that is difficult to overcome.

If this is argued, we say no; for the destination of a yogi who dies in the midst of yogic practice has been described in the *Vāsiṣṭha* within the exposition of the seven stages of yoga (*yoga-saptabhūmikā*),
and these stages shall be explained below.
Śrī Rāma said:
For one who is deluded, born of an ignoble family, engaged in base conduct, and has not attained the company of yoga— how could there be progress upward?
O Blessed One, what is the destiny of one who has died after having ascended either the first, the second, the third, or any other [ladder]?
Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who is deluded and has not ascended beyond faults, saṃsāra extends as far as the first stage (bhūmi) has not been awakened within hundreds of future births.
Alternatively, through association with the virtuous or by chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence,
dispassion indeed arises from reflecting upon the nature of worldly existence.
When dispassion arises in a person, the emergence of the stages [of realization] necessarily follows;
consequently, cyclic existence is destroyed—this is the summary of the Teacher’s meaning.
For an embodied being whose life has transcended the stages of yoga,
previous misdeeds are exhausted in accordance with the portions of those stages.
Then, she enjoys herself with her companions in the celestial chariots of the gods, in the cities of the world-protectors,
and in the groves of Mount Meru.
Then, when the accumulation of good deeds and the evil deeds committed in the past have both been exhausted through the consumption of their results, the yogin is born once again.
Having been born in the house of the pure, the prosperous, the virtuous, and the wise— well-guarded and endowed with excellence— he, being perfumed by yoga, pursues yoga alone.
Therein, the wise one, having observed the sequence of the stages of yoga previously practiced through cultivation,
leaps high up into the subsequent sequence of stages.
In the *Yogabīja*.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me, Mahādeva, what is the doctrine of the crows and monkeys?
Mahādeva said:
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall now declare what has been taught by me in other scriptures:
the Great Path of Ādinātha is indeed one alone, and not otherwise.
It may indeed be perceived in two ways due to the distinction between different births;
that which is to be attained is reached only through gradual practice, and not otherwise.
For some, through the gradual practice of yoga with this very body, perfection is attained after a long time; that indeed is the "monkey's leap" method.
If the body perishes through negligence before the accomplishments of yoga are attained,
one endowed with previous latent impressions will obtain another body.
Then, by the power of merit, one attains union with the Guru;
through the path of the western gate, the fruit arises swiftly.
Due to practice performed in previous lives, one quickly reaps the fruit;
this indeed should be understood as that supreme "crow-like" method (kākamatam).
Therefore, there is no state higher than practice;
thus it is said in the Bhagavad Gītā.
Arjuna said:
One who is endowed with faith, O Kṛṣṇa, but whose mind has wavered from yoga— failing to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does he go to?
O mighty-armed one, I fear that he, being without support and bewildered on the path to Brahman, may perish like a scattered cloud, fallen from his state through fear.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to completely sever this doubt of mine;
for indeed, no one other than you is fit to be the dispeller of this doubt.
The Blessed One said:
O Pārtha, there is no destruction for him either in this world or in the next;
for no one who performs wholesome deeds, my dear, ever goes to a state of misery.
Having attained worlds of merit and dwelt there for countless years,
one who has fallen from yoga is born again in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
He states the destiny of one who has fallen from yoga after practicing it for a long time, beginning with "Or else": "Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis."
For such a birth as this is indeed very difficult to obtain in the world;
therein one recovers the connection with the intellect acquired in a previous body.
O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more intensely for perfection;
indeed, by that very former practice, he is carried forward even against his will.
Even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman;
but the yogi who strives with diligent effort, having his impurities completely cleansed, [attains the Supreme].
"Perfected through many births, he thereafter attains the supreme goal.
Thus, desiring to know Yoga with faith— thinking, "What kind of Yoga is it that must be known even by me"—
and seeking to transcend the *śabdabrahman*, which is the Veda, [he realizes] this [Yoga], wherein all actions prescribed in all the Vedas [are transcended].

In view of the fruit, one attains for a much longer duration the fruit characterized by dwelling in the worlds of Brahmā and others; if such a fruit is obtained merely through the desire to know yoga, then what need is there to mention the superiority of the fruit resulting from the actual practice of yoga?
He states [the same] by way of a *kaimutika* argument (a fortiori) with the words "even one who desires to know," and so forth,
in the context of the *rājayoga*.
In ancient times, Umā, the primordial power (Ādiśakti), obtained [this] from me;
now, you alone have obtained it through the refinement of birth.
