Through the practice performed in other births, reality itself becomes manifest; like one who has just awakened from sleep, it is indeed perceived directly, even without instruction or the like.
Thus, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Even he who practices yoga with faith by means other than the [proper] path shall,
in time, certainly attain yoga after a long duration.
Just as the brahmin Jaigīṣavya and those such as Vaivasita, so too were the kṣatriyas Janaka and others,
and the vaiśyas Tulādhāra and others.
The seven Śūdras, such as Dharmavyādha and others, and Pailavaka and others, attained supreme perfection through their own previously practiced yoga.
Maitreyī, Sulabhā Gārgī, and the ascetic Śāṇḍilī—
these and many others, though born of low wombs, [attained perfection].
Having attained the supreme steadfastness in knowledge through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in previous births,

and moreover, having practiced yoga in previous births, some— according to the degree of merit from their own practice— attained the state of Brahmā, some the state of a celestial sage (*devarṣi*), some the state of being a son of Brahmā, and some the state of a Brahman-sage (*brahmarṣi*).

Some, having attained the state of liberation and even kingship, became self-realized there without any instruction; such were Hiraṇyagarbha, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Sanatkumāra, and others, as well as Vāmadeva, Śuka, and so forth, who were perfected from birth. Thus it is said.
It is heard in the Purāṇas and other such texts.
There is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation;
there is no god equal to Śambhu; there is no attainment equal to Yoga.

Regarding the stages (bhūmikās), however, the venerable Patañjali, while defining the knowledge of reality— which is the means for achieving liberation (kaivalya) characterized by the absolute abandonment of suffering— in the seventh wisdom (prajñā), has declared seven stages.
"Discriminative wisdom (*prajñā*) on the final stage (*prāntabhūmi*) of that [practice]"—this is according to the Sūtra.

Its explanation is as follows: for a person in whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, on the final stage—that is, at the conclusion of all meditative absorptions with an object (*sālambana-samādhi*)—wisdom becomes sevenfold. Among those, the task...
Liberation is fourfold in form:
"What was to be known has been known by me; there is nothing further to be known.
My defilements have been exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted."

"I have attained the cessation [of suffering]; I have reached discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). In that state, through the exclusion of other mental modifications (*pratyaya*), such wisdom (*prajñā*) alone arises. This intellect (*adhīḥ*) is called "liberation from the task" (*kāryavimukti*), because its nature is stainless knowledge regarding the object of the task. Liberation of the mind (*cittavimukti*) is threefold: "My purpose has been accomplished."
The intellect [is thus]. The qualities (guṇas), having completed their office, will not attain stability again, like rocks fallen from a mountain peak.

Since these are tending toward dissolution into their own cause, and because of the absence of the root-cause called delusion (moha) and because they are devoid of purpose, how could there be a further flow? And [the Self] has become its own essence.
When that samādhi exists, there is the realization "I am established in my own true nature"; such is the threefold liberation of the mind.
Since this entire wisdom has the form "I am established in my own true nature," and because of the nature of that true self—namely, "all this has that as its essence"—[it is so].

"That is the Truth; He is the Self; 'That art thou. What else could he say here? Thus indeed did he perceive the Person as Brahman, all-pervading. 'This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. There is no other seer than this. By such scriptural passages as "I am you, or you are I," and "That is indeed the Real," and so forth.

The form "I am Brahman" indeed arises within the discriminative knowledge (*vivekakhyāti*) due to the establishment of the non-difference between the individual self and Brahman. Even this [knowledge] does not directly constitute the means to liberation; rather, it is only by way of the subsequent non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpaka*) that it serves as a means, since that very primary yoga—consisting of the cessation of all mental modifications—is the actual means to liberation.

This is because it is so indicated in the scriptural and puranic passages cited previously. Furthermore, it will be explained that for the arising of this discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which serves as the means [to liberation], the practice of the limbs of yoga—restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*)—is the sole cause by way of purifying the mind (*cittaśuddhi*). These [practices] have been described in detail in the *Vāsiṣṭha*.
For thus Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, listen to this ground of knowledge consisting of seven steps;
once it is known, one no longer sinks into the mire of delusion.

Proponents of various systems speak in many different ways regarding the stages of yoga; yet these very stages, which are considered by me to be free from the sense of "mine-ness," are truly the bestowers of happiness.
They know that awakening is knowledge, and this consists of seven stages;
liberation, however, remains as the object of knowledge within the interval between the stages.
The first stage of knowledge is proclaimed as that called "Pure Desire";
the second is "Investigation," and the third is "Subtle Mind."
The fourth is the Satvāpatti; after that is the one named Asaṃsakti;
the sixth is the Padārthābhāvinī, and the seventh is known as Turyagā.
Liberation stands as the limit of these stages, wherein one no longer grieves;
hear now this definition of these stages.
"Why do I remain like a fool? Let me examine the scriptures with the company of the virtuous.
To desire preceded by dispassion is called "noble aspiration" (śubhecchā) by the wise.
The engagement in virtuous conduct through the study of scriptures, association with the wise, and the practice of detachment is called *vicāraṇā*.
Where there is detachment from the objects of the senses through both investigation and the desire for the auspicious,
that state is called "thin" (tanu) mental [discipline] because of its attenuated nature.
Through the practice of the three stages, by virtue of the mind's cessation from objects,
when the pure true self is established, that is declared to be the attainment of sattva.
Through the intense practice of the four stages, which yield the fruit of non-attachment,
this state in which sattva is firmly established and conduct is perfected is called "Non-attachment" (saṃsakti).
Through the firm practice of the five stages by means of delighting in one's own self, and through the contemplation of both internal and external objects, [the state of absorption is attained].
When awakening occurs after a long period of effort induced by another,
the sixth stage, called Padārthabhāvinī, arises.

The state known as the Fourth (turyagā) is that which, through long practice over six stages, results from the non-perception of difference and consists in abiding solely in one's own essential nature.
For this fourth state (turya) exists here among those liberated while living;
beyond that, the state transcending the fourth (turyātīta) pertains to the subject of liberation after death (videhamukta).
Śrī Rāma said:
How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed? And what are the signs for a practitioner regarding each stage?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Man is of two kinds: the one who is engaged in worldly activity and the one who has withdrawn from it.
Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively.
Having resolved, "Is it better that I have that which is called Nirvana, or rather that I remain in cyclic existence (saṃsṛti)?"— one who acts thus is described as "engaged" (pravṛtta).
Like the entry of a tortoise's neck into the hole of a yoke amidst the four oceans,
at the end of many births, a discerning person is born.
Since this worldly existence is devoid of essence, what is the use of my remaining in it? What is the point of these stale actions, when the day itself must be spent?
"What could be the supreme rest, free from the excess of activity?"—
one who has spoken thus with certainty is known as *sannivṛtta*.
"How may I, having become free from passion, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?"—
when the one of noble intellect is thus intent on such reflection, [he attains liberation].
Day by day, his inner latent impressions move toward detachment;
he engages in noble activities and rejoices daily.
He constantly doubts vulgar and dull-witted actions;
he does not praise worldly deeds and practices meritorious actions.
He practices gentle deeds that cause no agitation to others;
he is constantly afraid of evil and does not look toward worldly enjoyment.
He speaks words that are tender with affection and love, elegant, appropriate, and suited to the time and place.
When he has attained that first stage,
he serves virtuous people through mind, deed, and speech;
and having brought them from wherever they may be, he studies the treatises on knowledge.
One who possesses such investigation regarding the transcendence of saṃsāra is called "one who has attained the stage" (bhūmikāprāpta); the rest, however, are known as "noble ones" (ārya).
Having reached the other stage of yoga called *vicāra*,
he [performs] the acts of hearing, remembering, following right conduct, concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*).
Explained according to the primary interpretation, it will be followed by the wise,
who know the distinction between the meanings of words and the determination of what ought and ought not to be done.
The householder, having mastered what is to be heard, knows how pride, conceit, envy, hypocrisy, and delusion have been utterly transcended within his home.
Just as a snake sheds its skin like something external,
so too does one whose mind has been transformed by the study of the scriptures and service to the teacher and the virtuous cast off [worldly attachments].
One thoroughly and correctly understands the supreme secret,
namely the third stage of yoga called "Non-attachment."
Then that beloved one falls, as if onto a pure bed of flowers,
having established an unwavering intellect upon the meaning of the words of the scripture exactly as they are.
By means of sequences of discourse on the inner self (adhyātma) by those resting in the hermitages of ascetics,
and likewise by sequences of discourse on dispassion (vairāgya) that censure worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Seated upon a stone bed or seat, he wears away his extended lifespan by wandering through forest lands, graced by the tranquility of his mind.
The wise man passes his time in the bliss of unattached happiness,
through the diligent study of the scriptures and the performance of meritorious deeds.
Just as this vision of reality becomes clear to a person through the grace of the deity,
so too does the wise one, having reached the third stage, become enlightened by himself.
Listen to this classification of that non-attachment, which is of two kinds:
this non-attachment is twofold, namely, the ordinary and the superior.
"I am neither the agent nor the enjoyer, neither the oppressed nor the oppressor"—
this non-attachment toward objects is what is called "universal detachment."
Everything is fashioned by past karma and is entirely dependent on the Lord;
whether it be happiness or suffering, what agency do I have in this?
Enjoyments and non-enjoyments are great diseases; prosperities are supreme calamities;
unions lead only to separations; and mental anxieties are but physical ailments for the intellect.
The common notion that "Time stands ready to swallow, destroying all states of being" is a conceptual construction devoid of reality.
By this sequential yoga, through the association with great-souled ones,
through dissociation from the wicked, and through the practice of self-awareness, [one attains the goal].
Through human effort and by means of continuous practice,
when the object has attained firm clarity like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, [the goal is reached].
"I am not the Lord of All, nor am I the agent; surely my past karma has cast me far away"—such is the contemplation of the meaning of words.
That mental silence which is weary of the ocean of saṃsāra and directed toward the ultimate cause, the essence, on the further shore— that is called the highest company (saṅga).
That which is neither within nor without, neither below nor above, neither in the quarters nor in the sky;
neither in an object nor in a non-object, neither in the insentient nor in the sentient.
That which is seated, radiant, peaceful, non-radiant, and beyond cultivation;
without beginning or end, unborn, and beautiful—that is called the supreme state of non-attachment.
Sweet with the fragrance of the nectar of contentment, its tender leaves are the purity of one's own body;
nestled at the tip of the stalk of the mind, it is beset by the thorns of obstacles.
The lotus of discernment, having taken root within and been illuminated by the sun of discernment,
bears fruit in this third stage, which is characterized by non-attachment.
Through the conjunction of pure dispositions and the accumulation of meritorious deeds,
the first stage arises by way of a chance coincidence, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
That stage, like a sprout that has just emerged from the earth,
must be protected and nurtured with effort by the water of discernment.
If this [intellect] does not attain its rise through that very part which shines forth in inquiry,
then one should cultivate it daily with effort, just as a farmer cultivates a seed.
For this [first stage], once its interior has been polished, is the sole ground for the birth of the others;
through effort, one should then attain the second stage, and from that, the third.
For this third stage here is indeed declared to be "united with the best," wherein the person is free from the mental construction of all residual volitions.
O Rāma, these three stages are indeed known as the waking state;
it is called waking because, here, the perception of duality persists with clarity, as if one were actually awake.
In those engaged in yoga, there arises a state of pure nobility;
seeing which, even those of deluded intellect develop the desire for liberation.
One who performs what ought to be done, refrains from doing what ought not to be done,
and abides in natural conduct— he is remembered as an *ārya*.
He who adopts legal procedure according to custom, according to wealth, according to the scriptures,
and according to established tradition, is remembered as an Ārya.
In the first [stage], it is sown in the ground and then sprouts;
in the second and third [stages], the supreme state of nobility bears fruit.
A yogi who has died while in a state of nobility is purified by his accumulated intentions;
having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, he is born again as one possessed of yoga.
When ignorance has reached its end through the practice of the successive stages,
and right knowledge arises in the mind, which is then comparable to the rising of the full moon;
Those yogins who have reached the fourth stage perceive everything as equal, free from differentiation, and without beginning or end, their minds being firmly disciplined in yoga.
When non-duality has become firm and Māyā has been pacified,
those who have reached the fourth stage perceive the world like a dream.
The first three stages are called the waking state, and the fourth is called dreaming;
the mind, like a fragment of an autumn cloud, dissolves away in lamentation.
Having reached the fifth stage, one remains as a mere residue of existence;
no conceptualization of the world arises here, because the mind has been dissolved.
Having reached the fifth stage, known as the state of deep sleep,
he remains in pure non-duality, with all particular aspects stilled.
With the appearance [of objects] dissolved externally and awakened internally,
he remains as one dense in deep sleep, having reached the fifth stage.
Abiding in inwardness while casting outward activity upon others,
he appears as one perpetually asleep due to his state of perfect tranquility.
Practicing in this stage and becoming free from latent impressions,
one gradually descends to the sixth stage, which is designated as the Fourth (turyā).

Where there is neither the form of non-existence nor existence, neither "I" nor even the state of "not-I," there one remains with mere cessation of mentation, having emerged from both duality and unity.
Free from knots, with doubts pacified, liberated while living and free from mental constructs,
though not yet extinguished, he remains as one who has attained extinction, like a painted lamp.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky;
full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean.
He has attained something, or perhaps he has attained nothing at all;
having established himself on the sixth stage, he shall reach the seventh stage.
The seventh stage of yoga is said to be liberation while in the body (videhamukti);
it is beyond the reach of words, tranquil, and the ultimate limit among the planes of existence.
By some she was called Śiva; by others she was declared to be Brahmā;
by some she was proclaimed to be Viṣṇu; and by others she was remembered as the Void (Śūnya).
By some she is called "Artha," by others she is termed "Kāla," and by others she is conceived as the "Distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa."
Although it is eternal and inexpressible, it is nevertheless described in some way by others through various different conceptualizations of the self that they have imagined.
"O best of the Raghus, these seven stages have been described by me;
through the practice of these, no suffering is experienced."
[Thus ends the first chapter in the Yogacintāmaṇi composed by Śivānanda, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya Śrī Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī. || 1 ||
Now follows the determination of what should and should not be done by the practitioner of yoga.

One who has properly propitiated a true guru, who has attained yoga along with its secrets, limbs, and sub-limbs through his grace, and who is habituated to uninterrupted practice, certainly attains the aforementioned fruit;
as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having obtained the entire essence of yoga from the teacher and being himself firm in intellect,
he attains what has been described and thereby reaches even liberation.
Sureśvarācārya.
Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains the yoga endowed with its eight limbs;
through the grace of Śiva, one obtains the eternal perfection of yoga.
And there is scriptural authority as well.
For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and as toward the Divine so toward the Guru, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly.
"A person who has a teacher knows," as stated in the *Yogabīja*.
One should always serve that guru for whom mastery over the winds has been accomplished;
by the grace of the guru’s mouth, the wise one should effect the conquest of the vital breaths.
Yājñavalkya.
The gurus for all five [classes] are enjoined by the Śruti:
the mother, the father, the teacher (ācārya), the maternal uncle, and likewise the father-in-law.
Among these, three are declared to be primary: the teacher and likewise the two parents.
Yet among these, the most eminent is the one—the teacher—who knows the Supreme Self.
Therefore, at all times, by all those seeking the supreme good, teachers endowed with Vedic learning should be honored through speech, mind, and other means.
In the Rājayoga [configuration].
He who is not attainable through Vedāntic reasoning, scriptural declarations, various types of traditional lore,

collections of treatises, or through meditations and other virtuous practices— save for the one Guru who is like a wish-fulfilling gem; he whose vision remains steady even without an object of sight, and whose breath remains still without effort, his mind is truly stable.
He who remains without support—he alone is the yogi, he is the Guru to be served.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
There is nothing higher than the divine Guru; therefore, one should always worship him.
When the reality has been shown by the Guru, one becomes identical with it at that very moment;
considering oneself liberated, one is indeed liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Just as those [metals] become gold through contact with an alchemical elixir,
so too does a disciple become composed of reality by hearing the instructions of the Guru.
Success does not come from the mere instruction of a teacher alone;
everyone attains everything only through their own exertion.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
The hearing of the scriptures, the realization of the Guru, the realization of one's own Self, and the restraint of the mind—
all these combined together are considered by the wise to be the means for success in this world.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti]:
O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely for the sake of maintaining order;
the sole cause of realization, however, is the pure wisdom of the disciple alone.
No one can rescue another from the mire of worldly confusion— where all goals are obstructed and bondage is cast aside— except through one's own fortitude.
Then, through dispassion, the scriptures, and qualities such as greatness,
one should with effort cause the mind to blossom within itself for the sake of destroying obstacles.
The fruit that is obtained from a mind augmented by greatness is not attained even from the sovereignty over the three worlds, nor from a treasury full of wealth and grain.
In the Rājayoga [configuration].
Therefore, having properly received the innate [instruction] from a true guru, one should worship correctly and constantly remain devoted to the practice of the Self without effort.
For one whose nature is constant practice, that state becomes self-evident;
even by a guru, it cannot be described as "this is that."
One should diligently avoid the enjoyment of speech, mind, and body;
one should always maintain the self very firmly with the thought, "I am Brahman."
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
One should avoid friendship with the wicked, walking along paths where fire, women, or roads are present,
as well as bodily mortifications such as morning baths, fasting, and the like.
Excessive eating, over-exertion, excessive talk, adherence to restrictive rules,
attachment to people, and fickleness— by these six, yoga is destroyed.
Through enthusiasm, daring, fortitude, knowledge of reality, firm resolve,
and the abandonment of social contact— by these six, yoga is perfected.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a lump of ghee;
therefore, one should diligently avoid association with women."

One should diligently avoid the company of rogues, which is a source of great obstacles, just as one avoids association with women. The true nature of a rogue has been described by Dattātreya in the *Tattvaprakāśa* as follows:
"Whether he is joyful, or a bearer of a staff, or even one wearing saffron robes..."
He was one who spoke the words of Nārāyaṇa, wearing matted hair and smeared with ashes.
One who utters the word "Namas Śivāya," or one who perfectly observes his own conduct,
or one purified by the twelve places, or one adorned with an abundance of rosaries.
How can one who is devoid of action but brave in speech attain success?
Wearing a particular garb is not the cause of success; what then is the reason for that talk?
"O Sāṃkṛti, it is indeed true that action alone is the cause of success;
for those who merely wear the garb of yoga speak of it for the sake of their genitals and bellies."
But those unskillful and hypocritical men, devoid of actual practice, deceive all people with their various nonsensical prattlings.
"‘We are yogis,’ say the fools who are devoted to worldly enjoyments;
likewise, the wise man [should gradually distance himself] from those who have abandoned the practice of yoga."
One should avoid with mere words those who assume the outward garb [of practitioners] once their purpose is achieved,
for they are always obstacles to the practice of yoga.
"Wise men avoid such persons with great effort," thus it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha.

He who has a wife has a desire for enjoyment; for one without a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment? Having abandoned the woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the objects of the senses are the deadly poison.
Poison destroys one lifetime, whereas the objects of the senses destroy many lifetimes.
One should dwell according to the scriptures; one must not be in haste for accomplishments.
Accomplishment ripened over a long period of time will yield fruit in its wake.
Thus ends the section on Alarka in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear in truth about the conduct of the yogin,
by following which path of Brahman the yogin does not falter.
Dattātreya.
Suffering arises from the fault of attachment for those whose minds are bound by the sense of "mine-ness";
therefore, a man seeking liberation should strive to abandon attachment.
Due to the absence of attachment, the loss of this notion of "mine" arises;
freedom from possessiveness leads to happiness, and through dispassion, one perceives defects.
Detachment arises from knowledge alone, and knowledge is preceded by detachment;
that is one's home where one dwells, and that is one's food by which one lives.
That by which one is liberated is called knowledge; otherwise it is ignorance.
O King, [liberation comes] through the exhaustion of merits and demerits by means of experience.
And because of the non-performance of those obligatory duties that ought to be done, due to the absence of desire for them;
and because of the non-accumulation of new merit and the exhaustion of that previously acquired.
A person incurs bondage through karma, yet does not [again] obtain a body;
as for those two, honor and dishonor, which cause pleasure and aversion in men.
These same two, when their meaning is reversed, bring about the success of the yogi;
these very honors and insults are, respectively, poison and nectar for the arm.
In that case, dishonor is death, while honor is a poison more virulent than poison;
one should place a foot purified by the eye, and drink water purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth and reflect with thoughts purified by wisdom,
especially during guest-receptions, ancestral rites, sacrifices, and festivals for the deities.
A knower of yoga should never go among the great multitude for the sake of accomplishing his purpose,
lest people should despise him and treat him with contempt.
Thus, the yogi should practice with diligence, not defiling the dharma of the virtuous;
he should cultivate that essential knowledge which accomplishes what is to be done.
This multiplicity of knowable objects indeed creates an obstacle to yoga for one who would wander about thirsting, thinking, "This is to be known, this is to be known."
Even in thousands of aeons, one would not attain that which is to be known.
These three are the restraint of speech, the restraint of action, and the restraint of mind.
He for whom these three staffs are ever-restrained is a high-minded Tridaṇḍin;
he for whom the entire world, both moving and unmoving, is always of the nature of the Self.
O King, who is dear to him, and who is not dear, since he consists of both virtue and vice?

With pure intellect and equanimity toward all beings, like gold, dwelling with a concentrated mind, having gone to that supreme, eternal, and imperishable state, he is indeed never born again. Being thus concentrated—
A person who is supremely vigilant, pure, devoted to solitude, and has conquered the senses attains this yoga;
through that yoga, the high-souled one then achieves liberation.
One should not practice when bloated with food, hungry, exhausted, or when the mind is distracted.
O Indra among kings, one should diligently apply oneself to yoga for the sake of attaining yogic perfection.
Having veiled the activity of *tamas* with *rajas*, and likewise that of *rajas* with *sattva*, the knower of yoga, established in the stainless principle (*tattva*), should practice yoga.
All this has been fully explained to you, O Ālarka, according to its true meaning;
now learn from me in brief that Brahman by which you shall attain it.
Just as the moonstone (candrakānta-maṇi) releases water when in contact with the rays of the moon, yet does not do so when it is not joined [with them],
this is remembered as the application of the simile for the practitioner of yoga.
Just as the sun-stone, though not by itself, manifests fire through contact with the rays of the sun,
so too is the analogy for the yogi.
O Lord, ants, rats, house-lizards, and francolin partridges dwell in your home; when it is ruined, they depart for elsewhere.
But when that master is destroyed, there is no suffering for them;
O King of kings, this is used as an analogy to establish the point.
That house wherein one dwells, that food by which one lives, and that by which one’s own purpose is accomplished—this alone is "one's own"; all else is merely attachment.
Just as one performs an action with feet that are completely surrendered and fully employed,
so too should the yogi accomplish the Supreme by means of the intellect and other faculties that have been rendered alien [to the ego].
Even a tiny ant with a small body, by means of its extremely minute mouth, carries a burden of earth;
such is the instruction for the yogin.
Having taken up a vessel filled with substance, as he ascends from the earth and beholds the high, lofty path, through that the yogi attains supreme wisdom.
Observing the tip of the horn of a young ruru deer, which has the appearance of a tilaka mark,
the yogi who increases [his practice] along with it shall attain siddhi.
Having truly understood that exertion of a man which, when all his possessions are buried, is sufficient for his mere livelihood, the yogis have accomplished their purpose.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
One who knows yoga should practice yoga when he is neither over-satiated nor afflicted by hunger, nor oppressed by excrement and urine, nor exhausted by travel, nor distressed by anxiety.
The yogi who is moderate in diet and conduct, disciplined in his actions,
and regulated in sleep and wakefulness, perceives reality.
Thus, in the Bhagavadgītā.
Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all; it is not for him who is habitually addicted to excessive sleep, O Arjuna, nor for him who is ever awake.
For one who is moderate in diet and recreation, disciplined in actions,
and measured in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
"O Arjuna, he who sees everywhere with equanimity by means of the analogy of himself—
whether it be pleasure or pain— is considered the supreme yogin.
Thus it is said in the Brahmapurāṇa.
Well-composed during the latter part of the night and the first part of the day,
moderate in food, and with senses subdued, he should practice yoga during the forenoon and the middle of the day.
"One should practice yoga"—this is the connection [of the verse]. Yājñavalkya states in the Liṅga Purāṇa: "At dawn, at twilight, and at midnight, being composed..."

One who suffers from indigestion, one who frequently belches undigested food, one afflicted by the retention of feces and urine, one suffering from vomiting or diarrhea, one who has overeaten, or one overcome by fatigue [should not practice yoga].
He should not be overly devoted to ritual action, nor have his senses agitated by anxious thoughts;
he should be intent upon the teacher’s business and neither excessively hungry nor thirsty.
"One should not practice [this] when there is bodily affliction, as dejection and the like may arise"—
thus it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.
Immediately following the prohibition, "He shall never be afflicted by disease," it is said:
"Having ascertained these defects, if one indeed engages [in practice] through negligence,
his own defects will become provoked within his body, acting as obstacles."
Stupor, deafness, and muteness arise,
as well as blindness, loss of fortitude, and likewise fever and disease.
For these defects indeed become provoked when one practices yoga out of ignorance;
therefore, a yogi, being composed, should practice with pure knowledge.
"And by being ever vigilant, one shall never incur any faults.
Thus it is said in the Mahābhārata.
O lord of men, a yogi should never apply himself to yoga at the three times of urination, defecation, or eating.
Just as a vigilant archer, being fully concentrated, hits the target,
so too the disciplined yogi, properly engaged, attains liberation without a doubt.
Just as a person, having fixed his mind steadily upon a vessel filled with oil, ascends a staircase with a disciplined mind; so too should one proceed.
Just as you are disciplined, O best of kings,
so too is the knower of reality disciplined through yoga in the concentration of the self.
"O King, having abandoned this body, one attains a place that is difficult to reach," says Vyāsa.
The wise know that there are five defects of yoga to be completely eradicated:
desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth.

One conquers anger through tranquility and desire by abandoning volitional thought; by cultivating the quality of purity (*sattva*), the wise man makes his stainless self unshakable, appearing like the sun.
And just as a concentrated helmsman [guides] a ship, O son of Kuntī, |||

O King, one should swiftly lead a king who has fallen into the great ocean [of distress]; one ought to sever his sleep. With fortitude, one should guard the genitals and the belly, as well as the hands, feet, and eyes.
One should guard the eye and the ear with the mind, and the mind and speech with action.
One should abandon fear through heedfulness and deceit by cultivating wisdom;
in this way, one who is ever vigilant shall conquer these defects of yoga.
Having achieved one-pointedness of the mind and the senses, being well-composed,
one should fix the mind upon the Self during the first and last watches of the night.
Restraining the collection of his senses like one who guards a pot of gold, the sage, being self-controlled, should practice yoga at the three times of day.
One should always contemplate with one-pointed focus; through yoga, one should not allow the mind to wander, but rather employ whatever means are possible to restrain that flickering mind.
One should practice that with diligence and never deviate from it;
nor should one be attached to anything else, even in action, speech, or thought.
Being equanimous and moderate in food, one should remain the same whether gain or loss occurs;
for one might either rejoice in this [practice] or disparage it.
One should not contemplate the auspicious or inauspicious in either of these two states together;
one should not rejoice in gains, nor dwell upon losses.
Thus, for the virtuous person who is established in their own self and perceives equality everywhere,
the Brahman of Sound transcends after six months of constant practice.
"One who is devoted to this path should not desist, even if deluded.
Since yoga does not succeed in the absence of the proper place and time, those two must first be examined.
As stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
Having secured a suitable place, one should indeed practice the limbs of yoga in their proper sequence;
for the vision of yoga is not possible in an improper place or time.
Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
And since a sentient being does not arise, and is devoid of place and time, there is no perception of an existent in yoga; therefore, one should avoid that.
A yogi devoted to meditation should not practice during these times: when it is not too cold, nor indeed when it is hot, nor during the dual conditions consisting of fire and wind.
He [should avoid] a place with other noises, a place where practice has been worn out, a cow-pen, a crossroads,
dry leaves, a river, a cremation ground, or a place infested with reptiles.
One who knows the truth should avoid the practice of yoga in these places;
[as stated] in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Not near water or fire, not at a place called *jīrṇa* or a crossroads;
not where swarming with gadflies and mosquitoes, nor at a shrine or a public square.
One should not practice in a place defiled by hair, ashes, husks, charcoal, bones, and the like; nor in a place with a foul odor and so forth, nor in a place crowded with people.
Thus it is also stated in the Liṅgapurāṇa and other texts.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, prohibitions such as "one should not [travel] on an inauspicious day," "when infested by wicked people," or "when swarming with mosquitoes and the like" are to be observed.

Immediately after the prohibition beginning with, "One should never practice yoga in a place infested with gadflies and mosquitoes," it is said: "Indeed, for that fool who practices yoga while disregarding these defects,
I shall declare the defects that arise and act as obstacles."
Deafness, dullness, loss of memory, muteness, blindness, and cough arise immediately; likewise, these same afflictions arise for the one who possesses the yoga of knowledge.
Therefore, one who knows the yoga of protection should always guard [the body] with all one's being,
since the body is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Thus said Dattātreya.

Immediately after this refutation of [unfavorable] place and time, having stated those very defects such as dullness (*jaḍatva*) and so forth that arise solely from negligence (*pramāda*), he describes their remedy:
"If these defects of yogis should arise from negligence, then the remedy is as follows."
O Yogin, understand from me that which must be done for their destruction.
One who has vomited should hold very hot, unctuous gruel against that very spot for the sake of pacifying vāta-gulma; likewise, curd [should be held] in the case of udāvarta.
Just as one might cast away a thin gruel, wind, or a loose knot,
so too, when trembling occurs, one should hold the great mountain steady within the mind.

In the event of a failure of speech or deafness of the sense of hearing, one should likewise meditate on the fruit of attainment; and when afflicted by thirst, one should meditate on it regarding the sense of taste.

In whichever part of the body there is pain, one should apply a concentration (dhāraṇā) that provides relief for that specific area— cooling concentration for heat, and heating concentration for cold.
Having placed a kīla (stake) upon the head, one should strike wood with wood;
by this, the memory of the yogi whose memory has been lost is immediately restored.
One should sprinkle the pervasive Heaven and Earth, as well as Vāyu and Agni;
these non-human beings and creatures that cause no harm have thus been treated.
If a non-human being or an internal yogin should enter [the body],
this [practice]— through the concentration on air and fire— will utterly consume that which resides within the body.
Thus, O King, one who knows the yoga of protecting the body with one's whole being [should do so],
since the body is the means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus, the prescribed [times] are now described. Among them, time has been mentioned previously and will be discussed further in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Those who know the truth understand that the practice of yoga should be performed in solitary mountain fastnesses, at sacred fords, in temples, or in caves.
Yājñavalkya.
Having reached a well-provided penance grove abounding in fruits, roots, and water,
he stayed there in a delightful and pure place resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
It was filled with peaceful people devoted to their own duties and possessed of knowledge of Brahman,
and it was well-provided with water and endowed with various kinds of flowers.
In a place well-provided with fruits and roots, which grants all desired fruits—
whether it be a temple, a riverbank, a village, or even a city.
Having constructed a very beautiful hermitage endowed with all desirable things, one should practice yoga therein; this is the connection with what follows.
In the *Yogatattvaprakāśa*.
One should construct a very beautiful hut with a narrow door and devoid of external splendor,
carefully plastered either with cow dung or with lime.
It was always free from flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies,
and it was diligently swept every single day with a broom.
"And it is perfumed with fragrance and fumigated with guggulu and other substances," as stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
In a well-governed, righteous land, where food is abundant and free from calamity,
the practitioner of Haṭhayoga should reside within a small hut in a secluded place.
Provided with few doors, free from cracks, pits, or holes, neither too high nor too low,
well-smeared with thick cow-dung, free from impurities, and devoid of all living creatures; with an outer pavilion, a well,
and an altar constructed, and surrounded by a wall— this is declared to be the defining characteristic of a yoga-hermitage.
By the Siddhas who practice Haṭha:
"Staying in such a monastery, free from all thoughts,
one should always practice yoga alone according to the path instructed by the Guru."
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Free from all affliction, bringing happiness to all the senses,
generating clarity of mind, and gladdened by the fragrance of garlands and incense.
Thus it is stated in the Nandipurāṇa.
The temple was beautifully arranged, charming, perfumed with fragrances,
made sweet by the scent of incense, and adorned with heaps of flowers.
Adorned with sages' bathing places, rivers, trees, lotus ponds, and mountains,
it was like a work of art, variegated by various types of paintings.
The wise man should construct a beautiful meditation hall by means of an auspicious path;
for upon seeing the peaceful sages depicted therein, his mind attains tranquility.
Having seen the Siddhas depicted in the paintings, one's mind will be inclined toward spiritual exertion;
then, in the center of the yoga-hall, one should draw the maṇḍala of cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
And in some places, one should draw a most terrifying cremation ground and hells;
having seen those of such fearsome form, [one perceives] saṃsāra as devoid of essence.
The yogi who desires accomplishment does not become despondent,
even while observing diseased beings and noting those who are dead or intoxicated.

The connection is as follows: a pure-souled person of this kind, established in an auspicious yoga-hall, should practice the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*). This very definition of a yoga-hall is also stated in the *Liṅgapurāṇa* and other texts. Regarding the regulation of diet, its extreme necessity for yoga is [established] by way of the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*).

Furthermore, based on the scriptural statement, "From purity of food comes purity of being," the nature of food is first determined prior to the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*). Regarding that, Dattātreya [states] what is to be avoided:
Now I shall describe those things to be avoided, which cause obstacles to yoga:
salt, mustard, sourness, heat, dryness, and pungency.
"Excessive eating, excessive sleep, and excessive talking must be abandoned.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"One should abandon pungent, sour, and salty [foods], and one should always be an eater of sharp [tastes].
Thus it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.

They say that bitter, sour, pungent, salty, and hot foods; green vegetables, *sauvīra* (sour gruel), oil, sesame, mustard, fish, and wine; the meat of goats and sheep, curd, buttermilk, horse gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*kola*), oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), vermilion, and water from a well with a foul odor are unwholesome.
Furthermore, one should know that food which has been reheated or cut up is likewise harmful.
One should avoid food that is excessively salty, putrid, or dominated by śāka (potherbs).
Now, O Lord of Sages, those things which are not to be accepted: wheat, rice, barley, ṣāṣṭika rice, and other fine foods;
milk, clarified butter, cream, fresh butter, sugar, honey;
ginger, patola, fruits, and the five types of vegetables; mung beans and other pulses; raw water.
Beneficial is that food which is well-ground, very sweet, unctuous, derived from cow products, nourishing to the bodily constituents,
desired by the mind, and appropriate; such a meal a yogi should partake of.
Dattātreya.
And I shall declare what is to be accepted for the swift accomplishment of yoga:
milk, ghee, sweet food, and moderate eating are praised.
Some desire camphor and likewise beautiful betel-leaf;
however, that which is devoid of lime is recommended for yogis practicing the mastery of breath.
In the Compendium of Yoga.
When the vital breath has entered the solar channel (bhānunāḍī), the yogi should take food;
when the vital breath has entered the lunar channel (somanāḍī), eating is not at all recommended.
For one who delights in the self, milk alone is recommended during the first stage of practice;
at the initial period of practice, a diet of milk is praised.

Then, once practice has become firm, there is the adoption of such a restrictive rule (*niyama*). In this context, the constant consumption of betel leaf applies specifically to householders who habitually consume it, since its prohibition for others, such as mendicants and the like, has been stated. This is not a restrictive rule that one must eat only milk; rather, [it is a specific practice].

It should be understood that one should practice yoga after consuming whatever is obtained according to time and place, and whatever one’s own body can tolerate through its own natural inclination. As for what has been said— that a yogi should take food only when the *prāṇa* flows through the solar channel (*bhānunāḍī*)— that applies only when there is the capacity for traveling through the sky.

Then it should be known by the yogi; for at that time, it will be stated that there is no necessity for the practitioner of yoga to observe all the aforementioned rules, whereas during the initial practice, one must eat only when hungry. Otherwise, the fire of yoga would be extinguished.

Because liberation is not achieved when the knowledge of reality fails to arise due to the obstruction of *yoga* caused by the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), which gives rise to various diseases such as consumption (*bhasmaka*) and the like;
[one might object]: "But surely, eating in the evening and in the morning is ordained for humans by the gods."
One should observe the practice of eating only between meals; this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

Since the *Dharmaśāstra* prescribes eating only once or twice a day for all four *varṇas* and *āśramas*— stating that "an ascetic (*yatī*), a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), a widow, and a woman in her menses, having eaten a second time or consumed betel-leaf, shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance," and so forth— how can [eating] be considered unrestricted?

[Objection: Food is restricted [for the practitioner], and there is no other stage of life (āśrama) for yogins, because it has been shown in the cited Purāṇic and other scriptural passages that eligibility for the practice of yoga belongs only to the four previously mentioned classes and stages of life. [Reply: No, because that scripture concerns those who are not yet yogins. If it is asked, "How is this known?"—it is as follows: [text continues]
Because the practice of yoga is prohibited for one who is either satiated or afflicted by extreme hunger, and because its practice is prescribed at all times,

we understand that whenever there is hunger, one must indeed eat. Furthermore, eating at a single fixed time— which is a subordinate limb of knowledge— cannot override [the practice] which is primary in comparison to everything else.
The omission of the knowledge of the elements is appropriate, according to the maxim that "in a conflict between the primary and the secondary, the primary is stronger.
For this very reason, a restriction regarding food for practitioners of yoga is heard in another Śruti. To explain:
A Paramahaṃsa should eat once or twice a day;
by whatever means possible, the ascetic should be devoted to the practice of knowledge.
In this context, the word *yati* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all three stages of life (*āśrama*).
Now, that which must necessarily be known by the yogi within the body is being described.
And without that knowledge, there is no accomplishment through yoga.
Thus says Gorakṣa:
"The six cakras, the sixteen supports, the two objects of focus, and the five voids."
By what means do yogins know their own bodies and how do they achieve perfection?
How can yogis achieve perfection if they do not know that within their own body there is a house with one pillar, nine gates, and five presiding deities?
The six cakras and sixteen ādhāras will now be described. There are two types of objects of focus: external and internal.

These include the eyebrows, the nose, and so forth, as well as the mūlādhāra and the others. There is also the pentad of voids (*vyomapañcaka*), extending from the heart, throat, palate, and eyebrows to the *brahmarandhra*. This [body] is like a house supported by a single pillar, with the mind serving as that firm pillar.

By that [state], the mind itself, in the form of a pillar, sustains the body. In the Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, and Viśuddha [cakras], there reside, respectively, the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. Thus it is stated in the Yājñavalkya-gītā.
Gārgī said:
O Blessed One, my Lord, tell me the purification of the channels according to the prescribed method;
by what means may the channels of all embodied beings become purified?
Tell me also of the origin of the channels and their retention according to the rule;
what kind of bulb (kanda) is said to be there, and how many vital winds (vāyus) abide within?
Furthermore, O best of embodied beings, the locations and the individual functions of the vital airs within this body must be understood.
"You ought to tell me all of that, for there is no one who knows it better than you.
When his wife had spoken thus, he, with his mind fully intent upon her, replied:
Having examined the Gārgī-tantra, he explained it all as follows:
"This body indeed consists of only eight finger-breadths."
"Know, O beloved, that the life-force (prāṇa) of all living beings extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body by means of one's own fingers."
Some of the best of sages say it is fourteen finger-breadths,
while wise men say it is exactly twelve finger-breadths.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
These ten winds move through all the channels;
among these, five are known as the principal winds, beginning with prāṇa.
Among these, these two—prāṇa and apāna—are the most preeminent in the best of men;
of these two, prāṇa alone is always the primary one for all living beings.
To the one devoted to the yoga of Nakulīśa.
The vital air (vāyu) residing in the body, through its various functions such as sustaining life and so forth, sequentially assumes different designations,
beginning with prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and the rest.
In the *Amṛtabindu*.
Although it has been stated that there are innumerable winds within the body,
nevertheless, both prāṇa and apāna are established as the most excellent performers of action.
The purification of the channels will be explained later. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
They say that the abode of the vital breaths (prāṇa) is between the mouth and the nose, in the center of the heart, and in the center of the navel; and some say it is in the big toe of the foot.
Below and above the Kuṇḍalinī, the one known as Prāṇa stands on all sides;
within those four [channels], it illuminates like a lamp.
Some indeed say that the abode of the apāna wind is in the anus, the penis, the thighs, and the knees; others say it is in the abdomen, the eyes, the hips, the shanks, and the navel.
Vyāna resides in the ears, the eyes, the middle of the neck, the ankles, the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks; of this there is no doubt.
The udāna wind resides in all the joints, as do those in the feet and the hands;
the samāna wind alone is situated pervading the entire fire.

Along with the subtle elements (tanmātras), the five winds— nāga and the others— are situated throughout the entire body, including its limbs and sub-limbs, as well as within the skin, bones, and other parts.
The water, food, and the essential juices (rasa) and so forth, once combined within the belly,
are separated by the vital breath (prāṇa) located in the center of the abdomen.
Having placed water above the fire and food and other items upon the water,
one obtains the drink by oneself, yet not together with the wind.
Thereupon, the vital breath (prāṇa), situated in the middle, proceeds toward the fire;
the fire, fanned by the wind, is gradually moved upward by the downward breath (apāna).
Then, when the lord of brahmins blazes within the entire body,
the fire there, impelled by the vital breath (prāṇa), flares up with its flames.
Then the water made the food, along with its condiments, which had been placed upon it, extremely hot within the interior of the vessel.
Then Agni made it thoroughly cooked with heated water;
from the sweat and urine there would be water, while the form and potency became the essence (rasa).
O Gārgi, the prāṇa should carry the excrement to its end; it should distribute the nutrient essence separately into all the channels along with the samāna wind.
The vital air (māruta) moves through the body in the form of exhalation and inhalation;
and through the nine apertures of the void, it effects the discharge of feces, urine, and other waste.
All the winds act continuously within bodies as inhalation, exhalation, and coughing; this is celebrated as the function of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The function of the apāna-vāyu is the evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth;
the functions of vyāna are also held to include activities such as relinquishing and grasping.
The function of udāna is said to be that which raises the body and so forth;
the function of samāna is proclaimed to be the drying [of waste] and so forth within the body.
That which consists of belching and so forth is called the function of Nāga;
blinking and so forth belong to Kūrma, and sneezing belongs to Kṛkara.
O best of brahmins, the act of causing paralysis is proclaimed as belonging to Devadatta,
while all actions such as beautifying and so forth are proclaimed as belonging to Dhanañjaya.
Likewise, the locations, colors, and seed-syllables of the five [breaths], beginning with Prāṇa, are found in the Nakulīśayoga-parāyaṇa.
The vital breath (prāṇa) resides sequentially at the tip of the nose, the heart, the navel, and ending at the big toe;
it is joined with the seed-syllables beginning with "Soṃ" and the letter "Ra," which are blue in color.
With black shoes, situated at the neck, on the back, and at the heels;
he is thus applied with the seed-syllables ending in *tāra* (oṃ) and *nakāra* (na).
The Vyāna wind resembles Indra’s bow; it is the abode of the sense of touch and is resplendent with the seed-energy at its end, which is endowed with stars.
The udāna breath resides at the crown of the head, the middle palate, the tip [of the tongue], the throat, the heart, and the navel;
it has the luster of dawn and is joined with yellow, pervaded by the stars.
Equalizing the mind, he dwells in the heart, the navel, and all the joints;
he is exceedingly radiant by means of the seed-syllable ending with the letter *la*, which is pervaded by the *praṇava*.
The letter *ya* is the beginning of the letter *ra*; that same *ya*, together with the syllable *oṃ* (the *praṇava*), means the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Together with the *tāraka* (the *praṇava*), it is "with the *praṇava*"; and that which is the end of the letter *na* is the letter *pa*. By that seed-syllable, the downward breath (*apāna*) is colored.
The letter *la* ending in *yā*.
The meaning is that the letter *la* ending in *soṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the vyāna breath. "Exceedingly ruddy" means extremely red;
[it refers to] the tip of the palate and the edge of the uvula. "Pattala" means the sole of the foot. The letter *ra* ending in *yā* is the syllable *soṃ*.

The meaning is that the letter *repha* (ṛ) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *udāna* breath. Furthermore, this letter *va*, which is the final letter of the word *la* (i.e., *la-anta*), being preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), takes the form *soṃkāra*; the meaning is that this letter *va* is the seed-syllable of the *samāna* breath. In all these instances, although the vital airs (*vāyu*) are formless, specific colors such as blue and so forth are mentioned for the purpose of meditation (*dhyāna*).
It should be so understood.
Yājñavalkya.
In the center of the body is the seat of fire, with the luster of molten gold;
it is triangular for humans and quadrangular for four-footed creatures.
I shall describe this circle of the sunbeams as it is:
in its center always stands the slender crest of flame, which is purifying.
If you wish to hear where the middle of the body is, listen:
it is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis.
The middle of the body is said to be the center for humans;
for quadrupeds, it is in the middle of the heart, and for animals, in the middle of the navel.
O lady of excellent limbs, for the twice-born, the region of the navel is said to be the middle;
for human beings, the location of the *kanda* is nine finger-breadths from the center of the body.
With a width and length of four finger-breadths and likewise of that same measure,
its form is said by the proponents of reality to be like that of an egg.
In the middle of the belly of four-footed animals, birds, and twice-born beings, it is said that "abhi" is located in that center; from the navel arises the wheel (cakra).
That [wheel] is endowed with twelve spokes, and by it the body is established;
within this wheel, the individual soul (jīva) revolves, impelled by merit and demerit.
Just as a spider moves within the midst of its web,
so does this vital breath (prāṇa) move downward within the root-cakra of the individual soul (jīva).
The individual soul (jīva), mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), is always present within all bodies.
Above that is the location of Kuṇḍalinī, situated transversely below the navel.
Consisting of the eightfold nature, that Kuṇḍalinī is coiled eightfold;
she perpetually [regulates] the movement of the vital airs, as well as water, food, and so forth, exactly as they are.
Having fallen upon the sides of the *kanda*, it remains there always, having completely obstructed them; likewise, it completely envelops the opening of the *brahmarandhra* with its mouth.
At the time of yoga, however, she becomes awakened by the fire through the apāna breath;
throbbing in the space of the heart, she is of the form of a serpent, intensely radiant.
Then the wind goes through the *suṣumṇā* by means of its very companion, the wind;
the woman situated in the middle of the *kanda* is celebrated as the *suṣumṇā*.
All the channels known as *nāḍīs* stand surrounding this wheel;
O Gārgī, among all these *nāḍīs*, there are fourteen that are supreme.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Sarasvatī,
Vāruṇī, Pūṣā, Hastijihvā, and Payasvinī.
Viśvodarī, Kuhu, Śaṅkhinī, Yaśasvinī, Alambuṣā, and Gāndhārī— these fourteen are the principal ones.
Among them, three are the most prominent; of these three, one is considered the supreme.
That is called Suṣumṇā, the sustainer of the universe, which is said to be the path to liberation.
O Gārgī, the Suṣumṇā is well-established in the middle of the bulb (kanda);
situated in the middle of the back, it always remains at the top of the channel.
She is called the path to liberation and is celebrated as the *brahmarandhra*;
she alone is to be known as the unmanifest (*avyaktā*), subtle, and remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇavī*).
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.

Suṣumṇā, the path of the void, the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the great path, the cremation ground, the power of Śambhu (śāmbhavī), and the central way— these are synonyms for one and the same.

In this context, the *suṣumṇā* is the path of liberation; for it is stated in the forthcoming *Chāndogya* Śruti, "Rising upwards by that [path], one attains immortality," that it is a support (*dhāraṇā*) which is the means to liberation. For this very reason, it is designated as "Avimukta" (the Unreleased), just like Kāśī. Thus, it has been said that there is a threefold nature to Avimukta.

In the *Kāśīmīmāṃsā*, it is stated in the Sūtra: "There are three: the internal (ādhyātmika), the divine (adhidaivika), and the elemental (ādhibhautika). Furthermore, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the internal [state] is shown as follows: "O Bāli, Aruṇa said: 'The iḍā is considered to be the released (*vimukta*) channel, and the piṅgalā is the Varuṇā; within that [space] is the *vimuktaka*. Likewise:

That Suṣumṇā is the supreme channel; this [city] is Vārāṇasī and that is [the other]. Even in the Kūrma Purāṇa, because it bestows liberation upon those specific regions delimited by various particular locations, those respective places are designated as "Avimukta" (the Unreleased).
Between the eyebrows, in the center of the navel, in the heart, and also in the head—
just as it is liberated in the sun, so it is established in Vāraṇasī.
Likewise, between these two rivers, the Varaṇā and the Asī, is the city called Vārāṇasī;
here, the term "Avimukta" is used according to conventional linguistic usage. And thus is the connection here:
just as the word "vimukta" (released) is established in the Sun, which is the junction-form of the celestial and the terrestrial realms, so too [is it here].

Furthermore, with respect to the external (adhibhautika), he is established in the city known as Vārāṇasī located in the middle of Vārāṇasī; likewise, with respect to the internal (adhyātmika), he is established in the region of the Suṣumṇā canal as delimited by specific cakras— the space between the eyebrows, the heart, and the crown of the head.
Yājñavalkya.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are indeed on her left and right;
Iḍā is situated on her left, and Piṅgalā is situated on the right.
The Moon and the Sun move within the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā;
the Moon is to be known as being in the Iḍā, and the Sun is traditionally said to be in the Piṅgalā.

The moon is said to be of the nature of tamas, while the sun is said to be of the nature of rajas. The portion of the sun that is its poison is known as the portion of the moon, which is called "death."
These two sustain the entirety of time, consisting of night and day;
the Suṣumṇā is the consumer of that time—this is declared to be a secret.
In the ocean of nectar, the moon, endowed with sixteen digits, resides upon the peak of Mount Meru;
day and night, being composed of frost, it rains down nectar with its face turned downward.
Then, the nectar (amṛta) should be understood by the discerning as having become twofold:
through the path of the *iḍā* for the sake of nourishment, it is the sky; and [through the other path] it is the water of the Mandākinī.
Nourishing the entire body as it arrives via the path of the subtle channels,
this indeed has the nature of the Moon and is established on the left path.
Another moon, resembling a multitude of sacrificial pits and drawing a circle of joy,
proceeds by the middle path for the sake of creation.
The solar disc resides at the location of the root of the middle channel;
complete with twelve digits, it blazes with rays of light.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), whose form is sharp, carries [the breath] upward through the right [nostril];
this is the supreme fourth form for men on the southern path.
Flowing by means of the conjunction of the *lagna*, O cause of creation and destruction,
when the ocean becomes equal to Mount Meru, having abandoned its course to the left.
One should know that to be the equinox (viṣuva), the meritorious time within the body;
and having recognized this equinox in the body, those who possess the path [of practice] proceed with disciplined application.
Yogis easily effect their departure [from the body] through the conjunction of time;
[time consists of] the seasons, the twilights, the directions, night, the divisions of time such as kalās, kāṣṭhās, and kṣaṇas.
For both the taking up and the emission of everything indeed arise from the sun;
for when the sun becomes connected to the navel through yoga, [all things proceed].
Then the external creation is to be known, while yoga occurs from within;
one should certainly understand that grasping pertains to both the external and the internal.
Externally, it is the most meritorious time; internally, there shall be liberation when the sun eclipses the lunar orb within the circle of the moon.
The union of these two arises from one another; therefore, yoga is indeed attained when, by divine providence, the sun and fire move upward within embodied beings.
Then the lunar nectar descends below, and death occurs for men;
indeed, all the principles (tattvas) within the body then move upward.
"These two, the sun and the moon, shine forth as the givers of liberation," says Yājñavalkya.
Sarasvatī and Kuhū are situated on the two sides of Suṣumṇā;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are on the back and front of Iḍā.

Pūṣā and Yaśasvinī are in the east and west, Piṅgalā and Pṛṣṭhavāhinī are in the south and north; Kuha and Hastijihvā are in the southeast and southwest, while Viśvodarī is situated between them in the center.
Vāruṇī is established in the middle of Yaśasvinī and Kuhū;
and Yaśasvinī is situated between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī.
O best of Brahmins, Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī are situated in the middle,
while Śaṅkhinī and Alambuṣā are located below the center of the bulb (kanda).
In the eastern part of the Suṣumṇā, the Kuhū vein is situated as far as the penis;
it should be known as extending both downwards and upwards, being the Vāruṇī that reaches everywhere.
Yaśasvinī is held to extend from the southern [channel] to the big toe;
know, O my beloved, that Piṅgalā, which goes upward, extends to the tip of the southern nostril.
Pūṣan is at the southern end of the eye, behind Piṅgalā;
likewise, O Gārgī, Yaśasvinī is held to extend to the southern edge of the ear.
Likewise, Sarasvatī is established above the tongue;
O best of Brahmins, Śaṅkhinī is considered to extend upward from the left ear.
Gāndhārī is situated behind the left eye at the back of the iḍā;
the iḍā itself is established along the left side, extending to the middle of the nose.
Likewise, the Hastijihvā is held to extend from the left [nostril] to the big toe;
the Viśvodarī channel, however, is recorded as proceeding from the left to the left [side of the body].
O highly fortunate one, the Alaṃbuṣā extends downward from the root of the anus;
these other channels that have arisen, and others besides them, are also present therein.
Just as it is on the leaf of the *śvattha* tree, so too on the petals of the lotus;
O one whose wealth is austerity, it should be understood that [the breath] moves head-downward through all the white channels.
Thus it is in Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Within the center of the wheel are three channels, each presided over by a deity:
the channel Iḍā has Vaiṣṇava as its deity, and Piṅgalā has Brahmā as its deity.
That Suṣumṇā, belonging to Īśvara, is situated within Meru;
it is joined with the three knots located in the midst of the channels and is known as Triveṇikā.
The Gaṅgā is known to flow in the north, the Yamunā in the south, and the Sarasvatī in the west; their confluence is eternal.
Thus, in the *Amṛtasiddhi*.
Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā flows a single Sarasvatī;
having bathed at the confluence of these rivers, the fortunate ones go to the supreme goal.
Thus, in the Mānasollāsa.
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā run toward the corners of the eyes;
both, joined by the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), extend as far as the nose.
The *pūṣā* and *alambuṣā* channels, situated like the intestines of a cock, rest upon the navel region and extend to both ears.
Therefore, the channel called Śuklā ascends to the midpoint between the eyebrows;
the channel called Sarasvatī extends to the tip of the tongue, conveying speech.
The channel named Viśvodarī consumes the four kinds of food;
having drunk the water from the Payasvinī, it produces a sneeze when situated at the throat.
Emerging from the wheel of channels (nāḍī-cakra), three channels extend downward:
Rākā, joined with Sinīvālī, voids urine, while Kuhū voids feces.
Having taken up the essence of the food that has been consumed, the Śaṅkhinī vessel again goes to the cavity of the skull; one should contemplate the nectar there at the crown of the head.
There are one hundred and one channels, and of these, one has gone to the head;
by ascending through that one, one becomes liberated—such is the teaching of the Vedānta.
In this context, the mouth of the Suṣumṇā should be understood as being at the Mūlādhāra itself;
and thus says Sureśvarācārya:
The central location within the body is called the *mūlādhāra*;
it is situated two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis.
The tip of its mouth is downward-facing and triangular, resembling the vulva of a maiden;
therein is established the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī.
She who consists of the vital breath, fire, the bindu, and the nāda is Sāvitrī;
she is Sarasvatī, residing at the tip of the corner of the mūlādhāra, and passing through the suṣumṇā to the brahmarandhra.
With its lower half severed like a bamboo stalk, it is supported by the Bhāṣa;
from its two side corners, the two channels Iḍā and Piṅgalā arise and remain situated there.
They call it the "wheel of channels" (*nāḍīcakra*), for from it the channels have issued forth.

Furthermore, by piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), even the venerable Śaṅkarācārya stated that the mouth of the *suṣumṇā* is indeed at the *mūlādhāra*. For instance: "The Earth is situated in the *mūlādhāra*, and likewise the Fire resides in the *maṇipūra*."

Having pierced everything— from the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and the heart up to the wind and space, and even the mind at the center of the brows— along the path of the *kula*, you sport in the thousand-petaled lotus together with the Lord of the Night (Śiva). In all the mantra scriptures as well, that very point is declared to be the primary entrance for sages such as Yājñavalkya and Vasiṣṭha.
According to the view of Gorakṣa and other yogins, the mouth of the Suṣumṇā and Kuṇḍalinī are located within the *kanda* situated at the navel;

however, this opinion must be considered, as it is untenable because it would entail the dissolution of the knots known as Brahma and Viṣṇu, which are located in the Mūlādhāra and Svādhiṣṭhāna wheels respectively.
In the Yogabhāskara.
There are ten channels, ten bones, ten fires, and ten winds;
one should be devoted to the practice of yoga without causing conflict among these.
In that regard, the channels and the vital winds have already been described.
[The remaining parts are] the spinal column, the frontal bone, the neck, and likewise the chin.
The nasal bone, the chest, the arms, the feet, the thighs, and the knees—these are the ten bones; now hear of the ten fires from me.
The radiant, the coloring, the windy, and likewise the phlegmatic;
the digestive, the purgative as the sixth, the burning, and the eighth, the drying.
The nourisher and the binder— these are the ten fires within this body,
according to the *Amṛtasiddhi*.
Endowed with ten digits (kalās) and situated in the center of the solar orb,
the digestive fire (vahni) dwells in the region of the bladder, digesting food.
As long as the sun remains in the center of the body of the Fire of Time (Kālānala),
so long does this power of the Bindu remain uninterrupted and composed of nectar.
In this world, fire bestows strength; fire is the giver of longevity.
As long as this fire remains stable within, a man remains free from disease.
Therefore, the intention is that the practice of yoga must be performed in such a way as not to contradict that [scriptural injunction]. Now, the supports (ādhāras) in Śivayoga:
Now I shall specifically describe those sixteen supports:
one should fix the fire-meditation on the big toe, and the gaze should become steady.
Pressing the base of one foot with the heel of the other, which is known as the second support,
and remaining thus, the fire is ignited in an instant.
One should contract the base of the anus by means of contracting the feet;
from this, steadiness of the downward-moving wind (apāna) arises—this is the third [stage].
By contracting the penis at the base of the organ, one should first produce the three Brahma-knots;
thereafter, through the entry of the mind and the vital breath (vāyu) into the Brahma-nāḍī, the stabilization of the bindu occurs immediately.
By repeatedly offering the fifth support, oḍana,
the digestion of impurities, urine, and worms certainly occurs.
Then, the wise one should join the *praṇava* there as a support for the navel;
through one-pointed concentration, the arising of the *nāda* occurs for him.
One should restrain the vital breaths within that seventh support, the heart;
then, at that moment, the lotus in its center blossoms instantaneously.
One should press the base of the throat and the pit of the throat with the chin;
thus, the restraint of the breath in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels becomes very firm.
The ninth is the support of the uvula; one should place the tip of the tongue there.
This [channel] flows with a digit of nectar, and it brings about my complete satisfaction.
That which was long by means of swinging and milking becomes reversed;
when one causes it to enter the region of the interior of the palate-root, it attains the state of *unmanā*.
This is the *khecarī* mudrā; such is its essential nature and its power.
It will be explained in the section on mudrās.
If one who possesses the wealth of yoga should make the tongue the support for the terrible tongue (the uvula),
the taste of nectar will be perfected for him and his poetic skill will become manifest.
The twelfth is the support of the teeth; above that is the royal tooth (rājadantaka).
After six months, light becomes visible there by means of rubbing the tip of the tongue [against it].
The thirteenth [center] is the root of the nose; if one's gaze is fixed there constantly with the mind, the vital air (vāyu) will become steady therein.
The fourteenth support is called the forehead, where the knower of yoga,
having fixed the breath with the mind, shall attain all perfections.
The wise one, with his eyes directed upward toward that fifteenth support which is space, shall see it;
indeed, he perceives it very quickly in the form of rays.
The wise one should move that sixteenth [center], the support of the eyes, upward;
for he then quickly beholds within his own body that which consists of a mass of light—namely, Paramaśiva.
Now, the six cakras according to Sāṃkhya-yoga.
Henceforth I shall proclaim the six cakras; listen, O beloved:
Mūlādhāra, Adhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, and Anāhata.
Viśuddhi is located in the region of the throat; Ājñā is situated between the eyebrows.
The Foundation (Ādhāra) consists of four corners, while Sthiti has the form of a hexagon.
The Anāhata [cakra] is triangular and resembles a jewel with a crescent moon;
the Viśuddhi-cakra is proclaimed to be like a full moon.
O beloved, listen further to that which has the form of the crest of the divine command:
the Ādhāra is yellow in color, and the Svādhiṣṭhāna is of the nature of water.
The *maṇi* [cakra] resembles blue collyrium; the *anāhata* is red in color;
the *viśuddha* resembles crystal; and the *ājñā* possesses all colors.
Some say that the lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna is red in luster,
while the lotus of knowledge (jñānapaṅkaja) is white, revealing the Supreme Self.
In the case of the application of power.
Four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen,
and two are declared to be the number of petals for the lotus seats and so forth, based on their respective supports.
Herein, my [mandala] consists of Dviraṇḍa, known as Bālya, and likewise Cakra;
as well as Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī.
Sākinī and Hākinī are indeed the goddesses in sequence;
knowing this, all the wheels (cakras) truly become bestowers of all siddhis.
One should pierce those [cakras] in their proper sequence according to the method of the Guru’s instruction;
the manner of piercing the cakras is described in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
Then, having conquered the interior through the practice of inhalation (pūraka),
the wise man, being well-composed, should apply effort in the region of his own root-cakra to pierce the knots known as the *jopa* and *upapada*.
Just as one might gradually release all the coils of a conch-shell and then contract them back into their own place, so should the wise man [contract] the foundation (*ādhāra*).

With his self disciplined, he should forcefully contract the path of the *kaṃbu* (the throat); with his hand placed on the navel, he should repeatedly utter the sound *hūṃ* according to the sequence taught by the Guru. Then, the one whose source is the tip of the lotus consisting of light situated firmly between the anus and the *dhvaja* (penis), being self-restrained, should slowly draw back the wind from the *kaṃbu* in reverse order.

One should cause that [wind] to enter the root of the lotus-seat, which is difficult to attain according to the procedure taught by one's own guru. By performing this method repeatedly, that wind gradually enters the path at the base of the *ajapā*-lotus and effects the piercing of the knots.
Then, having avoided the path of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and of Candra, the jewel of the sky,
and having properly entered the lotus of the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) with its face turned upward,
he thereafter displayed a wondrous brilliance upon entering the supreme abode of the Paramaṣṭhin within his own home.
There arises lightness of body and a blazing radiance within the stomach that burns intensely;

it possesses a splendor like ten million flashes of lightning, surpassing the glow of the black fire with its own luster, and bears a beautiful brilliance resembling the massed rays of a thousand suns.
One should meditate upon Kāma, who wanders within the womb, possessing the luster of a throbbing, crimson bandhūka flower,
and as cool as ten million moons in his belly; above him is the flame of fire,
radiant with the splendor of a cluster of creepers, subtle, and situated within the interior of the path to Brahman.
The wise one should meditate with steady intellect upon his own Self as motionless, unified with the subtle portion of pure consciousness,
