like a lamp in a windless place, fearless, and having the nature of the *ahaṃsa*.
That which is called the power *Kuṇḍalinī*— designated by the syllables *Ā*, *Ī*, *Ma*, and *Sa*— is eternally intent upon the creation of the universe.

In the center of that [lotus], one should contemplate a lotus fiber (visalatā) resembling a flash of lightning, shaped like a conch-spiral, coiled like a sleeping serpent, enchanting the world, and as slender as a thread;
having awakened it from its sleep by means of the syllable *HŪṂ* according to the method taught by the Guru, one should join it with that [central] digit (*kalā*).
With a concentrated mind, one should mentally project that Kuṇḍalinī Māyā, who is united with the supreme unconscious form (acidrūpa),
the Kaulikī Śakti, together with the Great Path of Brahman from the Ādhāra by means of one's own self;
then, having pierced the three coils, the wise one [perceives] her as she ascends higher and higher through the Brahma-nāḍī.
From the abode born of the lotus, one should cause the power of the Self (ātma-śakti) to reach the sky-lotus—
the source of supreme bliss, the seat of emission (visarga), and the place where the red nectar flows above the moon.
Having drunk the divine essence of the nectar of the Kula, one should once again enter the center of the body.
With his self composed in meditative absorption, he should proceed from a *kula* to a *akula*, again by means of the application of the *mātrās* as taught by the most excellent of teachers.
That power (*śakti*), which has become the life-force of the entire body, is declared here by the masters of the *tantra* to be *prāṇa*.
The lords of sages declare that *udghāta* is *prāṇa* when it is brought gradually to touch that [point].

One who abides in right conduct, devoted to daily practice, full of faith, and constantly freed from all impurities, effects this; he is liberated from the flood of sufferings and is devoid of old age, affliction, and death. His qualities—

Endowed with this, one lives long on earth like a god. This very Yonimudrā, which has been described by me— even though it is difficult even for the gods— gives rise to all fourfold creation that exists here, and into it the entire universe, from Kālāgnirudra up to Sadāśiva, dissolves.

This [bond] is difficult to obtain. By means of this bond, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for the preeminent practitioner. Even the violation of the Guru’s bed, the drinking [of wine], the killing of a twice-born, and the theft of gold—by practicing this bond correctly even once, these go to destruction. That excellent minister, however...

That very yogi remains established in the supreme state beyond the attainment of the *guṇas*. He alone, who is constantly devoted to the duties and actions appropriate to his own station, practices here [this path] by means of this bond. For embodied beings, through this bond formed by constant practice, there is neither old age—the banner of the King of the Ancestors—nor death.
And fear has been explained. For by the thorough practice of this very bondage,
a person attains incomparable success such as *aṇimā* and the like, as well as unexcelled consciousness, peerless yoga,
victory over the vital breaths (*marut*), or even the mastery of time.
"The wise behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is higher than the high. Thus it is said in the Pārameśvara Tantra;
there, Īśvara said:
The linga facing west is proclaimed to be situated in the yoni;
it is conjoined with the heart-knot and the bindu, and denotes both the self-manifested (svayambhū) and the arrow (vāṇa).
The other is situated in the intermediate space, and likewise another is for the purpose of emission;
the Great Lotus Forest is proclaimed as the inner seat of yoga.
That desire, in the form of a drop (bindu), has the shape of a kadamba bud;
it is located right there within the mandala that supports the suṣumṇā at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The cavities beginning with earth are the designators of the threads;
the reality called Pūrṇa is the sandalwood situated between the two bows.
Above that, the one named Nāda is proclaimed as the seal (mudrā);
O beloved, the Śakti at Kāmarūpa is the incomparable Visarga.
I shall now describe its binding, by which one attains realization;
first, through the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one should again join it to the foundation of the bowstring (jyādhāra).
The womb is located between the anus and the penis; contracting it, one should awaken it, meditating on Kāma, who resides within the whirling womb and resembles a bandhūka flower.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
above that is the subtle and variegated fiery digit (*kalā*) of the crest-lock.
One should contemplate oneself as unified with her,
proceeding along the path of Brahman through the sequence of the three signs.
That nectar, characterized by supreme bliss, resides within the emission;
it is liquefied, red, rich with its own radiance, and set in motion by the falling streams.
Having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, one should enter the *kula* once again;
one should likewise go to the *akula* by means of the union of the *mātrās*, and not otherwise.
And that is designated as *prāṇa* in this tantra proclaimed by me;
it is the upward movement of sound, wherein resonance (*dhvani*) is produced from the vital breaths.
That measure is produced again by one who has mastery over exhalation;
that too is called an *udghāta* (upward stroke), when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) touches it.
For one who practices thus with daily resolution,
there is liberation from the bonds of existence through the floods of suffering caused by old age and death.
The fourfold creation which proceeds within that womb,
and in which it dissolves again, extends from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to Śiva.
This indeed is the supreme *yonimudrā*; its binding has been proclaimed.
By the mere binding of it, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish.
Those mantras which are severed, obstructed, pinned down, or paralyzed; those that are burnt, intoxicated, white, deficient, impure, or disregarded.
Those who were divided, those possessed by delusion, those cursed, those fainted, and those struck down; likewise the slow-witted, the aged, and those arrogant in their mature youth.
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, who are devoid of vigor and abandoned by living beings,
as well as those lacking conventional signs, have been cut into pieces by the hundreds.
When joined with this ritual procedure and duly appointed by the Guru, all of them quickly become bestowers of both spiritual perfection and liberation.
Whatever mantra-form, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the practitioner utters,
that indeed becomes accomplished without effort through the binding of the *yoni-mudrā*.
Having initiated them according to the prescribed rite and consecrated them in a thousand ways,
the mudrās are then proclaimed for the sake of their entitlement to the mantras.
"One might commit thousands of killings of Brahmins or even destroy the three worlds;
yet one is not tainted by sin through the binding of the *yoni-mudrā*."
Now, the wheels (cakras) utilized in the yoga of dissolution (*layayoga*) [are described] in the *Śivayoga*.

At the *mūlādhāra*, one should meditate on the *brahmacakra*, which has three revolutions and resembles the female organ (*bhaga*); within its bulb-like core (*kanda*), which is like fire, one should meditate upon the downward-facing Power (*śakti*) that grants all desires.
Then one should meditate upon the Svādhiṣṭhāna cakra, where there is a four-petalled lotus; that indeed is Oḍiyāna, wherein Śiva faces the west.

One should meditate there upon Kuṇḍalinī, the downward-pointing power (adhaḥśakti) who bestows perfect accomplishment, as being five-fold coiled at the navel-center, shaped like a serpent, and resembling lightning.
That wheel, joined with eight downward-facing petals, bestows desired fruits;
in its center, one should meditate upon this pericarp in the form of a light-linga.
The fifth is the throat-cakra; there, at a distance of four finger-breadths, one should meditate upon the iḍā and piṅgalā [nādīs], with the suṣumṇā situated in their midst.
The sixth is the *ghaṇṭikā-liṅga*, and its root is the *rājadantaka*;
one should meditate upon the tenth door there as empty for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
One should meditate upon the seventh, the brow-cakra, which is the single stalk-root that grants one's own speech; within its center is the divine form of a flame, the eye of wisdom.
The supreme wheel at the aperture of Brahmā is called Nirvāṇa; it bestows extreme subtlety.
Therein, one should meditate upon Jālandhara, which is smoky-colored and the bestower of liberation.
The ninth seed-syllable of space is praised; it is the triple-peaked [syllable] on the summit of Pūrṇagiri.
There, in the center of an eight-petaled lotus, one should meditate upon the upward-pointing power, auspicious and perfectly void.
Thus, in another treatise.
The first is the Wheel of Brahmā (brahmacakra), which is shaped like a yoni and has three revolutions;
they call it the Root-Bulb (mūlakanda) located in the apāna, and it is Kāmarūpa.
That very place shall be the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), and therein Kuṇḍalinī resides;
one should meditate upon her in the form of a seed-syllable, radiant with light, for the sake of liberation.
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should know that there is a second cakra situated in its center;
it is a liṅga facing westward, resembling a sprout of coral.
There, at the sacred seat of Oḍiyāna, having meditated upon that, one should attract the world;
the third is the navel-cakra, and within its center resides the serpent-goddess.
The central power has five whirlpools, is of the nature of consciousness, and has the form of lightning;
by meditating upon it, the wise one becomes a vessel for all accomplishments.
The fourth wheel is to be known as being in the heart, facing downwards;
one should diligently meditate upon the Haṃsa within its center, which is in the form of light.
For one who meditates upon that, the entire world shall become subject to his will; of this there is no doubt.
The fifth is the throat-cakra; therein, on the left, is the iḍā.
Piṅgalā is to be known as being on the right, and Suṣumṇā is situated in the middle;
by meditating there upon the pure light, one becomes a vessel for the supernatural powers (siddhis).
The sixth is the *tālukā-cakra*, which is said to be the location of the *ghaṇṭikā*;
they call that the path of the tenth door and the royal tooth (*rājadanta*).
Having brought about dissolution there in the void, one certainly becomes liberated;
one should know the seventh as the *bhrūcakra*, which they declare to be the station of the *bindu*.
Having meditated upon a circle between the eyebrows, one is liberated from light;
the eighth is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which indicates supreme nirvāṇa.
Having meditated upon that, one emits smoke from the tip of the needle;
and that supreme object of knowledge, which bestows liberation upon those of concentrated mind, is to be known as the stalk.
The ninth is the Sky-wheel (vyomacakra), endowed with sixteen petals;
and in its center resides the supreme Śakti, whose form is consciousness, standing upright.
There, at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Pūrṇagiri, one is liberated by meditating upon Śakti,
through the descent of the upward-moving power (ūrdhva-śakti) and the contraction of the downward-moving power (adhas-śakti).
"Through the awakening of the central power (madhya-śakti), supreme bliss arises.
This result has been explained in detail in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
For it is thus:
Now, I shall briefly describe the lotuses of the supports situated within the Suṣumṇā,
as well as the deities residing upon the petals of those lotuses, their respective colors, and the goddesses who are their supports.
O unborn one, that knot-lotus which was previously described by me, the sages here maintain as the primordial support;
it is golden-hued, endowed with four colors, possessed of petals accessible to yogis, and a source of great wonder.
Upon the petals of this fourth lotus, one should place the letters beginning with *nī*, *ru*, *ddhā*, *ja*, *la*, *rṇā*, and so forth, as the solitary Mother Goddesses. Sa...
The *bindu* is not merely a drop; it is the powerful and abundant goddess *Ḍākinī* who flashes with light.

Through the yoga of constant meditation upon her at the *mūlādhāra*, there arise for men, in due order, these excellent qualities: paralysis (*staṃbha*), stunning (*stobha*), levitation (*ūrdhvagati*), the power of the lizard (*dādurī*), the ability to leave the earth (*bhūmityāga*), and the state of moving through the sky (*khecara*).
Excellence of luster, clarity of voice, radiance of the digestive fire,

lightness of the limbs, sharpness of one's own senses, health, and freedom from dejection— by making the mind steady here in the *mūlādhāra-cakra* with constant devotion, men [attain] the past, the present, and even the future meaning.

They speak even of scriptures never before heard. Having immediately abandoned the lotus-wheel of the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā), Sarasvatī, assuming a divine form, dances as she arises from the lotus-circle accompanied by waves of joy.
Having attained the mastery of the mantra of the Lord of Rasas (Mercury), she awaits the [proper] time.

Having conquered that which is difficult to resist, and having attained the state of being ageless and immortal, he finally rejoices with delight in the station of supreme bliss. Previously, the entire world was submerged in the waters of a single unified ocean; within that [ocean] existed the primordial form of light, whose majesty is most highly honored.

The Lord Maheśa, whose self is presided over by the perfected ones (siddhas), who is praised by all the gods, who is endowed with six faces and six sheaths, and who is a swan that destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence, became the form of the *bhūḥ*-liṅga. The devotees of the Lord, who bear the bodies of the *aṅga*-liṅgas, are like a swarm of bees at his two limbs.
The eastern face of Śiva is Mahāla, while the upper face is likewise [Mahāla].

The southern face is this god Āśuśukṣaṇi, the wielder of the Pināka bow; furthermore, the western face is the blessed Chāgalaṇḍa, and the northern face of his became [the same]. That which is called Svādhiṣṭhāna is at the base with six petals.

Upon the lotus of the banner, resembling the rising sun, situated above the syllables of the *pṛṣṭha* and other *tarka* vowels, and with its head illuminated by the *bindu*, is the station of the Lord in the form of the *liṅga* who wields the trident; this is the sphere of perception for the best of yogis, and it is presided over by the goddess Ākīnī. Here, in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, one should fix one’s own mind.

With his heart stilled by a flood of intense bliss arising from absorption (*laya*), this excellent practitioner, though his body is joined with that of the deer-eyed women, remains free from passion;
yet, as he lies upon the ground, he delights their company with glances shimmering with love and radiant with beauty.
Here, having mastered various postures (*āsana*) and the vast collection of scriptures, he experiences the supreme state.

The Avadhūta, though subject to old age and mortal, lives for a very long time, free from the fear of death; he constantly effects the supreme purification of the human body, which is like a vessel that has been cleansed, yet remains as fragile as an autumn cloud.

The cool-rayed moon obstructs the dense mass [of darkness], and the great lord of elephants suddenly turns away from the lotus-pond of the sky upon seeing the lotus-like face. In this world, those virtuous ones who restrain [the senses] are indeed the wise and supreme among men; for even a great lordly elephant, whose temples are washed with rut, comes under control.

Just as by means of gentle methods, this powerful moon, though obstructed by the planets, necessarily comes under one's own control; so too, for one intent on the yoga of the thunderbolt and lotus, dissolution (*laya*) arises from the dissolution of the elephants of the senses such as speech, and through the power of that dissolution, consciousness becomes exceedingly exalted. [The fire] within is diminished, yet the great kitchen [of the body] remains.

For men who are running [on the path], the mind attains a non-trivial manifestation from its state of dissolution through the rising moon of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Therein is the *maṇipūraka* located at the navel, endowed with ten petals having the luster of blue collyrium;
there, the first ten syllables are situated upon the petals, their tips shimmering with *bindus*. [Therein resides] Lākinī...

Constantly established in meditative absorption through dhyāna, men perform only the subjugation, attraction, neutralization of poison, and the shaking of cities; for the virtuous who have dedicated themselves to this place,
there shall be the attainment of Pātāla-siddhi, as well as the accomplishment of the peerless Parā-ṣaḍga and whatever else is desired on earth.
Form is the abandonment of the [lower] planes, the power to enter another's body, the destruction of old age,

the pacification of all suffering and disease, and the deception of Time itself. In the heart is that lotus which they call "Unstruck" (anāhata), possessing the color of vermilion, twilight clouds, cinnabar, and gold, and containing the essence of mercury.
It is adorned with petals numbering twelve, graced by the Bhairavas beginning with Krodhīśa—twelve in number and endowed with staffs—and possessed of fierce power;
it is presided over by Kākinī and by the Goddess through her divine power, as well as eternally by the Lord in the form of a swan. In this [lotus]...

O one of excellent intellect, for the yogi whose mind is constantly established in the state [of the Self], divine women endowed with wondrous forms and beauty, though stationed in celestial palaces, become agitated; his knowledge becomes incomparable, pertaining to the three times, and there arises agitation within the city [of the body], as well as hearing from afar and vision.

The Union with the Yoginīs: At the throat is the lotus known as Viśuddha, endowed with the luster of smoke-colored bees, possessing sixteen petals associated with the vowels beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha. In this place resides the Goddess Śākinī, whose own power is equal to that of the Lord; she is the eternal Goddess who brings relief from the suffering of worldly existence.

For that bull among men whose mind is perpetually established here through the yoga of practice, there arises competence even in sciences not studied; he becomes the most excellent on this surface of the earth. A person whose mind is fixed on the place and the eyes becomes a seer of the three times, freed from all diseases.

Having conquered old age, with hair as black as collyrium, the yogi lives long on earth, free from death. If the enraged yogi, having restrained his breath and constantly fixed his mind upon this spot, were to move the entire three worlds,
neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Indra, nor even the sun could quell his power.

Nor is there impurity, nor even Gaṇapa. In the center of the pair of eyebrows is the Command (ājñā), endowed with a pair of petals, shining like the rays of the autumnal moon. Here too, the goddess Hākinī is joined; one should contemplate the two syllables on the pair of petals as being endowed with the nasal bindu. For one intent on the yoga of meditation, [the fruits] produced in previous births arise.

There is remembrance of past actions. Here, in the abode of the Bindu, the powers of seeing and hearing from afar are accomplished. In this place, a man whose own mental fluctuations are stilled performs conversation with a statue, travels to another city, and furthermore, brings back to life even one who is dead. [He attains] the supportless *mudrā* of his own...
Having mastered this very place through the oral instruction of the Guru, the excellent practitioner, with his intellect firmly established here,

constantly perceives through practice the infinite abode of the wind (Anilayāna), the entire series of Viṣṇu’s worlds, and even the Lord of the Stars (the Moon). He beholds Brahmā, whose pair of feet is worshipped by the hosts of gods.
Likewise, he [saw] Mukunda, Śambhu, the leader of the hosts of gods, the lord of the departed spirits, and the lord of the waters;
the fire of the days, the Lord Wind, Tārkṣya the sovereign of birds,
the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, the Siddhas with their hosts, and the renowned Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.

The yogi beholds within his mother the divine sages, bulls among men, and those of auspicious form— the Vidyādharas— endowed with a multitude of radiant splendors, as well as the river of the heavenly realm, its waters joined by lofty, dancing waves.
He possesses the luster of the ocean of milk and the golden mountain; his divine body is bent by the weight of high, full, and supple breasts; he is mounted upon an elephant as his vehicle;
his pair of eyes shine like flickering flames, while his glances are as tremulous as those of a startled fawn; and likewise, there is a multitude of celestial nymphs.

He beheld the best of mountains, charming with their lofty peaks that seemed to veil the expanse of the sky, adorned with girdles of various shimmering gems; likewise, he saw the delightful forest lands filled with deer and antelopes,
as well as the vast earth endowed with its diverse fields.
In this [ocean], there is a most wonderful expenditure of high waves that are like herds of elephants for the sun,
of formidable clouds that are like excellent mountains, and likewise of the oceans filled with the waters of the celestial river,
as well as of the lakes frequented by cranes and filled with rows of swans.

In that supreme state, the sole root of great bliss, the yogi whose mind is steady should unite his own mental faculty with the *mudrā*. Through this supportless [state], he gradually attains identity with That; thereafter, by the power of dissolution, his own innate great bliss manifests within. When the mind has dissolved therein...

In the abode of the universe, like sparks first seen from fire, and thereafter like radiant sprouts of a lamp; like the light of the young sun spreading through vast spaces, or like the moonlight shining within the interior of the earth— that splendor which is called "Eternal Bliss" and "Lord of Śrī."
The illustrious Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, is called the Self; for He is the Yogin of inconceivable majesty whom yogis perceive.
In this supreme station, that very Lord, the imperishable Witness, becomes manifest, residing within the orb of the moon and the sun, having entered into the innermost core of all.

This is the great abode of the Blessed One, the refuge of the universe; this is that state into which virtuous men, at the departure of their life-breath, place the vital wind and enter— that divine, supreme, ancient Puruṣa,
known through the Vedāntas, the Seer, the primordial source of all, the eternal and singular root of great bliss.

The Lord [resides] within the thousand-petaled lotus, which is below the *visarga* and faces downward, with its mass of filaments slightly reddened. Within that, the moon—devoid of its deer-mark, possessing three peaks, and shimmering with a network of rays—rests as nectar. Inside that is the extremely subtle *brahmarandhra*.

That which serves as the support for the channel known as Suṣumṇā— this very state is divine, exceedingly secret, inaccessible even to the gods, and must be guarded with great effort. This is the supreme Kula-state called Kailāsa, where the God of gods, Maheśa— the swan that destroys the darkness of the fear of worldly existence— dwells in the form of the Bindu and in the form of the Sky (Kha).

The primordial source of all beings, who pours forth a continuous, pure stream of liquefied essence within the inner self, bestowing desired fruits upon yogins and being attainable through yoga; by the mere knowledge of this place,
there shall be no further rebirth for men in this cycle of existence, as they continuously practice upon the assembly of elements.

Through yoga, one may possess complete power to create and destroy; having fixed the mind here upon the supreme abode named Kailāsa, the dwelling place of Haṃsa, the yogi—whose afflictions have been destroyed and whose obstacles removed—lives for a long time, liberated from death like one whose disease has vanished. In this place, [the power] is eternally risen, free from the states of decay and growth, and directed downwards.
She exists as the sixteenth digit of the moon, possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun;

she is similar to a single one-hundredth part of a hair-tip split into a hundred pieces, and because of her subtlety, she incessantly bears a stream of flowing nectar. Beyond her stands the Blessed Lady.

She is the sovereign lord of the presiding deities of the elements, known as Nirvāṇa; she is curved like the crescent moon and resides within the sixteenth digit. Because of her subtlety, she is comparable to a single strand of a hair split a thousandfold;
she is the mother of the three worlds, possessing the radiance of twelve suns. She is situated above the plane of the digit called Nirvāṇa, and she is Nirvāṇa itself.

The power (*śakti*) of the tip of a hair, which is as profound as the splendor of ten million suns at their furthest limit—this Mother of all beings is equal even to a ten-millionth part of that; she is eternally risen, stainless, the moon-like gateway to the state of eternal bliss, a supportless stream of liberation. Beyond this power of Nirvāṇa lies that which is higher than the highest.

The state of Śiva is eternal, immeasurable, stainless, perpetually manifest, and actionless. Regarding that, some wise ones declare it to be "the station of Viṣṇu," others "the station of Brahmā," some "the station of Haṃsa," some "the stainless station," and others "the supportless. Thus, having repeatedly superimposed their own powers [upon it].

Having meditated in sequence with a concentrated heart upon the single Self residing together with [the powers] in the stations ending with the Ājñā-cakra, and having led [the consciousness] from the beginningless up to the end of the sky, one should meditate on Her who resides within the great lotus of the *khagama* (the void) for the attainment of desired fruits— Her whose form is pure consciousness.
Having first [worshipped] Śakti,

one should drink the flood of divine nectar directly from the Swan residing in the great lotus-dwelling in the sky— which resembles lac-dye— and then enter once again the central region of the Kula; in every single wheel (cakra).
One should gradually satisfy all those deities, beginning with the Hākinīs, with the spreading nectar-essence;
then one should satisfy that Kuṇḍalinī who dwells in the lotus-born [lotus].
Now, the six acts (ṣatkarma). In the Haṭhapradīpikā:
Dhautī, vastī, netī, trāṭaka, naulika, and kapālabhāti— these are declared to be the six purificatory practices (ṣatkarma).
This sixfold ritual action, which purifies the vessel and bestows manifold virtues, is kept secret and is honored by the foremost among yogis.
Now, Dhautī.
One who knows the practice of *dhautakarma* should slowly swallow a cloth four fingers wide that has been moistened, and then withdraw it again; this is done through repeated practice.
Cough, asthma, splenic disorders, skin diseases, phlegmatic ailments, and abscesses—by the power of the *dhautī* practice, these surely vanish; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the enema.

In water reaching up to the navel, one who knows the practice of *vasti* should assume the *utkaṭāsana* posture with the nozzle inserted into the anus and perform the contraction of the *ādhāra*. Through repeated practice, this is accomplished.
Even gulmodara arising from vāta, spleen disorders, pitta, and kapha—
all such maladies are subdued by the power of the enema therapy (basti-karma).
The practice of water enema bestows clarity upon the elements, the sense organs, and the internal organs;
it grants luster and the power of digestion, and destroys the accumulation of all defects.
Then, "not this."
One should insert a thread, smooth as a span in length, into the nasal passage and cause it to emerge from the mouth; this is called *sāhinī* by the perfected ones (*siddhas*).
She is indeed the purifier of the skull and the bestower of divine vision;
she swiftly destroys the multitude of diseases born above the navel.
Now, the practice of *trāṭaka*.
With a concentrated mind and steady gaze, one should look at a subtle object until tears begin to flow; this is considered *trāṭaka* by the noble ones.
This churning is a bolt against eye diseases, drowsiness, and the like;
and this *trāṭaka* should be kept secret, like a casket of gold.
Now, naulī.
When one whirls the trunk rapidly to the left and right with the force of a swift vortex,
this is proclaimed as the *anāulī* yoga.
This Naulī, the crest-jewel of Haṭha practices, indeed kindles the weak digestive fire, maintains the pacifying fire, bestows bliss,
and likewise dries up all defects and diseases.
Now follows the Kapālabhātī.
Like the bellows of blacksmiths, with equal inhalation and exhalation and steady movement, it is known as Kapālabhāti; it dries up the disorder of phlegm.
Now, the mudrās.
In the *Pavanayogasaṃgraha*.
Mahāmudrā, the great bond (mahābandha), the great penetration (mahāvedha), and khecarī;
then śakticāla, mūlabandha, and beyond that, uḍḍiyāna.
The bindu called Jālandhara and likewise the inverted posture (viparītakṛti) are described in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Just as the Ganges is indeed the leader of all mountains, forests,
and the earth, so too is Kuṇḍalī indeed the leader of all Yoga-tantras.
Awakened by the grace of the Guru, she who was asleep becomes a giver of bliss;
likewise, all the lotuses and even the knots are pierced asunder.
The path of emptiness for the vital breath is like a royal highway;
likewise, the mind becomes supportless, and thus there is the deception of time.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be intent on the practice of *mudrā* in order to awaken the Goddess who is sleeping at the entrance of the door of Brahman.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), the Great Lock (Mahābandha), the Great Piercing (Mahāvedha), and Khecarī; Uḍḍiyāṇa, Mūlabandha, and the lock known as Jālandhara.
The Karaṇī, known as the Viparītā, and likewise the Śakticālana—
this indeed is the group of nine mudrās that is free from old age and death.
This divine [teaching] was proclaimed by Ādinātha; it bestows the eight sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya), is beloved by all the Siddhas, and is difficult even for the gods to attain.
It must be guarded with great effort, like a casket of jewels; it must never be told to anyone, just as the secret lovemaking of a woman of noble family is kept hidden.
Now, regarding Mahāmudrā, [it is stated] in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The purification of the network of channels, the joining of the moon and the sun,
and the thorough purification of the vital essences— this is designated as Mahāmudrā.
In that which was spoken by Īśvara.
In this tantra, I shall proclaim Mahāmudrā, my beloved,
by attaining which the Siddhas of old, such as Kapila and others, attained accomplishment.
Having respectfully pressed with the root of the foot using the *apasavya* (leftward) motion, one should,
according to the teacher’s instruction, [direct it] toward the *yoni* located between the anus and the genitals.
Holding both feet fully extended with the pair of hands,
having restrained the nine gates, and placing the chin upon the heart;
Having fixed the mind at the crossroads, one should begin the retention of the vital winds;
this is Mahāmudrā, which is concealed in all the tantras.
Having practiced with the left side, one should practice again with the right side;
the yogi, with a restrained mind, should perform the breath control (prāṇāyāma) equally.
Having obtained this mudrā, which is well-guarded, from the mouth of the Guru,
even a yogi of poor fortune attains success by means of this rite.
The movement of all the channels, the retention of the bindu,
and the digestion of the kaṣāya result in the destruction of sins.
It heats the Kuṇḍalinī, causes the vital breath to enter the aperture of Brahmā,
pacifies all diseases, and increases the digestive fire.
It bestows the beauty and splendor of the body, destroys old age and death,
fulfills desired aims, grants strength, happiness, and the subduing of the senses.
All these have been described for the yogin who has ascended the path;
through practice they shall surely come under his control—of this there is no need for doubt.
This mudrā, worshipped by the gods, must be guarded with great effort;
for by attaining it, yogins go to the further shore of the ocean of existence.
For this mudrā, which is like a wish-fulfilling cow for practitioners, has been taught by me;
it should be performed with secret conduct and must not be given to just anyone.
Indeed, this Mahāmudrā is praised by the great adepts (mahāsiddhas),
for through it the great afflictions, defects such as death and the like, are digested.
"And for that very reason, the best of the wise call it Mahāmudrā," so it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
Just as a snake struck by a staff takes on the form of the staff,
so too does the innate power Kuṇḍalinī become straightened.
Pressing the vulva with the left foot and holding the extended right foot with both hands, one should fill the mouth [with air].
Having applied the binding at the throat, one should hold the breath upwards;
thus it removes the state of death that rests within the two-legged being.
For indeed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all tastes become flavorless;
even if one has consumed terrible poison, it is digested like nectar.
Consumption, leprosy, constipation, abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and other such ailments—
the bodily humors of one who practices Mahāmudrā go to their destruction.
The Great Bond.
As proclaimed by Īśvara.
With one leg extended, place it upon the thigh;
contracting the anus and the perineum, draw the *apāna* upward.
Having joined them together and made them equal, the wise man should bind the prāṇa with its face turned downward for the sake of the upward movement of both apāna and prāṇa.
This great bandha has been described as the bestower of the path to perfection;
it leads the collection of fluids flowing through the channels upward for the yogi.
One should accomplish each [task] with both feet with great effort;
however, according to the opinion of some in this matter, one should avoid binding the neck.
One should raise the two "king-teeth" there with the tongue;
through practice, the vital air (vāyu) becomes joined within the middle of the suṣumṇā.
By this [practice], the luster of the body, the cage of bones with firm joints,
and the full heart— these become the hallmarks of a yogi.
By means of this bond, the lord of yogis shall accomplish all that is desired;
indeed, having effected the unification of the apāna and prāṇa breaths throughout the three worlds.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
One should place the heel of the left foot in the region of the vagina,
and likewise place the right foot upon the left thigh.
Having filled the mouth with air, one should likewise press the chin against the heart; then, having compressed the *yoni* and contracted it, one should fix the mind in the center.
And one should perform it very slowly; this is called the Great Bind (mahābandha).
Indeed, this Great Bind bestows the great siddhis.
He is skilled in releasing the great bond of the noose of time;
indeed, he is the one who obstructs the upward movement of all the channels.
It brings about the confluence of the three rivers (Triveṇī) and leads the mind to Kedāra;
now follows the Great Destruction (Mahāvadha).
Just as a woman or a man, though endowed with beauty and grace, is fruitless without a partner,
so too the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) and the Great Lock (Mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of penetration (vedha).
Established in the great bond (mahābandha), the yogi, having performed a single pūraka,
should arrest the movement of the vital airs by means of the throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā) while remaining perfectly still.
With the two hands joined together, one should slowly strike the buttocks against the ground;
by pressing down upon the two hollows of the abdomen, the vital air (vāyu) pulsates within the center.
The union of the moon, sun, and fire arises and becomes immortal;
since the state of immortality has been produced, whence can there be fear of death?
The Great Piercing (mahāvedha), which bestows great accomplishment through practice and destroys wrinkles,
gray hair, and disease, is cultivated by the most excellent practitioners.
This triad is a great secret that destroys old age and death,
increases the digestive fire, and bestows the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
It is indeed performed eightfold, every watch and day after day;
it always accumulates a mass of merit and shatters the flood of sins.
Even for those who possess perfect training, the first stage of accomplishment is very brief when spoken by Īśvara.
The wise yogi, established in Mahābandha and filling the abdomen with air, should strike the buttocks; this is proclaimed by me as Vedha.
Having pierced with this piercing, that bull among yogis pierces the knots along the path of the suṣumṇā and reaches the aperture of Brahmā by means of the vital air.
For one who constantly practices the well-guarded Mahābandha,
there shall be mastery over the vital winds (vāyu), which destroys old age and death.
The deities situated within the center of the wheel tremble from the blow of the wind;
even Kuṇḍalī, the Great Māyā, dissolves into the portion of Kailāsa.
Therefore, the yogi should diligently perform this triad in sequence;
he who performs this triad with diligence four times [attains the goal].
Within six months, one certainly conquers death; of this there is no doubt.
Only a perfected being (siddha) knows the majesty of these three, and no other.
Having known which, all the *siddhas* attained the title of "perfected" for a long time;
therefore, one who desires accomplishment (*siddhi*) should conceal this practice with great effort.
Otherwise, this determination of the mudrās would not be established. Thus [ends the section on mudrās]; now follows khecarī.
In the *Yogabīja*.
A length of one span (vitasti) and a width of four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula),
soft and white— this is declared to be the characteristic of the supporting cloth for wrapping.
Thus, in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
One should gradually lengthen the tongue by means of cutting, moving, and stretching, until it touches the space between the eyebrows; then the perfection of Khecarī is attained.
Having turned the *kalā* away from oneself, one should cause it to revolve in the triple path;
that becomes the *khecarī-mudrā*, and it is called the *vyomacakra*.
If one holds the tongue upward for even half a moment,
the yogi is liberated from sense objects and from disease, death, old age, and the like.
For one by whom the aperture above the uvula is sealed by Khecarīmudrā,
and who is embraced by the Kāminī, the bindu does not leak.
Even when the drop has moved and reached the fire,
it indeed goes upward and enters through the *yoni-mudrā* as Āniruddha.
In the procedure for the *saṃpātana* [offering], there is a drop (*bindu*) that is pale and likewise red;
"pale" is said to mean white, while that called "red" is *mahārajata* [gold].
The seed-syllable resembling vermilion is the *rajas* situated in the place of the sun;
the *bindu* is situated in the place of the moon. The unification of these two is extremely difficult to attain.
The *bindu* is Śiva and the *rajas* is Śakti; the *bindu* is the moon and the *rajas* is the sun. When they attain oneness with the *bindu*, then the divine body arises.
Semen is conjoined with the moon, and the menstrual flow is conjoined with the sun;
he who knows their equal merging into oneness is a knower of yoga.
The semen of men depends upon the mind, and life depends upon the semen;
therefore, both the mind and the semen must be protected with great effort.

That which exists in the netherworld, in the sky, on the peaks, and at the base of Mount Meru—that reality resides here before the rivers, as the wise one proclaims. From the moon, the essence flows from his body;
by that [essence], death comes to men. One should bind it with the clay of one's own senses; otherwise, there is no perfection of the body.
Just as fire does not leave its fuel, nor a lamp its oil and wick,
so the embodied soul never abandons the body, which is eternally filled with the digits of the moon.
One should cause the tongue to rise upward and drink the water thus made to flow;
one should daily eat beef and drink the blood of a horse.
I consider him to be of noble birth, and not others who are destroyers of their lineage;
for the tongue spoken of by the word "cow" (go) enters the palate.
That consumption of beef, however, is the destroyer of great sins;
it is indeed produced by the fire generated from the entry of the tongue.
From the moon let that nectar flow which is the wine of the immortals;
there is one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, and the single mudrā is Khecarī.
A single region is without support; a single state is *manonmanī*.
There is no posture equal to that of the Siddhas, and no *kumbhaka* comparable to the *kevala*.
There is no mudrā equal to khecarī, nor is there any dissolution (laya) like that of nāda.

Having forcefully restrained the tongue with the face turned upward, one should contemplate the supreme power (parā śakti) within the opening, [the power] which has flowed from the sixteen-petaled lotus of the head and been obtained through the vital breath (prāṇa).

The yogi who drinks that pure water, which is like the waves and digits of the moon, from the *jihvākula* (the family of the tongue), remains free from defects; with a body as tender as a lotus stalk, he lives for a long time. If the tongue, vibrating with its own essence, constantly kisses the tip of the *lambikā* (uvula) and tastes a flavor like salt, pungent, sour, or milk—[then he attains immortality].

It is always equal to honey and clarified butter; it removes diseases, brings an end to old age, and upholds the scriptures and traditions. For him, there shall be eightfold supernatural powers (siddhis) in this world, including the power to attract celestial women.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in the reverse direction,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that is the Khecarī Mudrā.
The mind moves through the void, and the tongue moves having gone into the void;
this is indeed that which is called Khecarī, practiced by those who have attained the siddhis of the mudrās.
As long as the seal of the expanded sky remains, the drop does not depart;
as long as the drop is stable within the body, whence can there be fear of time?
He who knows the khecarī-mudrā is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tainted by karma; he is not oppressed by time.
Placing the tongue in the cavity of the palate with the face turned upward, one should drink [the nectar];
having become immortal, one shall attain agelessness within six months—of this there is no doubt.
The knower of yoga who, having become steady, turns his tongue upward and performs the drinking of the moon (soma),
undoubtedly conquers death within half a month.
Pressing the great cavity of the upper teeth with the tip of the tongue and meditating upon the Goddess who consists of nectar, one becomes a poet within six months.
For the yogi whose body is filled with nectar, after two or three years,
semen begins to flow upward, and the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) arise.
The body of that yogi which is perpetually filled with the digits of the moon does not suffer from poison, even when bitten by Takṣaka; the venom does not spread within it.
Dattātreya.
Having drawn back the tongue and placed it within the cavity of the inner skull,
with the gaze fixed between the eyebrows— this is the Khecarī Mudrā.
For him who knows the Khecarī Mudrā, there is neither disease nor death, neither sleep nor hunger or thirst, and there shall be no fainting.
As proclaimed by Īśvara.
The wise practitioner should diligently join the tongue, turned upward, into the cavity situated above the uvula, within the well of nectar.
This mudrā is declared to be Khecarī out of consideration for devotees;
one who practices it continuously shall drink nectar every day.
By that, the accomplishment of the body occurs; this is the Khecarī Mudrā, known as Mṛtyumātaṅga-khecarī, which belongs to him who remains well-established and unwearied in it.
For even when a hundred Brahmās have passed, he indeed considers it but half a moment.
Now, the root-lock (mūlabandha).
Pressing firmly with the soles of his feet and well-restraining the anal passage,
he should forcefully draw up the *apāna* wind and practice its upward movement in gradual stages.

This root-lock (mūlabandha) has been described; it destroys old age and death, brings about the union of the downward-moving breath (apāna) and the upward-moving breath (prāṇa), and effects the cessation of urine and feces.
By means of this binding, the *yonimudrā* is most effectively accomplished.
When the *yonimudrā* is mastered, what on this earth is not accomplished?
By the grace of this *bandha*, the yogi, having conquered the wind in the sky and remaining in the *padmāsana* posture, moves about while leaving the earth behind.
O bull among yogis, if you wish to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, you should practice this binding in a well-concealed and solitary place.
Thus, in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Having pressed the perineum with the heel, one should contract the anus;
drawing the *apāna* upward, this is called *mūlabandha*.
The downward-moving *apāna* wind, by means of forceful contraction, one causes to move upward;
yogis call this the *mūlabandha*.
Thus, in the *Yogabīja*.
Pressing the anus with the heel, one should forcefully contract the wind;
in this manner, the vital air repeatedly moves upward.
When the prāṇa and apāna, as well as nāda and bindu, attain oneness through the mūlabandha, they reach the perfect accomplishment of yoga; of this there is no doubt.
When the apāna moves upward and reaches the region of fire,
it is struck by the wind and grows long like a flame of fire.
Then the downward-moving breath (apāna) and the fire departed, leaving the upward-moving breath (prāṇa) as their essential nature;
by that, the fire born of the body was utterly inflamed.
By that means, the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī is constantly awakened;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, she certainly attains straightness.
Just as one who has entered a house [sees its interior], so too does one proceed through the internal channels of Brahman;
therefore, the root-lock (mūlabandha) should be constantly performed by the best of yogis.
The Uḍḍiyāna-bandha, as described in the Yogabīja.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa), when bound by this [bandha], is made to fly upward through the Suṣumṇā,
it is therefore proclaimed by yogins as "Uḍḍīyāna."
For this reason, the great bird flies upward without ceasing.
That itself is known as Uḍḍīyāna, and it is called Mūlabandha;
one should perform the backward contraction of the abdomen above the navel.
Uḍḍiyāna is indeed the unbreakable bond, the lion that destroys the elephant of death;
Uḍḍiyāna is the innate state (sahaja), as it was taught by the Guru.
One who practices this without indolence becomes like a youth even if aged;
one should diligently perform the upward or downward movement of the breath from the navel.
If one practices for six months, one certainly conquers death; there is no doubt.
(From the *Haṭhapradīpikā*)
While in the vajra posture, one should firmly hold the feet with both hands near the region of the ankles, and press the abdomen against them.
One should cause the abdomen to extend toward the back and the chin to reach the heart,
very slowly, so that the vital breath does not enter the stomach.
Indeed, among all the locks (bandhas), Uḍḍiyānaka is the supreme;
when the Uḍḍiyāna lock is firmly established, the root [kanda] becomes natural.
As proclaimed by Īśvara.
One should practice the contraction [of the abdomen] intensely, both above and below the navel;
this is the Uḍḍiyāna Bandha, which destroys the flood of all suffering.
The yogi who performs this daily four times every day shall attain purification of the navel, by which the vital breath becomes perfected.
The yogi who practices for six months, knowing the reality, conquers death;
his digestive fire blazes and an increase in vital essence occurs.
By this, the accomplishment of the body is produced even more effectively;
furthermore, the destruction of diseases certainly occurs for the yogin.
Having received [the instruction] from the guru with diligence, the wise one should practice it in a secluded and well-situated place; for this supreme bond is extremely difficult to attain.
Now, Jālandhara.
Having bound the network of the neck and head, one should place the chin upon the heart;
this is declared to be the Jālandhara-bandha, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The fire residing in the navel of living beings drinks the nectar-like essence that has fallen from the thousand-petaled lotus; for that purpose, one should bind this [mudrā].
By means of this practice, the wise person drinks nectar himself;
and having attained immortality, he rejoices throughout the three worlds.
This is the Jālandhara-bandha, which bestows success upon the perfected ones;
it should be practiced constantly by the yogi who desires accomplishment.
In the *Yogabīja*.
Contracting the throat, one should fix it firmly at the heart with resolve;
this is the lock known as Jālandhara, which brings about the immortality and imperishability of *yama*.
Thus, in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
It binds the mass of hair here [at the head] so that the water from the sky flows downward;
therefore, it is called Jālandhara, the destroyer of the flood of suffering in the throat.
When the Jālandhara lock, characterized by the contraction of the throat, is performed,
the nectar does not fall into the fire, nor does the vital wind become agitated.
This middle wheel is to be known as the binding of the sixteen supports;
this triad of bindings is supreme, practiced by the great adepts.
For yogins in the practice of all the Haṭha Tantras.
Now, the practice that effects the reversal [of the flow] in Haṭhayoga.
The sun, whose nature is fire, resides eternally in the region of the navel;
and the moon, whose nature is nectar, resides eternally in the middle of the palate.
The moon rains downward while the sun swallows upward;
that method must be performed by which that nectar is obtained.
Having blocked the nectar of the lunar digit within the pure supreme wheel,
that which has been prepared travels by that path, bypassing the mouth of the Sun.
Having placed the nectar in the cave at the tip of the nose, it gradually moves upward on the peak;
having bypassed the mouth of the sun, it proceeds by its own power.
The pure water of the moon's digits increases and rises from the region of the throat to the tip of the nose;
from there, it reaches the sky through the aperture at the crown.
Standing above, one who has conquered the senses should drink this as it falls down upon the earth while he remains with his feet upturned; indeed, for such a person, there is no further rebirth.
Its exhaustion.
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Whatever nectar of divine form flows from the moon, the sun swallows it all; by that, the body is destroyed.
In that regard, the divine means of realization is the binding of the mouth of the Sun;
it is to be known through the instruction of the Guru, and not by millions of scriptural arguments.
The navel is above and the palate is below; the sun is above and the moon is below.
This practice called the "reversal" (viparītakaraṇī) destroys all diseases.
Dattātreya.
The sun is above and the moon is below; listen to this, O Sāṅkṛti:
on the first day, [the deity] remains for a moment with head downward and feet upward.
And one should practice for slightly more than a moment day after day;
within six months and a half, both strength and grey hair will be seen [to vanish].
He who practices this constantly for even a single watch (yāma) becomes a conqueror of time;
for one engaged in constant practice, the digestive fire is increased.
O Sāṃkṛti, abundant food mixed with clarified butter should be prepared for him;
for if the fire should have little food, it will surely cause a burning sensation.
Now, the movement of the *śakti*,
as spoken by the Lord.
The wise man, having drawn up the apāna wind and forcefully contracting it, should firmly awaken Kuṇḍalinī who is sleeping in the foundational lotus (ādhāra-cakra).
For he who practices the activation of the *śakti* in this manner every day,
there shall be an increase of digestive fire and the destruction of diseases.
Just as a female serpent abandons sleep and remains upright by her own power,
so too must a yogi who desires perfection practice this discipline.
He who constantly practices the supreme *śakticālana* will attain the perfection of the body (*vigrahasiddhi*), which bestows the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.

By means of the method of the guru’s instruction, whence can there be fear of death for him? For a period of two muhūrtas, one should practice the movement of the *śakti* according to the prescribed rule.
One should constantly practice for half a month while remaining in the vajrāsana posture.
The fire, kindled by the vital wind (vāyu), burns the kuṇḍalinī throughout the night.
By that intensely heated fire, the channel (nāḍī) and the power (śakti) that deludes the three worlds are purified.
Entering through the opening of the *suṣumṇā* with the diamond-beak [of the mind],
she pierces the *brahmagranthi* together with the wind and the fire.
Then, having pierced the Viṣṇu-knot, one remains at the Rudra-knot;
thereafter, one fills [the breath] intensely through kumbhaka again and again.
Just as knots are split in a bamboo stalk by a heated iron rod,
so too are the knots split in the spinal column by the vital wind (vāyu).
When an ant has bitten [the body], an itch arises there;
likewise, due to the breath, it occurs constantly through the wind in the *suṣumṇā*.
"Then, having pierced the Rudra-knot, one proceeds from there to that which is of the nature of Śiva," so it is said in the Haṭhayoga.
Just as one might forcibly open a door with a key,
so too the yogi should pierce the gate of liberation by means of Kuṇḍalinī.
Having covered with her mouth that gate through which one must go to the stainless abode of Brahmā, the Supreme Goddess lies fast asleep.
Above the bulb (kanda) resides the Kuṇḍalinī power; knowing this leads to liberation for yogis, while for the deluded it leads to bondage—he who knows this is a knower of Yoga.
Just as Śeṣa, the coiled serpent, is the support of the oceans, mountains, and islands,
so too is Kuṇḍalinī the support of all the Yoga Tantras without exception.
Kuṇḍalāṅgī, Kuṇḍalinī, Bhujaṅgī, Śakti, Īśvarī,
Kuṭilā, Arundhatī, and Devī are synonymous terms.
Coiled in the shape of a ring, she is proclaimed to be like a serpent.
He by whom that Śakti is set in motion is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā dwells the ascetic Bālaraṇḍā.
One should seize that supreme abode of Viṣṇu by force;
like a female serpent seizing a tail, one should awaken her who is asleep.
Abandoning sleep, she rises straight up with force;
remaining coiled like a serpent for half a watch from morning until evening,
she completes her circumambulation and, having cast off her garment, she goes forth, moving about.
The yogi, seated in the vajra posture, having stirred the kuṇḍalī,
should quickly awaken the kuṇḍalī by means of the bellows-breathing immediately after the solar breath.
One should perform the contraction of the sun and then stir Kuṇḍalinī;
for one who has done so, even if he has entered the mouth of Death, whence can there be fear of death?
The wind flowing through the right nostril, drawn in through the nose, lengthened, and filled with the lunar water to form a body of nectar, first reaches the uvula; then,
piercing the multitude of channels and apertures of the limbs that have fallen under the power of the vast fire of Time, it transforms that body.
Like the trunk of an old tree becoming new again,
one should move the *kuṇḍalinī* and especially perform the *bhastrā* [breathing technique].
Through such constant practice, Yama himself fears the self-controlled practitioner.
Then one should practice Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, and Śītalī;
for one who is thus engaged in practice, how could there be any lack of restraint for that self-controlled practitioner?
Indeed, by practicing intense movement for a period of two muhūrtas,
it is always beneficial for one who is devoted to celibacy and eats food that is wholesome and moderate.
Success in the maṇḍala is seen for the yogin who practices kuṇḍalinī;
it is the purification of the impurities of the seventy-two thousand channels.
Whence can there be a means of cleansing without the repeated practice of *kuṇḍalī*?

In this matter, regarding the activation of the power (*śakti*), only the *padmāsana* is to be seen, not the *vajrāsana*, because it contradicts actual experience. And so it is stated in another text:
Having joined the two hands in the *saṃpuṭita* gesture, firmly assuming the *padmāsana* posture, placing the chin tightly against the chest, and fixing the mind upon that meditation,
one should repeatedly expel the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) upward, fill the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and then release it.
"Awakening occurs with certainty through the arising of the awakening of power.
Thus were the nine mudrās proclaimed by Śambhu, the Primordial Lord;
each one bestows great accomplishment upon those who practice restraint.
Dattātreya.
The distinction [between the results] arises from the difference in practice, yet the fruit is indeed the same;
the sequence of practice has been explained in the *Pavanasaṃgraha*.
Having thoroughly practiced Mahāmudrā, one should thereafter certainly perform Mahābandha,
Mahāvedha, and the movement of the vital energy (śakticālana).
Having assumed a very firm posture and performed the mūlabandha,
one should likewise perform the uḍḍiyānabandha and then that known as the jālandharabandha.
The connection is with the word "should practice" (*abhyaset*), as found in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
Having drawn up the root-seat, one should perform the uḍḍiyāna-bandha;
having bound the iḍā and piṅgalā, one should cause [the breath] to flow along the western path.
By this very method, one should serve the abode of the wind;
then death, as well as old age, disease, and so forth, do not arise.
Thus, in the Yogabīja.
When the fourfold division of *kumbhaka* has arrived,
these three *bandhas* which I shall clearly describe must be performed.
At the end of inhalation (pūraka), the lock known as Jālandhara should be performed;
at the end of retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of exhalation (recaka), the Uḍḍiyāna lock should be performed.
Then, by quickly contracting [the anus] and constricting the throat,
and by extending the middle [channel] backward, the vital breath shall enter the Brahma-nāḍī.

Having raised the *apāna* upward and led the *prāṇa* down from the throat, the yogi, being liberated from old age, becomes sixteen years of age through his vital energy (*vayas*). Because of the natural occurrence of *uḍḍiyāna*, it should be performed during the state of *kumbhaka*. Regarding this, some say: "Even though [this practice] belongs only to perfected beings such as Kapila..."

They say that although [the practices of] Mahāmudrā and so forth are not accepted by sages such as Yājñavalkya, they should nevertheless be understood as being common [to all]. However, that is devoid of an understanding of the meaning of the text. For instance, in the section on the arising of the *nāda*: "Having drawn the *apāna* upward with the *praṇava*, one is composed."

Thus, the *mūlabandha* has been stated here explicitly; by its mention, the *uḍḍiyāna* and *jālandhara* [bandhas] are also implied, since the simultaneous performance of all three was previously demonstrated. Furthermore: "Having drawn the breath into the tongue, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue. Who [is this]?

Regarding the statement, "The wise man should drink the nectar and enjoy complete auspiciousness," it is evident that the drinking of nectar is impossible without the *khecarī* [mudrā]. Therefore, although the *mudrās* were intended for Yājñavalkya and others as well, they have not been specifically explained here because they are well-known in other texts.
This much has been explained; now, however,

for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who is endowed with the previously mentioned external and internal means (*sādhana*) and possesses knowledge of the *ādhāra*, *dhāra*, *mudrā*, *cakras*, and so forth, [this practice serves] as a means to liberation by way of the purification of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*).
The auxiliaries of the injunction that are conducive to the knowledge of the reality of things are now being defined; and so it is stated in the Pātañjala [Yoga-bhāṣya]:
"From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to the discriminative discernment.
This means that from the practice of the limbs of yoga which are about to be described, there occurs the destruction of impurity in the *sattva* of the mind, leading up to discriminative discernment.

The meaning is this: when impurity—known as the afflictions that veil the light—is destroyed, the radiance of knowledge that arises is a sattvic transformation; that [radiance], culminating in discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), is the cause of that discernment.
Furthermore, there is a sūtra intended to enunciate the limbs of yoga: *Yama-niyamāsana*...
"Prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi are the eight ancillaries," so says Yājñavalkya.
I shall explain the constituent parts to you correctly, just as I heard them before;
O Ārgī, with a concentrated mind, listen together with the sages.
Yama and Niyama are proclaimed to be tenfold;
there are eight excellent Āsanas, and among them, three are the most excellent of all.
Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold, and pratyāhāra is fivefold;
dhāraṇā is said to be fivefold, and dhyāna is proclaimed to be sixfold.
Among these, three are declared to be supreme, while samādhi is of a single form;
some, however, desire them to be manifold, explaining each separately in detail.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion,
straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten restraints (yamas).
Not causing distress to any living being at any time, through action, mind, or speech—
that alone is declared by the yogis to be non-violence (ahiṃsā).
Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings, not merely speaking according to the facts;
it is freedom from longing for the property of others through action, mind, and speech.
"Not stealing"—this has been proclaimed by the seers who perceive reality:
[the practice of] never at any time, in any state, and through action, mind, or speech.
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all circumstances is declared to be *brahmacarya*;
it belongs to those established in the stage of *brahmacarya*, to ascetics (*yatis*), and to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).
Indeed, that very practice is called *brahmacarya* for those dwelling in the forest,
as well as the union with one's own wife according to the prescribed rule during each fertile season.
That very same practice is declared to be the life of celibacy (brahmacarya) for those dwelling in the householder stage of life;
indeed, the life of celibacy is proclaimed even for the king who is a householder.
Constant service to the guru is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya);
compassion toward all beings is remembered as universal benevolence.
When other prescribed actions are performed through the deeds of mind, speech, and body—
whether in engagement or in withdrawal— to possess a single, uniform nature is integrity (*ārjava*).
That state of equanimity which embodied beings maintain toward all things, whether pleasant or unpleasant,
is declared by the learned who proclaim the Vedas to be patience itself.
Fortitude is the steadying of the mind in all circumstances— whether in the loss of wealth or kinsmen, in the performance of duties, in prosperity, or in the attainment of those two.
Eight morsels are prescribed for a sage, sixteen for forest-dwellers,
thirty-two for householders, and as much as desired for students of sacred knowledge.
For us, this is measured food, while for others it is eating little;
likewise, purity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External purification is traditionally taught to consist of earth and water, while internal purification is the purification of the mind;
and the purification of the mind is to be understood as being achieved through dharma and the science of the inner self (adhyātma-vidyā).
O sinless one, by means of the dharma of inner knowledge, through one's father or teacher,
[one practices] austerity, contentment, faith in the hereafter, charity, and worship of the Lord.
Listening to the established doctrine, modesty, intelligence, recitation, and vows—these are declared to be the observances (niyamas); hear now all of them individually.
Ascetics declare that the emaciation of the body through the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances, performed according to the path prescribed by rule, is the highest austerity.
This, however, should be observed even before the practice of yoga,
because during the time of practice, physical exhaustion, fasting, and the like are prohibited.
The characteristics such as silence (mauna) mentioned in the Bhagavadgītā are appropriate; for it is said:
"Worship of gods, the twice-born, gurus, and the wise, purity, and uprightness."
Celibacy and non-violence are said to be bodily austerity;
and speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, [is verbal austerity].
The practice of reciting sacred texts is said to be austerity consisting of speech;
serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, and self-restraint constitute austerity of the mind.
"Purity of disposition— this is called mental austerity," says Yājñavalkya.
The sages have declared that contentment, characterized by happiness, is that state of mind which always considers it sufficient for a person to obtain whatever comes by chance.
Faith in what is righteous and unrighteous is called *āstikya*;
and wealth, food, or anything else that is given away, having been acquired through just means.
This is declared to be the gift given with faith to those who seek it;
[it is that which is offered] to Viṣṇu or indeed to Rudra with a serene disposition.

Worship according to one's ability with devotion is indeed the worship of the Lord; a heart free from passion, speech free from falsehood and the like, and a body free from violence— this is the worship of the Lord.
The hearing of the Siddhānta is declared by the wise to be the hearing of the Vedānta;
for a Kṣatriya, as for a twice-born, the hearing of the Siddhānta has been so described by the wise.
And some desire [the protection] of the Vaiśyas who are virtuous and well-conducted,
of the Śūdras, of women, and indeed of ascetics who abide in their own duty.

The wise have declared that listening to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is equivalent to listening to the Purāṇas; however, whatever action may be contemptible according to the Vedic or worldly paths [is not].
The shame that arises toward that [transgression] is indeed proclaimed as *hrī*. Furthermore, when all prescribed duties are performed, that state of mind which consists of faith is *mati*.
Instructed by the Guru and avoiding external distractions, one should drink [the nectar];
the practice of mantra according to the path prescribed by the rule is known as *japa*.
Having studied the Vedas, the Sūtras, the Purāṇas, or the Itihāsas—
that study which is performed upon these is known as constant practice and recitation (japa).
Regarding the subject of the ascetic, Dattātreya stated the specific [vows]:
"Non-stealing, celibacy, renunciation, as well as freedom from greed—
these five are indeed the supreme vows for mendicants, characterized by non-violence."
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food, lightness [of diet],
and daily study of the Vedas— these are proclaimed as the five observances (niyamas).
Also in the Pātañjala [Yogaśāstra].
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the yamas;
purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the niyamas.
Thus it is stated in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Compassion, freedom from laziness, detachment, supreme honesty,
lack of fickleness, fortitude, truthfulness, and knowledge— these they know as *yama*.
In this context, non-cruelty means the absence of killing.
Purity, regulation of diet, freedom from possessiveness, detachment, tranquility,
forbearance, self-restraint, and contentment— these are remembered as the eight observances (niyamas).
Now, regarding the seat;
concerning this, Patañjali says:
Posture is that which is steady and comfortable.

That by means of which one sits is the "seat" (āsana), such as the lotus posture and others; when it becomes immovable, comfortable, and free from agitation, then it attains the status of being a limb of yoga. To that same end—namely, for the attainment of stability and comfort—there is the aphorism: "By relaxation of effort and meditative absorption. In this context, the reading is with the abstract suffix *tva* attached to the word *ananta*.
Bhojadeva [comments]: The connection is that through the relaxation of effort and the attainment of infinity, the posture becomes steady and comfortable.
When one thinks, "I shall assume this posture," it is not accomplished without difficulty even when there is relaxation of effort; when—

When, through focused attention, the mind is brought into meditative absorption (samāpatti) within the infinity of space and attains identity with it, then, due to the absence of the ego-sense of the body, the posture no longer produces discomfort. And when this mastery of posture is achieved, the physical ailments that serve as obstacles to samādhi do not arise.

Regarding "jayatvādayaḥ" and so forth: the traditional interpretation of the Bhāṣya is that the reading of the Sūtra is *ananta-samāpattibhyām* without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*). In this context, the mind is absorbed (*samāpanna*) in Ananta, the leader of the serpents, upon whose many thousand steady hoods the entire circle of the earth is supported.

Vācaspati Miśra explains that [the sūtra] "produces the posture" (*āsana*) provides the definition. However, the general definition of posture (*āsana*) is: "A posture is a particular configuration of the hands and feet.
The specific definitions, however, are found in the *Dharmaputrikā*.
The two feet should be placed upon the ground by the yogin seated on his seat;
the right foot on the left side, and the left foot on the right side.
Having turned the two hands into the form of a deer's head facing each other,
it is called the *mṛgasvastika* for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga.
Standing with the left foot [extended] and the right knee [bent], one should form the hollow of the hands; this they know as the Ardhacandra (Half-moon) posture.
Standing on the ground with both knees [on the floor], the yogi should place his hands together at the heart; this is to be known as the añjalikāsana posture.
With the feet comfortably extended, well-joined, and resting on the ground, one sits with the upper body upright;
this is known as the staff posture (daṇḍāsana).
With both feet placed evenly on the ground while seated,
and having placed the palms of the hands upon the two knees, this constitutes the pīṭhāsana posture.
Thus says Mataṅga.
Having gone behind, one should bind the cross-legged posture with a yoga-band,
properly drawing up both knees, starting from the right sole of the foot.
On the outside, one should place the left calf below the right [thigh] on the exterior;
having drawn it out slightly, one should remain standing while bending the hip.
The posture known as paryaṅka bestows the perfection of yoga.
In the Āgneya Purāṇa.
Having doubled both feet, one should place the hands horizontally and vertically respectively,
with the fingers joined and the nails resting upon the bandage.
This yogapaṭṭa seat is indeed honored by all;
now hear briefly concerning the half-moon [seal].

In the same way, having placed the two feet together with the soles joined, it is called the "Half-moon" (Ardhacandra). This means that, like the lotus posture (padmāsana), one should place the two feet doubled over; likewise, one should arrange the two feet such that their faces are bent toward each other.
Extending both hands so that they rest upon the pillow behind the back—
this is indeed called the Extended Seat (Prasāritāsana), which bestows the accomplishment of yoga.
Vasiṣṭha:
Restraining the anus with the two ankles in reverse order while remaining composed—
those who know yoga recognize this as *kūrmāsana*.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
Then, placing one foot upon the other and remaining with the body erect, he sat; this is the supreme means for accomplishing yoga, known as the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka).
Yājñavalkya.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this they call the Svastika posture.
Having placed the two ankles of the feet against the sides of one's own torso at the seam,
one should place the right ankle on the left side of the back.
Likewise on the right, the left [leg] should be positioned like that of a cow;
then, having placed one foot upon the other thigh, he stands.
Likewise, in the other [posture], the Vīrāsana is described as placing the thighs [on the ground] and the two ankles below the scrotum on either side of the perineal seam.
Placing the right ankle over the left [ankle] and likewise the other with the right,
one should place both hands upon the knees and extend the fingers.
With his face covered, he should gaze at the tip of his nose, well-composed;
this is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogins.
One should place the ankles and testicles on either side of the lower seam (perineum),
and having firmly bound the sides and feet with the hands, remain perfectly motionless.
This is the Bhadrāsana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons;
it is formed by pressing the subtle seam [of the perineum] with the left ankle.
Placing the left foot over the right ankle is called *muktāsana*;
one should firmly press the ground with the palms of both hands.
One should place the hands and elbows at the sides of the navel;
with the head and feet raised, standing like a staff in the air—
this indeed is the Mayūrāsana, which destroys all sins.
All internal diseases and poisons are destroyed;
[as stated] in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
I shall describe some of the postures adopted by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and by yogis such as Matsyendra.
Since it is the first limb of Haṭha, posture (āsana) is described first;
one should practice that which brings stability of posture, health, and lightness of the limbs.

Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs and resting them on the ground, one establishes the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana), which is situated in the void.
Having bound the neck with both arms while assuming the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana), one should remain supine like a tortoise; this is the Uttānakūrma [āsana].
Grasping the two big toes with both hands up to the ears and drawing the bow is called the Dhanurāsana (Bow Posture).

Placing the right foot upon the root of the left thigh and grasping it with the right arm wrapped around the outside of the knees, one should remain with the body turned; this shall be the posture (āsana) declared by the illustrious Matsyanātha. It is the seat of Matsyendra, a weapon for shattering the circle of fierce diseases that have increased within the belly.

Through practice, this awakens the *kuṇḍalinī* and brings stability to the staff-like body of men. Extending both legs on the ground like a staff and grasping the two feet with both hands, one should place the forehead upon the knees and practice this limb known as *paścimatāna*. Thus is the supreme posture, *paścimatāna*.

It causes the wind to flow toward the west; it brings about the awakening of the digestive fire and, for men, leanness and freedom from disease in the abdomen. Pressing the earth with both hands while placing the sides of the navel upon the elbows, rising from that seat like a staff—this is the *Khāmayūra* posture.

The virtuous declare that this glorious *madhura* (mercury) is a seat for all diseases, swiftly removing ailments such as abdominal tumors and enlargements, and subduing the [three] humors (*doṣas*). It reduces to ashes everything eaten, even an abundance of *kadamba* fruits; it generates the digestive fire of the stomach and would digest even *kālakūṭa* poison.
Lying face upward on the ground like a corpse is known as the corpse posture (śavāsana). This corpse posture removes fatigue and is the means for achieving rest of the mind.
Placing one's head on the ground and likewise the elbows on the hands, one should position the feet like a staff; this is declared to be the Naraka posture.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
There are as many types of seats as there are sources of life, all of which are effective; however, among them, two grant swift accomplishment.
Gorakṣa.
Each one is said to consist of eighty-four lakhs;
Maheśvara alone knows all the various divisions of these.
Then Śiva established one hundred and sixteen seats;
these two categories were declared from among all the thrones.
One is declared to be Siddhāsana, the second is Kamalāsana;
thus it is stated in the Haṭhapradīpikā.
Eighty-four postures have indeed been taught by Śiva;
taking from among them a group of four that constitutes the essence, I shall now speak of them.
The fourfold [postures] are Siddha, Padma, Bhadra, and Siṃha;
among these, the Padma is indeed the best, and that is what constitutes Siddhāsana.
On the previously described auspicious lion-throne, Yājñavalkya says:
One should press the *sīvanī* vessel with the left ankle;
it is subtle, located below the two knees, and the right [ankle] is placed upon the left.
O Gārgī, one should bind the calves and thighs above them firmly and without gaps.
With neck, head, and shoulders symmetrical, with back and belly symmetrical,
he stood looking upward at his right ankle with both eyes.
This is called Siddhāsana, which bestows swift accomplishment;
likewise:
