Pressing the anus with the left ankle and likewise pressing the joint with the other [right ankle],
placing the other hand upon the left hand, one should gaze at the crest of the fire.
O Gārgī, when the vital breath (prāṇa), which causes the destruction of life, is indeed restrained by means of one's own posture (āsana),
it then gradually enters the family of fire through drinking.
In the *Pavanayogasaṃgraha*.
Having firmly established the root of the perineum joined with the ocean-base (the perineal junction),
one should place one foot upon the penis; then, with a focused mind, keeping the body perfectly straight and the senses restrained, like a pillar,
one should gaze with a steady vision at the space between the eyebrows.
This Siddhāsana is said to be that which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation for the conscious self; likewise:
Placing the left ankle upon the penis and likewise placing the other ankle upon that,
this becomes the Siddhāsana.
They call this Siddhāsana, and others know it as Padmāsana;
some speak of it as Guptāsana, while others call it Vajrāsana.
Some call this supreme posture "Muktāsana";
thus it is stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*.
Just as moderate diet is primary among the observances (niyamas), even as non-violence is among the restraints (yamas),
so do the wise know this Siddhāsana to be the foremost among all postures (āsanas).
One should practice the Siddhāsana among the eighty-four pīṭhas,
as one would the Suṣumṇā among the seventy-two thousand channels.
Meditating on the Self and restricting his food, for as long as twelve years,
the yogi shall attain perfection through the constant practice of *siddhāsana*.
When the Siddhāsana is attained, what is the use of many other seats that grant tranquility?
For when the vital breath (prāṇānila) is bound with vigilance in the Kevalakumbhaka, [all else is rendered superfluous].
Just as the state of Unmanī will arise spontaneously and without effort when the Siddhāsana is always firmly established in this very manner.
The three bandhas arise spontaneously and without effort.
Now, the *padmāsana*. Yājñavalkya says:
O best of Brahmins, one should bind the two thumbs with the hands in reverse order,
having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs.
This is the lotus posture (padmāsana), honored by all;
having placed [the feet] upon the surface of the earth in a pleasant and level place, one should remain in meditative absorption (samādhi).
Placing the left foot upon the right thigh and the right foot upon the left thigh,
one should draw both shanks together.
For this indeed is called the lotus, the supreme seat of Brahmā,
in Haṭhayoga.
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and likewise the left foot upon the right thigh,
holding them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method, and placing the two big toes at the heart,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose; this is the *padmāsana*, which destroys the afflictions of disease.
It is said: Dattātreya.
Having carefully placed the palms upward and resting them upon the thighs,
one should then place the hands with palms up in the middle of the thighs and likewise fix the gaze there.
One should place the root of the upper front teeth against the tip of the nose with the tongue,
lift the chin toward the chest, and slowly raise the breath.
Having drawn [the breath] in as much as possible, one should slowly fill the abdomen;
then, likewise according to one's capacity, one should slowly exhale the air.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all diseases;
it is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is obtained on earth by the wise.
The yogi, seated in the lotus posture, should fill [the breath] through the openings of the channels;
he who holds the vital air in this manner is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having mastered the postures and overcome fatigue, the lord of yogis should practice the purification of the channels and the movement of the vital breath by means of the mudrās.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the Yogacintāmaṇi composed by Śivānandasarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya Śrīmad Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī. || 2 ||
Salutations to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

Then, in a monastery located in the aforementioned place and characterized by the aforementioned features, at an auspicious time, on a lunar day endowed with favorable stars, the strength of the moon, and an auspicious conjunction of moments (*muhūrta*), one should worship Vināyaka, Śiva, Śivā, Viṣṇu, Kṣetrapāla, and the Guru along with his disciples, as well as the lords of yogis, according to one's capacity.
Seated upon a seat of kuśa grass, deerskin, or cloth sixteen-fold, endowed with virtues such as self-restraint (yama) and the rest,

and facing either east or north, one should bow to Śiva and other deities as well as to the gurus of the yogis; then, according to the path taught by the Guru and the scriptures, one should first perform that which is the most intimate internal limb of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the purification of the channels (nāḍīśodhana). [As stated] in the Gītā:
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—
neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deer-skin, and kusha grass, one upon the other.
In the Rājayoga [chapter].
Seated upon a comfortable seat in a secluded, solitary place that is pure and pleasing to the mind,
he should remain leaning slightly backward.
With all his limbs abiding in great ease, his self well-stabilized and perfectly pure; as stated in the Śruti:
"In a secluded place, seated on a comfortable seat, pure, with his neck, head, and body held straight."
"Abiding in the state beyond the āśramas, having restrained all the senses, and having bowed with devotion to one's own guru"—
this is the word of Śiva in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
Having paid homage to the lords of yogis along with their disciples, to Vināyaka,
and to his own guru, the yogi, being well-composed, should then engage in yoga.
Yājñavalkya.
Having acquired knowledge and subdued his anger, he was devoted to truth and righteousness;
he delighted in serving his guru and was intent on devotion to his father.
Abiding in his own hermitage, practicing virtuous conduct, and well-instructed by the learned,
he should worship Vināyaka thoroughly with fruits, roots, water, and other offerings.
Having bowed to one's chosen deity and the guru, and then having ascended the seat,
one should thus understand the arrangement of the channels (nāḍīs) as well as the locations of the vital winds (vāyus).
Perform the purification of the channels according to the path prescribed by the rule, as stated in the Vāsiṣṭha-yoga.
Engaged in the duties prescribed by the injunctions, free from all desires,
endowed with qualities such as tranquility, and devoid of all attachments.
Then, having gone to a penance grove provided with fruits, roots, and water—
in a delightful and pure place there, whether by a river or in a forest—
Having constructed a very beautiful monastery endowed with all means of protection,
one should remain pure and composed, performing ablutions at the three times of day.
The wise one, whose body is infused with mantras and who always wears white ashes,
should spread kuśa grass upon a soft seat or else upon a horse-skin.
Having thoroughly worshipped Vināyaka with fruits, roots, water, and other offerings,
and having bowed to one's chosen deity and one's guru, one should then ascend the seat.
One should face either the east or the north, having mastered one's posture;
with neck, head, and body held straight, the mouth closed, and remaining perfectly motionless.
Seated with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, having placed one hand upon the other,
he beheld at the tip of his nose the orb of the moon, overspread with a canopy of lunar rays.
Having perceived with both eyes and the mind the fourth letter of the seventh group, conjoined with a bindu and situated in the center of the orb.
One should fill the external air through the *iḍā* for twelve *mātrās*;
then one should meditate upon the fire as before, endowed with powerful, flickering flames.
Meditating upon the letter *ra* conjoined with the *bindu*, situated within the circle of fire,
one should then exhale slowly through the *piṅgalā* channel.
Then, having filled the breath through the right [nostril] by means of Piṅgalā,
the wise one should likewise exhale slowly through the left [nostril], Iḍā.
For three or four years, or even for three or four months,
one should practice this diligently six times a day at the three periods of the day.
One attains the purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs:
lightness of the body, radiance, and the increase of the digestive fire.
"The manifestation of the *nāda*—this is the sign indicating its attainment;
as long as one perceives these, one should practice in this manner."

"Engaged in the actions prescribed by the injunctions" means being engaged in the performance of the duties ordained for one's specific caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*) as appropriate. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "Yama and so forth," the observances (*niyama*) and postures (*āsana*) are included. Of those [practices], namely Yama, Niyama, and the rest—

"Endowed with" (*āḍhya*) means possessed of those qualities, the signs of their accomplishment, and the conduct [consisting of] the excellence of what is to be achieved, such as the renunciation of enmity, self-disgust for one's own body, and non-affliction by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). By the passage beginning "Having gone from there to the forest of austerity" (*tapovanaṃ tato gatvā*), this is a rule regarding the restriction of place for the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*), because the sentence is intent upon the sequence [of the stages].

Therefore, this [verse] is a restatement of a single portion of those places for yoga practice that have been established as having five limbs, such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the others. In the phrase "having spread out the kuśa grasses, or the horse-skin," the word "or" (atha vā) does not intend to express an option; rather, it refers to what was not previously mentioned.
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because indeclinables possess multiple meanings. Thus, the meaning is as follows:
"even having given a garment made of soft kuśa grass over a skin. And so it is said in the Gītā:

"Not too high, nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass. Regarding the phrase "covered with kuśa grass" (*kuśottara*), since the rule that "the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)" applies, the sequence is reversed from the order of the text; this has also been stated by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya. Thus, [it means] upon the kuśa grass, [a skin] of a deer or a tiger.

Or it should be explained as a hide with a soft cloth upon it. There is no inconsistency whatsoever in explaining "cailājinakuśottara" as a seat upon which a cloth, a hide, and kusha grass are placed in that order, with the kusha on top. [As stated] in the Yogasāra:
"Spread with kusha grass, cloth, and deerskin," as stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
Seated there with soft, cut kuśa grass and a sacred thread made of maṇi grass,
one should constantly practice the limbs of yoga.
Yājñavalkya.

"Then, having spread out soft grass and *kuśa* grass, [he should worship] the Conqueror (*ajina*)," so it is said. Others, however, say that the word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an option between the *kuśa* grass and the *ajina*. That is incorrect; for the meaning of another statement must necessarily conform to the meaning of the words of the Blessed Vāsudeva, the teacher of all the world. Furthermore, in the *Vasiṣṭha-gītā*:

Since no specific cloth has been mentioned, there is an option between *kuśa* grass and deerskin; for it is established by experience that the practice of yoga is impossible on a seat made solely of *kuśa* grass or one made solely of deerskin. [Objection: But surely the seat is filled with cotton, covered with a white cloth, and topped with a black antelope skin?

Regarding "gentle action," it is stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*; and in the words of Dattātreya, "One endowed with great fortitude should always [use] a cloth or indeed a horse that is neither too high nor too low," there is also the requirement for the absence of *kuśa* grass.

If it is argued that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is indeed appropriate for the act of seeing and so forth, we say no; because even in that case, according to the principle of the *adhikaraṇas* in all the scriptures, just as in the scriptural passage concerning the "threefold" (*trivṛt*) there must necessarily be the inclusion of two elements, so too must there be the inclusion of the *kuśa* grass.
Thus, it is also logical to state: "Posture (*āsana*) is that which is steady and pleasant. Here, however, [the seat] is filled with cotton.

The seat covered with white cloth should be understood as referring to those other than ascetics (*yati*), because in the *Dharmaśāstra* there is a prohibition against both cotton and white cloth for them. For it is said:
"The collection of commentaries, disciples, and so forth, as well as beds, seats, water-pots, and books [is forbidden]."
Cotton wool and a cotton garment—these six lead to the downfall of ascetics.

By this, it is shown that even in those cases where only the six ancillaries beginning with posture (*āsana*) are mentioned, the inclusion of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is also indicated; for these two are common to all vows (*vrata*), and thus they should be understood as being taught in their entirety in certain texts. Furthermore, this rule for posture (*āsana*) does not aim merely at the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*), but rather—

The meaning of *sāṅgayoga* (yoga with its ancillaries) should also be understood here, based on the statement of Nārada: "Seated there, one should practice the ancillaries of yoga. One should visualize the orb of the moon at the tip of the nose, dripping nectar. The seed-syllable for the seventh group, beginning with *ṣa-ṣa-sa-ha*, is *haṃ*. One should fill [the body] with air.
It should be understood as "mixed with nectar. By this, the inhalation (*pūraka*) which is the means for purifying the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*) is shown.
Here, some maintain that by the passage beginning with "Then fire" (*tato 'gnim*) and ending with "again" (*punar*), the exhalation (*recaka*) is shown.
By the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*), there is also a reference back to "at the tip of the nose" (*nāsāgre*). And thus, [the sequence involves] the moon, fire...

In this context as well, it is only inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*) accompanied by meditation (*dhyāna*) that are taught as the means for purifying the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*), and not retention (*kuṃbhaka*) either. For this very reason, the *Yogasāgara* states: "Having filled [the breath], one should subsequently exhale through the path of the black-pathed one (fire)."
Adorned with the second *soṃ* syllable situated in the center,
one should fill the wind [element] three or five times by way of the lunar path.

"Then one should purge slightly through the channel by means of the fire. Regarding this, some say that for one devoted to the yoga of Nakulīśa, only inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*) are prescribed as the means for purifying the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*). That is not correct; for if that were the case, the sequence following inhalation would be contradicted by the word "then" (*tataḥ*) in the phrase "then [one should kindle] the fire."

Since [the meaning] is already obtained by the word "after" (*paścāt*) itself, the word "again" (*punar*) in the phrase "again after" (*paścāt punaḥ*) would be redundant. Furthermore, since the meditation that constitutes a limb of exhalation (*recaka*) is already obtained by the word "meditating" (*dhyāyan*), the hearing of the word "should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) again would yield little fruit; thus, [the intended sense is simply] "one should exhale while meditating."

Because the optative suffix (*liṅ*) prescribes exhaling (*recana*) as qualified by meditation (*dhyāna*), the phrase "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) enjoins meditation as a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward an object. Furthermore, that meditation is not merely a continuous flow of consciousness (*cittasaṃtati*); rather, it is accompanied by breath-retention (*kuṃbhaka*), due to the force of its syntactic unity with the preceding and following passages. To illustrate: this meditation [is prescribed] in the *Naraka* [chapter].

By the phrase "one should fill [the breath] when possible," the completion of the *pūraka* (inhalation) is stated, according to the maxim that the completion of all verbal roots constitutes the meaning of the word. Likewise,
by the phrase "thereafter one should meditate on the fire," meditation is enjoined immediately after the completion of the *pūraka*, and not otherwise.

This [practice] occurs during exhalation (*recaka*); for one should meditate [on the mantra] and subsequently exhale, since according to the previously established rule, the performance of exhalation is prescribed immediately after the completion of meditation.

Therefore, by the force of the scriptural authority (*vākya-pramāṇa*) and the consideration of what precedes and follows—namely, "prior to exhalation" and "immediately after inhalation" (*pūraka*)—[the practice is determined].
By the word "should meditate" (*dhyāyet*), it is precisely meditation accompanied by the restraint known as *kumbhaka* that is prescribed as the means for attaining the fruit;

such is the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s statement. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that *pūraka* and *recaka*, when devoid of *kumbhaka*, possess the capacity to purify the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*). As stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
In the section on the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*), one should draw in the breath with the lunar [channel] and, having drawn it up to the navel, retain it.
Having retained it for as long as possible, one should then exhale slightly through the solar [channel].
In this manner, one should purify the breath situated from the big toes upwards.
"Because the wind is always all-pervading, the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana) is desired [through breath control].

Likewise, in many other texts as well, kumbhaka is clearly taught in the sections concerning the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi). Therefore, by the force of corroboration from other texts and through the syntactic unity of the preceding and following passages, [this is established].

It is appropriate here to hold that meditation accompanied by breath-retention (*kuṃbhaka*) alone is prescribed. Nor should it be argued that such an interpretation fails to provide for the meditation on deities and so forth which constitute the limb of exhalation (*recaka*), because the expectancy of the passage beginning with "the fire" (*agnim*) has been satisfied by its connection with the previously mentioned phrase "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*).

In accordance with the requirement of the expectant phrase "meditating, one should expel," and because it is well-established in all yoga treatises that Agni is the presiding deity of the *suṣumṇā* and the Sun is the presiding deity of the *piṅgalā*, the word "Sun" (*sūrya*) must be supplied here. Consequently, [the meaning is]: meditating on the Sun, which is red and of the nature of fire...

Thus, the meaning of the sentence "one should cause to purge" is established. For this very reason, with the intention of meditating upon the Sun as having the form of fire, [the text says] "by the path" and "of the black-pathed one"; and by the phrase "from the channel of Jātavedas," it is because in the *Yogasāra*, the word "fire" (*agni*) is applied specifically to the Sun for those devoted to the *Kulīśa-yoga*.
And likewise in the *Amṛtabindu*:
He who is indeed Vahni is Sūrya; he who is Sūrya is Hutāśana.
These two are seen as one, yet differentiated by a subtle distinction.
And thus, even the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the phrase "and again by Piṅgalā" is purposeful;
for it is only when [the word] "again" is understood as "meditating again" that the consistency of the connection between the words is maintained.
Otherwise, since the immediate succession of the *pūrvaraṅga* was not previously mentioned,
the word "again" (*punar*) in the phrase "one should perform it again" (*punārecayet*) would be incoherent.

This is what must be considered here: in the phrase "the orb of the moon on the tip of the nose," the term "tip of the nose" indicates the midpoint between the eyebrows. This is because the midpoint between the eyebrows is well-known in all yoga treatises as the locus of the moon, and therefore meditation upon it is appropriately directed toward that very place.

Regarding the phrase "one should meditate as before," this refers specifically to a period of time measured by twelve *mātrās* and nothing else; however, the words "in the middle of the body" must be supplied as an ellipsis, because it is precisely there that the breath is retained during *kumbhaka*.
Consequently, the meaning is as follows: [one should meditate on] the lunar disk, joined with the seed-syllable, from which flows a continuous stream of trickling nectar.

Gazing with both eyes at the space between the eyebrows, one should fill [the breath] for twelve *mātrās* with air mixed with nectar. Then, while meditating upon the fire-mandala— a triangle situated within the center of the body, joined with the seed-syllable and encircled by flickering flames— one should [hold] the air in the *suṣumṇā* for twelve *mātrās*.

One should retain [the breath]. Then, meditating on the sun in the form of fire at either the heart or the navel, one should exhale the air for twelve *mātrās* through the *piṅgalā*. Again, preceded by meditation and so forth, having filled [the breath] through the *piṅgalā*, one should restrain it in the heart and exhale through the *iḍā*.
In the Yogabhāskara.
One should fill the breath through the iḍā, retain it in the suṣumṇā, and exhale it through the piṅgalā nāḍī; this is remembered as the sequence for prāṇāyāma.

And thus, as long as the signs indicative of the purification of the channels have not appeared, one should practice six times daily—at dawn and at midday. Thereafter, the yogi whose collection of channels is purified will become capable in *prāṇāyāma*. This is what has been stated:
"As long as one perceives these, so long should one practice in this manner. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"When the entire wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*), which was clouded by impurities, becomes pure, at that very moment the yogi becomes capable of binding the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
With the mouth firmly closed, one should fill the breath with the moon (the left nostril) according to one's capacity, and then exhale it through the sun (the right nostril);
this is called *prāṇāyāma*.
Meditating on the moon as it pours forth a continuous stream of nectar,
the lord of yogis attains bliss in that very instant through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having drawn in the breath with the sun (the right nostril), the yogi should fill the cavity of the belly;
having retained it, he should then slowly exhale through the moon (the left nostril).
Meditating upon the sun in his heart as having the appearance of a mass of blazing fire,
the lord of yogis shall become a partaker of bliss by means of this southern watch (yāma).
Thus, through three months of practice and the cultivation of both types of *āyāma*,
the yogi whose channels are purified is called one who has mastered the vital breath (*siddhaprāṇa*).
"By the purification of the channels, there occurs the ability to hold the breath as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and good health."
Also in Haṭhayoga:

If one restrains the breath with the iḍā and then exhales it through the other [piṅgalā], or having inhaled the air through the piṅgalā, holds it and then releases it through the left [iḍā]— for those self-controlled ones who meditate upon the two orbs of the sun and moon according to this method, their entire collection of channels becomes purified.
After three months,
when the purification of the channels has occurred, then all anxiety is dispelled;
at that time, the emaciation of the body and a radiant luster will certainly arise.
One should practice the kumbhakas four times a day— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight— gradually increasing up to eighty repetitions each time.
In the lowest degree there is perspiration; in the middle degree there is trembling;
in the highest degree, while seated in the lotus posture, the vital breath is suspended.
One should perform a massage of the body with water produced from physical exertion;
by that, firmness and lightness of the body are produced.
In another treatise:
A person should perform sixty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) at the break of day,
forty at midday, and twenty at the twilight (saṃdhyā).
"At midnight there should be twenty; such is the restraint of the vital breath," thus says Dattātreya.
Having spread out a waveless seat in that monastery,
the wise man, assuming the lotus posture, sat down there.
With an upright body and palms joined in reverence, one should bow to the chosen deity;
then, with the thumb of the right hand, [one should touch] Piṅgalā.
One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* channel very slowly by means of restraint according to one's capacity; thereafter, one should perform the *kumbhaka*.
Then one should exhale through Piṅgalā very slowly and not with force;
having again filled [the breath] through Piṅgalā, one should fill the abdomen slowly.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale slowly through the *iḍā*.
Having filled [the breath] with that same [nostril] through which one would exhale, one should retain it without conflict.
In this manner, one should perform twenty *kumbhakas* at dawn according to one's capacity;
this is the *kumbhaka* known as *sahita*, which is free from all restrictive constraints.
Having thus performed twenty kumbhakas at the time of midday,
one should then perform twenty kumbhakas in the same manner in the evening.
In this very manner, one should also perform twenty kumbhakas at midnight,
together with exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), every day.
Therefore, the *sahita-kumbhaka* consists of [breaths] accompanied by exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūra*).
One should perform it in this manner four times every day without laziness.
One should practice in this manner for three months; thereafter, the purification of the channels occurs.
When the channels are purified, then the signs of the yogin appear.
Those qualities indeed arise within the body; listen as I describe them to you:
lightness of the body, radiance, and the increase of the digestive fire.
"And at that time, emaciation of the body will certainly arise," so it is stated in the *Yogabhāskara*.
Drawing the thread through the pair of nostrils and rubbing it;
consuming more than a pinch of cumin with sugar; and vomiting forth water and food.
Regarding the purification of the channels, the means taught by the sages are indeed the *mādas* and so forth;
it is my conviction that these consist of eating as prescribed and the binding of the vital breath (*vāyu*).
Yājñavalkya.
One should not release the breath through the out-breath (apāna) or with forceful gusts of air,
by which one might cause the flour held in the hand to be moved by the force of the breath.
One should release the air from the nostrils slowly and not with force;
one should not cause the body to tremble—for such a yogi is considered supreme.
Thus, in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Alternatively, the knower of yoga, having assumed upon any external seat— such as the *svastika* or others— in which comfort arises for him, should practice yoga.
With his feet placed on his thighs and the left hand resting on the right thigh,
he should slightly raise his face upward and steady it with his chest.
With eyes closed, established in the quality of goodness (sattva), not touching tooth against tooth,
with the tongue fixed on the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly motionless.
Having thoroughly restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should then undertake the middle and the highest forms of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The characteristics of the three types of breath control—mild, medium, and intense—will now be described in sequence.
When practiced correctly, it leads one wherever one desires;
through disciplined breath control, there occurs the destruction of all diseases.
Through the practice of improper yoga, all diseases arise, including hiccup,
labored breathing, coughing, and pains in the head, ears, and eyes.
Various diseases arise from the derangement of the vital air (vāyu). One should exhale the air little by little and fill it in little by little.
One who knows yoga should bind [the breath] again and again as it is joined; in this way, success is achieved.
If this prāṇa is forcibly restrained, it will escape through the pores of the skin.
This [wind] tears apart the body and even gives rise to leprosy and other ailments;
yet, once it has been brought under control, that very same wind gradually becomes like the sky, or like an elephant in the forest.
Whether it be a wild elephant or a lion, they gradually attain gentleness;
they follow the instructions of the treatise and do not transgress them.
Likewise, this vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the heart, when grasped by the yogi through the yoga of stages and being cultivated, attains a state of full confidence.
As long as the vital breath remains in the body, so long is it called "life";
when that has departed, death occurs; therefore, one should restrain the vital breath.
As long as the vital wind (marut) is bound within the body, the mind remains without support;
as long as the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, whence can there be fear of death?
Out of fear of death, Brahmā always practiced supreme breath control (prāṇāyāma);
thus, yogis attain perfection through the complete restraint of the vital breaths.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā].
Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, how do yogis live for such a long time?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O best among all knowers of Brahman."
Vasiṣṭha said:

The movement [of the mind] arises from the throbbing of the vital breaths; when those cease, it becomes like a stone. Therefore, through steady concentration, those [breaths] do not perish for the yogi.
Whether it be the movement of the mind, the vital breath, or the bodily wind—both internal and external—for him no such movement exists;
therefore, both transformation and decay remain far removed from him.
When the movement of both the breath and the mind has become peaceful within and without,
the bodily constituents never again abandon their stability within the body.
When the breath carries the *āsana*, the channels fall into disorder,
just as the order of the castes and stages of life collapses when the king is improperly situated.
Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Listen, O protector of the earth, to the characteristics of prāṇāyāma,
as well as the manner in which the seat is prescribed for one who is constantly engaged in yoga.
Having assumed the lotus posture, the half-lotus posture, or likewise the svastika posture,
the yogi should practice yoga, placing the syllable *praṇava* within his heart.
Having become well-composed in posture and drawing together both feet,
with the mouth closed and likewise firmly bracing the thighs together in front;
Standing with self-restraint, he touched his penis and testicles with his two heels; with his head slightly raised, he kept his teeth from touching one another.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking around in any direction,
the yogi, thus restrained in diet and devoted to breath control, [should practice].
One should gradually ascend the conquered and won territory as if it were one's own home;
likewise, one should overcome faults, disease, delusion, and even the ground that has been overrun by them.
One should cause [the qualities] to increase but not ascend to a stage that has not been conquered;
the means for this has been taught here by the yogis and supreme sages.
By means of which the defects such as disease do not arise for the yogi,
just as one seeking water [obtains it] gradually from a machine, a pipe, and so forth.
Likewise, the yogi who has conquered fatigue should drink air;
for even lions, tigers, and elephants become gentle when they are being served.
Just as they enter, so does the vital breath become subject to the control of the yogin;
like a mahout leading an elephant at his will, he brings it under his command through trust.
In the same way, the yogi leads the mastered vital breath according to his own will;
for just as a mastered lion kills deer and not human beings.
In the same way, the restrained breath does not [leave] the body of men with sin;
therefore, a disciplined yogi should always be devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus says Yājñavalkya.
Therefore, O beautiful woman, you should always perform your daily rites,
or else constantly practice the restraint of breath during the periods of the twilights.
All those who are devoted to breath control, who have breath control as their ultimate refuge,
and who are purified by breath control— they go to the supreme goal.
There is nothing other than breath control (prāṇāyāma) that delivers those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra from the hells and other realms; breath control is the savior.
Now follows the definition of *prāṇāyāma*.
In that regard, the Blessed One Patañjali [says]:
Regarding this, the author of the Commentary [Vyāsa] states: "Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
Therein, inhalation (*śvāsa*) is the drawing in of external air, and exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is the expulsion of internal air;
the cessation of their movement is [prāṇāyāma].
"Prāṇāyāma is the state of the absence of both. Regarding this, Vācaspati’s commentary states:

"In exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka), there is a cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. Even in the case of exhalation, where the air within the lungs is expelled and held outside, there exists a cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.

Thus, in *kumbhaka* as well, there is the absence of both [inhalation and exhalation]. Bhojadeva, however, states: "When stability in that posture has been attained, the specific limb of yoga characterized by *prāṇāyāma*, which is caused by it, should be practiced. Of what nature is it?
It consists of the threefold expulsion, filling, and retention of inhalation (*śvāsa*) and exhalation (*praśvāsa*) through the external and internal channels."

"In the locations of the tip of the nose, the heart, and the navel, the retention [of breath] through the cessation of the flow of movement is called *prāṇāyāma*," so it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
The *haṃsa* (the breath) moves externally for a measure of thirty-six finger-breadths by way of the left and right paths; therefore, it is called *prāṇa*.
"Prāṇa is the wind residing within the body; āyāma is its restraint. Thus it is stated in the Āditya Purāṇa.
The restraint of the internal and external winds that move within is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*; it is said to be of two kinds.
Yājñavalkya says that [prāṇāyāma] is of two kinds: with seed (sagarbha) and without seed (nirgarbha).
Prāṇāyāma is said to be the union of prāṇa and apāna.

Prāṇāyāma is said to be threefold, consisting of pūraka, kumbhaka, and recaka. Regarding the definition of pūraka: it is the filling of air from the outside into the abdomen; that indeed is pūraka. (From the Kālikā Purāṇa)
Pūraka is so called because of filling; Devala says: "Filling is the inflation [of the body] by exhalation"; thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
One should fill the body with external air like a leather bag;
remaining thus completely filled, it is known as *pūraka* because of that filling.
Yājñavalkya.

Drawing in the air situated outside through the nostrils and gradually filling all the channels with that very breath from every side—that is what is called *pūraka*, the great restraint (*mahānirodha*). Devala says: "The entry of that [air] into the interior of the belly by that same path is called *pūraka* because of the act of filling."
By means of the characteristics of the nostrils, the mouth, and the *brahmarandhra*. In the *Vāyusaṃhitā*:
"Having pressed one nostril with a finger, [one should block] the other with the other [finger]."
One should fill the body with the external wind, like an inflated leather bag.
Pūraka is known as the filling [of the breath] through the other nostril. Now, the definition of kumbhaka:
Yājñavalkya.
"Kumbhaka is the retention of breath like a jar being completely filled," as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
One neither releases nor inhales the air situated inside or outside;
having filled [the body] like a jar, one should remain motionless—this indeed is *kumbhaka*.

Yogī Yājñavalkya says: That state in which the breath, remaining fixed at the tip of the nose, is neither exhaled nor inhaled, and is held perfectly motionless in due order— this they call *kumbhaka*.
Those who know it say:
that which consists of exhaling, inhaling, and releasing, wherein the breath is held in bliss, is called prāṇāyāma; all of this is indeed kevala-kumbhaka (pure retention).
Having exhaled, one should perform inhalation; that indeed is the *sahita-kumbhaka*.
Other specific varieties of *kumbhaka* will be described later. [Now follows] the definition of *recaka* (exhalation). Yājñavalkya says:
The exhalation of air from the abdomen is known as *recaka*.
Likewise:
"The complete vital breath (*prāṇa*) exits through the opening like wind into a void."
When one stands without breathing and the upward-moving air [is retained], that is called *recaka*, the great restraint (*mahānirodha*).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"One should release the breath, joined with all the limbs, through the right nostril during the solar nāḍī;
when preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, that is known as Recaka."
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having pressed one nostril with the finger, one should exhale the air from the abdomen through the other; this is known as *recaka* because of the exhalation (*recana*).
Devala says: Continuous exhalation is *recaka*. Continuous, fragmented exhalation is the expulsion [of air].
That which is the expulsion of the abdominal air through the *brahmarandhra* and the nostrils and mouth—this evacuation of the internal air is *recaka*.
In the Yogaśāstra of Jaigīṣavya.
Exhalation (recaka) is proclaimed to be the expulsion of the air within the abdomen;
pranayama is said to be of three kinds, distinguished as light, medium, and superior.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"By means of the divisions of *mātrās*,
that breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) is proclaimed as the minor, the middling, and the superior."
This [measure] exists, distinguished by its divisions, as two or three times the measure of a Brahmin.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
That which consists of twelve short mātrās is the low [pitch]; that which is double that is the middle;
and that which consists of triple the mātrās is declared to be the high [pitch].
By the first [stage] one should conquer perspiration, by the middle trembling, and by the third dejection;
thus one should overcome the defects in successive order.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
The shortest *yama* consists of twelve *mātrās*,
while the middle one is proclaimed to consist of double that number of *mātrās*.
The eldest [breath] is said to consist of three qualities; one should bring about the stability of that which is eldest.
Devala says:
"Furthermore, by means of one, two, or three *udghātas*, it becomes mild, slow, or sharp."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
The shortest [breath] consists of twelve measures (mātrās) with a single exhalation;
the middle, however, has two exhalations and twenty-four measures.
The highest [type of breath-retention] is known to consist of thirty-six *mātrās* and involves three upward thrusts;
it is considered the best because it generates perspiration, trembling, and physical impact.
By these signs, the perfected vital breath within should be marked by the yogi;
as stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
The restraint of prāṇa and apāna occurs according to the sequence beginning with the lowest [breath] and so forth;
it is taught as fourfold, distinguished by its measures and qualities.
The lowest [breath] has one expulsion and consists of twelve measures;
the middle, however, has two expulsions and consists of twenty-four measures.
The *uttara* [prāṇāyāma], however, is known to have three exhalations (*udghāta*) and thirty-six measures (*mātrā*);
it is the superior breath-control that produces perspiration and so forth.
In this state, the yogi experiences the arising of bliss, horripilation, rolling of the eyes, contortion of the limbs, as well as incoherent speech, dizziness, fainting, and so forth.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
The measure of prāṇāyāma is traditionally held to be twelve mātrās;
a single udghāta (upward impulse) is said to consist of twelve mātrās for one of inferior capacity.
The medium [breath] consists of two udghātas and twenty-four mātrās;
the primary, however, is said to consist of three udghātas and thirty-six mātrās.
Perspiration arises, followed by the emergence of trembling; in this state, bliss is born, as well as sleep and drowsiness, respectively.
When horripilation, the perception of sound, the twisting and trembling of the limbs,
whirling, perspiration, muttering, and so forth, as well as unconsciousness and fainting, arise, one should conquer them.
Then, that most excellent and beautiful prāṇāyāma is said to be accomplished;
"ghūrṇa" is the oscillation of the mind, and "dhvani-saṃvitti" is the manifestation of the internal resonance (nāda).
In the Vāsiṣṭha-yoga.
He who produces perspiration during the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) is considered inferior;
he is said to be middling by means of trembling, and superior by means of rising [from the seat].
As for the definition of a *mātrā*, it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"A *mātrā* is the duration of an eyeblink, or likewise two short syllables (*laghu*).
Also in the *Nandipurāṇa*.
"It is remembered as being swift, consisting of light syllables, and having twelve mātrās," so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Having performed the circumambulation neither too quickly nor too slowly,
as long as it takes to snap one's fingers— that duration is what is sung of as the measure [of time].
Thus says Dattātreya.
One should release three fingers and rub the knees;
one should give a single snap of the fingers, for in this way the number of measures (mātrās) is reckoned.
Likewise: the shortest [measure] consists of twelve challenges; the middle is recorded as double that;
and the longest should be double again—this is proclaimed as the distinction of measures.
Yājñavalkya.
The wise praise the signaling of three finger-snap releases, the wiping above the knees, and even the clapping of three hand-claps.
The milking of a cow, the drinking by a calf, the flight of an arrow,
or even the ringing of a bell— these are indeed cited as exceeding the proper measure.
"They should always be practiced gradually, in accordance with place and time.
As for the definition of the *udghāta* (the upward stroke), it is as stated in another treatise:
"When the *apāna* is compressed by the *prāṇa* being expelled [upward]."
Having gone upward, one should return; this is the characteristic of the *udghāta*.
Now, the specific meditations and recitations for inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) are demonstrated. Vyāsa says:
One should meditate upon Kaṃ, who is red in color and situated in the navel-lotus, by means of inhalation (pūraka);
and one should meditate upon Janārdana, who has the luster of a blue lotus and is situated in the heart-lotus, by means of retention (kumbhaka).
One should contemplate the white Śiva, situated on the forehead, by means of exhalation (recaka);
he resembles pure crystal, is stainless, and is the destroyer of sins.
Bṛhaspati.
One should meditate on Prajāpati as red, Viṣṇu as having the luster of a blue lotus, and Śaṅkara, the three-eyed one, as white; by so meditating, one is released from bondage.
Yājñavalkya.

During the retention of breath (kumbhaka), one should meditate upon the lotus-seated Brahmā, the Grandfather, whose body is reddish-fair in hue and who possesses four faces, located in the region of the heart.
One should meditate, by means of inhalation (pūraka), upon the Great-Souled One, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, established in the center of the navel, and possessing four arms.
By means of the exhalation (recaka), one should know Maheśvara, the Lord, residing in the forehead—
resembling pure crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins.
Through inhalation (pūraka), one attains union with Viṣṇu; through retention (kumbhaka), one reaches the presence of Brahmā;
and by means of exhalation (recaka), the third, one may attain the state of the Lord (Īśvara).
When, through the conjunction with cessation, one contemplates the three deities by means of the union with fire,
wind, and water, then indeed one is purified by these three.
From cessation wind is born, and from wind fire is born;
from fire water is produced; thereafter, [the body] is purified within by these three.
Prāṇāyāma is said to consist of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka);
these—beginning and ending with the three syllables—are the inhalation, retention, and exhalation.
This very one is declared to be the Praṇava, and the prāṇāyāma consists of that;
having drawn in the air through the iḍā and filled the belly, he remains [therein].
One should slowly contemplate the syllable *A* there for sixteen measures;
thereafter, one should retain the filled breath for sixty-four measures.
Even here, while recollecting the form of the syllable *ukāra*, one should mutter the *praṇava*;
or, for as long as possible, one should perform the *japa* accompanied by the *vāraṇa*.
After filling [the vessel], one should then retain the breath joined with the external air;
slowly, O Gārgī, through the Piṅgalā for thirty-two mātrās once again.
Even here, being well-composed, one should recollect the form of the letter *ma*;
this constitutes breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and one should practice it again in this same manner.
That which produces perspiration during breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) is said to be inferior;
that which causes trembling is declared intermediate; and that which results in rising [from the ground] is remembered as superior.
One should perform each preceding stage until the highest is attained;
when the highest breath control (prāṇāyāma) is achieved, O Gārgī, one becomes happy.
By that very [vitality], the prāṇa conquers even more within the body;
and by that, the body rises up, having assumed its seat.
Exhalation and inhalation never exist for him,
even though both of those natural qualities may still be present in his body.
Nevertheless, those two [the breaths] are destroyed by the supreme *prāṇāyāma*;
indeed, upon their destruction, one becomes capable of performing *kevalakumbhaka*.
One should practice *kumbhaka* daily, either with breath-retention (*sahita*) or alone (*kevala*);
one should practice the *sahita* method until mastery of the *kevala* is attained.
When kevala kumbhaka, devoid of both exhalation and inhalation,
is mastered, there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult for him to attain.
One attains swiftness of mind and such things as grey hair perish;
this is the great path to liberation, consisting of the internal self known by the letter 'Ma'.
This kumbhaka, which is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), produces the internal sound (nāda).
What is called the restraint of the vital breath is the holding of the prāṇa within the body.
This method of conquering the vital breath is the destroyer of all death in Haṭhayoga.
From *kumbhaka* comes the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī;
from the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, she enters the *suṣumṇā*, and the perfection of *haṭha* arises.
In the Vāyusaṃhitā.
This triad of exhalation and the others should be performed neither too quickly nor too slowly;
through the application of the sequence of upward impulses (udghāta), you should practice this means of yoga.
The practice of the three breath-controls, beginning with *recaka* and preceded by the purification of the channels,
is declared to be the path for following yoga until the point of voluntary departure from the body.
Prāṇāyāma is of six kinds, distinguished by the categories of sagarbha and vigarbha;
for it is so stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
A wise person should practice either yoga with a seed (sagarbha) or without a seed (agarbha);
thus it is stated in the Nandipurāṇa.
Prāṇāyāma is its first [limb]; its application at the outset is now described. It is proclaimed to be of two kinds: with seed (sagarbha) and without seed (agarbha).
The "churning" (*mathana*) of this wind called *prāṇa* is what constitutes *prāṇāyāma*, because it serves as the locus for the knowledge of the self, which is like butter (*navanīta*).
Their definitions are as follows, according to the *Liṅga Purāṇa*:
The "womb" (garbha) is said to be "with womb" (sagarbha), while the "victory" (vijaya) is [the practice] accompanied by recitation (japa); this is stated successively in the Vāyusaṃhitā:
"Without recitation and meditation it is 'wombless' (agarbha); that which is endowed with those two is 'with womb' (sagarbha)."
Prāṇāyāma joined with *agarbha* and *garbha* is more than a hundredfold [in merit].
Japa performed mentally is mental recitation (*prasaṃkhyāna*). In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"One should perform the japa with the muttering of the mantra, neither too slow nor too fast;
however, in the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should always perform the mental recitation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) by means of the mind alone."

Regarding recitation (*jāpya*) with the *praṇava*, *gāyatrī*, and other mantras, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "The practice of contemplating the meaning of words, moving from letter to letter and from word to word within the sequence of syllables that is to be meditated upon— that is called mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*)."
In the Nandipurāṇa: "Because he meditates upon the deities who are the portions of the *mātrās*, he is proclaimed as 'Possessing Flames' (*sa-jvāla*).
But because he is pierced by the speech of the mantras, he is proclaimed as ending in wisdom (*prajñā-anta*)."
The mantra is said to be the syllable Oṃ, which conquers all mantras;
it is the assembly of all deities and the support for all yogis.
Within its belly, the entire collection of mantras is established;
it alone is the yoga of yogis, for it is indeed equal to a wish-fulfilling gem.
But that [sound] is joined with three measures: *a*, *u*, and *ma*; these are so remembered.
In this triad of measures, everything—both existence and non-existence—is established.
The three measures (mā) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are traditionally taught in sequence; Skanda, Umā, and Śaṅkara are likewise declared, as are Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
The three fires are said to be praised as the *mātrās* born from the *praṇava*;
through meditation on its three *mātrās*, the breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) becomes "with smoke" (*sadhūmaka*).
Through meditation on the deities who are the portions of the digits (kalā), he is proclaimed as being with flames;
through the support of the yoga-nāḍīs, the measure (mātrā) is the reality free from even a trace of smoke.
In the scriptures, the "tranquil" (praśānta) is said to be that which has emerged from all states of being.
These are the varieties of the "pregnant" (sagarbha) [prāṇāyāma]. Here, three varieties of the pregnant prāṇāyāma are observed.
Regarding "with smoke," "with flame," and "tranquil": therein, it is "with smoke" due to meditating on the three measures (*mātrā*);
it is "with flame" due to meditating on the forms of the measures, which are the constituent parts of the *praṇava*, as well as their respective deities.
"Speechless regarding mantras" means being tranquil. "Pierced by the non-speaking of mantra" means being joined with mental reflection;
by this, it is implied that one is devoid of meditation on the meaning expressed by the mantra.

"Kalāmātra, dhūmāṃśa," and so forth; "mātrātadartha" means devoid of meditation and tranquil. Here, by the word *aṃśa*, the deities who are the objects of the *mātrās* are intended. One is "tranquil" (*praśānta*) because of taking refuge in the entities that have emerged in the form of the deities of the *mātrās*—namely smoke, [fire], and flame—and because of taking refuge in the yogic channels (*yoganāḍī*).
The *suṣumṇā* is the channel of yoga (*yoganāḍī*).
Thus, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *praṇava* at its core has been demonstrated,
as stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
By the utterance of "Oṃ," everything that exists and does not exist is grasped;
this is the imperishable Brahman, known as the supreme Oṃkāra.
The syllable Om is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and the Brahmin is indeed the one equipped with the weapon;
with undistracted mind, one must pierce the mark, and like the arrow, become absorbed in that.
Yājñavalkya.
The syllable Om is said to be the ultimate conclusion of all established doctrines, as well as of the Vedas and Vedānta, and of other scriptures too.
The Vedas, beginning with the syllable Om, are established within the syllable Om;
the entirety of speech resides in the syllable Om; therefore, one should practice the syllable Om.
Likewise, during the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), the twice-born should mutter three Gāyatrīs joined with the syllable Om and accompanied by the Vyāhṛtis.
By this, the *prāṇāyāma* consisting of the *gāyatrī* is shown. Manu states its definition:
"The *vyāhṛtis* are prescribed to be recited constantly during *prāṇāyāma*:
Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahas, Janas, Tapas, and likewise Satyam. This is according to the statement of Yogi Yājñavalkya.

And here, the mantra from the Yajurveda beginning with "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" is used for the head. Likewise, Vyāsa states: "Yogī Yājñavalkya prescribes the conjunction of the Praṇava (Oṃ) with all nine [worlds], beginning with Bhūḥ, as follows:
'Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, Tapaḥ, and Satyaḥ.'"
Then, joined with the individual *oṃkāras*, follows the mantra "tatsavitur vareṇyam."
One should employ the mantra "oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" at the back of the head;
for it is declared that prāṇāyāma consists of the practice of repeating [the mantra] three times.
The syllable *oṃ* should also be seen here at the beginning of the mantra; likewise, Yama says: "One should recite the seven *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*."

"One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Śiras; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the supreme austerity. In this context, it should be understood that the word "mentally" (manasā) is to be supplied. And so says Saṃvarta:
A twice-born man should daily recite the seven Vyāhṛtis joined with the Praṇava,
and the Sāvitrī together with its Śiras, three times mentally.
Yājñavalkya.
A Brahmin endowed with Vedic learning and always devoted to his own duty should recite Vedic mantras, and never those that are worldly.
Some desire to recite Vedic mantras for the sake of the welfare of living beings;
the recitation during breath control (prāṇāyāma) prescribed for a Kṣatriya is said to be the same as that for a twice-born (dvija).
O Gārgī, for Vaiśyas endowed with dharma, for women, Śūdras, and ascetics,
there is no mantra at the time of restraining the vital breaths (prāṇa), except for the Praṇava.
The wise desire either a Śiva-mantra ending in *namaḥ* or a Vaiṣṇava mantra;
or else, a Śūdra should practice one that is worldly (*laukika*), according to the prescribed rules.
"A Śūdra and women should never recite Vedic mantras.
Thus, this distinction between those born from the womb and those not born from the womb has been explained.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Exhalation (recaka), the void (śūnyaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka)—
the suspension of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) is thus fourfold, known as prāṇāyāma.
Among those, some characteristics such as *recita* and others have been indicated; the definition of *śūnya* is stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*.
Then, having abandoned all practice, one should contemplate the inner self;
one should restrain the wind situated outside, and that is designated as "void."
"Then," meaning having performed the exhalation (*recaka*) through the *bhānudevatā* channel with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *praṇava*, and so forth; as stated in the *Jaigīṣavya-yoga-śāstra*:
"One who is fatigued by the five breath-restraints (*āyāmas*) should perform them in order, beginning with exhalation."
Exhalation, inhalation, retention, upward movement, and downward movement.
The connection is that the weary yogi attains perfection;
thus it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
The vital breaths are the wind consisting of breath; this wind is declared to be the Self. Its extension has been fully described by the wise as being of six kinds.
It is rightly described as being joined with the cessation of even the vital air (vāyu).
Furthermore, it has six modes: two, namely exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), along with the combined breath (sahita) and the isolated breath (kevala).

There are two types of *kumbhaka*: the upward-drawing (*utkarṣa*) and the downward-drawing (*apakarṣa*). Devala states: "The *kumbha* is to be known as sevenfold, according to the divisions beginning with *recita*."
Recaka, pūraka, śānta, pratyāhāra, uttara, adhara,
and sama— thus is kumbhaka described as having seven varieties.
Likewise, he states the definition for all seven types, beginning with *recita*:
"The external retention of the breath is *recita-kumbhaka*."
When the abdomen is filled, the obstruction [of the breath] is called *pūrita-kumbhaka*;
when there is a pervasion throughout the interior and exterior of the body, it is called *śānta-kumbhaka*.
The obstruction between two locations is the kumbhaka known as pratyāhāra;
it is the upward obstruction [of breath] in the heart and other centers, filling them sequentially from below.
The *uttara-kumbhaka* (upward retention) occurs when the breath is held below the navel; the *adhodha-mūrdhata-dhara* (downward-to-head-holding) occurs when it is held above the head.
*Kumbhaka* is the steady holding of the vital air (*marut*) by the mind, having abandoned both exhalation (*recana*) and inhalation (*pūraṇa*).
In regions such as the vehicle (the feet) and so forth, the "equal pitcher" (sama-kuṃbha) is proclaimed.

Regarding the body, this means that by abandoning exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), there is a pervasion through the retention of the vital air (vāyu) within and without the body by means of the mind. In the phrase "in the two places," a distributive repetition (vīpsā) is to be understood. [These places are] the soles of the feet, the secret organ, and the navel.
The heart, chest, throat, uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) are the locations.
The retention of breath within these locations, specifically in the interval or middle between two [locations], is the kumbhaka known as pratyāhāra.
Regarding the locations: from the head down to the heart, there is the process of exhaling and filling [the breath] in these locations.

There is a distinction between the equalized (*sama*) and the tranquilized (*śānta*) [breaths] due to their difference. Your venerable Patañjali states the definition of the fourfold breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), beginning with exhalation (*recaka*): "Exhalation, inhalation, and retention have their movements observed by place, time, and number; they are long and subtle. The fourth is that which transcends the objects of the external and internal. This is its meaning.

The outward movement is inhalation (*śvāsa*), which is exhalation (*recaka*); the inward movement is exhalation (*praśvāsa*), which is inhalation (*pūraka*); and the state of internal suspension is retention (*kumbhaka*). When that [breath] is obstructed by a single, powerful effort of restraint, setting aside both exhalation and inhalation, it remains motionless like water [in a jar].

The suspension of the breath is *kumbhaka*. Just as water placed on a heated stone dries up completely from all sides and undergoes contraction, so too is the subtle [breath] held rigid within the body; thus it is the function of *stambha* (stiffening). This threefold *prāṇāyāma* is characterized by space, time, and number, and is [thereby] long.
It becomes subtle in perception. In terms of place, it is characterized by the nose, the *dvādaśānta*, and so forth;
in terms of time, it is characterized by number, such as a measure of thirty-six *mātrās* and so on, and it is also characterized by number in terms of how many times [it occurs].

The inclusion of the mention of number is for the purpose of knowing that "the first *udghāta* occurs after this many inhalations and exhalations. And an *udghāta* is the striking of the air, impelled from the base of the navel, against the head. This very practice, when cultivated in the sequence of days, fortnights, months, and so forth, [attains its result].

It is called "long-subtle" (*dīrghasūkṣma*) because it is long by virtue of pervading great space and time, and subtle by virtue of being the object of perception. As for the second meaning: the external object refers to the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*) and so forth, while the internal object refers to the heart, the navel-cakra, and so forth; these two are the objects.
That which, without prior reflection, consists of a state of suspension like a pillar and involves the cessation of movement, is the fourth *prāṇāyāma*.

This is the *kumbhaka* (retention) of the third [type]. Its distinction is that it is accomplished suddenly through a state of suspension—like water falling upon a heated stone—after having reflected upon both external and internal objects. This one, however, is preceded by reflection.

One who is dependent [on external aids] and practices with great effort first attains that particular stage, and then, through the sequence of mastering each successive stage, he proceeds. He now states the fruit of all four types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The Blessed Patañjali [states]:

"From that, the veil over the light is destroyed and the mind becomes fit for concentration. From that—namely, from that breath control (prāṇāyāma)—the veil over the light, which is the nature of omniscience residing in the *cittasattva*, is destroyed.

When the obscuration consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*) is exhausted and destroyed, the mind becomes fit for the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) whose characteristics will be described below; by means of the vital breaths, the mind, its defects diminished, wherever it is held, [remains there].
The meaning of the Sūtra is that it becomes stabilized in each respective place.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Just as ghee is obtained by the virtuous through the application of milk and other [ingredients],"
Just as fire is obtained from wood or wind from the atmosphere, so too is the self subject to passing away.
Prāṇāyāma is its churning; its method is first explained. Likewise:
"The functioning of all the senses is proclaimed to be the vital breath (prāṇa), which is air."
For by the conquest of that [intellect], the senses themselves are indeed conquered;
since it is proclaimed that there is no difference between the modification (vṛtti) and the subject of the modification (vṛttimat).
Therefore, by the conquest of the mental modifications (vṛtti) alone, the possessor of those modifications (the mind) becomes conquered;
this occurs through the excellence of knowledge and dispassion, and by the striking away of the impurities of the vital breaths.
Having swiftly conquered the senses, everything indeed becomes conquered;
for both heaven and hell are entirely dependent upon the senses alone.
The body is called a chariot, controlled by which one goes either to heaven or to hell; the senses are said to be its horses.
The person is said to be the charioteer, and breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is remembered as the bridle;
by means of the reins of knowledge and dispassion, the mind is restrained and held steady.
In Haṭhayoga, [the mind], struck by the whetstone of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), gradually attains stillness.
Sūryabheda, Ujjāyī, Śītkāra, Śītalī, Bhastrikā,
Bhramarī, and Mūrchā— these are the eight types of Kumbhaka.

In that regard, the characteristics of the *sahita* [practice] have already been explained previously. Through the constant application of practice by the lords of yogis, a certain play of bliss arises in the mind: the inhalation (*pūraka*) is the humming sound of a bee’s flight, and the exhalation (*recaka*) is the slow, gentle resonance of a female bee.
Mūrcchā:

At the end of the inhalation (pūraka), one should perform the Jālandhara lock very firmly; then one should exhale slowly. This is called Mūrcchā, which bestows the bliss of mental absorption (manomūrchā).
One should produce the sound "śīt" in the mouth and must never release it through the nose;
by practicing yoga in this manner, one becomes a second Kāmadeva.
He is to be served by the circle of yoginīs and is the agent of creation and destruction;
neither hunger nor thirst, nor sleep, nor drowsiness, nor laziness arises [for him].
By this method, the lord of yogis who [practices] upon the circle of the earth shall have a body that acts according to his own will and is free from all afflictions.
He who constantly drinks the vital breath through the union of the tongue and the palate will,
within half a year, experience the total destruction of all diseases.
In the *Yogabīja*: Sūryabhedaṇa.
Then, on a comfortable seat, the yogi, having assumed the vajrāsana posture,
should slowly draw in the external breath through the right nāḍī.

The wise practitioner should perform a kumbhaka (retention) extending from the tips of the hair on the head down to the tips of the nails; thereafter, he should slowly exhale the breath through the left channel (nāḍī).
One should perform the excellent Sūryabheda [prāṇāyāma], which purifies the skull, destroys defects, removes the afflictions of worms, and bestows repeated purification.
Ujjāyī.
Having restrained the mouth and drawn the breath back through the two channels,
it resounds as it reaches from the throat and heart down to the base of the heart.
Then, as before, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] like a jar;
this removes phlegm disorders from the throat and increases the digestive fire of the body.
This kumbhaka known as ujjāyī is to be performed while walking or standing; it destroys the defects located in the channels, the water, and the bodily tissues.
The bellows.
Having placed both soles of the feet likewise upon the thighs,
this becomes the correct lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all sins.
Having correctly assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), with neck and belly held straight, the wise one,
carefully restraining the mouth, should exhale the breath through the breath.
Just as it settles in the heart and throat, one should fill [the breath] up to the skull;
one should properly fill the wind with force up to the limit of the heart-lotus.
One should purge again in that same manner, filling [the vessel] repeatedly,
just as the bellows of smiths are moved by the force of the wind.
In the same way, that which resides within one's own body is moved by the intellect of the vital air (pavana);
one should fill it with such force that exertion occurs within the body.
Just as the belly becomes full, one should hold it light with air;
one should firmly hold the middle of the nose with the two index fingers, excluding the thumbs.
Having performed the *kuṃbhaka* as before, one should then exhale through the *iḍā*;
this removes wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases the digestive fire of the body.
One should perform the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī, which destroys sins, bestows happiness, and is auspicious;
it resides at the mouth of the Brahma-nāḍī and effects the destruction of the bolt of the skull.
This kumbhaka known as *bhastrā* must specifically be performed for the purpose of piercing the three knots (*granthi*) that have arisen in the body.
Śītalī.
Having drawn in the air through the tongue as before, and following the retention (kumbhaka),
the pure-minded practitioner should slowly exhale the breath through both nostrils.
Or even abdominal tumors and enlargement of the spleen.
Having drawn the breath from the outside and filled the belly,
one remains focused with effort on the center of the navel, the tip of the nose, and the big toe.
One should retain the breath within the mind during the periods of twilight or at all times;
thus liberated from all diseases and free from fatigue, the yogi shall live long.
O Gārgī, fixing [the mind] on the tip of the nose is the cause of victory over the vital breath (vāyu);
by fixing it in the center of the navel, there shall be the destruction of all diseases.
The body attains lightness through concentration on the big toe;
that man who, having fixed the tongue upon the breath, drinks [it] constantly, [attains this].
Fatigue and fever are destroyed for him, and likewise his diseases perish,
who, during the two twilights or at the time of Brahma, draws in and drinks the air.
O auspicious lady, after three months, Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, arises within him;
through the practice of six months, he is liberated from great diseases.
Having projected the self into the Self within the Kuṇḍalinī, one should hold it there;
those who know the highest truth declare that his diseases of consumption and the like are destroyed.
Having drawn the wind into the tongue, one should place it at the root of the tongue;
the wise man who drinks this nectar enjoys every auspiciousness.
He who, having drawn the self into the self within the space between the eyebrows by means of the iḍā,
drinks the food of the thirty gods, is liberated from diseases.
He who, having drawn the vital air through the two channels, causes it to move in the navel, or on the sides of the belly,
or at the uvula, is liberated from diseases.
For one month, during the twilight hours, one should inhale air through the tongue and drink it; he who consumes this food of the gods should hold it within the center of his abdomen.
Furthermore, diseases such as abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders (plīha), and stones (aṣṭhilī) produced by the three humors,
as well as all other ailments located within the abdomen, perish along with their underlying sins.
All fevers are destroyed, as are various kinds of poisons;
what is the use of saying more, O Gārgī? Even gray hair and other such signs of old age perish.
In the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.

Touching the tips of the two upper front teeth and placing the tongue near them, one should drink the breath through the hollow of the crow’s beak; this is the supreme restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma).
For one who slowly inhales the breath through both nostrils while drawing it in from all sides,
fatigue, burning sensations, diseases of the throat and stomach, fever, and abdominal tumors indeed come to an end.
For both twilights, for a period of three months, one should inhale the scent for even a single muhūrta;
by drinking that essence with the two-fold beak, the fragrance-bearing wind, there shall be the supreme accomplishment of Sarasvatī upon the earth.
Poison brings about the total destruction of even the most exalted serpents who possess supreme valor;
how much more so, then, those such as scorpions, insects, and spiders, by merely drinking the wind from the mouth of a raven?
If a man, free from sloth, drinks the wind from the two wings of a crow day and night,
he will certainly hear [the voice of the deity] within a year and even see [the deity] from a very great distance.

What is the use of these words spoken repeatedly in many ways? For when the wind is seized by the double-beaked bird [Time], the powerful fear of death brought about by old age quickly reaches its end through exhaustion.
Having placed the tongue at the root of the palate and firmly pressing the teeth against the teeth,
he who drinks the breath very slowly along with the internal flowing streams of nectar— such a supreme practitioner, freed from all diseases and devoid of sin, is liberated within six months.
Having conquered the messenger of death, who arrives once every year, he shall live for a long time upon this earth.

By the power of practicing this for three years, one whose hair becomes as dark as a blue lotus will perceive both the past and the future. Poison does not take effect in his body, even if he is bitten by the most terrible lords of serpents; nor do artificial poisons, whether of mineral or organic origin.

Or is it poison? What need is there for other *kālakūṭas*? Or is it Bhairava himself, who, having attained the eightfold qualities by the power of Time, sports upon the surface of the earth? [She is] the divine stream, white as the mist of the food [offered] within the hollow of the pillar supporting the *yāmaṇḍa*, flowing from the moon within the hollow of the sky-lotus, carrying [it] along. Of that—

For one who causes the hollow of the sky-going channel (nāḍī) known as Vajra to enter the center of the belly, there shall be the dissolution of the vessel of the Brahma-egg, a solid death even unto Death himself. Having entered a state of swoon, it truly destroys the multitude of diseases; when firmly bound, it brings about for men movement through the sky. The wind is dead.
Through practice, the complete conquest of death becomes truly easy for one who has mastered the breath; this is the word of Śiva in another scripture:
"The fickleness of the vital essence (rasa) and of the mind is equal."
When nourished by rasa, why should that which is bound to the mind not achieve perfection on this earth?
O Bhairavī, when swooned, the mind-wind removes disease; when dead, it restores life by itself; and when bound, it bestows the power of moving through the sky.

Some, however, describe these very breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) as a form of medical treatment for the various diseases arising from the negligence of yogis; that is incorrect. For [the scriptures state]: "One who is not afflicted by disease," "one whose consciousness is not distracted," "one who is not tormented by anxiety," and "one should not practice when there is bodily affliction, as it may give rise to despondency and the like"—and much more to this effect.

Because the practice of yoga is prohibited during a state of illness, as has already been shown previously, and because it would contradict direct experience; furthermore, the scriptural mention of the fruit consisting of the destruction of disease applies to the [practice] common to all its constituent parts, and not to merely two or three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*). For instance, among all living beings...

It is clearly observed in all the Yoga scriptures that all diseases, ailments, fevers, and the like, which exist on earth in a subtle form like seeds, are destroyed— some by postures (āsanas), some by breath control (prāṇāyāma), some by withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and some by concentration (dhāraṇā) and other such means.

We have also previously demonstrated this in various contexts. It will be stated that the propitiation of the Supreme Lord alone is the remover of all obstacles, such as diseases and ailments born of fate.
Furthermore, other means for mastering the vital breath (*prāṇa*) have been described incidentally in the very first chapter.
The specific method for conquering the downward breath (apāna) and the others is found in the Yoga Sāgara.
Exhalation and so forth should be understood in their proper sequence through the separation from their respective locations;
the meaning is that this occurs by means of the extensive practice of exhalation (*recaka*).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
One should direct the apāna wind toward the region of the hips and the back;
by always holding it right there, this is the method for conquering the vital winds.
Through the gradual restriction of the common location [of the breath], one attains mastery;
here too, the restriction of the location occurs through the alternation of exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka).
Likewise:
One should fill the body with air through the solar channel (bhānu) and, having pervaded the body, retain it;
thus the knower conquers the samāna breath, and if he gazes while it is blazing, he attains vision.
Then, trembling and drenched in perspiration, the yogi should blaze;
the sage should cause even that all-pervading one to be deluded by his pores.
In the *Yogasāra*:
By means of the yoga of nasal extraction, this [soul], being drawn up sequentially from the heart and other centers, attains subjugation; whether restrained or unrestrained, it reaches its fruit.
Moving back and forth from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet,
following the sequence of the previously mentioned locations, it quickly comes under one's control.

Having first fixed [the mind] on the tip of the nose, and having successively restrained [the breath] at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head, it is drawn upward; this refers to the activity of going and coming,
meaning the domain of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Drawing [the breath] with the head raised and making a loud sound, one should hold it;
thus the udāna, whose deity is Vāyu, is surely conquered.
The conquest of the *vyāna* [wind] is in the ocean of yoga.

Through the practice of *kuṃbhaka* (retention) in one's own field (*svakṣetra*), by means of the sequence beginning with contraction and the yoga of the heart’s pervasion of the universe, the *vyāna* breath is said to be conquerable. One's own field is the body.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Inhalation, retention, and exhalation are thus described;
by contemplating the subtle with inner radiance, the yogi shall gradually conquer vyāna.

In this regard, it should be understood that the specific methods for mastering the vital winds (prāṇa), beginning with breath control, must be practiced only in conjunction with the previously mentioned contemplation of locations, phonemes, seed-syllables (bīja), and so forth; they are not independent. Now, the methods for simultaneously mastering all the vital winds:
To the one devoted to the yoga of Lakṣmī.
Bringing [the breath] from its own place— the heart-lotus— along with the letters, seed-syllables, and so forth,
and unifying it with Brahman and Fire, one should perform the recitation simultaneously.
