Having unified [the elements] within the heart-lotus and mentally contemplated the multicolored sphere of all the winds together with fire, one should then lead that [wind] through the intermediate stations in succession up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
and from the aperture of Brahmā, by bypassing the intermediate stations, [lead it] to the tip of the big toe.
The meaning is that one should conquer [the breath] simultaneously through practice until it turns back; as stated in the *Yogasāra*:
Having joined the function of the prāṇa with the apāna and drawn it up into the heart,
one should bring the vyāna there and thus achieve its unification with the udāna.

Having led it, one should bring it to the middle of the chest, then to the middle of the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the surface of the forehead, and finally to the crown of the head.
"Having performed [the preliminary], one should then perform everything else either in the Brahma-fire or even in the Āgneya-fire";
thus was he instructed by Sarvavāyu regarding the gradual and simultaneous conquest [of the elements].
Even though it is not explicitly mentioned here, it is understood because of its connection to that [context],
as stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Having drawn the wind into the navel, one should release it slightly from the fire-element;
through such practice, the sage conquers all winds within the mouth.
Likewise:
Having assumed the posture, one should hold the breath according to the sequence of *dhāraṇā*;
with effort, the practitioner of yoga should remain straight and free from drowsiness.
Through such practice of yoga, one perceives a subtle light at the tips of the toes,
at their bases, on the heels, the ankles, the thighs, and the knees.
It is situated equally in the anus, the generative organ, the bladder, the navel, the heart, the throat, the chest,
the tongue, the nose, the eyes, the mouth, and the head.
One should contemplate the supreme reality; by that, one becomes absorbed in it as a sage.
—From the Yājñavalkya-gītā.
But here, other yogins of even mind, devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and purified, declare that one should be free from both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka).
One should press the vein at the suture with the right ankle, [placing it] below the two shanks;
the subtle [vein] is on the left, and the right [ankle] is placed upon it.
O Gārgī, one should bind the space between the calves and thighs firmly so that there is no gap;
with the neck, head, and shoulders aligned, the back straight, and the abdomen level.
Gazing with both eyes at the right ankle situated above,
one should hold [the mind] together with the mind while uttering the syllable Om.
O lady of excellent hips, those twice-born ones, their minds fixed on another, would constantly recite the syllable *praṇava* to the Kṣatriya in private while seated.
Seated in a secluded place, those of steady mind who have conquered their senses—
Vaishyas, Shudras, women, and other men devoted to the practice of yoga— [attain this].
Whether reciting a Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, or even any other sacred text,
those whose minds are fixed elsewhere remain seated, glancing at the lamp held in their hand.

Since the vital breath (prāṇa) is the cause of the destruction of life and because of this [breath] the lineage of fire [is maintained], one should practice thus until the conquest of the smoke-bannered [fire] occurs; otherwise, it is merely blindness.
For one who performs its retention, the vital wind reaches the seat of power;
the body attains lightness, and the digestive fire is kindled.
Then, having perceived the sign and mentally superimposing the wind upon that [sign],
one should recite the mantra for a long duration and restrain it within the center of the navel.
As long as the movement of the mind remains within this solar orb at the navel,
for that long the yogi, restrained and fixed in posture, should practice.
By this means, when the vital air is held in the center of the navel, it enters the Kuṇḍalinī and the fire burns there; of this there is no doubt.
Heated there by fire and stirred by the wind itself,
she then expands her hood and attains consciousness.
When this wheel at the root of the navel has awakened and is moving,
that which is designated as the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds into the *suṣumṇā* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
O fair-faced one, when that wind has reached the *suṣumṇā*,
the wise practitioner, having mentally uttered the mantra, should fix it within the center of the heart.
One should fix [the mind] upon the heart, the pit of the throat, and the middle of the eyebrows;
then, with one-pointed intellect, having ascended from there, one should carry the fire along with the vital breath by means of the mind.
O best of Brahmins, while reciting the syllable *praṇava*, one should hold [the breath] in the void;
when the void within the body, along with its limbs and sub-limbs, has been filled by the vital air.
Then his self shines like the sun in the sky;
if he desires to cast off the body, he should practice correctly in this manner.
Meditating on the single-syllabled supreme Brahman, the Lord Praṇava,
he [pierces] the crown of the heads of those whose minds are dissolved by means of that vital air at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Thereafter, one should release the vital breath into the center of the Great Sound (Mahāpraṇava),
which transcends the body, is the life-force of the universe, and is the void, eternal, and immutable state.
O Gārgī, the pure one should unite the self with the supreme bliss in the ether;
he becomes Brahman itself and shall not be subject to rebirth again.
Likewise, Gārgī said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, devoted to the welfare of all beings! O Lord of Yogis, that which has indeed been described by you for the sake of liberation—"
Indeed, the extensive yoga endowed with eight limbs was [practiced] by me;
all of that has now been forgotten in your presence, O Omniscient One.
O Omniscient One, having instructed me today in yoga along with its constituent limbs in a concise form, you ought to protect me from the ocean of birth and saṃsāra.
Thus addressed by the woman who speaks of Brahman, the Brahmin who knows Brahman then looked upon them with compassion and, preceded by a smile, spoke as follows.
Arise, arise! Why do you lie on the ground, O Gārgī of lovely countenance?
I shall explain the yoga to you in brief; listen now.
Yājñavalkya.
Pressing the anus with the left ankle and likewise pressing the joint with the other [right ankle],
and placing one hand upon the hand resting on the left knee, always gaze at the crest of this fire.
O Gārgī, when the vital breath that obstructs longevity is indeed restrained by means of the posture (āsana),
it then gradually enters the fire through drinking and carries the lineage.
Stirred by the wind and by the apāna breath very gradually,
the fire then blazes within the bodies of all in the center of their own [respective] families.
Being composed in mind, one should practice thus for a single muhūrta during the morning, at dusk, and at midnight, until two five-day periods have passed.
Then, O best of Brahmins, various signs of mastery arise individually within his own self for him by whom the vital breath (samīraṇa) has been conquered.
Lightness of the body, radiance from the fire residing in the stomach, and the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda)— by these signs, indeed, the two feet [of the yogic path] are attained.
There will be little urine and feces for six months or even a year;
once the seat has been worn through, one should not move on for three years.
Then, having mentally ascended that blue [wind] together with its companion, one should restrain it;
one should constantly meditate upon the unawakened, ever-slimy Kuṇḍalinī as having entered the navel.
Having fixed the opening with the mouth, the middle part with the body, and likewise the head;
having properly grasped its own tail with the mouth and restrained it, just as one would restrain the hosts of Maruts.
Breathing like the awakened king of serpents, ever-awakened and blazing with splendor,
that Kuṇḍalī always resides at the navel within the bodies of animals and among men.
He who, while recollecting her form, burns the Kundalinī— who resides within the navel at the center of the kanda and is fanned by the wind with flames of fire— is indeed the best among men.
Heated there by fire and agitated by the wind,
she then extends the coils of her serpent’s body and awakens.
When awakening has occurred at the center of the navel of the Cakriṇī, all the vital breaths (prāṇas) gather together in this body and move along with the fire,
just as the movement of threads occurs within a cloth.
Having indeed pierced the station of the Discus-bearer, one who is devoted to constant practice should then lead the apāna upward from the navel while maintaining mindfulness.
O friend Vāyu, when you have entered the body and moved beyond the navel together with the life-force (vāyusakha),
diseases perish, strength increases, and then a preeminent luster arises.
The vital winds here enter the aperture of Brahmā and, together with the fire, proceed into the midst of the sky;
I tell you this because of my observation of the well-kindled flame of the lamp within your heart.

When the wind, together with its friend, is restrained in the heart and enters the opening of the thousand-petaled lotus in the center, O best of the twice-born, it should then be made to face upward once more.
In this city of Brahman, within the lotus of the awakened heart,
the wind ceased its movement like a row of young suns in the sky.
Situated within the *suṣumṇā* from the center of the heart,
that consumer of oblations shines like a streak of lightning amidst banks of water-laden clouds.
When the fire is well-established in the awakened heart-lotus and the vital breath (prāṇa) is likewise fixed therein,
external as well as internal signs— such as the appearance of lamps and the like— become visible to him.
While ascending the vital air (vāyu), he utters the fire-syllable (vahni) together with the Praṇava mantra and the bindu;
then, resembling the crescent moon, he gazes upon the crescent moon at his forehead.
Having then mentally placed the fire upon the wind between his eyebrows, he,
with undistracted mind, should subsequently meditate upon the inner self within himself.
O Gārgī, even in the middle of the heart and on the forehead, the invisible linga blazes like a pillar;
this is the supreme reality—behold it, behold it with your mind as a beautiful form.

He who perceives the light consisting of knowledge within the center of the forehead or the lotus of the heart beholds that Śakti blazing like the tip of a lamp; with a single-pointed vision, he perceives Brahman itself.
Just as the mind of yogis among men attains dissolution in the space between the eyebrows,
there occurs the flow of nectar at the root of the tongue and the vision of the Self between the eyebrows.
There is trembling at the crown of the head and the vision of the Self by means of the mind alone;
as well as the delightful celestial gardens, the stars, and the moon.
The ṛṣis, siddhas, and gandharvas become visible to yogins as long as the mind remains dissolved in the state of Viṣṇu situated between the eyebrows, until it reaches full awakening.
Having practiced thus for a while, one should again contemplate the form of the eternal Radiance in the midst of space;
when the vital breath has entered the station of Viṣṇu and the individual soul remains there, neither dead nor yet alive.
If the mind always attains dissolution in that [Self], they say this is near to liberation—
for you, O one of pure intellect, who are established in the Self and whose breath has entered the station of Viṣṇu.
O Gārgī, behold today with a purified intellect this most wonderful truth that exists:
having thus practiced for a very long time, disciplined in body through the restraints (yama) and other yogic limbs, and moderate in diet.
Having reached the Self that has entered the cave, you shall again attain liberation in the city of Brahman;
from whom all beings—both moving and unmoving—arise at creation, yet do not truly live.
All declare that the Knower of Brahman is that in which all things born reach their dissolution;
it is the one-formed reality within the space of the heart-lotus, eternally consisting of bliss and exceedingly subtle.
That Brahman is known to be within the cave [of the heart], as the Śruti also declares:
"Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being. They bring these two together.
At the time of departure, you, free from sorrow, behold that Supreme Will with a purified intellect;
for, through the instruction of the Guru, you have attained by means of the mind that Wind which has reached the crown of the head and carries the Fire.
Having pierced through the crown of the head, cast the vital breath again into the midst of space while recollecting the syllable *oṃ*;
if you wish to know the voluntary relinquishment of the body, my friend, I shall explain it to you.
Uttering the Praṇava, perform the upward piercing of the crown and create a body for yourself; thus it is said in the Gītā.
Having restrained all the gates [of the senses] and fixed the mind within the heart,
and having placed his vital breath in the head, he remained established in the practice of yoga-concentration.
"Uttering the single syllable 'Om', which is Brahman, and remembering Me, he who departs,
casting off the body, goes to the supreme goal."
And it is stated in the Śruti as well.
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing [from this world].
If a yogi desires to remain for a long time in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta), he should nourish his body;
thus says Dattātreya.
"If the desire arises in the yogi, 'I am a liberated soul while living, moving through the three worlds,' then listen to me regarding that."
This body is never to be abandoned by anyone, anywhere;
therefore, a yogi must exert effort for the sake of protecting the body.
A yogi must constantly and with effort investigate the signs of death (ariṣṭa), so that time may not strike him unawares.
But the undesirable [results] will now be explained.
Having correctly understood that time and resorted to the place of dissolution,
one should practice yoga so that this time may yield its fruit.
Having assumed the bound posture (baddhasiddhāsana), one should fill the body with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu);
having made the body steady through the intellect, one should restrain the ten gates.
One should bind the Khecarī Mudrā, Jālandhara at the neck,
Mūlabandha at the perineum, and likewise Uḍḍiyāna in the abdomen.
Having raised up the serpent-like power (śakti) residing in the lotus of the mūlādhāra,
auspicious and piercing through the five cakras within the suṣumṇā;
Having led the living soul, which resides in the heart, along with the intellect and mind as they depart,
[one should contemplate them] merged into Śiva, who abides in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus and consists of nectar.
Then, one should meditate upon her sprinkling the entire body from its very base with the nectar produced from the moon, completely flooding it.
Then, together with her, the yogi shall attain identity with Śiva;
having become composed of supreme bliss, he should even abandon the activity of consciousness.
Then, how could Time destroy that which is without an object of perception, devoid of the sense of "I," free from all conceptualization of limbs, and beyond all mental constructs?
That alone is the auspicious Time; everything is nothing at all.
There, who is slain by whom? No one dies there either.
Then, after some time had passed, he was awakened by Time, whose form is delusion,
as a yogi awakens from sleep upon rising.
Thus, having deceived time and the cycle of existence through extraordinary human effort according to the prescribed rule, the yogi shall become perfected.
Then that yogi wanders alone throughout the three worlds,
beholding the manifold variety of saṃsāra by his own will, free from the sense of "I" and devoid of agency.
Now, one should observe the signs in the mastery of the vital airs, beginning with prāṇa; as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
When the vital breath (prāṇa) has been properly conquered, one should observe its signs:
a diminution of the impurities of feces, urine, and phlegm occurs.
Capacity for abundant food, slow breathing,
as well as health, long-distance travel, enthusiasm, and excellence of voice.
Strength, complexion, clarity, and likewise the destruction of all diseases—
such signs as these arise in one who is established in sattva.
In the Vāyusaṃhitā.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) has been properly conquered, one should observe its signs:
lightness, swiftness of movement, enthusiasm, and excellence of voice.
The destruction of all diseases, strength, splendor, and beauty;
fortitude, intelligence, youthfulness, stability, and the attainment of the goals of human life.
Dattātreya.
From practice even more intense than that, great power arises,
by which one attains the accomplishment of moving on the earth, which strikes fear into those who move upon the earth.
Whether it be a tiger, a buffalo, a wild ox, a gayal, or even an elephant,
or a lion— by that yogi, they are all killed with a mere stroke of the hand.
To the one devoted to the yoga of Nakulīśa.
Through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), long exhalation and the conquest of disease occur;
through the conquest of form, there is the reduction of feces and urine, as well as luster and beauty.
The subsiding of thirst and hunger, the keenness of the digestive fire, and the healing of wounds,
fractures, and skin eruptions are considered the results of conquering the *samāna* wind.
From *jaya* comes the upward departure of the *udāna* breath and the ascent from water and other elements;
from *dhyāna* comes the destruction of all Rudras and non-attachment to cold and heat upon the skin.
When victory is achieved simultaneously, all this should be understood as the fruit itself;
through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*), the remainder is brought to destruction by means of conceptualization.
Thus, the fruits of exhalation (recaka) and the other breath-control techniques for the vital winds such as prāṇa and the rest are recorded in tradition;
it is also stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa regarding the nature of these winds:
By conquering these, the wise man conquers the reality known as earth and the rest;
by conquering them, the sage who knows yoga truly becomes omniscient.

By desiring sensual pleasures, one obtains them; by [controlling] desire, great dignity arises. When the wise man conquers the vital air (vāyu), there occurs a reduction in the production of feces and urine.
The yogin will certainly attain [mastery] over Pātāla and the other regions through effortless play;
likewise, there is the ascent of the digestive fire within the stomach and its state of equilibrium.
He will surely become a great eater; the sage becomes one whose essence is the *sattvas*.
From that identity with the *sattvas*, there is oneness; and from that oneness, he becomes composed of that.
It is not cut by weapons at all, nor indeed do waters moisten it;
neither disease nor poison takes hold of it, due to the governance of the vyāna breath.
In the Yogabhāskara.
As long as the internal sound vibrates and as long as the mind dissolves, for that long one is a yogi of the arisen state; thereafter, one becomes a master of the ascended yoga.
And one shall become a master of yoga within ten years or ten months;
likewise, it has been stated that this occurs immediately after the purification of the channels (nāḍī).
Thus one becomes a yogī of the "arisen" (utpanna); listen now to the description of the yogī who has ascended.
The body of the yogī of the arisen stage, even if well-nourished, attains a state of emaciation.
The body of one who has ascended to yoga may become emaciated yet regain its bulk;
the mind of one in whom yoga has arisen is forcibly led to a single point.
The mind of one who has ascended to yoga never becomes unsteady;
the arisen yogi is free from world-weariness, while the ascended yogi is always happy.
The practitioner who has attained yoga has a weak digestive fire, whereas one who has ascended is a great eater;
for him, even fruits, flowers, and leaves that he consumes are digested.
When the vital air has reached beyond the three locations, one is said to be "perfected" (siddha).
For the perfected one, there are three signs: he is a giver, an enjoyer, and one who does not deceive.
Thus, in the *Yogabīja*.
By the grace of the Guru, Marudeva accomplished [the practice]; by that very breath, the mind was mastered.
He alone is the yogi, he who has conquered his senses and is happy; the fools who argue with fallacious logic do not know this.
If the mind, though seemingly lost, indeed shines forth, then even the wind is perceived as having perished there;
yet if it were not so, there would be neither scripture for it, nor self-realization, nor a guru, nor liberation.
Just as a leech certainly draws out blood by force,
so too does the Brahma-nāḍī draw out the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Through the yoga of constant, continuous practice and by always maintaining the postures,
the mind attains dissolution, and the bindu likewise does not fall downward.
Having abandoned both exhalation and inhalation, one remains for a long time with the breath;
various sounds arise, and the lunar orb flows forth.
When that is so, all defects such as hunger and thirst perish,
and one attains a state of abiding in the absolute nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

Freedom from greed, health, lack of harshness, a pleasant fragrance, clarity of urine and feces, luster, serenity, and gentleness of voice— these are indeed the first signs of the commencement of yoga.
People feel affection upon hearing the praise of one's virtues even when they are out of sight;
and living beings are not harmed—this is the supreme sign of success.
For one who experiences no affliction from the most intense cold, heat, and so forth,
and who feels no fear from others, accomplishment has arrived.
In this way, for the yogi who is disciplined in yoga and self-restrained,
all defects perish and he becomes truly established in well-being.
And he beholds the Supreme Brahman and the material qualities separately,
as well as space and the other elements down to the atoms, and likewise the stainless Self.
Listen to its fourfold state which bestows the fruit of liberation:
destruction (dhvaṃsti), attainment (prāpti), consciousness (saṃvit), and grace (prasāda) are glorified.
Listen now to their essential nature as it is being described in due order:
through these actions, whether auspicious or wicked, the exhaustion of their fruits occurs.
Where, due to the slight turbidity of the mind, right conduct is prescribed,
[one should abandon] whatever desires of this world or the next, as well as greed, delusion, and so forth.
The ever-yoked yogi remains in a state of cessation; this is the attainment that fulfills all desires, whereby he perceives past and future objects, as well as those that are remote or concealed.
O King, when a yogi, through the perfection of knowledge, perceives the moon, the sun, the stars,
and the planets as being of an identical nature, he attains that state.
Then that state of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is known as "consciousness" (saṃvit),
by which his mind and the five vital airs attain serenity.
"The sense organs and the objects of the senses are called *saprasāda*," says Vasiṣṭha.
"At both twilights, one should always [perform the rite] with the Gāyatrī or with the *praṇava*."
A Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of the Vedas should practice the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma).
One should always perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in this manner;
performed daily, they purify even the killer of an embryo within a month.
After three seasons, one is indeed purified from the sins committed in another birth;
after a year, one becomes a knower of Brahman. Therefore, one should practice these constantly.
Those who are devoted to the practice of yoga and those who are intent on their own duty— indeed, all such people become liberated through the restraint of the vital breath.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, following the description of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
it is stated: "A celibate student who has conquered anger, conquered greed, and is free from envy— by practicing in this manner constantly for a year, he is called a yogi."
In the Haṭhapradīpikā.
The postures, the various breath-retentions (kumbhakas), the practice known as mudrās, as well as the application of the sounds (nādas), according to the sequence of practice.
A celibate practitioner who eats moderately, practices renunciation, and is devoted to yoga shall become perfected after one year; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Emaciation of the body, brightness in the face, clarity in the voice, and utter purity of the eyes;
freedom from disease, the conquest of the vital drops (bindu), stimulation of the digestive fire, and purification of the channels—these are the signs of success in Haṭha Yoga.
In that which was spoken by Īśvara.
The initial stage, the pot-like stage, as well as the stage of mastery,
and the stage of perfection— these are the states of yoga in all yogic practices.
For it is thus:
when the channels of the yogin who perceives reality become purified, then,
for one whose sins have been destroyed, the possibility of spiritual commencement arises.
The signs [of progress] appear upon the body of the yogin due to the purification of the channels;
I shall describe them briefly for my devotee.

He possesses an even body, is fragrant, is very handsome, and has a voice like that of a swan; he is one whose digestive fire is mature, enjoys excellent pleasures, is happy, and is beautiful in every limb.
With a fully perfected heart, the yogi becomes endowed with all enthusiasm and strength;
thereafter, the yogi shall possess the power to retain the vital breath (vāyu) as desired.
Through the retention of breath according to one's will, *kumbhaka* is certainly accomplished;
once *kevala-kumbhaka* is mastered, what is there that cannot be achieved here for the yogi?
Sweat arises on the body of the yogi; this is the first, the lowest stage. Trembling arises as the second; it is difficult to restrain and is considered the middling stage.
When perspiration arises, one should perform gentle massage;
otherwise, the constituent element (dhātu) of the yogin is destroyed within the body.
Then, through even more intense practice, the lord of practitioners, the yogi,
even while remaining in the lotus posture, proceeds by leaving the earth behind.
Then the accomplishment of the vital air (vāyu-siddhi) should be known as that which destroys the darkness of saṃsāra;
for that duration, one should observe the restraints prescribed for yoga.
For the yogi who perceives reality, sleep and excrement become very slight, and what must be wiped away is minimal; he is free from dejection and free from disease.
Sweat, saliva, and dizziness never arise at all;
nor do phlegm, bile, or wind [disturbances] occur within the body of the practitioner.
The lord of yogis should chant that mantra for a long time for the sake of destroying obstacles,
and through breath control (prāṇāyāma), he attains the eightfold sovereign powers.
Having crossed the ocean of sin and merit, one shall attain lordship over the three worlds;
[as stated] in the *Amṛtasiddhi*.
When the wind is mastered within the body, then consciousness arises;
and from that consciousness, all supernatural powers (ṛddhi) come to be for the yogins.
But when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is accomplished, then non-attainment (*asiddhi*) is not far off;
for that wind which has the nature of attainment is conjoined with the path of the central channel (*madhyamā*).
Then the mind, consisting of bliss, becomes of a single form, composed of space;
when the mind consists of bliss, it is free from external afflictions.
Then, by enduring the sufferings of existence, meditative absorption (samādhi) arises;
it is always perfected in absorption and filled with innate bliss (sahajānanda).
Then this mind is perfected, removing all suffering and fear;
whatever the yogi performs at that time, all of it comes to pass in that very instant.
One should certainly know the characteristics of a yogin whose body has attained perfection:
the experience of bliss (*hlāda*) and so forth within the bodies [of others], as well as the entry into another's body (*parapurapraveśana*).
Seeing and hearing from a distance—these are established as the characteristics of air;
and when there is the accomplishment of these three—the body, air, and mind.
That is to be known as the great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi), which bestows the fruit of liberation while living;
having attained liberation while living, the yogi shall proceed to the state of great liberation.
Then the lord of yogis indeed becomes perfected in the meditative absorption of his own will;
then there is the great meditative absorption known as the Cloud of Dharma.
Then the yogi, consisting of bliss, becomes omniscient and all-seeing;
he is to be worshipped in all worlds and his command is forever unimpeded.
Possessing unimpeded movement, wise, and filled with obstructed bliss,
he is endowed with all qualities of sovereignty and accompanied by all perfections.
The lord of yogis is unfailing toward all beings and is free from defects;
therefore, the yogi consists of all things, for he is indeed composed of all beings.
When contented, he delivers the worlds; when angry, he is the destroyer of all.
When a yogi has attained realization, he is no longer terrifying.
In this manner, for thousands, hundreds of thousands, and hundreds of years, she dwelt in caves on mountain peaks; she was Nanda, a perfected yoginī.
Thus it is stated in the Īśvaraprokta.
Then, through the very sequence of practice, the triad beginning with the jar shall arise,
by which the yogi’s desired complete accomplishment will certainly be attained.
Mastery of speech, the power to move at will, the ability to see from afar,
as well as hearing from a distance, subtle vision, and the power of entering another's body.
By anointing with feces and urine, gold becomes invisible; these qualities belong to the great ones, as does the power of moving through the sky for yogins.
When the supreme state of the "pot" (ghaṭāvasthā) occurs for those practicing with the vital wind,
then there is nothing in this wheel of saṃsāra that they cannot accomplish.
The yogi should be firm in posture, just like Jñānadeva;
when the posture has become very firm, that vital air enters the center.
Through the entry of even a slight amount of vital energy (vāyu), the arising of knowledge occurs for the yogin;
once the accumulation of vital energy has been produced, the yogin becomes equal to a god.
Free from defects, suffering, hunger, sleep, old age, and death,
he becomes equal to the Lord of Yogis, the creator and destroyer of the universe.
Whether there be success for you two or not, here alone is uninterrupted bliss:
the prāṇa and apāna, the nāda and bindu, and the individual self and the supreme self.
Because it is joined together (ghaṭate) by being assembled (militvā), it is therefore called a "jar" (ghaṭa);
when one is capable of holding [it] for at least one watch (yāma) without weariness, [it is complete].
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) occurs only at that time and certainly not in between;
whatever the lord of yogis perceives, he should contemplate that very thing within himself.
By means of those faculties through which the practice is performed, there shall be mastery over those very faculties;
when, through the application of practice, a state of whirling occurs for the duration of a watch (yāma).
Then the yogi should perform the kumbhaka once;
when the breath becomes motionless for eight staff-lengths (daṇḍas), he is a yogi.
Then, having concealed his own power, the wise one should remain like a blade of grass;
thereafter, through practice, the stage of familiarity arises for the yogin.
When the vital air remains motionless, having abandoned the moon and the sun,
and when the air is thoroughly mastered, it moves through the suṣumṇā into the ether.
And having grasped the power of action and having certainly pierced through the wheels,
then the state of familiarity arises through the yoga of practice.
Then the yogi certainly perceives the three peaks of karma;
thereafter, having destroyed the peaks of his own karma with the Praṇava.
The yogi should manifest a multitude of bodies for the sake of experiencing his own karma;
at this time, the great yogi should practice the fivefold retention.
That by which the accomplishment of moving upon the earth is attained removes the fear of those respective elements;
there are five *ghaṭikās* in the foundation (*ādhāra*) and likewise in the region of the navel.
Above that, for five ghaṭikās, one should likewise hold [the breath] at the navel and between the eyebrows;
above the midpoint of the eyebrows, the wise man should likewise hold it for five ghaṭikās.
At that time, the lord of yogis who has mastered the earth and the other elements shall certainly not perish—
he who is wise and practices the concentration upon the five elements.
Even after the passing of a hundred Brahmās, death does not exist for him;
thereafter, through the very sequence of practice, the perfection of yogis comes to be.
By which one may cut through the nets of beginningless karma and attain immortality;
when perfection is achieved, meditative absorption (samādhi) occurs according to one's own will.
Within a month, the power of absorption arises for the yogi who is liberated while living;
having seized the vital air and the power of action, he becomes possessed of great speed.
Having quickly shattered all the wheels, one dissolves into the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "the three peaks of karma" (*trikūṭaṃ karmaṇaḥ*): some karmas are to be experienced exclusively in heaven, while others are to be experienced in hells such as Avīci.
Certain objects of enjoyment belong to the mortal world; this constitutes the threefold nature of karmas.
For the sake of experiencing those enjoyments and for the sake of experiencing his own sovereignty, the yogi should practice the creation of a network of bodies (*kāyavyūha*).
The procedure for this is as follows, according to the *Pātañjala*:

For the yogin who has realized reality (*sākṣātkṛtatattva*), in order to experience simultaneously the fruits of karma and to enjoy sovereign powers such as becoming minute (*aṇimā*) and so forth, minds are produced simultaneously; these arise from the root cause [the *citta*] by means of mere latent impressions (*vāsanāmātra*). Like sparks from a fire, those minds [arise] during the time of yogic practice.

It is not because they follow that [mind] that they lack the nature of being impelled by the single fundamental mind; rather, the cause for their distinctness from the minds arising at birth and so forth is their freedom from the latencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*). Furthermore, it has been stated that the karma of yogis is different because it is performed with the intention of relinquishing the fruits [of action].
It is stated that karma which is distinct from the [threefold]— namely, neither-white-nor-black—

is the undertaking of performance through the intention of renouncing the fruits of even previously mentioned karma; and regarding the production of results such as experience in the assumption of various bodies, this occurs even for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of knowledge acquired over thousands of previous births.

Or rather, the immediate succession of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is beginningless; yet even though they are beginningless, because they are rooted in experience, passion, and ignorance, they are removed through knowledge and yoga, or by means of wisdom (*vidyā*). Because they are like a mere mental construction (*kalpa*), actions (*karman*) are easily abandoned. [Objection: But surely [they are removed] only through experience?

If it is argued that the destruction of karma would render the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and other texts prescribing expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) invalid, we say no; for there is a diversity of karma. To explain:

Indeed, among the various karmas of all living beings, some are to be destroyed by penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, which end with the destruction of the body; others are to be destroyed by means of knowledge, meditation, yoga, and so forth; while yet others are to be destroyed solely through experience (*bhoga*). For the sake of experiencing those [latter], a yogin must certainly create a manifold of bodies (*kāyavyūha*). And as for that which...
The statement beginning with "Karma is not exhausted without being experienced" refers specifically to *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma), which is destroyed solely through experience.

It concerns those living beings who have not performed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), meaning that for them, karma is not exhausted except through experience. Otherwise, [the scriptures] teaching expiation would be rendered purposeless.

The lack of authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa would thus be unavoidable; this is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, these states—known as tāmasa, rājasa, and sāttvika—are distinguished by the differences among practitioners who are mild, moderate, intense, or most intense, and they occur either over a long period of time or a short period of time.
Thus it is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi*:
Men who are diseased, weak, aged, lacking in fortitude, living as householders,
of little enthusiasm, and of feeble vigor should be known as mild.
Within twelve years, these attain a single state:
they become mature in policy, equal in practice, equal in vigor, and equal in disposition.
Those who abide in the middle paths of yoga, likewise through middling yoga,
possessing middling enthusiasm, middling passion, and middling valor, are to be known as the middling [practitioners].
Within eight years, one of these stages is accomplished;
they become heroic, compassionate, patient, and high-minded.
Established in their own place, they shall be healthy and firm in intellect;
they shall be learned, always engaged in practice, and always endowed with respect.
Those who perform meritorious deeds and are indeed superior yogins should be known;
for those who are superior in even a single state, success is achieved within six years.
These men possess great strength, great bodies, great heroism, and great virtues;
though arisen from great delusion, they are peaceful and possessed of great compassion.
They had practiced all the sciences, were adorned with all auspicious marks,
possessed forms resembling those of the Omniscient One, and were free from all diseases.
Endowed with excellent youth, these best of men were free from physical change,
stainless, free from disease, unimpeded, and undisturbed.
Those of noble lineage and great resolve, who have practiced in previous lives,
deliver sentient beings and cross over themselves as well.
Beings possessing all the marks should be known as being of the highest degree;
this single stage is accomplished in three years.
Through four stages, yoga reaches completion;
thus it is stated in the Yogaśāstra.
Having blocked the nine gates, having firmly retained the wind after drinking it in,
and having led the apāna together with fire upward by means of the śakti, one should perform self-meditation; by this method,
having placed [the breath] at the crown of the head, for as long as it remains there, [one attains mastery] over the winds.

It is produced through attachment. Having restrained the mind at the navel and forcefully suppressed the downward movement of the breath, one should contract the root of the apāna and the flame of the fire, which is as subtle as a thread.
Having led that [flame] to the lotus of the heart, and then to the throat, the palate, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one pierces through the void beyond the void.
Where the god Maheśa enters the sky— thus it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha.
Know Kuṇḍalinī to be the life-sustaining essence within the living soul— known by the other name of the "City of Eight"— just as a flower-cluster is the essence within a fragrance.
When that [vital energy] is filled and stabilized evenly through the practice of inhalation (pūraka),
then the stability of Bhairava is attained, as well as the plumpness of the body.
When the vital breath, dependent on the interior filled by inhalation,
is led upward along with consciousness in order to endure the sequence of heat and fatigue.
Moving swiftly like a serpent, it ascends, assuming the likeness of a staff;
taking hold of all the channels, it is bound to the body like a slender creeper.
Then it completely floods this body,
just as a boat filled with dense wind is submerged by water.
Thus, through yoga characterized by the play of practice, yogis attain the power of moving through the sky,
just as the Danavas attained the high state of Indra.
By the flow through the Brahma-nāḍī, the Kuṇḍalinī power is bestowed;
it is outside, above the door-panel, at a height of twelve finger-breadths.
By means of the practice of exhalation, when the hundreds of channels are obstructed, one attains stability for a muhūrta; then, there is the vision of the sky-like state.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect situated not far from consciousness,
the sky-faring Siddhas are seen, like dreams, even as they bestow their own purposes.

By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), when the vital breath is led to remain for a long time outside the mouth at the distance of twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta), it enters the supreme city.
If, when the self is perceived in every way, both upward movement and downward descent are abandoned,
then the disease of that person is destroyed due to the internal obstruction of the vital airs.
O Raghava, all prosperities, from kingship down to liberation, are achieved by everyone through mastery over the body and the vital breath.
Now follows the exposition of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
In this regard, the venerable Patañjali states the nature and the result of withdrawal (pratyāhāra):
"Withdrawal is the senses' imitation of the nature of the mind during contact with their respective objects."
This follows from the two sūtras beginning with "Then, having brought the senses under complete control.
The meaning of this is as follows:
*pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) is that in which the senses are drawn back (*āhriyante*) against (*prati*) their respective objects. How is it performed?

And because of this [point regarding] the object, he says: the objects of the sense organs such as the eye are form and so forth; "application" (prayoga) is their functioning toward those [objects], that is, being directed toward them.
"Oneness with that" (tadekabhāva) is the state of remaining in one's own essential nature alone, having abandoned that directedness. When that [state] exists...

All the senses follow the mind, imitating its movements just as all bees follow the queen bee; therefore, by the cessation of the mind, they are withdrawn. Thus, when withdrawal is practiced in this manner, it becomes so.
They become submissive and dependent; that is to say, even when being led toward external objects, they follow along.
In the Śivagītā.
The restraint of the senses as they naturally wander among their objects is called *pratyāhāra* by the virtuous.
In the Yogaśāstra.
The sun draws back the stream consisting of lunar nectar;
that drawing back of it is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
Just as the sun situated in its third period withdraws its radiance,
so too the yogi established in the third part withdraws mental modification.
Yājñavalkya.
The forceful withdrawal of the senses as they naturally wander among their objects is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
Whatever one perceives, all that one should perceive within oneself as being like the Self;
this is declared by the great-souled masters of yoga to be withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Those rites which are prescribed as obligatory for embodied beings—
the performance of them within oneself by means of the mind, without external action.
Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is also a supreme means for achieving yoga;
it is highly praised and always practiced by yogis.
The withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is said to be the concentration on the vital points (marmasthāna) of the wind within the eighteen locations, drawing [the breath] from one place to another.
The Aśvins, the two foremost physicians among the gods, as they were requested by Gārgya,
[taught] the vital points in the body for the sake of success in yoga and liberation.
I shall describe all of them exactly as they are; listen, O lady of excellent vows:
[they are located] on the big toe, the ankle, and likewise in the middle of the calf.
At the base of the throat, at the knees, and in the middle of the two thighs;
then the root of the anus, followed by the middle of the body and the penis.
The navel, O Gārgī, the heart, as well as the pit of the throat,
the root of the palate, the tip of the nose, and the circles at the roots of the eyes.
O best of sages, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head—
these are the vital points (marmasthānas), and their measurements are as follows, each individually.
The measurement from the foot to the ankle is four and a half finger-breadths;
the distance from the ankle to the middle of the calf should be known as ten finger-breadths.
From the middle of the shank to the base of the altar (citi) is eleven finger-breadths;
from the base of the altar, O lady of beautiful hips, the knee is two finger-breadths away.
The lords of sages have declared that the middle of the thighs is nine finger-breadths above the knees;
likewise, O Gārgī, the root of the anus is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the thighs.
Likewise, from the root of the anus, two finger-breadths [above] is the center of the body;
and from the center of the body, the penis is likewise one and a half finger-breadths [below].
From the penis to the navel, O best of the twice-born, it should be known as twelve and a half finger-breadths; from the navel to the center of the heart, however, it is fourteen finger-breadths.
Six finger-breadths from the center of the heart is the pit of the throat;
likewise, from the pit of the throat, the base of the tongue is four finger-breadths away.
The root of the nose is four finger-breadths from the root of the tongue;
the location of the eyes is held to be half a finger-breadth from that root.
Therefore, the distance between one's own eyebrows is half a finger-breadth;
the region called the forehead should be three finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows.
From the forehead, one should mentally place the wind— known as "space" (vyoma) and measuring three finger-breadths— in those aforementioned locations and hold it there.
For one who performs pratyāhāra by withdrawing [the senses] from place to place,
all diseases perish and his yogic powers indeed become perfected.
Some men who are skilled in yogas say thus;
O lady of noble limbs, listen as I describe to you that practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Having filled the air like a water-pot from the big toe up to the middle of the head, one who is impelled by the practice of *prāṇāyāma* holds the vital breath (*anila*) with the intellect.
Having drawn [the breath] from the aperture of space, one should hold it again at the forehead;
having drawn the wind from the forehead, one should restrain it between the eyebrows.
Drawing the vital breath from the eyes, one should restrain it at the root of the nose;
from the root of the nose, one should then restrain the vital breath at the root of the tongue.

From the pit of the throat to the center of the heart; from the center of the heart to the center of the navel; from the center of the navel again to the penis; from the penis to the abode of the body;
from the center of the body to the anus, O Gārgī; and from the anus to the root of the thighs.
From the base of their thighs, one should restrain [the breath] between them, and from there, at the knees.
Then, from that root of the consciousness, likewise into the middle of the two shanks;
having drawn the wind up from the shanks, one should restrain it at the ankle.
O Gārgī, one should restrain that [vital energy] from the ankles and toes up to the feet;
indeed, he who thus holds it with his intellect, drawing it from place to place.
With his soul purified of all sins, he lives as long as the moon and stars endure;
this has been proclaimed even by Agastya for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga.
Among all forms of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), this is praised by yogis:
having filled the breath through both nostrils, a person [places it] on both sides of the kuṇḍalinī.
Even one afflicted by disease, if he should maintain this, is liberated from the diseases of existence;
having raised the vital air as before, he should hold it in the space of the heart.
O lady of excellent limbs, he too shall again attain the state of the Supreme Self;
however, his diseases—both external and internal—will persist.
Having drawn in the breath through both nostrils and filled the belly, he remains steady;
having fixed his gaze between the eyebrows and behind the eyes, he is composed in meditation.
Even he who holds [this] for a mere moment attains the supreme goal;
what need is there to say more, as he constantly performs his obligatory duties?
Having fixed the vital breath of the self within the suṣumṇā between the eyebrows,
practice restraint for as long as it takes for the mind to dissolve therein.
But Tattātreyas says:
That yogi who clearly withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses by resorting to *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) is said to practice *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Whatever one sees with the two eyes, one should contemplate that within oneself;
whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that within oneself.
Whatever the yogi tastes with the tongue, he should contemplate that within himself;
whatever the yogi touches with the skin, he should contemplate that within himself.
Thus, every day for the duration of one watch (three hours), the yogi, diligent and unwearied, should with effort contemplate everything within the self as being composed of the organs of knowledge.
Then, having reflected upon his capacity, the power of the yogin certainly arises:
distant hearing, distant vision, and likewise the ability to travel a great distance in an instant.
Mastery over speech, the ability to assume any form at will, and likewise the power of invisibility.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Yogacintāmaṇi* composed by Śivānanda Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī. || 3 ||
Now, concentration (dhāraṇā) is defined.
Regarding this, Patañjali states the definition in the sūtra: "Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a place. The meaning of this is as follows:

"Place" refers to internal locations such as the navel-cakra, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the space between the eyebrows, or the crown of the head; or external locations such as the tip of the nose and so forth. "Binding of the mind" is that state of the mind which, by abandoning other objects, [remains fixed].

This placement is called "common" (sādhāraṇā). The meaning is as follows: in a place free from disturbances, by a yogi whose internal organ has been perfumed with friendliness and the other [brahmavihāras], who possesses the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), who has mastered posture (āsana), who has eliminated the fluctuations of the vital breath (prāṇa-vikṣepa), who has withdrawn the collection of sense organs through pratyāhāra, whose body is straight, and who has conquered the pairs of opposites (dvandva).
Through the practice of conscious concentration (*saṃprajñātasamādhi*), the mind should be made steady upon the tip of the nose and so forth;
as it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
Having brought the vital breath under control through breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) and the senses through sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
one should then direct the fluctuations of the mind toward a virtuous object.
In the Śivagītā.
In the lotus of the heart, at the tip of the nose, on the crown of the head, or wherever it may occur—
in such places as these, *dhāraṇā* is the binding of the mind.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Endowed with the practice of posture, joined with breath control,
and perfected in the withdrawal of the senses, one should thoroughly practice concentration.
The separate concentration upon each of the five elements within the heart,
through the immobility of the mind, is designated as *dhāraṇā*.
One should meditate in the heart upon the earth as being like yellow orpiment, marked with the syllable *la*, together with the Creator (Brahmā), and shaped as a square; this is the earth-dhāraṇā.

One should meditate upon the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, which resembles the water of the throat, is like the crescent moon, is endowed with Viṣṇu, and has the luster of a kunda flower; by meditating thus, one conquers the waters.
Having properly meditated upon the fire situated at the palate— triangular, resembling an indragopa insect, joined with the letter *ra*, and presided over by Rudra— one shall conquer the fire.
One should conquer the wind by meditating on the air-principle (vāyutattva) located between the eyebrows, circular and resembling collyrium, with the seed-syllable *ya* as its presiding deity, Īśa.

The space situated at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) is like pure water; it is the tranquil letter *Ha*, accompanied by the Lord Sadāśiva. Having drawn the vital breath (*prāṇa*) there for five *ghaṭikās*, one should hold it together with the mind, becoming skilled in splitting open the door of liberation for the Goddess.
The five types of concentration (dhāraṇā) for the elements have been declared:
the stabilizing, the flooding, the burning, the whirling, and likewise the pacifying. These are the five concentrations of the elements.
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"The stabilization of the mind, endowed with qualities such as restraint (yama) and the rest, within the Self is called 'dhāraṇā' by the virtuous who know the purport of the scriptures."
O Gārgī, within this city of Brahman, which is this lotus of the heart,
it is precisely in that internal space that the support of the external space exists.
And this is called "dhāraṇā" by those learned in the Yoga-śāstras—
by thinkers, by scholars who know the Yoga-śāstras, and by the wise who are well-informed.
The concentrations (dhāraṇās) are said to be fivefold, and they are each distinct:
earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The retention of these five deities is considered to be fivefold.
The region from the feet up to the knees is said to be the location of the Earth.
The region from the navel down to the anus is proclaimed as the seat of water;
that which extends from the anus up to the heart is called the seat of fire.
The region from the center of the heart up to the midpoint between the eyebrows is known as the family of air (vāyu-kula).
From the midpoint between the eyebrows up to the crown of the head is called the element of space (ākāśa).
O Gārgī, one should place Brahmā Parameṣṭhin upon the earth;
Viṣṇu in the waters; Rudra in the fire; and Īśvara in the sphere of the wind.
Likewise, being well-composed, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva in the ether;
having established the wind upon the earth, conjoined with the syllable *la*.
Meditating on Brahmā, the cause of creation, who has the form of four faces, one should maintain [the concentration] for five ghaṭikās; thus, through the earth-mantra, one attains the fruit of japa.
Having mounted Vāyu upon the syllable *vā* (the presiding deity of Varuṇa), conjoined with the letter *va*,
one should remember the god Nārāyaṇa, who has four arms and a pure smile.
One should wear [an amulet] resembling pure crystal, clad in yellow garments, and infallible for five ghaṭikās; one is then liberated from all diseases.
Having superimposed the wind [seed-syllable] upon the fire, conjoined with the syllable *ra*,
one beholds the three-eyed Rudra, the bestower of boons, resembling the rising sun.
Meditating with a serene mind upon Him whose entire body is smeared with ashes, one should hold [the breath] for five ghaṭikās; he will not be burned by fire.
One should hold the Māruta [breath] in the station of the Maruts, endowed with the deity of its color; for five ghaṭikās, one becomes like the wind, moving through the sky.
Having superimposed the wind upon the ether, one should contemplate Śaṅkara above the letter *ha*— Mahādeva in the form of the *bindu*, Sadāśiva whose nature is the void.
Resembling pure crystal, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
endowed with five faces, peaceful, ten-armed, and three-eyed.
With hands raised holding all weapons, adorned with every ornament,
his body half-formed as Umā’s, the granter of boons, the cause of all causes.
He who, reflecting with his mind, should hold [this] even for a moment—
having been thus addressed, he [should do so] three times with those trained in chariot-riding.
This is what is meant here, O Gārgī: the most excellent among those who know Brahman, having withdrawn all effects beginning with Brahmā into their respective causes, [remains].
Having fixed his mind upon that Sadāśiva, who is the cause of his own self,
he— possessing a disciplined mind— constantly united his very soul with the Supreme Lord.
Regarding that matter, other yogins who are the best among the knowers of Brahman say:
"Having withdrawn all effects into their respective causes by means of the Praṇava."
One should dissolve the vital breath and the mind into that Sadāśiva, the own cause,
at the end of the resonance (nāda) of the Praṇava, whose form is supreme bliss.
The virtuous perceive with their mind the Supreme Brahman as Ṛta and Satya, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny— the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
Therefore, by means of the *praṇava* alone, through three *prāṇāyāmas* each,
you should dissolve the effects, beginning with Brahmā, into their respective causes.
Others, who are yogins and the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, say regarding this matter: "One sees the Supreme Lord at the end of taking [the breath] with a purified mind."
O lady of excellent limbs, the best of physicians are thoroughly proficient in these applications;
for the body indeed consists of the five elements.
In that regard, O lady of excellent limbs, there may arise a condition consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm;
[this applies] to all those of windy temperament who are self-restrained in their yogic practices.
The body does not wither at all during the restraint of breath;
however, for those whose constitution is dominated by bile, the body withers away quickly.
For those whose nature is dominated by blood, the desired result shall be fully accomplished without delay;
moreover, for one who performs the retention [of breath] in the fire, all disorders born of wind are destroyed.
For one who constantly practices *dhāraṇā* upon the earth element and the water element,
diseases born of phlegm (*śleṣman*) as well as those born of wind (*vāta*) perish without delay.
For one who constantly performs concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the portion of space and the portion of air, diseases born of the three humors (*tridoṣa*) perish; of this there is no doubt.
In this matter, the two Aśvins, the best of physicians,
have likewise declared that the restraint of breath alone does not pacify the three humors (doṣas) in human beings.
Dattātreya said:
Having diligently discerned in secret both auspicious matters and those that are harmful, one should perform the fivefold concentration; for that which has become such brings fear.
One should hold the breath for five *ghaṭikās* below the navel and above the anus;
from that, earth arises, provided there is no danger during the retention.
For that yogin, death originating from the earth shall not occur;
therefore, he should hold the vital air at the location of the navel for five nāḍikās.
Then there is no fear of water, nor does death occur in water for the yogi;
he should hold the breath in the circle above the navel for five nāḍikās.
This is the fire-element concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā); for him, death does not come by fire, nor is his body burned when the mass of flames has subsided.
One should hold the breath for five ghaṭikās in the space between the navel, the eyebrows, and the nose, measuring three spans; this indeed is the Vāyavī [mudrā].
By the retention of the breath, the state of a yogin indeed arises;
he should hold it for five nāḍīs above the space between the eyebrows.
The yogi should diligently practice this concentration on space regarding the vital air;
by performing the concentration on space, one conquers eternal death.
And thus the wise yogi should perform the five dhāraṇās;
then, for one whose body has become firm, death does not exist.
Thus, for one who practices this fivefold elemental retention (bhūtadhāraṇā),
even through the dissolution of Brahmā, death does not exist for him.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
The yogi, ever engaged in yoga, having obtained food and conquered his senses,
should maintain the seven subtle dhāraṇās, beginning with Bhūḥ, in the crown of the head.
Supporting the earth, the yogi attains its subtlety;
he regards himself as the earth and abandons its odor.
In the same way, one should practice the concentration on that subtle form of the Apsaras within fire,
and likewise on touch within air, while maintaining that very same meditative hold.
Just as it abandons the subtle activity of space and its sound, so too,
when [the yogi] enters the mind of all beings by means of his own mind, he likewise abandons them.
Bearing mental concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the mind attains subtlety;
likewise, the knower of yoga reaches the intellect of all living beings.
Having attained unsurpassed subtlety of intellect,
the knower of yoga abandons all these seven constituents.
Once that which has been attained is correctly understood, no further activity toward it exists;
however, the self-possessed one perceives the subtlety of these seven elements.
Having seen [this] again and again, one should then abandon even accomplished success and proceed toward the supreme;
for, O Lord of the Earth, wherever one directs one's attachment toward worldly existence, [there one remains bound].
Having attained attachment to this or that, one perishes;
therefore, having understood these subtle things to be mutually attached, [one should abandon them].
The embodied soul who renounces these attains the supreme state;
O King, having joined together these very seven threads.
For one who knows the true nature of detachment from the elements beginning with earth,
this entire world— which is deeply attached to odors and other sense objects— is for the sake of liberation.
O King, having transcended these seven concentrations, that yogi may, if he so desires, attain the state of Brahmā, including the gods and humans, from which there is no return.
O Lord of Men, within each respective subtle element,
there occurs the dissolution of gods, asuras, gandharvas, uragas, and rakshasas.
It dissolves within the bodies and does not incur attachment anywhere;
likewise,
first in the navel, then in the heart, and thirdly in the chest.
In the throat, the mouth, the tip of the nose, the eyes, between the eyebrows, and on the crown of the head.
Beyond that, there is another which is known as the supreme common [concentration].
Having attained these ten concentrations, one attains equality with the Imperishable.
Now, meditation.
Patañjali states the definition of that [meditation]:
"Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointed flow of cognition upon that [object].
In this context, "one-pointed flow of cognition" refers to the continuity of cognition directed toward that object which has been made the support (*ālambana*) in concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
That which consists in making the flow of mental modifications uniform by setting aside heterogeneous cognitions is called *dhyāna* (meditation). As stated in the *Śivagītā*:
The wise know that meditation to be the continuous flow of the activity of the intellect, which, while taking the spatial location as its object, remains untouched by other modes of activity.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

"O King, that continuous flow of one-pointed cognition directed toward that [object], which is free from longing for anything else—that is dhyāna; it is accomplished by means of the first six ancillaries."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: The verbal root *dhyai* is remembered as having the meaning "to contemplate"; contemplation is the unwavering [fixation] upon reality.
That which is called *dhyāna* (meditation) is twofold: with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*).
That which possesses qualities is considered to be characterized by all differentiation, while that which is devoid of qualities is held to be absolute.
Know that which is accompanied by mantras to be with qualities, and that which is free from mantras to be without qualities.
As long as the subtle elements of sound and the rest remain within the ears and other sense organs, so long is it considered to be meditation (dhyāna); beyond that is concentration (samādhi).
Neither by the horse sacrifice nor by the royal consecration does one obtain that merit which a yogi of steady posture gains through a single moment of meditation.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Having abandoned attachment, subdued anger, eating light food, and having conquered the senses,
one should close the gates [of the senses] with the intellect and fix the mind in meditation.
Whether in empty places, in open spaces, in caves, or in forests,
the ever-disciplined yogi should always properly undertake meditation.

The Vedas are supreme; one who is free from all negligence, pure, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses—that great-souled one shall attain this yoga, and through that yoga, he attains liberation.
Yājñavalkya.
I shall now explain meditation; listen, O Gārgī of lovely countenance, for meditation alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for living beings.
Dhyāna is indeed the perception of the nature of the Self by means of the mind;
it is both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa), and that which is with attributes is said to be manifold.
The best of the twice-born say that there are five supreme Vedas;
among these, three are most excellent, while one alone is indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Having understood the vital points (marmas), the individual locations of the channels (nāḍīs),
and the positions and functions of the vital airs (vāyus), one should practice self-knowledge.
It is one, consisting of light, pure, all-pervading like space,
firm, unmanifest, stainless, eternal, and indeed devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
It is gross and subtle, formless space, intangible and invisible;
it has no taste, nor is it rich in fragrance; it is immeasurable and free from affliction.
Blissful, undecaying, and eternal; the cause of both the existent and the non-existent, and of all things;
the support of all, whose form is the universe itself, unborn and imperishable.
Invisible yet situated within the visible, standing outside while facing every direction;
all-seeing with feet everywhere, all-touching with a head everywhere.
The realization of the truth that "I am indeed Brahman, consisting of Brahman"—
this, the knowers of Yoga understand, is meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa).
Alternatively, having realized through the instruction of the Guru the Supreme Self, whose form is supreme bliss— the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny—
And in this city of Brahman, situated in the midst of the path of fire,
the wise perceive with their mind that which is the remedy for the disease of saṃsāra.
In this heart-lotus, endowed with eight petals, arisen from the center of the *kanda*,
having a stalk twelve finger-breadths long and opening upwards four finger-breadths wide.
Having visualized the desired deity, who grants all desires, with the mind within the pericarp adorned with filaments that has been opened by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
The cognition "I am that Self" is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna),
performed within this lotus of the heart, whose pericarp consists of primordial nature (prakṛti).
It is endowed with the petals of the eight sovereign powers, joined with the filaments of knowledge,
possessing the stalk of wisdom and the great bulbous root awakened by breath control.
[He meditated on] Vaiśvānara, the Lord whose body is a crest of flames, the great fire with universal radiance, blazing with faces on all sides, and who is contemplated as the universe itself.
He beheld the fire blazing within his own body, from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head,
like a lamp in a windless place.
With his vision, he beheld the imperishable Supreme Self in the center of his crest-lock,
radiant like a streak of lightning situated in the midst of a dark rain cloud.
Having known the god Vaiśvānara— who is as subtle as the awn of wild rice, who has the luster of a lamp, and who is the cause of all— to be "I am that Self," such is the realization.
Those who know yoga understand that among meditations with attributes (saguṇadhyāna), this meditation is the supreme;
having attained the state of Vaiśvānara through it, one goes to liberation by that very means.
Alternatively, one should perceive within the mandala of the sun of great splendor oneself as the Person (Puruṣa), the cause of the world, having the form of gold.
He has golden beard and hair, golden nails, and is tawny;
his face is beautiful with its exquisite form, and he is the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Seated in the lotus posture, gentle, with a face resembling a blossomed lotus,
possessing lips like the interior petals of a lotus, he bestows fear upon all the worlds.
He who always knows everything, who gladdens the righteous,
who illuminates the entire world with his vision, and who is the unique witness of the universe.
The realization "I am that" is praised in meditation;
O lady rich in austerity, this alone is the great path to liberation.
Through this solar meditation, the wise shall attain liberation by beholding the inner self between the eyebrows— whose form is light and who is the cause of all.
Like a pillar, it rose from the middle of his body up to the top of his head—
the unmanifest cause of the universe, blazing with immeasurable splendor.
The highest meditation is this: "May I become that which is perceived by the mind.
Alternatively, one may sit in the bound lotus posture with the body relaxed.
Having himself become Śiva, he fixes his gaze for a moment upon the tip of the nose;
or else, [he meditates] upon [the lotus] endowed with eight petals, possessing ears and filaments.
Within the center of the lunar orb in the lotus of his awakened heart,
he beholds his own self in the form of a child, the imperishable enjoyer.
His head, endowed with the sixteen Vedic meters, was covered by moonbeams emitting the essence of nectar from its downward-facing lotus.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon that person there being drenched on all sides by thousands of streams of nectar flowing forth, one should contemplate.
By that very nectar-like essence, my body, along with its limbs and minor members, becomes the Supreme Brahman; I alone am the Supreme Self, the imperishable.
Thus, whatever sensation arises therein is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna).
In this way, the entire nectar of meditation shall become the conqueror of death within six months.
He shall undoubtedly be liberated even while living after one year;
for one who is liberated while living, there is no suffering whatsoever in any way.
How much more difficult, then, is liberation for one who is constantly engaged [in worldly affairs]?
For the Śruti says:
"Having meditated upon the lotus of the heart as stainless and pure, one perceives within it that which is luminous and free from sorrow."

Having meditated upon the inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite-formed, auspicious, tranquil, immortal source of Brahman; likewise, the one, all-pervading, wondrous Lord who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless, accompanied by Umā, the Supreme Lord, the Master, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful.
The sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness;
then, meditating upon it, he beholds that partless reality.
It is seen, however, by those who perceive the subtle, through a sharp and subtle intellect.
"It is to be attained by the mind alone," and so forth—thus says Dattātreya.
Then one should practice meditation for exactly sixty *ghaṭikās*,
restraining the vital breath (*vāyu*) while focusing on some chosen deity who bestows desired boons.
This is indeed meditation with attributes (saguṇadhyāna), which bestows qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest;
but by meditating on the attributeless (nirguṇa) like space, one enters the path of liberation.
Yogī Yājñavalkya.
There is no purifier of evil deeds equal to meditative absorption;
even while eating among outcaste dog-cookers, the meditator is never defiled.
Meditation alone is the supreme Brahman; meditation alone is the supreme austerity;
meditation alone is the supreme purity; that meditation is the highest state.
Even one who is addicted to every kind of sin, by meditating for a single wondrous moment,
then becomes an ascetic, a purifier of those who purify the assembly.
In the Mahābhārata.
Even one who is devoid of all proper conduct or joined with all sins,
shakes off all that evil by meditating on Śiva within the self.
In another treatise:
In all sins, and even in great sins,
having entered the first quarter of the night, one should practice meditation on Brahman.
In the Vasiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa], in the section on the worship of the Self, following the description of the nature of meditation,
the Lord said:
The self is indeed the offering of meditation; meditation is my great worship.
Without this, and by no other means, can this Self be attained.
O wise one, by means of this meditation, even a fool, having worshipped the Lord for thirteen moments, shall obtain the fruit of gifting a cow.
Having worshipped the Lord for the duration of one hundred nimeṣas,
a human being obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having worshipped his own self as the Lord for half a ghaṭikā,
a human being obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
He who, by means of his own self, worships himself for one *ghaṭikā* with the offering of the garland of meditation (*dhyānavali*), shall obtain the merit of the *rājasūya* sacrifice.
By thus performing the midday worship and other rites, one partakes in the merit of a hundred thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
having worshipped in this manner throughout the day, a person shall dwell in the supreme abode.
This is that supreme means; this is that supreme art, as stated in the *Ātmagītā*.
Even if one is unable to realize Me directly, one should contemplate Me without hesitation;
in time, having ascended to direct experience, one will certainly become successful.
Just as there is no means for obtaining a treasure buried deep in the earth other than digging,
so too, even when wealth is present, there is no way to obtain it except through contemplation of one's own self.
For having fashioned this body with ease,
know that a man may further take me as his treasure from the earth, using the hoe as a plow and the mind as the field.
And in another treatise as well:
Even if direct experience is absent, one should simply contemplate, "I am Brahman.
If even that which is non-existent can be attained through meditation, how much more so the eternal Brahman?
If one does not meditate day after day while perceiving that the fruit of meditation is the daily weakening of the notion of self, tell me, who is more of a beast than such a person?
If one disregards that [obligation] and performs only pilgrimages, recitations, and the like,
the maxim "having cast away the rice-ball, he licks his hand" would apply.
Now, concerning concentration (*samādhi*), [the following is] Patañjali:

At that very moment, there is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which manifests only the object and is, as it were, devoid of its own [subjective] form. That very entity which has become the support for meditation appears solely as the thing-in-itself, manifest without doubt and in its entirety as a perfectly complete form by its own nature; therefore, it is entirely [the object].

When a particular state of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) appears as if devoid of its own nature because it is free from objective referents (*viṣaya*), that is called "concentration" (*samādhi*). This is the general definition of the two types of concentration;
the specific definitions should be understood as they have been explained in detail in the first chapter. Others, however, [say...]
They say that *samādhi* is that wherein the mind is properly fixed and made one-pointed by abandoning all objects of cognition;
thus says Yājñavalkya.
Now I shall explain the meditative absorption that liberates one from the bonds of existence;
you ought to listen correctly to how it benefits one bound by the snares of worldly life.
Samādhi, however, is the state of equanimity between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
it is that abiding of the inner self (pratyagātman) in Brahman alone.
In whatever manner one meditates upon the Self, one's samādhi becomes exactly like that;
having thus meditated, the Self must be established within the self, for the Self cannot exist otherwise.
In this very way, wherever a man exerts effort,
he himself is present right there, and he shall surely attain that very object.
Just as water poured into the lord of rivers reaches dissolution without distinction,
so too the self, though appearing distinct here, attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
There may be a concentration of a single form, free from spatial objects;
for the cognition by means of the object alone is the supreme means of accomplishing yoga.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
That very [state] which is devoid of conceptual construction and intended for the apprehension of the true nature,
accomplished through mental meditation— that is designated as *samādhi*.
Nor should it be suspected that there is no difference between *dhyāna* and *samprajñāta-samādhi*.
