For even in *dhyāna*, which is accomplished through great effort, there still occurs the shifting of other mental impressions (*pratyaya-antara-saṃcāra*). In *samprajñāta-samādhi*, however, there is absolutely no opportunity for the shifting of other mental impressions in any respect whatsoever.
Such is the distinction between the two.
Sureśvarācārya states:
"The contemplation and meditation upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, they call [meditation]."
The absence of movement of the intellect arising from meditative absorption is designated as samādhi.
In the Śaiva Dharma.
Samādhi, however, is the state of equilibrium between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme soul (paramātman);
it is the attainment of the waveless state, consisting of supreme bliss.
Whether accompanied by inhalation and exhalation, or motionless with eyes unmoving,
one who meditates on Śiva and is well-absorbed is said to be established in samādhi.
When one hears nothing, sees nothing, smells nothing,
and does not perceive any touch, one is said to be established in samādhi.
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That state of equality between these two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—
in which all volitional constructs have perished, is designated as samādhi."
The lord of yogis, absorbed in samādhi, knows neither self nor other, neither cold nor heat, neither pleasure nor that which is other than pleasure.
The yogi who is disciplined in samādhi is not affected by time, nor is he stained by karma; he is not pierced by weapons or missiles.
Just as water poured into water becomes that very water, and milk [poured] into milk likewise; so too the yogi should attain identity with that.
Dattātreya.
Endowed with the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), one should then practice samādhi;
indeed, within twelve days, one shall attain that samādhi.
By restraining the vital breath, the wise man will certainly become liberated while living;
Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self and the supreme self.
If one should desire to cast off one's own body, one may abandon it oneself;
having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, one shall merge into the Supreme Brahman.
Now, if one does not wish to relinquish one's own body because it is dear,
one may wander through all the worlds endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.

And thus, for the yogi who practices the yoga of the limbs according to the manner described, there arise obstacles that are sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. All of these are trivial and must be abandoned by the yogi.
As Dattātreya has said:
O Sage, at the time of the first practice, however, various obstacles arise;
laziness is the first obstacle, and the second is now described.

Those who know yoga understand that there are four [pursuits]: the assembly of rogues mentioned before, the third is the accomplishment of mantras, and the fourth is the alchemy of the elements (dhātuvāda).
Just as is the form of Kandarpa, so too is that of this very yogin;
noble women, being under the sway of his form, long for union with him.
For in this way, O Sage, many obstacles arise for one who is steady, like mirages in a desert; having recognized them, the wise man should abandon them.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"When the Self is perceived, obstacles indeed arise for the yogi.
I shall explain these to you; listen to them in brief."
Likewise, one desires desirable actions and human pleasures;
[one seeks] women, the fruit of giving, knowledge, illusion, base metals, wealth, and heaven.
Divinity, the status of lord of the immortals, the elixir that effects the reversal of aging,
leaping from Mount Meru, performing sacrifice, and likewise entering into water or fire;
The fruits of ancestral rites (śrāddha), the giving of power (śakti-dāna), as well as observances (niyama), fasting (upavāsa), works of public utility (pūrta), and even the worship of deities;
The mind thus proceeds toward various actions, being impelled by them; therefore, the yogi should restrain it with effort.
Making his mind one with Brahman, he is liberated from the *upasargas*;
once these *upasargas* have been conquered, the *upasargas* [of worldly existence] cease thereafter.
Yogins proceed according to their qualities—sāttvika, rājasa, or tāmasa.
There are eight types: the prāpti, the śrāvaṇa, the daiva, and likewise the other two, the bhrama and the āvarta.
These five are obstacles for yogins, resulting in bitter consequences:
the meaning of the Vedas, the meaning of poetic and scientific treatises, all branches of knowledge, and all arts without exception.
The intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) of the yogin is that by which all words and meanings appear as if manifest before him,
and he perceives every word and understands its meaning.
It is said that [the sound] is heard from thousands of yojanas when the divine beings are seen on all sides at a distance of eight [yojanas].
The wise call even that an affliction caused by fate,
when the mind of a yogi wanders without support due to a defect, like one who is insane.
That which arises from the collapse of all supports is proclaimed as "delusion" (bhrama);
it is like a whirlpool, wherein the whirlpool of knowledge becomes turbulent.
Where the mind is destroyed, that is called an "upasarga" (affliction).
By these [afflictions], O God, all the divine births have their yoga destroyed.
Due to extremely terrible afflictions, they revolve again and again;
therefore, the yogi should cause that which consists of mind to revolve solely as the pure [Self].
"One should contemplate the Supreme Brahman, having made the mind inclined toward it.

Furthermore, those obstacles to the mind— such as disease, unfitness for action, the presence of doubt regarding the fruits of yoga, negligence, laziness, attachment to sense-objects, delusion of nature, failure to attain the stages of meditative absorption (*samādhi-bhūmi*), and instability of the mind— are to be understood.

Even those [mental states] designated as *vikṣepa* (distractions) do not cease at all during the contemplation of Brahman. This has been stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra], following the definition of yoga in the passage beginning with "From devotion to the Lord" (*īśvara-praṇidhānāt*), etc.:

"The designator of that [Lord] is the *praṇava*; its repetition and the meditation upon its meaning [lead to it]. From that comes the realization of the inward-facing consciousness and the cessation of the obstacles."

And [this is established] by the sūtras beginning with "and the state of being" (bhāvaḥ). Nor is there any room for obstacles even in that cultivation (bhāvana) for the sake of that [state], because that cultivation is itself of the nature of restraint; for in the worship of the Blessed One, which is like a fire to the cotton of all sins, there is no possibility for obstacles.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Just as fire with uplifted flames, aided by the wind, burns dry grass, so too Viṣṇu, residing in the mind, consumes all the sins of yogis."

Thus, for the sake of eliminating all previously mentioned obstacles known as distractions (*vikṣepa*), as well as those that arise simultaneously with distraction— such as pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, labored breathing, and sleep— one should cultivate a continuous flow of meditation upon the desired object; this is what has been stated.
For the purpose of prohibiting that, the Sūtra states: "The practice of a single principle.
In the Vāsiṣṭha, these are desire, anger, and so forth.
O Brahmin, these great evils, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra,
do not disturb even for a moment a mind that is concentrated in one-pointedness.
Indeed, the sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, stirred up by great delusions, do not disturb a mind that is single-pointedly concentrated.
Within whom truth and wonder constantly flash forth,
the lords of the directions protect his entire, indivisible world as if it were their own.
Thus it is said in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"One who is endowed with right vision cannot be overcome by those devoted to ritual action;
the yogi whose self is united with yoga attains supreme liberation."
And there is also scripture:
"Therefore, he who knows thus—'I am Brahman'—becomes this All; even the gods are not able to prevent his becoming, for he becomes their very Self," and so forth. Furthermore:
The supernatural powers (*siddhis*) that arise prior to liberation must be regarded as nothing but obstacles,
because for a yogi whose mind is attached to such powers, liberation becomes difficult to attain. And so it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
In this world, obstacles arise for the yogin that cause the ruin of his yoga;
yet news from afar is heard, and even what is far away is seen.
One would be able to travel a hundred yojanas in half a moment;
indeed, scriptures never before considered would come to one's lips through recitation from memory.
The power of retention becomes exceedingly fierce; a great burden becomes light;
in one moment it is emaciated, in one moment it is stout, in one moment it is small, and in one moment it is vast.
He enters the bodies of others, understands the speech of animals,
assumes a divine fragrance, and utters divine words.
Divine maidens may entreat him, and he may long for a divine body;
such obstacles as these may arise as indicators of the imminent perfection of yoga.
If his mind is not agitated by these obstacles,
then he attains the supreme state that is difficult even for Brahmā and others to reach.
"O Kalaśodbhava, that which one does not turn back from upon reaching, and that upon reaching which one does not grieve— that is obtained through the six-limbed yoga."
In the *Yogabhāskara*.
For the yogi who has conquered the senses, who is self-controlled, who has mastered his breath,
and who fixes his mind upon Hari, the supernatural powers (siddhis) manifest.
One should abandon all powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, even when cultivated through meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇās*), because they are useless and, moreover, are creators of obstacles.

One who is bound by the latent impressions of supernatural powers and the like, and is attached to various enjoyments, generally falls from his station and remains within the state of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Resorting to sattvic fortitude, the renunciant, well-stabilized through sattva,
meditates upon the attributeless with the mind and is liberated from all obstacles.
Thus practicing yoga, free from desire for the status of Śakra and other such positions,
and by abandoning the latent impressions of supernatural powers and the like, the sage becomes liberated while living.
For fear of excessive prolixity, I have not mentioned that there are indeed numerous obstacles;
these must be warded off by the yogi through meditation upon Hari and Hara.

Such is the established conclusion of all the scriptures. And thus, for the sake of inspiring confidence and for the sake of testing the yogin who, favored by the Supreme Lord, practices yoga with its constituent limbs free from obstacles, the attainments of intermediate fruits—culminating in liberation—manifest in succession. There are five kinds of attainments in the world:
And so says Patañjali:

The supernatural powers (*siddhis*) born of birth, herbs, mantras, and meditation are as follows: the power born of birth (*janma-siddhi*) consists of such things as the ability to travel through the air possessed by Yakṣas and others,
and the knowledge and other qualities that arise immediately upon birth in the case of Kapila and others.

For some, there is the accomplishment of medicinal herbs characterized by the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and so forth in Pātāla and other realms; for others, there is the accomplishment of mantras that yield fruits as vast as space; for Viśvāmitra and others, there is the accomplishment through austerity (*tapas*); and for yogins such as Yājñavalkya, there is the accomplishment through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
In that regard, for all the perfections (siddhis) such as birth and so forth, the sole cause is the perfection of meditative absorption (samādhi) practiced in previous lives;
it should be understood that mantras and the like are merely instrumental conditions.
This is illustrated by the case of Ānandīśvara and others, who attained transformations such as changes in their kinsmen within this very life.

Because of the fulfillment by means of the primordial material causes (*prakṛti*). For it is the very same primordial material causes from the previous [life] that, through the gateway of another birth and so forth, fulfill the modifications (*vikāra*) characterized as the body and senses composed of gross elements in this present life.
While the performance of *dharma* and other such acts is the motivator for the fulfillment of the primordial material causes, it is nevertheless [only] from that...
The destruction of those factors that constitute obstructions occurs; just as the function of a dam is merely to stop the force [of water],
while the outflow of water happens of its own accord, so too there is no consequence of the collapse of the previously mentioned cause— the meditative concentration practiced in other lifetimes.
And thus Patañjali [states] in two sūtras:
"The transformation into another species occurs through the influx of the primary causes; the external cause is not the motivator of the primary causes.
However, it effects the removal of obstructions, like a farmer."
In the *Yogabhāskara*:
"Whatever accomplishments exist here through birth, herbs, austerity, or mantras—one attains them all through yoga; by no other means does one attain the state of yoga."
In the *Yogabīja*: "O Goddess, I shall now tell you the fruit of practice:
first diseases perish, and afterwards the dullness born of the body."
Then, having attained a state of equilibrium, the moon rains down incessantly;
the fire, fanned by the wind from all sides, absorbs the essence of the minerals.
Various sounds arise and the body becomes supple;
having conquered the inertia of the earth element and the others, the man becomes a sky-walker who can traverse the air.
He becomes omniscient, able to assume any form at will, and possesses the speed of the wind;
he sports in the three worlds, and all the supernatural powers (siddhis) arise for him.
When camphor dissolves, what hardness remains therein? Likewise, when the ego is conquered, whence can there be any solidity in the body?
He becomes omniscient, the creator of all, independent, and possessed of universal form;
he is liberated while living, a great yogi—of this there is no doubt.
The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, whatever web of conceptual constructions there may be, that does not lead to liberation.
What will supernatural powers (siddhis) accomplish in the non-conceptual Self of Consciousness?"
"O Lord, O Purifier, you ought to sever this doubt of mine. The Lord said:
"What you have spoken is true; I shall tell you, listen, O beautiful one."
O Śivā, the accomplishments (siddhis) in this world are of two kinds: the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized.
Those accomplishments which are achieved through the means of medicinal elixirs, rituals, timing, mantras, yantras, and so forth,
are proclaimed as the "imagined" (kalpitā) attainments.
Those accomplishments arising from the practitioner are impermanent and of little power;
for indeed, in this way they are born spontaneously even without the means of practice.
But those perfections which are produced from the state of lordship due to one's own sovereignty, when one is solely established in the yoga of one's own Self,
are remembered as being free from conceptual construction.
Pure, impermanent, and of great vigor, these forms assumed at will arise from one's own yoga;
they are produced after a long time even among those devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The great yoga, which is to be cultivated within the imperishable state of the Supreme Self, is eternally radiant even without the sun; this is the characteristic of one perfected in yoga.
Just as various holy places are seen along the way by travelers journeying toward Kāśī, so too are the supernatural powers (siddhis) found on the path to liberation.
They arise spontaneously, free from gain and loss;
one should recognize accomplishment through the signs of accomplishment, as well as liberation while living.
Due to his supramundane qualities, the eternal [state] is sometimes perceived;
this, O Goddess, has been described as the characteristic of one perfected in yoga.
One should recognize that man as bound who is deprived of the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis);
for he alone is truly liberated while living, possessing a body that is neither subject to decay nor death.
O beautiful one, for those who meet their death by dogs, cocks, insects, and the like, can there truly be liberation through the offering of funeral cakes?
The vital breath does not go outside; how then can there be the falling of the body?
That which is called liberation through the falling of the body is not truly called liberation.
Just as a lump of salt attains the state of water, so the body attains the state of Brahman;
when it thus reaches the state of mindlessness, it is then called liberated.
In the *Mānasollāsa*: "When the mind has attained immobility and has dissolved into the midst of the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
these signs arise individually from the conquest of the five elements."
Scarcity of feces and urine, absence of phlegm, health, lightness of the body,
a pleasant fragrance, and a golden complexion are the primary signs of yoga.
Not being attached even to the tip of a thorn, not sinking even in water or mud,
and endurance of hunger, thirst, and so forth— this is the second characteristic of yoga.
The capacity to consume abundant food and drink, endurance of heat and fire,
and the ability to see and hear from a distance— this is the third characteristic of yoga.
Leaping upon the earth like a frog, leaping upon a tree like a monkey,
and traveling through the sky— this is the fourth characteristic of yoga.
Knowledge whose object is the three times, sovereignty such as the power of becoming small (aṇimā) and so forth,
and the possession of infinite power— these five are the characteristics of yoga.
Now, the characteristics of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*: *Aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*,
as well as *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, and *vaśitva*— these are the eight *siddhis*.
The attainment of extreme minuteness and entry [into all things] as one's own self is the sovereignty known as *aṇimā*, belonging to the all-pervading Supreme Self.
The state of pervading externally the entire aggregate of the thirty-six principles, beginning from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) up to Śiva, is the sovereignty known as "magnanimity" (mahimā).
In the act of uplifting one whose limbs are like Mount Meru,
the Buddhas know that its gravity is equal to the weight of Meru itself.
For a person dwelling in the netherworld, the sight of the realm of Brahmā,
the attainment of a great name, and supreme sovereignty are exceedingly difficult to achieve for those who lack yoga.
The complete accomplishment of other perfections, such as traveling through space and so forth,
by the mere will of one's own desire, is designated as *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will).
Some declare that this sovereignty, known as *prākāmya*, consists in the illumination of all objects by means of the light of one's own body.
The agency in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds by one's own mere will,
as well as the power to direct the sun and other celestial bodies, is designated as "lordship" (īśitva).
All the world-protectors and all the worlds are subject to their control;
that sovereignty known as "mastery" (vaśitva) is easily attained by the yogins of Śiva.
For those whose splendors constitute the sovereign empire of all embodied existence and whose meditative absorptions are fully ripened, what indeed is there that cannot be accomplished?
For that brahmin who possesses such knowledge, even the gods remain subject to him;
how much more so then kings, tigers, serpents, women, men, and the like?
One should abandon desire for inferior fruits that result in rebirth in heaven and the like;
for a wise person does not prize even sovereignty over heaven or universal empire as much as the state of being a human.
That alone is his true sovereignty which is sovereignty over the self;
[all else, such as] the abundance of sons, grandsons, houses, fields, wealth, and grain, is merely a semblance of it.
And those who are modern also achieve success in the realms of heaven, the netherworld, and on earth,
just as one who is engaged in cooking avoids cold and other such obstacles.
And all incidental powers are always accomplished through the practice of yoga;
his sovereignty and lordship do not exist as something separate from that.
Even while the person is running, his shadow follows him;
likewise, infinite power, sovereignty, and the supernatural faculties such as atomization (aṇimā) remain motionless.
When one's own lordship is fully established, [all powers] indeed become accomplished by themselves;
for just as fragrance is experienced by one bringing a flower, even without a separate desire.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, though their manifestations are limited, are encompassed by me through my overflowing sovereign power when I am endowed with the state of fullness.
Those who possess sovereignty shine; that very Self is Sadāśiva.
All supernatural powers attend upon one who possesses the realization of being the Self of all.
"Therefore, one whose mind is restrained should exercise sovereignty over the self.
Thus it is stated in the *Layakhaṇḍa* as well;
following the description of the practice of *samādhi*, it is established that perfection is attained precisely through the sequence of its practice.

The sequence has also been stated. For it is as follows: "Seated comfortably on a cushion in a secluded place, having moved back slightly, with arms extended to the length of a forearm, with steady gaze and relaxed limbs, free from anxiety, perform your practice."
Seated in a comfortable posture, one should practice the contemplation of reality;
through constant practice, one should effect the manifestation of the supreme reality.
Brahmā resides within the five elements, and his body is composed of the five elements;
since everything consists of the elements, one should contemplate that nothing exists apart from them.
One should not meditate on anything with the mind, being free from all thought;
that yogi, both externally and internally, becomes face-to-face with reality.
When the reality (tattva) becomes manifest before one, the state of non-mind (amanaska) arises;
once non-mind has been produced, the dissolution of the mind and its functions occurs.
When the dissolution of the mind and other faculties has occurred, the dissolution of the vital breath (pavana) takes place;
through the destruction of both the mind and the breath, one abandons the objects of the senses.
When one is liberated from the objects of the senses, external cognition does not arise;
and when external cognition has perished, one then becomes equal toward everything.
When one has become equal toward all and free from activity,
the yogi is then bound to the supreme Brahman and has attained dissolution therein.
I shall describe the characteristics of that supreme dissolution which arises for those who are constantly devoted to practice and whose minds are liberated.
Having entered into absorption (laya), he does not perceive pleasure or pain, nor does he experience cold or heat;
indeed, he knows no deliberation regarding the objects of the senses.
Neither living nor dead, he neither sees nor blinks;
devoid of life, he remains like a log of wood, and is thus called one who has entered the state of dissolution (laya).
Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot shines motionlessly,
so the yogi who has attained absorption, being freed from the activities of the world, shines unmoving.
Just as a lake, when freed from them, becomes motionless and stainless,
so too is he seen established in dissolution, abandoned by the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest.
Just as salt thrown into water gradually dissolves,
so too the mind, through the practice of yoga, dissolves into Brahman.
Just as salt, through contact with water, becomes composed of water,
so too the mind, through contact with Brahman, becomes composed of Brahman.
Just as salt is certainly obtained from alkaline earth with effort,
so too is the knowledge of Brahman attained effortlessly, and through that, the liberation of the mind.
Just as ghee that is mixed with ghee is not separate from it and is absorbed into it,
so too the yogi absorbed in reality finds no state of separateness.
Through moments, breaths, instants, nāḍīs, watches,
days, months, and years— by means of these durations of time— he who abides in dissolution attains that which is supreme.
Prāṇa consists of inhalation and exhalation; six prāṇas are known as one pala.
Sixty palas shall constitute the duration of one ghaṭikā.
By means of absorption, the yogi certainly attains contact with the supreme reality in a mere twinkling of an eye,
as well as rising from it again and again.
For the yogin who has attained absorption within the dissolution, there arises a cooling of the fever of worldly existence, as well as frequent sleep and fainting,
occurring within a mere six moments.
By the dissolution of even the two breaths, the kūrma-vāta and other winds cease, and they bring about the binding of the bodily constituents (dhātus) within the constituents themselves.
By that very dissolution of even a single breath,
the vital winds such as prāṇa and the rest flow through their respective locations due to the connection with the stream of breath.
Even with the rhythm of four breaths, the essences that have entered the seven constituents produce perfect nourishment, owing to the harmonious combination of the constituents.
Remaining seated, one does not become fatigued even by a *pala* of *prāṇāyāma*;
the yogi’s breath becomes minimal, and likewise, his perspiration is very slight.
Even with the movement of only two finger-widths, there occurs a vibration in the heart-channel;
that is to be known as the Unstruck (anāhata), and one should not fix the mind right there.
Through a process lasting four palas, there arises an experience;
suddenly, an auspicious or inauspicious sound falls upon the ear.
Even by means of a mere eighteenth part [of a moment], his desire ceases;
yet it would not cease at all for one embraced by a passionate woman.
Flowing through the path of the *suṣumṇā* even with the rhythmic beat of a *kalāpa*,
she proceeds by means of the final path of the *kalāpa* through its very absence.
Even in half a ghaṭikā, Śakti certainly moves;
awakened by the stirring of the vital air, she rises upward through the western path.
Even by the dissolution of a single *kalā*, power (*śakti*) certainly vibrates;
and even by the dissolution of two *kalās* and the vibration of power.
In an instant, a trembling arises in his mind;
he has brought about that state where even sleep does not occur within the abode of the four *kalās*.
The yogi perceives the orb of light like a spark within the heart;
even by the dissolution of a quarter of a day, the person should consume very little food.
There is scantiness of urine and feces, lightness, and unctuousness of the body;
even through the partial dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), the light of one's own Self shines forth.
Like the sun shining with its rays, the reality of yoga is revealed;
even through dissolution for a mere day, the reality of one's own self is revealed.
The expansion of sensory perception proceeds within the cosmic egg;
yet the yogi, established in his own self, remains so even through the dissolution of day and night.
By the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, the yogi perceives fragrance from afar;
even after two days and nights, there is no dissolution within for the yogi.
The consciousness of far-sighted vision functions by its very nature;
even within three days and nights, the bliss of dissolution arises.
Even from afar, the yogi who is free from conceptualization perceives the essential flavor (rasa) through the power of the state of dissolution within four days and nights.
The lord of yogis perceives touch even from afar, there is no doubt;
through the dissolution of the five nights, his [liberation] also certainly arises.
The cognition of hearing from afar is a cause of wonder for the mind;
this is the great knowledge of the five senses, consisting of direct personal experience.
By means of this, the lord of yogis knows the entire course of the universe;
even through the dissolution of six nights, the one of great intelligence flourishes.
Even for a yogin who has merged into the Supreme, universal knowledge— which is inconceivable and transcendent— continues to function despite his dissolution for seven nights.
The state of knowing all things up to Brahmā and the knowledge of the Vedas remain;
even by means of dissolution in eight nights, the yogi becomes free from affliction.
Established in his innate state, he is not afflicted by conditions such as hunger and thirst;
he beholds whatever most secret and wondrous things there may be.
Then, on the eleventh day, due to the arising of momentum in that which remains in dissolution, the body,
even though accompanied by the mind, desires to go.
Indeed, mastery over the earth is accomplished even in twelve days;
and in the measure of half a blink of an eye, the surface of the earth is truly filled.
Then, within thirteen days, even through dissolution,
the lord of yogis attains the most wonderful accomplishment of Khecarī, even by means of meditation alone.
If he remains established in dissolution for fourteen days,
the siddhi called aṇimā shall belong to him, by which atomicity is attained.
Absorbed in the Self by means of the self, the yogi attains the perfection of greatness for sixteen days,
assuming a form equal to that of Mahādeva.
And if one remains established in dissolution until the end of eighteen days,
one attains the siddhi called "heaviness" (garimā), by which one becomes weightless upon the earth.
If one remains motionless for twenty-four hours,
the perfection known as *laghimā* arises, by which one becomes minute while supporting a burden.

For one who has attained dissolution into the *svalakṣya* for twenty-two days, the perfection of attainment (*prāptisiddhi*) shall arise; he shall cause whatever exists in the world to be brought forth.
If the yogi enters into dissolution (laya) for twenty-four days,
he shall attain the perfection of irresistible will (prākāmya-siddhi), by which he obtains whatever he desires.
He whose mind remains concentrated for exactly twenty-six days indeed attains the lordship of the world, by which he becomes a teacher of the universe.
If one’s dissolution remains steady in the firm posture for twenty-eight days,
one shall attain the perfection of mastery, by which one indeed brings the world under control.
For anyone who desires to go to dissolution in the state of the Supreme Brahman,
all their spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) become causes of destruction for them.
He whose absorption lasts for one month, remaining unbroken,
that lord of yogis does not wake up until he attains liberation.
Even with a delay of nine months, the earth reaches its true nature;
once the earth-element is fully perfected, the lord of yogis becomes like a diamond.
Even for a yogin who remains in dissolution for one and a half years, there shall be the accomplishment of the water-tattva; he becomes composed of the water-tattva.
Even for a yogin who remains in dissolution for three years,
the perfection of the fire-principle (tejas-tattva) shall be attained, and his fire-element will become continuous.
The perfection of the principle of space shall occur, and one becomes composed of the principle of space,
for one who remains in dissolution continuously for twenty-four years.
The perfection of the Śakti-tattva occurs, for he is indeed composed of the Śakti-tattva;
he beholds the entire universe as if it were a pearl resting in the palm of his hand.
Having established the true nature of one's own body exactly as it exists, one should practice the conduct of reality while remaining within that body, appearing in the world accordingly.
He indeed performs the practice of reality for the sake of dissolution within the principle of power (śakti-tattva);
thus, through the yogin’s practice of dissolution that has increased progressively, [he attains the goal].
The yogis, like great souls such as Bhuśuṇḍa and others, enjoy supreme bliss even during the dissolutions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
The great-souled ones, such as Bhuśuṇḍa and others, enjoy supreme bliss.
Here, after defining the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), the venerable Patañjali describes the sequence of accomplishments (*siddhi*).
In the Vaiśeṣika system, this refers to the meaning of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).

For the sake of linguistic brevity, he designated the term "saṃyama" for the objects of perception, retention, meditative concentration, and absorption themselves; he then demonstrated the fruit and the application of that saṃyama through two sūtras as follows:

"From its mastery comes the light of wisdom; its application is upon the stages. This means that from the mastery of that *saṃyama*—through practice leading to its becoming natural—the light, that is, the expansion, of wisdom in the form of discernment (*viveka*) arises. Its characteristic is a state of flow that is stainless and not overwhelmed by other forms of wisdom.
The meaning is that light arises. One should apply that *saṃyama* to the mental fluctuations established upon the stages (*bhūmi*s), according to the distinction between gross and subtle objects.
Having mastered each successive lower stage of the mind, one should [apply it] to each successive higher stage of the mind.

Restraint (*saṃyama*) must be practiced. For one who has not made the lower stages his own while practicing restraint on a higher stage does not partake of the fruit. To effect the purification of the object of the aforementioned restraint, he shows the threefold transformation by means of three sūtras. [The first concerns] the opposition to emergence (*vyutthāna-virodha*).

The transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) is the sequence of the mind characterized by the cessation [of fluctuations], consisting in the suppression and emergence of the two types of mental formations (*saṃskāra*). "Emergence" (*vyutthāna*) refers to the three stages known as the distracted, the deluded, and the occasionally distracted.
Cessation is the transformation of the mind through the predominance of *sattva* as a constituent factor; from these two, emergence...

The two formative forces (*saṃskāra*) produced by the two cessations (*nirodha*) abide respectively as being overcome and as having become subordinate, due to their lack of capacity to produce an effect; whereas their manifestation occurs in the present.

It is the persistence of the mind in a state manifested as resonance (*dhvani*). In that regard, the first transformation with cessation (*sanirodha-pariṇāma*) is the persistence of the substratum—the mind—which exists at the moment of cessation, remaining in its own essential nature throughout both states known as emergence (*vyutthāna*). This is the intended meaning: when the form of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence...

The *dharma* (the property) disappears and the *saṃskāra-rūpa* (the form of the latent impression) appears; thus, the mind (*citta*), by virtue of its nature as the substratum (*dharmī*), is perceived as persisting through both states. That cessation is designated by the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
Although there is no absolute immobility for the mind because the functioning of the *guṇas* is inherently mobile, nevertheless, it is thus...
The actuality of transformation is said to be stability. This, however, is the fruit of transformation for the mind:

the state of being a flow of similar moments in which distraction and fatigue have been removed. Likewise, the transformation of the mind as samādhi consists in the waning of the capacity for all objects and the arising of one-pointedness.

The state of having all things as its object (*sarvārthatā*) is the non-arising of distraction due to its absolute suppression; this is the "destruction" (*kṣaya*) characterized by the entry [of the mind] into past sounds, and not merely their prior non-existence. The emergence, or manifestation, of one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*)—characterized by a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*) with respect to a single objective support—is the intensification of the mind.

The persistence of the essence (*sattva*) through its continuity while in a state of manifestation during the present sound—meaning its state of being manifest—is the second transformation, which is accompanied by meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The ultimate limit of this very [absorption] is the transformation into one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).

This is as follows: when the subsided and the arisen [cognitions] have identical objects, that is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness; this belongs specifically to one who is in a state of meditative absorption.

One mental modification (*pratyaya*) of the mind is a specific state that has entered the past time as it subsides; another has arisen and is manifesting in the present time. Both are equal by virtue of being concentrated minds (*samāhita-citta*), and similar by virtue of having the same form as their object (*ālambana*). In both cases, it is precisely for one who is concentrated [that they occur].
The persistence of the mind through its continuity is called concentration (*samādhi*), which is the transformation into one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).

This very threefold nature is to be seen elsewhere as well; by this [explanation], the transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) in the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) are explained. By this, which has been stated in three ways—

Through the transformation of the mind (*cittapariṇāma*), it should be understood that a threefold transformation— distinguished by attributes (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*)— is explained as occurring within the elements (both gross and subtle), the sense organs, and the intellect (*buddhi*), which exists as the distinction between the instrument of action (*karma*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is defined as the modification of a persisting substrate (*dharmī*) from its previous attribute...

In cessation, there is the transcendence of attributes (*dharma-parāpatti*). Among these, transformation of attributes (*dharma-pariṇāma*) is as follows: the substratum (*dharmin*), characterized by clay and so forth, abandons its attribute in the form of a lump and assumes another attribute in the form of a jar; likewise, that very jar abandons the future time-period (*adhvan*) and assumes the present time-period.
By the relinquishing of that [present state], there is transformation characterized by the grasping of the past time-period, as in the case of the transformation of states.

This refers to the persistence of that very jar through its similarity between the first and second moments; for the activity of the *guṇas* is mobile, such that it does not remain fixed in a single modification.

He remains even for a moment. Now, he demonstrates the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arising from the power of *saṃyama*. "From *saṃyama* on the three-fold transformation, there is knowledge of the past and the future. Regarding this subject (*dharmin*)—the aforementioned three-fold transformation consisting of *dharma*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *avasthā*—[one knows]: "This is its *dharma*, this is its *lakṣaṇa*, and this is its *avasthā*."
Having come together with the future time-path, [the action] performs its own function in the present time-path and then enters the past time-path;
by thus avoiding distraction and thereby acting without restraint, one knows all that is past and future. "Sva" and so forth...

When the obstruction caused by mental distraction has been destroyed through *saṃyama*, the innate capacity of the mind to grasp all objects is manifested. Thus, regarding the question—"What is the word? What is the object? What is the cognition?"—there occurs a mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) among the distinct cognitions of the meanings of those words.

From the subsequent imparting of the form "cow" (gauh), there arises for those who possess the established knowledge of the word "cow" and its referent a single uniform manifestation as "cow. Because this brings about a state of uniformity within the cognition, there is a differentiation of what was previously intermingled: namely, that "this word 'cow' is the denoter" and "that which possesses the dewlap and so forth is the denoted."

The *Piṇḍovāca* states: "That [knowledge] is of such a nature as being both that [object] and its illuminator. Having explained the knowledge of the cries of all beings through the mastery of that [power], [it continues]: regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by merit and demerit, the mind of another arising from facial coloration, and the bodily form—[one realizes] that "there is no such form in this body."

Through *saṃyama* on the characteristics of karma—whether ripening quickly or slowly—as it is being cultivated; on the strength of friendliness and the other [immeasurables] as being like an elephant and so forth; on the sun; on its color; and on the pole star (*dhruva*), there arise, respectively:
knowledge of previous births, certainty regarding the specific objects of another's mind, and the suspension of the power of grasping.
It has been described that there arise the knowledge of the disappearance of previous [bodies], the knowledge of the yoga of the body and internal organ as delimited by specific place and time,

the attainment of power such as being a friend to all, the knowledge of the worlds, the knowledge of the stellar wheel known as the *tārāvyūha*, and the knowledge of the movements of the stars; this is so because of the application of the world-orders as they have proceeded.

By the phrase "knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote," it is meant that when the previously mentioned [states]— the state characterized by engagement with objects (*viṣayavatī*), the state characterized by luminosity (*jyotiṣmatī*), and the state characterized by ideation (*lakṣaṇā*)— occur, there is a sattvic expansion of light;
through the withdrawal of that [light] from various objects, [one attains knowledge] by means of the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) of those respective objects.

When the senses, together with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), have attained preeminent power, there arises knowledge of the subtle— such as atoms— or of the remote— such as a treasure hidden beneath the ground out of sight, or an elixir located on the far side of Mount Meru; thus having demonstrated the external perfections (*bāhyasiddhi*), [the author] now describes the internal ones.
From the mastery of the wheel-marks (*cakracihna*), the hollows situated beneath them known as *gartta* and *kūpakaṇṭhakūpa*,

the tortoise-channel (*kūrmanāḍī*) situated below those, and the upward-light in the form of the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), one gains, respectively: knowledge of the arrangement of the channels within the body, the cessation of hunger and thirst, and the perfection of stability.

The perfections characterized by vision have been explained. Likewise, by the sūtra "From *saṃyama* upon the specific aspect of the cognition of the absolute distinction between *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are utterly unmixed, there arises knowledge of the *puruṣa* as distinct from that which exists for another," it is shown that the nature of *sattva* and the *puruṣa* consists in their being essentially luminous.

The experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) and the locus of experience (*adhiṣṭhāna*), being utterly distinct due to their respective natures as conscious and unconscious, possess a specific characteristic of cognition (*pratyaya*): because they do not appear as separate, the agency belongs to the *sattva* alone.
That which is the perception of pleasure and pain through this cognition is "enjoyment" (*bhoga*), and that occurs through the *sattva*'s lack of regard for its own self-interest.

The goal of the person for the sake of another is different from that which is the goal for one's own sake, having as its object only the essential nature of the person (*puruṣasvarūpa*). When the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) has been transferred into the being in which egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) has been abandoned, knowledge of the person arises for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon that [reflection]. Once that knowledge has arisen, that very knowledge, having that form, becomes the object of focus.

The person established in *sattva* knows [the truth], yet the person does not again become an object of knowledge for that which is known and unknown. By the phrase "having attained insentience," the fruit of the direct realization of the *puruṣa* has been stated;
thereafter, there arise the supernormal powers of intuition (*prātibha*), hearing (*śrāvaṇa*), feeling (*vedanā*), seeing (*darśa*), tasting (*āsvāda*), and the knowledge of news (*vārtājñāna*).

By this [verse], there is the intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) which has as its fruit the perception of subtle objects and the like; the auditory knowledge (*śrāvaṇa*) which has as its fruit the knowledge of divine sounds; the tactile knowledge (*tvāca*) known as sensation (*vedanā*) which has as its fruit the knowledge of divine touches;
and the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśa*) which has as its fruit the knowledge of divine forms.

Visual knowledge has as its fruit the knowledge of divine taste, which is called the fruit of tasting; the knowledge of touch has as its fruit the knowledge of divine fragrance; the knowledge known as *bhūti* is that produced by the olfactory faculty, which perceives sound existing within;
and the knowledge called *rūpavartāka* is said to be form (*rūpa*).

Having thus stated the distinction between the results—namely, that there are obstacles in concentration (*samādhi*) and perfections (*siddhi*) in emergence (*vyutthāna*)—and the division of their respective objects, [the author states: "By the loosening of the cause of bondage and by the awareness of the movement of the mind, there is entry into another's body. By this, [he explains] the pervasive nature of the self and the mind.

By the power of determinate karma alone, within the body itself, there arises a consciousness characterized by the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed—such as "happiness," "the body is mine," "I am its enjoyer," and "this is I" or "this is mine.
This is called the bondage of the body. For example:
Due to the power of *samādhi*, the cause known as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) becomes loosened; it reaches a state of attenuation.
That movement of the mind which flows from the region of the heart toward the objects through the doors of the senses—that perception [of that flow] is thus the channel for the movement of the mind.
The mind flows by means of this [channel] in such a way that it is distinct from the channels that carry the vital fluids, the breath, and so forth.

When one knows the movement of the bodiless [mind] within both one's own body and another's body, then, by means of the movement of the mind, one enters another's body—whether dead or living. The mind [enters] the other's body.
The senses follow [the mind] as it enters [a new body], just as bees follow the king of bees; thereafter,
the yogi who has entered another body conducts himself through that body as if it were his own, because the all-pervading consciousness,
having been freed from the karma that causes the contraction of the person's experience, is liberated by samādhi.

Having stated another established doctrine—that there is the perfection of the experience of autonomy—[the text continues]: through mastery over *udāna*, there is non-adherence to water, mud, thorns, and so forth; through mastery over *samāna*, there is radiance; and through *saṃyama* on the relationship between the ear and space, characterized by the location and the located, there arises the divine [power] capable of perceiving subtle, obstructed, and distant sounds and other objects.

Having described the attainment of the ear [hearing through the body], the connection between the body and space, the attainment of states consisting of lightness like cotton-wool and so forth, and the mentalization of space, [the sūtra] states: "The external, non-conceptualized function is the Great Bodilessness (mahāvidehā); from that follows the destruction of the veil over illumination. By this [it is meant]:

The mental modification (*manovṛtti*) that consists of the identification with the body is called "the imagined" (*kalpita*). When, however, having abandoned the state of identifying with the body, the mental modification occurs independently, it is called "the imagined great bodilessness" (*kalpitā mahāvidehā*).
Through *saṃyama* upon that, the destruction of the impurities of the mind (*cittamala*) occurs; thus another perfection (*siddhi*) has been stated. In this way...

Having established the various perfections (*siddhis*)— arising from the internal and external sense organs which are conducive to *samādhi*, as well as those arising from mastery over the vital airs such as *prāṇa*— for the sake of the yogi’s mental firmness and the production of confidence, the various means for the attainment of *sabīja* and *nirbīja* *samādhi* have been demonstrated by means of the aphorisms (*sūtras*).
These are presented along with their explanations as follows:
"From *saṃyama* upon the gross form, its nature, its subtle [cause], its inherence, and its purposefulness, mastery arises.
The gross form of the elements is the visible form possessing specific characteristics. Of the five—

The subtle causal elements, known as the *tanmātras*, are characterized respectively by hardness, moisture, heat, motility, and the provision of space for the gross elements (*bhūtas*). The pervasive qualities (*guṇas*) are illumination, activity, and inertia. And their capacity to produce purposeful results consists in the accomplishment of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) within those very qualities.

"Power" refers to the five stages; by practicing *saṃyama* through the process of reabsorption (*pratyava-saṃkrama*) among the differentiated elements, one becomes a conqueror of the elements. For example:
first having performed *saṃyama* upon the gross form, and subsequently upon the subtle form, and so forth.

For one who has practiced self-restraint in due order, the primary elements of nature (bhūtaprakṛti) become obedient to his will, like cows following their calves. He states the fruit of that very mastery over the elements: "From that, there arises [the attainment of] the powers such as atomization (aṇimā), and the non-obstruction of qualities (dharmas) wherever one may be. (YS 3.45)
Aṇimā is the attainment of the state of an atom; from that, one enters even into the interior of diamonds and other such substances. || 2 ||
From *laghimā* comes the attainment of lightness, like that of a tuft of cotton. || 3 ||
Majesty is the attainment of greatness. || 4 ||
The capacity to touch diamonds and other hard substances with the tip of a finger;
and *prākāmya* (irresistible will), which is the non-obstruction of the body and the internal organ by one's desire.
*Sovereignty* (*īśitva*) is the power of mastery over all things. *Control* (*vaśitva*) is such that all beings, being subject to one's will, do not transgress what has been commanded.

"Where there is the power of fulfilling desires (*kāmāvasāyitva*)" means that in whatever object the yogin has a desire or wish, his resolve regarding that object comes to pass; the meaning is that he leads that object to the fulfillment of his longing by means of its appropriation. These eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*, which are conducive to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), are called the "great accomplishments" (*mahāsiddhi*). [The body...]

He states the characteristics of perfection (*saṃpad*) by means of a verse: perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, adamantine compactness (*vajrasaṃhananatva*), and so forth. "Adamantine compactness" means that his body possesses a firm cohesion like a diamond (*vajra*).
The rest is clear. The qualities of that body, such as its form and so on, are not destroyed by fire, wind, or other elements.
It does not exist. Now, having described the conquest of the elements (*bhūtajaya*), he speaks of the conquest of the senses (*indriyajaya*) for one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*):
"From *saṃyama* upon the essence of the objects—namely, grasping, essential nature, self-sense, and purpose—the senses are conquered.
Grasping is the activity of the senses directed toward their respective objects. Essential nature is [their nature] in general.
[The characteristics of the senses are] luminosity, the accompaniment of smiling and egoism, and the meaningfulness of their conjunction, as previously stated.

By performing *saṃyama* upon these five states of the senses as before, one becomes a conqueror of the senses. He states its fruit: "From that, [one attains] swiftness of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over *pradhāna*."

The threefold fruit consists of: the attainment of a supreme movement for the body as if it were the mind; the attainment of the functioning of the senses independent of the body; and mastery over all things. These perfections (*siddhis*) manifest for one who has conquered the senses. They are called "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*), because even a single drop of honey is sweet to the taste.
"Thus each of these individually maintains its own transformation. Now he describes the conquest of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*):

"For one who possesses the mere discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. This occurs for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon that pure, *sāttvika* transformation."

Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) arises between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, consisting in the loosening of the false attribution of agency to the *guṇas*. By virtue of its greatness, for the yogi established therein, there arises from *samādhi* the state of presiding over all states of being— all the transformations of the *guṇas*.

Like a master, there is mastery over them; there is the presiding over all of those very [objects] which exist as the nature of being designated as "quiescent" or "arisen"; and there is omniscience through discriminative knowledge arising exactly as it is.
And this occurs within this state known as "mastery."
When the stage called *viśokā* (free from sorrow) is attained, its perfection is described. He now states the subsequent stage in sequence:

"From detachment even toward that, upon the destruction of the seed of defects, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). When detachment arises for the yogi even toward the *viśokā* stage, then, because of that, the seed of those defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth—which is ignorance (*avidyā*)—is destroyed.

Upon their destruction and uprooting, there is isolation (*kaivalya*), which is the absolute cessation of suffering for the *puruṣa*, the completion of the *guṇas'* mandate, and the state of abiding in one's own essential nature. Regarding this very *samādhi*, he states the means for its maintenance: "In the event of an invitation from celestial beings, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest there be a recurrence of undesirable consequences. (IV. 27) There are four [verses].

There are stages for the yogin. Among them, the first is called "the beginner" (*pravṛttamātrajyotis*) or "the first stage" (*prathamakalpa*), who possesses practice. The second is characterized by "truth-bearing wisdom" (*ṛtambharaprajñā*). For one who directly realizes the stage known as "honeyed wisdom" (*madhumatīprajñā*), this is the stage designated as "honeyed."
The gods who dwell there become his inviters; they present him with celestial women, elixirs, and the like.

In response to that invitation, he must not form an attachment, nor should he feel pride. By forming such an association, he would fall back into the enjoyment of sense-objects; by feeling pride, he would come to consider himself as one who has already accomplished all that was to be done. He must not do so.

He exerts himself toward samādhi; therefore, he must avoid attachment and pride. Regarding this very discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the fruit [of practice], he states another means distinct from the previously mentioned *saṃyama*:
"From *saṃyama* on the relationship between the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination arises."
A *kṣaṇa* is the smallest unit of time, such that its constituent parts (*kalās*) cannot be further divided.
Through *saṃyama* upon the sequence—the successive transformation—of such moments of time, the previously mentioned discriminative knowledge (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arises. This is the meaning.

When, through the practice of *saṃyama* on such a sequence as "this is a moment (kṣaṇa), this follows from that moment, and this precedes that," there arises direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) even of the extremely subtle succession of moments,
then there occurs direct perception of other subtle things as well, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth.
The arising of discriminative knowledge. He now states the means for distinguishing the objects of this very *saṃyama*:
"From that, there is the discernment of two things that are otherwise indistinguishable due to identity of genus, characteristic, or location.

Genus, characteristic, and location are the causes of differentiation among entities. For example, in the case of "cow" and "spotted or ruddy [cow]," the genus and characteristic [serve as differentiators].

Regarding the differentiator: for two things of equal transformation, space is the differentiator. However, in a case where a difference cannot be determined—such as between two white, earthy atoms situated in the same location—when knowledge of the distinction arises for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon such an object, then through that practice...

Even subtle principles, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, are perceived through their distinctions. The following *sūtra* is intended to explain the name, the object, and the nature of the aforementioned discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*):
"It is the deliverer, having all things as its object, and encompassing all modes of objects."

And this is the knowledge born of discernment (*vivekaja-jñāna*). Knowledge that arises in the final stage through the power of the aforementioned *saṃyama* "rescues" the yogi from the unfathomable ocean of *saṃsāra*; thus it is called "salvific" (*tāraka*).
He states its object: all principles (*tattva*), beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are its objects; therefore, it is "all-objected" (*sarvaviṣaya*).

And its nature is to be the object in every respect (*sarvathā-viṣayatvam*). Since all principles (*tattvas*) exist in every manner—through all states distinguished as gross and subtle, and through their various transformations—it has them as its object; thus he states another nature [of the intellect] as being "the object in every respect. Furthermore, by saying "and non-sequential" (*akramam*), he means "without remainder" (*niḥśeṣa*).

Because it grasps objects in their various states—whether two, three, or one—as they have undergone transformation, its sequential process does not exist; thus, it is "without succession" (*akrama*). The meaning is that it perceives everything simultaneously, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. He then states what results from this discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) called "the star": "When there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). This "equality" belongs to the *sattva*.

Purity for the *puruṣa* consists in the cessation of the conceit of agency in every respect and the consequent entry into its own cause; this purity is the absence of even figurative experience (*upacarita-bhoga*). When both [the *puruṣa* and *prakṛti*] have attained this same purity, liberation occurs. Thus, through the sequence of practice, as the various accomplishments (*siddhis*) arise—beginning with sovereignty and culminating in liberation—
The yogin must not disclose anything, nor should he harbor pride or wonder; for if he does so, success will not be attained.
And thus says Dattātreya:

Because the consciousness of the yogin dissolves through the astonishment caused by the exposition of the characteristics of worldly activity (pravṛtti) and so forth, such activities must be kept secret.
In this way, even one's practice (*karma*) should not be disclosed; if it were disclosed, the result would arise [as a hindrance].
Thus, it is said in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"The science of Haṭha must be kept strictly secret by the yogi who desires accomplishment."
It shall be powerful when kept secret, but powerless when revealed.

Now, whether through a successful yoga (*siddhayoga*) or an unsuccessful yoga (*asiddhayoga*), the signs of time must always necessarily be observed; these are now written down. Among them, by means of a successful yoga, one who desires liberation while living acts for the purpose of deceiving Time (*kāla*).
By means of an unsuccessful yoga, however, at the time of death there is the recollection of yoga, so that yoga may be attained in another future birth.
And so it is said in the Gītā:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state."
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding even at the time of death in this state, one attains the liberation of Brahman.
The method for cheating death has already been explained previously in passing. Its signs are as follows, according to the Skanda Purāṇa:
"He in whose left nostril the breath flows day and night..."
Indeed, his entire, single lifespan perishes within three years.
The sun flows continuously for two days and nights, or three days and nights;
the rule regarding his lifespan here is said to be up to one year.
If the wind flows continuously through both nostrils for ten days,
and there is a transition [of breath] during that time, then one shall live for three seasons.
Except for the two nostrils, the wind, emerging from the mouth, does not proclaim his departure; therefore, one should know that his journey on the path of the sky is prior to that.
When the sun is situated in the seventh zodiac sign and the moon is in the natal asterism,
that time of the constellation Puṣya is not to be desired, provided that the sun is moving toward the southern path.
Death may suddenly approach him at any moment;
therefore, one who fears death should reflect upon that time with diligent effort.
He who suddenly beholds a man who is dark-brown in complexion shall live for two years with that very form at that very moment.
If the semen, feces, urine, sneeze,
or even the excrement of such a person should fall upon this [place] at any time, his lifespan is said to last for one year.
He who sees a multitude of serpents, resembling sapphire,
moving here and there in the sky, lives for six months.
One whose death is near shall not behold Arundhatī, Dhruva, the three steps of Viṣṇu, nor the fourth, the circle of the Mothers (Mātṛmaṇḍala).
Arundhatī is the tongue, and Dhruva is said to be the tip of the nose;
the stations of Viṣṇu are the space between the eyebrows, the eyes are the glau, and the circle of the Mothers is the forehead.
One who perceives colors such as blue and so forth, or tastes such as bitter and sour,
to suddenly change into something else, will meet with death within six months.
For one whose death is six months away, the throat, lips, tongue,
and palate constantly dry up, as do the tongue and the palate as the fifth.
If semen, the nails, and the corners of the eyes possess a bluish tint,
then that man shall go to the city of Yama in the sixth month.
If a three-colored lizard quickly climbs onto someone's head,
that person's life will come to an end within six months.
Even for one whose mouth, heart,
feet, or hands quickly become parched, his life remains for only three months.
If one's shadow trembles even when the body is perfectly still,
the messengers of Death bind that man in the fourth month.
The intellect falters, speech wavers, and Indra’s bow is seen;
two moons appear at night, and two suns appear by day.
The sky was devoid of stars by day and devoid of the moon at night,
while simultaneously in the four directions there appeared the circle of Indra’s bow.
Whether at the foot of a tree, on a mountain peak, or in a city of the Gandharvas,
or even witnessing the dancing of Piśācas by day— these indeed are the causes of death.
If one observes even a single one of all these signs,
then one should await death within a month’s time, and not longer.
For he is indeed cast away and devoured by piśācas, asuras, and crows;
by bhūtas, pretas, dogs, vultures, jackals, donkeys, and pigs.
One who sees śarabhas, young elephants, kīras, hawks, mules,
and cranes in a dream will give up his life at the end of the year and behold Yama.
The man who, during the time of a dream, sees his own body adorned with red perfumes, flowers, and garments, lives for eight months.
He who indeed climbs upon a heap of dust, an anthill, pus,
or even a staff in a dream, perishes in the sixth month.
Whoever sees himself mounted on a donkey, anointed with oil, and shaven-headed, being led toward the direction of Yama, he likewise [attains the same result] as before.
That man who, in a dream, sees grass or white wood upon his own head or even upon his body, perishes in the sixth month.
If one sees a black man wearing black garments and holding an iron staff standing at the head of the bed, he shall not survive beyond three months.
If Kālīkumārī should bind one with her arm-nooses in a dream, one should,
in brief, behold the desired woman as the mistress of the city.
A man who, while sleeping, dreams that he is mounted upon a monkey and travels toward the eastern direction,
shall behold the city of Saṃyamanī in just five or six days.
If even a miser were to become generous, or a generous man were to become a miser,
then nature would undergo a transformation, and he would meet his death.
These are the signs of the time; there are many others as well.
Having recognized them, a man should practice yoga or else take refuge in the state of space (ākāśikā).
"O Sage, I did not previously understand that this [life] is subject to the deception of time.
Thus it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"And one whose bonds of karma are not exhausted, having perceived death as something undesirable..."
By recollecting this at the time of departure from the body, one attains the state of a yogin once again.
Therefore, whether by means of unsuccessful practice or successful practice,
one should always understand those undesirable factors so that one does not falter during the departure of the vital breath.
O Great King, listen as I describe those undesirable omens to you,
by the sight of which the knower of yoga recognizes his own death.
Having seen the sun without its rays, as well as the fire garlanded with flames,
a man lives for no more than eleven months, or at most one year.
He who vomits urine and feces, or likewise gold and silver—
whether in waking reality or in a dream— has but ten months of life remaining.
Having seen pretas, piśācas, and others, as well as gandharva cities and trees of golden hue, he lives for nine months.
He who was stout becomes thin, or he who was thin becomes stout,
and he who deviates from his natural constitution— his lifespan is eight months.
If a person's foot has a crack on the heel or at the tip of the toe,
they will live for seven months amidst dust and mud.
If a pigeon, a vulture, a crow,
or even a raven, or a carnivorous bird should perch upon one's head, it indicates a lifespan of six months.
Furthermore, he is struck by rows of crows or by a shower of dust;
indeed, his lower left side withers away from the vital point [of that wound].
One should know that death has approached for him within five months;
however, having seen his own shadow otherwise, he lives for four months.
Having seen lightning in a cloudless sky situated in the southern direction,
or likewise a rainbow in the north, one's life remains for only two or three months.
He who sees his own body without a head in ghee, oil, a mirror, or even in water, shall not live beyond seven days.
If a scent equal to that of a musk deer is found on the body of even a common person,
the life of that yogi, O King, should be known to last for half a month.
He whose heart-lotus withers immediately after bathing,
and whose lips become parched while drinking water— even he shall live for ten days.
When his vital airs are disordered and he feels as if his vital points (marmasthāna) are being cut,
and he finds no joy from the touch of water, death has arrived for him.
He who, in a dream, travels toward the southern direction while singing and seated upon a bear or a monkey, for him death does not come at its appointed time.
If a woman wearing red and black garments leads one toward the southern quarter while singing and laughing in a dream, he too shall not live.
If one sees a naked, laughing, and very powerful ascetic (kṣapaṇaka) in a dream,
or likewise sees the end of his strength, one should know that death is at hand.
That man who, in a dream, sees himself submerged up to the surface of his head in a sea of mud, dies immediately.
Having seen hair, charcoal, ashes, a serpent, or a river without water in a dream, death occurs within ten days on the eleventh day.
If one is struck with stones in a dream by terrifying, hideous, black men with raised weapons, one shall meet death immediately.
If at sunrise a female jackal approaches one's face,
whether by circling to the left or to the right, that person shall meet death immediately.
If, immediately after eating, one's heart is oppressed by hunger and the grinding of teeth occurs, his life has undoubtedly departed.
He who does not perceive the scent of lamps and the like during the day as well as at night,
nor sees his own reflection in the eyes of others, does not live.
Seeing Indra’s weapon at midnight, or likewise an eclipse of the sun or moon,
the knower of the self should consider his own life to be nearly exhausted.
He whose nose becomes crooked, whose ears do not rise evenly,
and whose left eye leaks— his life has reached its end.
When the face becomes reddish and the tongue turns black,
then the wise man should know that his own death is near.
O Lord of Men, one who travels toward the southern direction in a dream by means of a vehicle drawn by camels or donkeys should be known as facing immediate death.
He who, covering his ears, does not hear the internal sound produced within himself,
and whose light of vision perishes— he too does not live.
If one who has fallen into a pit sees a door in a dream,
yet does not emerge from that dream, his life ends there.
The gaze is upward and not fixed; it is reddened and rolling about.
There is heat in the face and coldness at the navel; these are the final signs for men before the departure of the body.
If one enters fire in a dream and does not emerge again,
or likewise enters water, his life ends there.
And that man who is struck by wicked spirits, whether by night or by day,
will undoubtedly meet his death at the end of seven nights.
If a man sees his own garment as stainless white, red, or black,
one should indeed predict that he has met with death.
The reversal of one's own nature and the inversion of primordial matter—
these two, Yama and Antaka, declare to be the causes of death for human beings.
He recognizes as his own those who have been constantly disciplined by him, yet he reviles even those who are considered most worthy of honor.
He does not honor the gods, the elders, his teachers, or the Brahmins;
he treats his parents with disrespect and behaves likewise toward his sons-in-law.
This should be understood by the wise as the time for yogis, the learned, and other great-souled ones when it has arrived.
O Lord of the Earth, the yogi should constantly and with effort observe the omens until the end of the year; thus, day and night, they yield their fruit.
O Lord of Men, these [omens] should always be observed by one who is intent on the fruit [of his actions]; having understood them in his mind, he should act at the proper time.
Having correctly understood that time and having taken refuge in the state of fearlessness,
one should apply oneself to yoga so that this time does not pass fruitlessly.
Having thus perceived the signs of death, the yogi abandons the fear born of dying;
having contemplated that very nature [of reality], he remains until the appointed time arrives.
In that same portion of the day, the knower of yoga should practice yoga every single day,
whether in the forenoon, the afternoon, or at midday.
On whichever lunar day that misfortune was observed,
one should apply [the remedy] on that very day until that specific day arrives.
Then, having conquered that time and abandoned all fear,
the self-possessed one remained right there in his dwelling, where he found his own steadfastness.
Having conquered the three qualities within the Supreme Self, the yogi should unite himself with it;
then, becoming one with that through his own self, he should even abandon the activity of consciousness.
Thereafter, he partakes of that supreme nirvāṇa which is beyond the senses, not within the sphere of activity, which is not accessible to the intellect, and which cannot be described.

In the *Brahmayāmala*: "In the sky, when the [mental] limit has vanished, during the bright fortnight at night, he who— day by day, with a mind steady and one-pointed— [focuses] on the navel, the heart, or the surface of the forehead, should then behold the first shadow and subsequently the eye."
Then he beholds that supreme reality there, the Person of Time (Kālapuruṣa), who resembles the ocean of milk and the jasmine flower.
By the mere sight of him, one is liberated from all sins;
and when one beholds him in his fullness, whence can there be any fear of death?
When one beholds him, stainless and endowed with all the perfect marks,
then for certain no time remains until the end of that year.
If the head is missing, death shall occur within six months; of this there is no doubt.
If the arms are missing, there will be disease, or else the destruction of one's uterine siblings.
If there is a crack on the dark side, there will be loss of wealth; if there is a crack at the vulva, the woman will die;
if there is a crack in the middle, there will be a wound from a weapon or a famine will occur.
If it is yellowish-white, there will be prosperity and an abundance of food, and the calamity of a broken neck will perish;
if it is yellow, there will be paralysis; if it is black, it brings death.
If it is red in color, there will be sovereignty; if it has a white luster, there is long life.
Merely by the sight of it, rebirth no longer exists.
Having realized the supreme reality— which is devoid of colors such as white and the like, free from sound and form, and beyond the reach of mind and speech— [one attains liberation].
For if [the practice] is concealed, it removes death even from one's guru, but not if it is seen;
however, there is no fruit in public display, whereas in secrecy they behold the Slayer of Time (*Kālahan*). (There is a lacuna here. This is the general direction.
This very practice of nididhyāsana, together with its means of accomplishment, has been described by me in brief, according to the scriptures and according to my own understanding.
Hearing and reflection, along with their specific details and full extent, are to be sought in the Vedāntas alone; they have not been stated here for fear of prolixity.
Whatever secret remains of Rājayoga and Haṭhayoga has been revealed by me here in its entirety for the delight of yogins.
However, because it cannot be accomplished by those of recent times,
I have not written down that haṭhayoga which was practiced by Uddālaka, Bhuśuṇḍa, and others.
The ritual procedures and other such matters prescribed by the Kāpālikas have not been recorded by me, for they are in contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti.
For one by whom Mahādeva, Gaurī, Brahmā, or Hari,
or even Lambodara or Ravi has been propitiated, their yoga becomes successful.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
"By whomsoever the Lord who has the moon as his crest (Śiva) was previously propitiated,
he may quickly attain this, even if it be Hari, Brahmā, or the Sun."
The *Yogacintāmaṇi* should be constantly contemplated by those seeking liberation,
who desire the great attainment of liberation while living and who long for agelessness and immortality.
O friends, having conquered the suffering born of dwelling in the womb, that arising from childhood, youth, and old age,

that produced by the loss of the beloved and the occurrence of gain and loss, that born from the separation of body and life-force, disease, and the ripening of hellish torments such as the *kumbhīpāka*—
worship this great medicine for malignant maladies, the venerable *Yogacintāmaṇi*.

O best of beings, for one who practices yoga, the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of the Vedas— whose branches are frequented by the twice-born— is the pacification of the suffering of worldly existence.

[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Yogacintāmaṇi composed by Śivānandasarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī; and this work, the Yogacintāmaṇi, is hereby completed.]
May there be auspiciousness in the Śaka year 2014.
